lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ πρὸ οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς παρερχόμενα
lexical_decisions.chosen: the things passing away before heaven and earth do
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρό is temporal here: these things pass away earlier than the promised passing of heaven and earth.

passages.text: Since, then, while heaven and earth still remain, sacrifices, kingdoms, the “among those born of women” prophecies, and all such things have passed away because they were not commands of God—hence indeed he says, “Every planting that the heavenly Father did not plant will be uprooted”—for this reason he himself, being a true prophet, said, “I am the gate of life; the one who enters through me enters into life,” since no other teaching capable of saving exists. Therefore he also cried out, saying, “Come to me, all who toil,” that is, those who seek the truth and do not find it; and again, “My sheep hear my voice”; and on another occasion, “Seek and find,” since the truth does not lie plainly exposed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the “among those born of women” prophecies
lexical_decisions.rationale: The quoted prepositional phrase is retained without supplying an unstated agent or referent; it may characterize the prophecies by their place among those born of women.

lexical_decisions.chosen: every planting
lexical_decisions.rationale: φυτεία can denote either a planting or what has been planted; “every plant” is a viable smoother alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the gate of life
lexical_decisions.rationale: πύλη denotes a gate or gateway; the genitive may be understood as a gate belonging or leading to life.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δεῦτε πρὸς μὲ πάντες οἱ κοπιῶντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: Come to me, all who toil
lexical_decisions.rationale: κοπιάω emphasizes laboring or becoming weary through labor; “all who are weary” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: and on another occasion
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἄλλοτε is temporal, marking another time or occasion rather than another location or textual position.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Seek and find
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both forms can be read morphologically as indicatives or imperatives, but their setting as a direct exhortation supports imperatives; the Greek does not contain a future equivalent to “you will find.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς μὴ προδήλως κειμένης τῆς ἀληθείας
lexical_decisions.chosen: since the truth does not lie plainly exposed
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὡς with the genitive absolute is taken causally. It could instead be rendered “on the understanding that the truth does not lie plainly exposed.”

passages.text: But a voice bearing witness was also heard from the heavens, saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I delighted; listen to him.” And besides these things, wishing to expose them as having gone still further astray, he declared that the prophets—from whom they indeed insisted they had learned—had died desiring truth and without having learned it, saying, “Many prophets and kings desired to see what you see and to hear what you hear, and, amen, I tell you, they neither saw nor heard.” What is more, he said, “I am the one concerning whom Moses prophesied, saying, ‘The Lord our God raises up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me as well; listen to him in all things. But whoever does not listen to that prophet will die.’”

lexical_decisions.chosen: a voice bearing witness … from the heavens
lexical_decisions.rationale: μάρτυς is a noun, literally presenting the voice as a witness; the rendering preserves that function without reducing it to merely “a heavenly voice.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ πλεῖον αὐτοὺς πεπλανημένους ἐλέγξαι θέλων
lexical_decisions.chosen: wishing to expose them as having gone still further astray
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering attaches ἐπὶ πλεῖον to πεπλανημένους, expressing a greater degree of error. Alternatively, it may qualify ἐλέγξαι: “wishing to demonstrate more fully that they had gone astray.” Its position immediately before αὐτοὺς πεπλανημένους supports the chosen scope but does not make it certain.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτοὺς πεπλανημένους ἐλέγξαι θέλων τοὺς προφήτας
lexical_decisions.chosen: wishing to expose them … he declared that the prophets
lexical_decisions.rationale: αὐτούς is taken as the object of ἐλέγξαι, while τοὺς προφήτας is taken as the object of ἀπεφήνατο later in the sentence. Alternatively, τοὺς προφήτας could stand in apposition to αὐτούς, making the prophets themselves those whom he wished to expose as having gone astray.

lexical_decisions.chosen: from whom they indeed insisted they had learned
lexical_decisions.rationale: βεβαιόω here means to maintain or affirm firmly; the object of “learned” remains implicit as in the Greek.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπιθυμοῦντας ἀληθείας καὶ μὴ μεμαθηκότας τελευτήσαντας
lexical_decisions.chosen: had died desiring truth and without having learned it
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participles characterize the prophets at death; “truth” supplies the natural object of “learned” from the immediately preceding genitive.

lexical_decisions.chosen: amen, I tell you
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀμήν is retained rather than replaced with a harmonized familiar formula such as “truly I say to you.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Προφήτην ἐγείρει ὑμῖν κύριος ὁ θεὸς ἡμῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: The Lord our God raises up for you a prophet
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐγείρει is printed as a present-tense form. It could function as a prophetic present with future sense, but the main rendering preserves the selected edition’s observable tense.

passages.text: Therefore, without his teaching it is impossible to attain truth that saves, even if someone searches forever where the object of the search does not exist. But it was and is in the word of our Jesus. At any rate, knowing the true things of the law, when Sadducees asked on what grounds Moses had allowed seven to marry, he said, “Moses gave you permission because of your hardness of heart, for from the beginning it did not happen that way. For the one who created the human being from the beginning made him male and female.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: to attain truth that saves
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐφίστημι with the dative here conveys arriving at or coming upon something; σωζούσῃ explicitly characterizes the truth as saving.

lexical_decisions.chosen: even if someone searches forever
lexical_decisions.rationale: The accusative τὸν αἰῶνα expresses extended duration; “for an age” would preserve the noun more formally.

lexical_decisions.chosen: where the object of the search does not exist
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantival participle means “what is being sought”; the location introduced by ἔνθα is left general.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in the word of our Jesus
lexical_decisions.rationale: λόγος may mean his word, discourse, or teaching. The rendering preserves the genitival attachment to “our Jesus” without identifying Jesus himself as “the Word.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καθ’ ὃν λόγον Μωϋσῆς ἑπτὰ συνεχώρησεν γαμεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: on what grounds Moses had allowed seven to marry
lexical_decisions.rationale: καθ’ ὃν λόγον asks for the reason or principle. The indeclinable numeral ἑπτά is taken as the infinitive’s subject: “allowed seven [people] to marry,” a contextual reading of the Sadducees’ question. It could instead be the object: “allowed [someone] to marry seven [people].” The wording does not explicitly identify the seven as brothers, men, or women. Under the chosen subject reading, the object of “marry” remains unstated.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ ἐποίησεν αὐτόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the human being … made him male and female
lexical_decisions.rationale: The selected wording has singular τὸν ἄνθρωπον and singular αὐτόν, followed by both “male and female”; the singular is preserved rather than changed to a plural familiar from other forms of the saying.

passages.text: To those who suppose, as the Scriptures teach, that God swears, he said, “Let your yes be yes and your no, no, for anything beyond these comes from the evil one.” And to those who say that Abraham and Isaac and Jacob died, he said, “He is not God of the dead but of the living.” To those who think that God “tempts,” as the Scriptures say, he said, “The evil one is the one who tempts,” the same one who also tempted him. To those who assume that God does not know beforehand, he said, “For your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things before you petition him.” And to those who believe, as the Scriptures say, that he does not see everything, after saying, “Pray in secret,” he said, “And your Father, who sees secret things, will repay you.”

source_issues.source_quote: Ἀβραὰμ καὶ Ἰσαὰκ καὶ Ἰακὼβ ἀπέθανεν
source_issues.issue: The selected text has the singular verb ἀπέθανεν after three coordinated names. This is a grammatical irregularity or singular agreement centered on the coordinated group; ordinary English requires the plural “died.”

source_issues.source_quote: τοῖς δὲ πιστεύουσιν (ὡς αἱ γραφαὶ λέγουσιν) ὅτι μὴ πάντα βλέπει, „ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ εὔχεσθε“ εἰπὼν „καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ὑμῶν ὁ βλέπων τὰ κρυπτὰ ἀποδώσει ὑμῖν“
source_issues.issue: The final construction uses the participle εἰπών but supplies no new finite speech verb before the second quotation. The preceding ἔφη is naturally understood by ellipsis, so the translation expresses it without emending the Greek.

lexical_decisions.chosen: anything beyond these
lexical_decisions.rationale: τὸ περισσόν denotes what exceeds or goes beyond the stated yes and no; “the excess beyond these” would be more formally literal.

lexical_decisions.chosen: from the evil one
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive form can mean either “from evil” or “from the evil one.” The immediately following explicit ὁ πονηρός favors the personal rendering here.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκ ἔστιν θεὸς νεκρῶν, ἀλλὰ ζώντων
lexical_decisions.chosen: He is not God of the dead but of the living
lexical_decisions.rationale: The implied subject is God from the preceding clause. The Greek describes the two groups substantivally as dead and living persons.

lexical_decisions.chosen: The evil one is the one who tempts
lexical_decisions.rationale: πειράζω can mean either test or tempt, but attribution to the evil one and the following reference to his tempting Jesus support “tempt.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: the same one who also tempted him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The pronoun is retained as “him”; in context its most likely referent is Jesus, though the sentence does not rename him.

lexical_decisions.chosen: before you petition him
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀξιόω most commonly concerns deeming worthy, but with a personal object it can carry the contextual sense of making a request or petition; “before you ask him” is a smoother alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: secret things
lexical_decisions.rationale: The Greek is a substantival neuter plural, distinct from the preceding singular phrase ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ, “in secret.”

passages.text: To those who thought that he was not good (as the Scriptures say), he said, “Which of you will, if a son asks him for bread, give him a stone instead? Or if the son also asks for a fish, will he give him a snake instead? Therefore, if you, though evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give good things to those who ask him and to those who do his will?” To those who asserted that he was in a temple, he said, “Do not swear by heaven, because it is God’s throne, nor by the earth, because it is the footstool of his feet.” To those who had assumed beforehand that God desires sacrifices, he said, “God wants mercy and not sacrifices, knowledge of him and not whole burnt offerings.”

source_issues.source_quote: μήτε τὴν γῆν, ὅτι ὑποπόδιον τῶν ποδῶν αὐτοῦ ἐστίν. τοῖς δὲ προλαβοῦσιν
source_issues.issue: The supplied edition does not print a closing quotation mark after ἐστίν before the narrative resumes with τοῖς δὲ. The syntactic boundary is clear, so the English supplies the closing quotation mark without proposing missing words.
source_issues.proposed_reading: μήτε τὴν γῆν, ὅτι ὑποπόδιον τῶν ποδῶν αὐτοῦ ἐστίν.“ τοῖς δὲ προλαβοῦσιν

source_issues.source_quote: ἔφη „ὁ θεὸς ἔλεος θέλει καὶ οὐ θυσίας, ἐπίγνωσιν αὐτοῦ καὶ οὐχ ὁλοκαυτώματα.
source_issues.issue: The supplied edition opens this final quotation but prints no closing quotation mark after ὁλοκαυτώματα. The English supplies closure at the end of the intelligible quotation; this is an editorial-punctuation feature, not a restoration of wording.
source_issues.proposed_reading: ἔφη „ὁ θεὸς ἔλεος θέλει καὶ οὐ θυσίας, ἐπίγνωσιν αὐτοῦ καὶ οὐχ ὁλοκαυτώματα.“

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τίνα ὑμῶν αἰτήσει υἱὸς ἄρτον, μὴ λίθον ἐπιδώσει αὐτῷ;
lexical_decisions.chosen: Which of you will, if a son asks him for bread, give him a stone instead?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The son is the subject of αἰτήσει, while the person addressed by τίνα ὑμῶν is the understood subject of ἐπιδώσει. The conditional English expresses the paratactic relationship, and the rhetorical question preserves μή’s expectation of a negative answer.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those who ask him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The middle-form participle is rendered idiomatically as requesting something from him.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῖς δὲ αὐτὸν διαβεβαιουμένοις ἐν ναῷ εἶναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: To those who asserted that he was in a temple
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαβεβαιόομαι conveys confident assertion; the pronoun’s referent remains as implicit as it is in the Greek.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῖς δὲ προλαβοῦσιν ὅτι θυσιῶν ὀρέγεται ὁ θεός
lexical_decisions.chosen: To those who had assumed beforehand that God desires sacrifices
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here προλαμβάνω presents a prior assumption or preconception. Unlike the preceding διαβεβαιουμένοις, it does not by itself establish that they voiced a confident assertion.

lexical_decisions.chosen: knowledge of him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive is taken objectively, referring to knowledge of God; “recognition of him” remains a viable lexical alternative.

passages.text: To those who had been persuaded that he was evil (as the Scriptures say), he said, “Do not call me good, for the one who is good is one.” And again, “Become good and compassionate like the Father who is in the heavens, who makes the sun rise upon the good and the evil and brings rain upon the righteous and the unrighteous.” To those who had been deceived into supposing that there are many gods (as the Scriptures say), he said, “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God, the Lord, is one.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μή με λέγε ἀγαθόν· ὁ γὰρ ἀγαθὸς εἷς ἐστίν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Do not call me good, for the one who is good is one
lexical_decisions.rationale: The masculine singular substantive ὁ ἀγαθός and masculine εἷς refer to a personal singular, “the one who is good.” The rendering preserves the unusual numerical predication without adding “God” or substituting a familiar canonical formula.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Become good and compassionate
lexical_decisions.rationale: γίνεσθε denotes becoming, while οἰκτίρμονες emphasizes compassion or mercy.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ πατὴρ ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς
lexical_decisions.chosen: the Father who is in the heavens
lexical_decisions.rationale: The attributive article and phrase are represented explicitly, and the plural οὐρανοῖς is retained as “heavens.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: brings rain
lexical_decisions.rationale: This preserves the verb φέρει rather than assimilating it to the wording of a familiar parallel.

lexical_decisions.chosen: supposing that there are many gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπονοέω denotes supposing or imagining; English supplies “there are” to express the predicate construction naturally.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κύριος ὁ θεὸς ὑμῶν κύριος εἷς ἐστίν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the Lord your God, the Lord, is one
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering retains both occurrences of κύριος and the plural possessive ὑμῶν. An alternative syntactic presentation is “The Lord, your God, is one Lord,” but the main wording more visibly preserves the repeated title and final numerical predicate.

passages.text: All the same, Simon, recognizing that Peter was compelling him to use the Scriptures as Jesus had taught, did not want an examination of the discourse about God to take place, although Peter had changed the examination, as Simon himself had demanded, so that it would proceed by question and answer. Nevertheless, the inquiry continued for three days. As the fourth day began to dawn, Simon set out by night for Tyre in Phoenicia. Not many days later, some of those who had gone ahead came and told Peter, “Simon, performing great wonders in Tyre, has astounded many of the people there and, through many slanders, has caused you to be hated.”

source_issues.issue: The image-checked edition prints ὁμῶς, which can mean “similarly” or “in the same way.” The context permits the adversative force normally written ὅμως, “nevertheless.” “All the same” is a provisional contextual rendering, while the printed form remains unchanged and its interpretation is not certain.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Πέτρος αὐτὸν συνάγει ταῖς γραφαῖς χρῆσθαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: Peter was compelling him to use the Scriptures
lexical_decisions.rationale: συνάγει can express constraint or compulsion in this construction; “bringing him to use” is a possible but weaker alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς τὸν περὶ θεοῦ λόγον ἐξέτασιν γενέσθαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: an examination of the discourse about God to take place
lexical_decisions.rationale: λόγος may mean discourse, teaching, or argument; “discourse” preserves the broad sense without identifying it with a particular doctrine.

lexical_decisions.chosen: although Peter had changed the examination
lexical_decisions.rationale: The implicit object of μετατίθημι is supplied from ἐξέτασιν, and the following phrase identifies the new question-and-answer format.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the inquiry continued for three days
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπικρατέω literally suggests holding sway, but with the duration expressed by τριῶν ... ἡμερῶν it indicates that the inquiry persisted throughout that period.

lexical_decisions.chosen: some of those who had gone ahead
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantival expression denotes people preceding the main party; “members of the advance party” and “forerunners” are viable alternatives.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through many slanders, has caused you to be hated
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative πολλαῖς διαβολαῖς expresses the means by which Simon caused hostility toward Peter.

passages.text: When Peter heard this, on the following night he had the crowd of hearers assemble. All the same, when they had assembled, he said, “Since, as I was setting out toward the nations that declare that there are many gods, to proclaim and teach that God is one, ‘who created heaven and earth’ and everything in them, so that by loving him they might be able to be saved, evil got there first and, by the law of pairing, sent Simon ahead, so that, if people cease declaring that there are many gods, they may condemn those called gods on earth but suppose that there are many gods in heaven, so that, having never honored the good of sole rule, they may perish completely after punishment. And what is most terrible, because the true word possesses incomparable strength, by getting there first with his slanders he persuades them not to accept it from me at all, lest the slanderer himself be exposed as a devil in reality and the true word, once shown forth, be able to be believed. I must therefore overtake him quickly, so that the slander, if allowed to persist, does not gain complete control of everyone.”

source_issues.issue: The image-checked edition again prints ὁμῶς. It can be read as “similarly,” but the context permits the adversative force “all the same,” normally written ὅμως. The main rendering is provisional, and the printed form is not treated as an OCR defect.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν ἀκροατῶν τὸν ὄχλον συνελθεῖν ἐποίησεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: he had the crowd of hearers assemble
lexical_decisions.rationale: The causative construction with ἐποίησεν and the infinitive indicates that Peter caused or arranged for the gathering.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ ἔθνη τὰ πολλοὺς θεοὺς λέγοντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: the nations that declare that there are many gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: λέγειν with πολλοὺς θεούς conveys asserting the existence of many gods, not merely pronouncing the words.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by the law of pairing
lexical_decisions.rationale: συζυγία denotes conjunction, yoking, or pairing and here evokes the work’s paired-agent framework; “law of conjunction” remains a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they may condemn those called gods on earth
lexical_decisions.rationale: “Gods” is supplied from the immediately preceding πολλοὺς θεοὺς λέγειν. The more formally elliptical “those spoken of on earth” is possible but obscures the contextual referent.

lexical_decisions.chosen: having honored the good of sole rule
lexical_decisions.rationale: μοναρχία denotes rule by one or sole sovereignty. The preceding μηδέποτε negates the participle: they never honor this good.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτὸ μηδὲ τὴν ἀρχὴν ἀναδέξασθαί μου
lexical_decisions.chosen: not to accept it from me at all
lexical_decisions.rationale: αὐτό most naturally refers to the true word, while μηδὲ τὴν ἀρχήν is idiomatic for “not at all.” The more temporally explicit “not to accept it from me even at the outset” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ διαβάλλων αὐτὸς τῷ ὄντι διάβολος
lexical_decisions.chosen: the slanderer himself be exposed as a devil in reality
lexical_decisions.rationale: Rendering διαβάλλων as “slanderer” and διάβολος as “devil” preserves the source’s wordplay.

lexical_decisions.chosen: overtake him
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπικαταλαμβάνω here means catching up with someone who has gone ahead.

passages.text: “Since, then, it is necessary to appoint someone in my place, one who will fill my position, let us all pray to God with one resolve, so that he himself may make evident the best of those among us, in order that, seated upon the Messiah’s chair, he may administer his church devoutly. Who, then, will be appointed? For by God’s counsel that man is shown to be blessed whom his lord will appoint over the service of his fellow servants, to give them their provisions at their proper time, neither thinking nor saying in his heart, ‘My lord is delaying his coming,’ nor beginning to beat his fellow servants while eating and drinking with both prostitutes and drunkards. And the lord of that servant will come at an hour that he does not expect and on a day that he does not know, and he will cut him in two and place the unfaithful part of him with the hypocrites.”

source_issues.source_quote: μὴ ἐννοούμενον καὶ λέγοντα ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ Χρονίζει ὁ κύριός μου ἐλθεῖν καὶ ἄρξηται τύπτειν τοὺς συνδούλους αὐτοῦ, ἐσθίων καὶ πίνων μετά τε πορνῶν καὶ μεθυόντων
source_issues.issue: The construction begins with accusative participles connected to ὃν, shifts to the finite subjunctive ἄρξηται, and then uses the nominative participles ἐσθίων and πίνων. The scope of μή is also uncertain. The main text takes it broadly over the coordinated misconduct because the surrounding clause identifies the appointed man as blessed and charges him with timely provision. A narrower scope, in which only ἐννοούμενον is negated and the saying and abuse are affirmative, remains possible and better prepares for the following punishment. The sentence is anacoluthic, but both readings arise from the supplied wording and no conjectural restoration is required.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with one resolve
lexical_decisions.rationale: προαίρεσις denotes deliberate purpose or resolve; the phrase calls for united intention in prayer.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν ὄντων ἐν ἡμῖν τὸν κρείττονα
lexical_decisions.chosen: the best of those among us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The comparative κρείττονα selects the superior member from the group and therefore functions contextually as “the best”; “the one who is better among us” is a more formally comparative alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: upon the Messiah’s chair
lexical_decisions.rationale: χριστός functions independently as a title and is rendered “Messiah”; καθέδρα denotes an authoritative seat or chair.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he may administer his church devoutly
lexical_decisions.rationale: οἰκονομέω denotes managing or administering, while εὐσεβῶς describes reverent or devout conduct. The pronoun’s precise antecedent remains implicit in English as in Greek.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ τῆς θεραπείας τῶν συνδούλων αὐτοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: over the service of his fellow servants
lexical_decisions.rationale: θεραπεία may denote service, attendance, care, or a body of household attendants. “Over the care of his fellow servants” and “over the household of his fellow servants” are contextual alternatives.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μὴ ἐννοούμενον καὶ λέγοντα ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ Χρονίζει ὁ κύριός μου ἐλθεῖν καὶ ἄρξηται τύπτειν τοὺς συνδούλους αὐτοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: neither thinking nor saying in his heart, ‘My lord is delaying his coming,’ nor beginning to beat his fellow servants
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering takes μή broadly over the coordinated misconduct, keeping it within the characterization or warning attached to the appointed man. English “neither ... nor” expresses that broad negative scope. A narrower reading—“not taking thought, and saying ... and beginning”—is grammatically possible and more directly anticipates the ensuing punishment, but it turns the latter actions into affirmative narrative and fits the description of the blessed appointee less readily.

lexical_decisions.chosen: My lord is delaying his coming
lexical_decisions.rationale: χρονίζειν with an infinitive means taking a long time or delaying the action. Lowercase “lord” preserves the servant-master imagery without deciding whether a divine referent is foregrounded.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he will cut him in two
lexical_decisions.rationale: This preserves the literal and violent image of διχοτομέω rather than weakening it to “punish severely.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ ἀπιστοῦν αὐτοῦ μέρος μετὰ τῶν ὑποκριτῶν θήσει
lexical_decisions.chosen: place the unfaithful part of him with the hypocrites
lexical_decisions.rationale: The neuter participle ἀπιστοῦν directly qualifies μέρος, producing the unusual image of an unfaithful or unbelieving part of the servant. The rendering does not replace it with the textually different idea of assigning the servant a portion.

passages.text: But if any of those present, though able to manage people’s unreasonableness, draws back, caring only for his own rest, let him too expect to hear, “Wicked and lazy servant, you should have put my silver before the bankers, and when I came I would have collected what was mine. Cast the useless servant into the outer darkness.” And rightly so. “For it was your responsibility,” he says, “human being, to put my words before bankers like silver and to test them like currency.” Therefore, the multitude of believers must obey one particular person, so that in this way it may be able to continue in harmony. For a system that culminates in the rule of a single authority, as an image of monarchy, puts those who submit in a position to enjoy peace because of good order; but when all are eager to rule and unwilling to yield to one alone, they are also certain to fall because of division.

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a Greek question mark between χρήματα and δοκιμάσαι, interrupting two coordinated infinitives. The translation follows the defensible syntactic coordination while disclosing the punctuation rather than treating it as missing wording.

source_issues.source_quote: τὸ δὲ πάντας φιλαρχοῦντας ἑνὶ μόνῳ ὑπεῖξαι μὴ θέλειν, καὶ αἰτίᾳ διαιρέσεως πάντως καὶ πεσεῖν ἔχουσιν
source_issues.issue: The sentence begins with a neuter substantivized infinitival construction but shifts to the plural finite verb ἔχουσιν, with the semantic plural πάντας supplying the sense. This is intelligible as an anacoluthon, so no restoration is required.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διοικεῖν δυνάμενος τὴν ἀγνωμοσύνην τῶν ἀνθρώπων
lexical_decisions.chosen: though able to manage people’s unreasonableness
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here ἀγνωμοσύνη denotes deficient judgment or unreasonable conduct; “ingratitude” is lexically possible but fits the governing context less well.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Wicked and lazy servant
lexical_decisions.rationale: Following the supplied policy, δοῦλος is rendered “servant”; the context still carries the subordinate status of a servant answerable to his lord.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I would have collected what was mine
lexical_decisions.rationale: πράσσω here means exacting or recovering what is due, rather than merely “doing” what belongs to the speaker.

lexical_decisions.chosen: For it was your responsibility, he says, human being
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive σοῦ with the following infinitives is understood as an elliptical expression of obligation: “it was your part” or “it was your responsibility.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: to test them like currency
lexical_decisions.rationale: δοκιμάζω evokes testing or assaying currency; “them” refers to the preceding λόγους, though the Greek does not repeat the object.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ γὰρ εἰς ἀρχὴν μιᾶς λῆγον ἐξουσίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: a system that culminates in the rule of a single authority
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantivized neuter phrase describes an arrangement or system ending in one governing authority.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as an image of monarchy
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative εἰκόνι characterizes the single-authority arrangement as a likeness or representation of monarchy.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they are also certain to fall
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔχειν with an infinitive expresses what lies ahead or is inevitable; “they must also fall” is a viable alternative.

passages.text: But furthermore, let what happens before our eyes persuade us: now, with many kings throughout the whole earth, wars happen continually. For each has the other’s rule as a pretext for war. But if one person is leader of the whole, having nothing for which to wage war, he has perpetual peace. Ultimately, then, for those deemed worthy of eternal life, God appoints one king over the whole in that age, so that, because of monarchy, unfailing peace may come about. Therefore, everyone must follow one person as guide, honoring him as an image of God, while the guide must know the entrance leading into the holy city.

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a period between the elided ἀλλ᾽ and ἔτι. It appears to be stray editorial punctuation rather than a lacuna marker; no wording has been supplied in its place.

lexical_decisions.chosen: let what happens before our eyes persuade us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb has no expressed object; “us” represents the assembled hearers, while “persuade the observer” or “be persuasive” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἔχει γὰρ ἕκαστος πρόφασιν εἰς πόλεμον τὴν ἑτέρου ἀρχήν
lexical_decisions.chosen: each has the other’s rule as a pretext for war
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόφασις may mean a pretext, occasion, or stated reason; “pretext” preserves the author’s critical force.

lexical_decisions.chosen: having nothing for which to wage war
lexical_decisions.rationale: The relative expression is understood impersonally as the absent reason or occasion for war; “having no one against whom to wage war” is a contextual alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Ultimately, then
lexical_decisions.rationale: πέρας functions adverbially as “at last,” “in the end,” or “as the final outcome,” introducing the eschatological arrangement.

lexical_decisions.chosen: unfailing peace
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἄπτωτος literally describes what does not fall or collapse; “secure peace” or “unshakable peace” are viable alternatives.

lexical_decisions.chosen: honoring him as an image of God
lexical_decisions.rationale: προτιμάω conveys assigning precedence or special honor; “preferring him” would be more literal but less clear in this context.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς εἰς τὴν ἁγίαν πόλιν εἰσούσης εἰσόδου
lexical_decisions.chosen: the entrance leading into the holy city
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the source’s repeated entrance-and-entering image without reproducing an awkward English cognate construction.

passages.text: “Whom else among those present shall I choose except Zacchaeus, to whom our Lord also went in and rested, judging him worthy to be saved?” After saying this, he laid his hand on Zacchaeus, who was standing there, and pressed him to sit in his chair. But Zacchaeus fell at his feet and begged him to release him from governing, while making this promise and saying, “Whatever a leader must do, I will do; only grant me not to bear this name. For I am wary of putting on the name of office, for it is full of bitter envy and danger.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς ὃν καὶ ὁ κύριος ἡμῶν εἰσιὼν ἀνεπαύσατο
lexical_decisions.chosen: to whom our Lord also went in and rested
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording says that the Lord entered or went in to Zacchaeus and rested; it does not explicitly name a house.

lexical_decisions.chosen: judging him worthy to be saved
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive articular infinitive depends on ἄξιον and identifies that of which Zacchaeus was judged worthy.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐβιάζετο ἐπὶ τὴν αὐτοῦ καθεσθῆναι καθέδραν
lexical_decisions.chosen: pressed him to sit in his chair
lexical_decisions.rationale: The middle verb can mean compel, constrain, or strongly urge. “Pressed” preserves the insistence without necessarily implying physical force.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to sit in his chair
lexical_decisions.rationale: αὐτοῦ most naturally refers to Zacchaeus, though Peter remains a grammatically possible referent; the English pronoun preserves that ambiguity.

lexical_decisions.chosen: release him from governing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive infinitive names the responsibility from which Zacchaeus asks to be released.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I am wary
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb may express caution, apprehension, or reverential fear; “I am afraid” is possible but somewhat stronger.

lexical_decisions.chosen: putting on the name of office
lexical_decisions.rationale: The translation retains the clothing image of ἐνδύομαι and renders ἀρχή as governing office in this context.

passages.text: And Peter said, “If this is what you are wary of, do not be called a ruler, but ‘the one appointed,’ since the Lord permitted this expression to be used when he said, ‘Blessed is that man whom his lord will appoint over the care of his fellow servants.’ If, however, you do not want it known at all that you have authority to administer, you seem to me not to realize that the acknowledged authority of the one presiding has considerable power to inspire deference in the multitude. For each person obeys one who has received the authority, since he regards his conscience as a powerful constraint. What then? Do you not also know for certain that you are to rule, not as the rulers of the nations do, but as a servant (ministering to them), as a father (to those being wronged), as a physician (attending to them), as a shepherd (guarding them)—in short, I say, having every concern for their salvation? Do you think I am unaware what sort of toils I am pressing you to undertake when I require you to be judged by crowds whom it is impossible for anyone to please? Yet one who acts well is fully able to win God’s favor. Therefore I ask you to undertake it willingly, for God’s sake, for the Messiah’s sake, for the salvation of the brothers, for their proper ordering, and for your benefit.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἄρχων μὲν μὴ καλοῦ, ἀλλὰ ὁ καθεστώς
lexical_decisions.chosen: do not be called a ruler, but ‘the one appointed’
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὁ καθεστώς is a perfect participial title meaning the person who has been established or appointed, deliberately distinguished from ἄρχων.

lexical_decisions.chosen: since the Lord permitted this expression to be used
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive absolute says that the Lord granted or allowed this designation to be spoken; “gave this to be said” would be more formally literal.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ τῆς θεραπείας τῶν συνδούλων αὐτοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: over the care of his fellow servants
lexical_decisions.rationale: θεραπεία can denote care, service, attendance, or a body of attendants. “Over the company of his fellow servants” is therefore possible, but “care” fits the ensuing description of pastoral duties.

lexical_decisions.chosen: fellow servants
lexical_decisions.rationale: Following the supplied policy, δοῦλος and its compound are rendered with “servant”; the compound stresses shared subordination to the same lord.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to inspire deference in the multitude
lexical_decisions.rationale: δυσωπία concerns restraint produced by respect, shame, or awe. “To overawe the multitude” is possible but gives the phrase a harsher tone.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς μεγάλην ἀνάγκην τὴν συνείδησιν ἔχων
lexical_decisions.chosen: since he regards his conscience as a powerful constraint
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle most naturally continues with ἕκαστος as its subject; conscience supplies the compelling reason to obey recognized authority.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐχ ὡς οἱ ἄρχοντες τῶν ἐθνῶν ἄρχειν ἔχεις
lexical_decisions.chosen: you are to rule, not as the rulers of the nations do
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔχεις with the infinitive expresses what Zacchaeus is expected or obliged to do.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Do you think I am unaware
lexical_decisions.rationale: The initial ὅτι introduces an elliptical rhetorical question; “Is it because you think I am unaware?” is a more explicit alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: when I require you to be judged by crowds
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀξιόω with an infinitive can mean require, expect, or deem appropriate, rather than necessarily “consider worthy.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: θεὸν δὲ εὖ πράττοντα πείθειν δυνατώτατον
lexical_decisions.chosen: Yet one who acts well is fully able to win God’s favor
lexical_decisions.rationale: The person acting well is taken as the subject of πείθειν and God as its object. More literally, “to persuade God” or “to prevail upon God” is possible; context favors the idiom of gaining divine approval.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for the Messiah’s sake
lexical_decisions.rationale: Χριστός functions independently as a title here, so it is rendered “the Messiah” under the supplied policy.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for their proper ordering
lexical_decisions.rationale: οἰκονομία can denote administration, management, arrangement, or stewardship. The genitive may be understood as the proper ordering or administration of the brothers.

passages.text: Also consider this other point: to the degree that administering the Messiah’s church involves toil and danger, the reward is that much greater. But furthermore, the punishment is also greater for one who is capable and disobeys. Therefore, knowing that you are more learned than those present, I want you to lend out the good counsels with which you have been entrusted by the Lord, so that you may hear, “Well done, good and faithful servant,” and not, like the one who hid the single talent, be found liable to punishment after receiving an accusation. But if you do not wish to become a good guardian of the church, identify someone else in your place, more learned and more faithful than you. But you will not provide one. For you were with the Lord, gave an account of the marvelous deeds, and learned how to administer a church.

lexical_decisions.chosen: administering the Messiah’s church
lexical_decisions.rationale: οἰκονομεῖν denotes managing or administering, and Χριστός is rendered as the independently functioning title “Messiah.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: the reward is that much greater
lexical_decisions.rationale: τοσούτῳ supplies the proportional counterpart to the preceding toil and danger: the greater the burden, the greater the reward.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for one who is capable and disobeys
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantival participles describe someone able to accept the responsibility who nevertheless refuses or disobeys.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to lend out the good counsels
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering retains the financial metaphor of δανείζειν. γνώμαι may also be rendered “teachings,” “judgments,” or “principles.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: with which you have been entrusted by the Lord
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect passive treats the counsels as a trust committed to Zacchaeus by the Lord.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Well done, good and faithful servant
lexical_decisions.rationale: The isolated εὖ implies commendation, conventionally expressed in English as “Well done”; δοῦλος follows the supplied “servant” policy.

lexical_decisions.chosen: be found liable to punishment after receiving an accusation
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔγκλημα is a charge, accusation, or ground of blame, and ἀναφανῇς means being shown or found to occupy the stated condition.

lexical_decisions.chosen: identify someone else in your place
lexical_decisions.rationale: μηνύω here means disclose, point out, or name a suitable alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: But you will not provide one
lexical_decisions.rationale: The object is unexpressed but is supplied by the previously requested alternative person; “you will not produce one” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: gave an account of the marvelous deeds
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἱστορέω can mean recount or report what one has learned, supporting the narrative rendering chosen here. In view of the preceding statement that Zacchaeus was with the Lord, the experiential alternatives “observed the marvelous deeds,” “witnessed the marvelous deeds,” or “became acquainted with the marvelous deeds” are also contextually viable.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the marvelous deeds
lexical_decisions.rationale: θαυμασίους may be analyzed as the feminine accusative plural of a two-termination adjective agreeing with πράξεις; the printed form therefore does not require correction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: learned how to administer a church
lexical_decisions.rationale: The Greek uses the noun “administration” with “church”; the verbal English form expresses the acquired practical knowledge without adding a new claim.

passages.text: And your task is to command what is necessary, while the brothers’ task is to submit and not disobey. Those who submit, then, will be saved, but those who disobey will be punished by the Messiah, because the one presiding has been entrusted with the Messiah’s place. Therefore, either honor or insult shown to the one presiding is carried to the Messiah, and from the Messiah it is referred to God. I have said this so that the brothers themselves may not be unaware of their own danger from disobedience toward you: whoever disobeys when you command disobeys the Messiah, and one who has disobeyed the Messiah provokes God to anger.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: σοῦ μὲν ἔργον ἐστὶν κελεύειν ἃ δεῖ, τῶν ἀδελφῶν ὑπείκειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: your task is to command what is necessary, while the brothers’ task is to submit
lexical_decisions.rationale: The second clause elides ἔργον ἐστίν, which is supplied in English without adding a new claim.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the one presiding has been entrusted with the Messiah’s place
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive πεπίστευται presents the presider as entrusted with a representative position; it does not identify him as the Messiah.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἤτοι τιμὴ ἢ ὕβρις τοῦ προκαθεζομένου
lexical_decisions.chosen: either honor or insult shown to the one presiding
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive is understood objectively in context: the honor or insult is directed toward the presider. A less likely formal alternative is “the presider’s honor or insult.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: Messiah
lexical_decisions.rationale: Χριστός functions independently as a title throughout the passage rather than as part of a personal-name construction.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς πρὸς σὲ ἀπειθείας τὸν κίνδυνον αὐτῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: their own danger from disobedience toward you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The placement of αὐτῶν is awkward but defensibly identifies the danger as belonging to the brothers; the genitive ἀπειθείας indicates the disobedience from which that danger arises.

passages.text: The church, therefore, like a city built on a height, must have a God-loving order and good administration. Above all, let the bishop, as ruler, be listened to in the matters about which he speaks. Let the elders be diligent to see that what is commanded is done. Let the deacons, going all around among the brothers, look after their bodies and souls and confer with the bishop. Let all the other brothers accept being wronged; but if they want their cases concerning the wrongs done to them to be judged, let them be brought to agreement before the elders. The elders are then to report the settlement also to the bishop.

lexical_decisions.chosen: like a city built on a height
lexical_decisions.rationale: This preserves both the city comparison and its elevated location without turning the image into a quotation from another text.

lexical_decisions.chosen: have a God-loving order
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective φιλόθεον directly characterizes the community’s τάξις as devoted to or loving God.

lexical_decisions.chosen: let ... be listened to in the matters about which he speaks
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive of ἀκούω can imply being heeded or obeyed; “be listened to” preserves that force without making obedience more explicit than the wording requires.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐκπεριερχόμενοί τῶν ἀδελφῶν τὰ σώματα καὶ τὰς ψυχὰς ἐπισκεπτέσθωσαν καὶ τῷ ἐπισκόπῳ ἀντιβαλλέτωσαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: going all around among the brothers, look after their bodies and souls and confer with the bishop
lexical_decisions.rationale: Ἐπισκέπτομαι includes visiting, inspecting, and caring for. The uncommon ἀντιβάλλω may indicate conferring with, reporting back to, or laying the findings before the bishop; “confer with” leaves the precise exchange open.

lexical_decisions.chosen: let them be brought to agreement before the elders
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive or middle συμβιβάζεσθαι can denote reconciliation or the settlement of a dispute; the following συμβιβασμόν supports an agreed settlement.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν δὲ συμβιβασμὸν ... τῷ ἐπισκόπῳ προσαναφερέτωσαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: report the settlement also to the bishop
lexical_decisions.rationale: Προσαναφέρω here denotes referring or reporting the elders’ settlement upward or additionally to the bishop.

passages.text: Let them expedite the marriages not only of the young but also of those advanced in years, lest seething desire bring a plague upon the church through an occasion of sexual immorality or adultery. For above every sin, the impiety of adultery is hated by God, because it destroys not only the sinner himself but also those who share his table and strive alongside him. It resembles rabies, for by nature it imparts its own madness. For chastity’s sake, therefore, let not only the elders but everyone be eager to complete marriages. The sin of the adulterer forces its way upon everyone. Therefore, urging the brothers to live chastely is the first act of mercy, for it is care for the soul; food for the body is relief.

source_issues.issue: The selected print joins the two particles with a hyphen. This is an orthographic or editorial feature and does not alter the ordinary construction “but also.”
The dative πρώτῃ does not agree with the predicate noun ἐλεημοσύνη. The intended predicate sense is nevertheless clear, and the translation represents it as “the first act of mercy.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: let them expedite the marriages
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb calls for actively hastening the marriages rather than merely recommending them.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those advanced in years
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect participle describes people who have progressed in age; “older people” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through an occasion of sexual immorality or adultery
lexical_decisions.rationale: Πρόφασις can mean pretext, occasion, or ostensible cause. “Through an occasion” best fits the warning that seething desire may bring the stated plague; a more literal but less clear alternative is “under a pretext of sexual immorality or adultery.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: those who share his table and strive alongside him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The two participles depict people dining with the offender and engaging alongside him. The second can also be understood more generally as associating or sharing his pursuits.

lexical_decisions.chosen: It resembles rabies
lexical_decisions.rationale: Λύσσα can denote rabies or raging madness; the following image of contagious madness supports the disease sense while retaining its association with frenzy.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ οὖν σπεύδειν σωφρονεῖν τοὺς ἀδελφούς
lexical_decisions.chosen: urging the brothers to live chastely
lexical_decisions.rationale: Σπεύδειν is taken transitively as hastening or urging the brothers toward σωφροσύνη. The syntax also permits “the brothers’ being eager to live chastely.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: for it is care for the soul
lexical_decisions.rationale: Θεραπεία can mean care, treatment, or healing; “care” preserves the contrast with bodily nourishment without asserting a specific medical image.

passages.text: Nevertheless, if you love your brothers, you will take nothing away from them, but you will share what you have. You will feed the hungry, provide drink for the thirsty, clothe the naked, visit the sick, help those in prisons as far as possible, eagerly welcome strangers into your own lodgings, and hate no one. As for how you must act devoutly, your own understanding will teach you, since you are discerning. Above all—even if it is necessary to tell you—meet together more frequently; would that it were every hour, but at least on the customary days of assembly. For if you do this, you are within walls of refuge, since desertion from the ranks is the beginning of destruction. Accordingly, let no one be absent from meeting together on the pretext of petty resentment toward a brother. For if anyone among you is absent from gathering, that person will be counted among those who scatter the Messiah’s church and will be punished as one who has become one of those opposed to the Messiah’s disciples. That person will be cast out with adulterers. For, like an adulterer, he has separated himself on some pretext under the influence of the spirit within him, and has given the evil one room against himself to seize a sheep as one found outside the folds.

source_issues.source_quote: συνεχέστερον συνέρχεσθε, εἴθε καθ’ ὥραν, ἐπεί γε ἐν ταῖς νενομισμέναις τῆς συνόδου ἡμέραις
source_issues.issue: The wish εἴθε καθ’ ὥραν is followed by a verbless ἐπεί γε phrase. The translation treats the latter as an elliptical minimum—“but at least on the customary days of assembly.” The more formally connective alternative “since at least on the customary days of assembly” leaves the same gathering verb implicit. No missing wording has been restored.

source_issues.source_quote: ὡς γὰρ μοιχὸς ὑπὸ τοῦ ἐν αὐτῷ πνεύματος προφάσει τινὸς ἑαυτὸν ἀφώρισεν
source_issues.issue: The opening comparison and the agent phrase permit more than one attachment: the absent person may be compared with an adulterer, or ὡς μοιχός may characterize him directly as one. The main rendering takes it as a comparison and attaches “by the spirit within him” to his self-separation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you will take nothing away from them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The middle form can mean taking something from others for oneself or depriving them; the following promise to share one’s possessions supplies the contrast.

lexical_decisions.chosen: since you are discerning
lexical_decisions.rationale: Εὐγνωμονέω can describe being sensible, fair-minded, or well-disposed. Here it concerns the readers’ capacity to recognize how piety should be practiced.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you are within walls of refuge
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the enclosing-wall image and takes ἀσυλία as safety, immunity, or inviolable refuge.

lexical_decisions.chosen: desertion from the ranks is the beginning of destruction
lexical_decisions.rationale: Λειποταξία is a military term for abandoning one’s assigned position, here applied metaphorically to absence from the assembly.

lexical_decisions.chosen: on the pretext of petty resentment toward a brother
lexical_decisions.rationale: Μικροψυχία literally suggests smallness or faintness of spirit and can denote pettiness or discouragement. In this interpersonal setting, “petty resentment” is contextually defensible; “discouragement concerning a brother” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the Messiah’s church
lexical_decisions.rationale: Χριστός is used independently as a title, not within a personal-name construction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: under the influence of the spirit within him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase identifies the spirit as the agent of his self-separation but does not explicitly identify it as his own spirit, the Holy Spirit, or an evil spirit; lowercase wording preserves that uncertainty.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρόβατον ἁρπάσαι ὡς μανδρῶν ἔξω εὑρεθέν
lexical_decisions.chosen: to seize a sheep as one found outside the folds
lexical_decisions.rationale: The absent person is depicted through the sheep image. The ὡς with the participle presents the sheep as regarded or found outside, while μανδρῶν is plural, “folds.”

passages.text: However, listen to your bishop, and do not grow weary in rendering him every honor, knowing that, though ostensibly directed to him, it is carried to the Messiah; from the Messiah it is referred to God, and it is repaid many times over to the one who offered it. You will therefore honor the Messiah’s throne, since you were also commanded to honor Moses’ seat, even if those who preside are regarded as sinners. These things have been said to you sufficiently. But as for how he must live blamelessly, I consider it superfluous to speak, since he is a proven disciple of the one who taught even me.

lexical_decisions.chosen: listen to your bishop
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive with ἀκούετε can include heeding or obeying; “listen to” preserves that range while the surrounding commands establish the authoritative setting.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: προφάσει τῇ πρὸς αὐτὸν εἰς χριστὸν φέρεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: though ostensibly directed to him, it is carried to the Messiah
lexical_decisions.rationale: The implied subject is the honor just mentioned. Πρόφασις marks its outward or apparent direction toward the bishop, while the author says its ultimate recipient is the Messiah.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Messiah
lexical_decisions.rationale: Χριστός functions independently as a title throughout the passage rather than as part of a personal name.

lexical_decisions.chosen: it is repaid many times over
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverb indicates a multiplied return rather than merely an equivalent repayment.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the Messiah’s throne ... Moses’ seat
lexical_decisions.rationale: Distinct English terms preserve the source’s distinction between θρόνος and καθέδρα rather than harmonizing both as “seat” or “chair.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: he is a proven disciple
lexical_decisions.rationale: Δόκιμος describes someone tested and found approved or dependable; “proven” conveys that evaluative force.

lexical_decisions.chosen: of the one who taught even me
lexical_decisions.rationale: The crasis κἀμέ means “me also” or, with rhetorical emphasis, “even me”; the latter suits the speaker’s appeal to the bishop’s teacher.

passages.text: Nevertheless, brothers, there are some things you should not wait to hear, but should also recognize for yourselves what is reasonable. Is Zacchaeus alone to labor for you? Having given himself over entirely to being occupied, since he has a belly and has no leisure for himself, how can he obtain the necessary food? Is it not reasonable for all of you to take thought for his livelihood, without waiting for him to ask you? For that is the act of a beggar, and he would die of hunger rather than undertake to do this. How, then, will you yourselves not incur punishment if you fail to consider that “the worker is worthy of his wages”? And let no one say, “So then, is the word that was provided freely being sold?” By no means. For if someone who has the means to live should accept support, that person is selling the word. But if someone without the means to live receives food in order to live—as the Lord also received food both at dinners and among friends, possessing nothing though he is the one who will possess everything hereafter—he does not sin. Accordingly, honor elders, catechists, useful deacons, widows who have lived well, and orphans as children of the church. Moreover, whenever a need for some resource for a necessary purpose arises, all of you should contribute together. Act piously toward one another, not hesitating to endure anything at all for the sake of your own salvation.

source_issues.issue: The confirmed editorial question punctuation leaves the clause without an expressed predicate. The main rendering supplies the idea of labor from the immediately following occupation language; alternatively, the words may be represented more literally as “Is Zacchaeus alone for you?” or ὑμῖν may be understood closely with the following infinitive despite the punctuation. No textual correction is required.

The selected edition spells the name here with one χ but uses Ζαχχαίῳ in 3.72. This is an orthographic variation; both are represented by the conventional English name “Zacchaeus,” without altering the supplied Greek.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Is Zacchaeus alone to labor for you?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The printed question is elliptical. “To labor” is supplied contextually from the following description of his complete occupation; a more formally literal but obscure alternative is “Is Zacchaeus alone for you?”

lexical_decisions.chosen: Having given himself over entirely to being occupied
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase depicts complete dedication to an occupation or lack of leisure, without specifying a separate office or activity.

lexical_decisions.chosen: since he has a belly
lexical_decisions.rationale: This preserves the source’s concrete bodily image rather than reducing it to the abstract statement that he has needs.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to take thought for his livelihood
lexical_decisions.rationale: The construction calls for active provision or care concerning the means by which he lives.

lexical_decisions.chosen: For that is the act of a beggar
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive denotes conduct characteristic of one who begs or solicits alms.

lexical_decisions.chosen: both at dinners and among friends
lexical_decisions.rationale: The two coordinated expressions differ slightly in sense—one denotes occasions and the other company—but both can be retained without emendation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: honor
lexical_decisions.rationale: The immediate context includes material provision, but the verb itself means to honor; the translation does not restrict it to payment alone.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Act piously toward one another
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb denotes the practice of piety or dutiful reverence, here directed toward fellow members of the community.

passages.text: After saying these things, he laid his hand on Zacchaeus and said, “Sovereign and Lord of all, the Father and God, you yourself preserve the shepherd together with the flock. You are the cause; you are the power. We are those who receive help; ‘you are the helper’, ‘the physician’, ‘the Savior’, ‘the wall’, the life, ‘the hope’, ‘the refuge’, the joy, the expectation. You are rest. To sum it up, I will say: you are everything to us. Work with us toward the eternal possession of salvation; rescue us; guard us. You can do all things, for you are ruler of rulers and Lord of lords, master of kings. Give the one who presides authority to loose what must be loosed and to bind what must be bound. Make him wise. Through him as through an instrument, preserve the church of your Messiah as a beautiful bride. For yours is eternal glory, the praise of Father and Son and Holy Spirit, throughout all the ages. Amen.”

source_issues.source_quote: ἡμεῖς τὸ βοηθούμενον, „σὺ ὁ βοηθός“, „ὁ ἰατρός“, „ὁ σωτήρ“, „τὸ τεῖχος“, ἡ ζωή, „ἡ ἐλπίς“, „ἡ καταφυγή“, ἡ χαρά, ἡ προσδοκία. ἡ ἀνάπαυσις,
source_issues.issue: The selected edition marks six expressions as quotations and places a full stop after προσδοκία. The translation preserves the quotation distinctions and treats ἡ ἀνάπαυσις as an elliptical predicate, “You are rest.” It could instead be punctuated as a continuation of the preceding enumeration. No textual correction is proposed.

The relation between ὕπαρξιν and σωτηρίας is interpretively open: the phrase may mean “eternal possession of salvation,” “an eternal state of salvation,” or “eternal existence in salvation.” The main rendering is grammatically and contextually defensible, so no conjecture is needed.

source_issues.source_quote: σοῦ γὰρ ἐστὶν δόξα αἰώνιος, ὕμνος πατρὸς καὶ υἱοῦ καὶ ἁγίου πνεύματος
source_issues.issue: The syntax allows ὕμνος to stand in apposition to δόξα, as in the main translation, or to function as a second predicate: “For yours are eternal glory and the praise of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.” The supplied wording supports either construction.
The selected edition spells the name here with two χ letters, whereas 3.71 has Ζακχαῖος. This nonblocking orthographic variation is represented by the same conventional English name, “Zacchaeus.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: Sovereign and Lord of all
lexical_decisions.rationale: “Sovereign” conveys the authority of δεσπότης while distinguishing it from the following κύριος, “Lord.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: You are the cause
lexical_decisions.rationale: In this prayer πρόφασις is read as the originating cause or ground, rather than its frequent negative sense “pretext.” “You are the ground” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: We are those who receive help
lexical_decisions.rationale: The singular neuter participial expression is treated collectively as the party being helped.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: „σὺ ὁ βοηθός“, „ὁ ἰατρός“, „ὁ σωτήρ“, „τὸ τεῖχος“, ἡ ζωή, „ἡ ἐλπίς“, „ἡ καταφυγή“, ἡ χαρά, ἡ προσδοκία
lexical_decisions.chosen: ‘you are the helper’, ‘the physician’, ‘the Savior’, ‘the wall’, the life, ‘the hope’, ‘the refuge’, the joy, the expectation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The six expressions separately marked as quotations in the selected edition retain distinct inner quotation boundaries, while the intervening unquoted attributes remain outside them.

lexical_decisions.chosen: You are rest
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun names rest or repose as a divine attribute. The predicate “you are” is carried forward from the surrounding enumeration so that “rest” cannot be mistaken for an unspecified remainder.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Work with us toward the eternal possession of salvation
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὕπαρξις can denote possession, state, subsistence, or existence. “Eternal possession of salvation” gives a coherent objective-genitive sense; “an eternal state of salvation” is a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who presides
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle literally describes the person seated in front and contextually denotes the community’s presiding leader.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Make him wise
lexical_decisions.rationale: The unexpressed object is understood from the immediately preceding presiding leader.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the church of your Messiah
lexical_decisions.rationale: χριστός functions independently as a title possessed by God, so its titular meaning is rendered rather than treated as part of a personal name.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: σοῦ γὰρ ἐστὶν δόξα αἰώνιος, ὕμνος πατρὸς καὶ υἱοῦ καὶ ἁγίου πνεύματος
lexical_decisions.chosen: For yours is eternal glory, the praise of Father and Son and Holy Spirit
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering takes ὕμνος as an appositional description of the glory. It leaves “praise of” able to express either praise associated with or praise directed toward Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

passages.text: After saying these things, he then said, “All of you who wish to be baptized, begin fasting tomorrow, have hands laid on you each day, and inquire about whatever you wish. For I want to remain with you for ten more days.” After three days, when he had begun baptizing, he called me, Aquila, and Nicetas and said, “Since I intend to set out for Tyre after seven days, I want you, after leaving this city, secretly lodging as guests with Bernice the Canaanite, Justa’s daughter, and learning from her precisely the matters concerning Simon, to write to me. For this is of great help to me, so that I may adjust myself accordingly. Therefore, depart from this city in peace.” And so, leaving him baptizing just as he had commanded, we went ahead of him to Tyre in Phoenicia.

source_issues.issue: The phrase occurs twice. Tyre is an explicit feminine antecedent candidate immediately before the first occurrence, while the main translation instead supplies an implicit reference to the current city. At both occurrences, ἐξ αὐτῆς may also function idiomatically as “at once.” The ensuing journey to Tyre is compatible both with departure from the current city and with immediate departure, so it does not by itself decide between those readings. No source correction is proposed.

The neuter singular pronoun does not directly refer to the masculine Simon and does not formally agree with the preceding neuter plural τὰ. It can nevertheless refer collectively to the matter or situation concerning Simon, yielding “adjust myself accordingly” or “adapt myself to it.” No emendation is necessary.

lexical_decisions.chosen: All of you who wish to be baptized
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here ποτε gives an indefinite force comparable to “whoever”; it does not require a separate temporal phrase in English.

lexical_decisions.chosen: have hands laid on you each day
lexical_decisions.rationale: In the preparation of baptismal candidates, the passive verb naturally refers to receiving the laying on of hands; “be appointed” is contextually less likely.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after seven days
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase marks the intended interval before the departure for Tyre.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Μέλλων ἐπὶ τὴν Τύρον ὁρμᾶν μεθ’ ἡμέρας ἑπτὰ βούλομαι ἐξ αὐτῆς ὑμᾶς ἀπελθόντας
lexical_decisions.chosen: Since I intend to set out for Tyre after seven days, I want you, after leaving this city
lexical_decisions.rationale: Tyre immediately precedes the first ἐξ αὐτῆς and is formally a feminine antecedent candidate. The main rendering instead understands an implicit reference to the current city. The phrase may also be idiomatic and temporal, “at once,” rather than spatial.

lexical_decisions.chosen: secretly lodging as guests
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverb conveys remaining unnoticed or concealed, while the participle denotes receiving or taking guest lodging.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: παρ’ αὐτῆς τὰ κατὰ τὸν Σίμωνα ἀκριβῶς μαθόντας
lexical_decisions.chosen: learning from her precisely the matters concerning Simon
lexical_decisions.rationale: τὰ κατά with a person denotes the facts, circumstances, or matters concerning that person.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πολὺ γὰρ μοι συμβάλλεται, ἵνα πρὸς αὐτὸ ἁρμόσωμαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: For this is of great help to me, so that I may adjust myself accordingly
lexical_decisions.rationale: The neuter singular αὐτό is taken collectively as the matter or situation disclosed by the requested report. A more formally explicit alternative is “so that I may adapt myself to it.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διὸ ἐξ αὐτῆς πορεύεσθε μετὰ εἰρήνης
lexical_decisions.chosen: Therefore, depart from this city in peace
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering again supplies the current city as the spatial referent of αὐτῆς. An idiomatic temporal rendering, “Therefore, depart at once in peace,” is also viable.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς Τύρον αὐτὸν προήξαμεν τῆς Φοινίκης
lexical_decisions.chosen: we went ahead of him to Tyre in Phoenicia
lexical_decisions.rationale: With the personal object αὐτόν, προάγω here means to precede or go ahead of him rather than to lead him.

passages.text: Leaving Caesarea of Strato, I, Clement, together with Nicetas and Aquila, arrived at Tyre in Phoenicia. At the instruction of Peter, who had sent us, we were received as guests by Berenice, daughter of Justa the Canaanite. She welcomed us most gladly. She exerted herself greatly in the honor she showed me and in her affection for Aquila and Nicetas; in her joy she treated us warmly, speaking freely as though she were an old acquaintance, and hospitably pressed us to care for our bodies. Perceiving, then, that she was allowing us to make a brief postponement, I said, “You do well to hasten to fulfill the duties of love. But fear of our God must be preferred to this. For, since we are engaged in a struggle on behalf of many souls, we are afraid to prefer our own rest to their salvation.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: Leaving Caesarea of Strato
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive identifies the city historically; “Strato’s Caesarea” or “Caesarea Stratonis” would also be possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: speaking freely as though she were an old acquaintance
lexical_decisions.rationale: συνήθης can describe someone familiar or intimate, while παρρησιαζομένη denotes speaking with freedom or frankness.

lexical_decisions.chosen: allowing us to make a brief postponement
lexical_decisions.rationale: The object of the postponement is left implicit in Greek, so the English does not specify whether it was their mission, inquiry, or departure.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ πρὸς τὸν θεὸν ἡμῶν φόβος
lexical_decisions.chosen: fear of our God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The placement of ἡμῶν naturally permits attachment to θεόν, yielding “our God”; “our fear toward God” remains grammatically possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὲρ πολλῶν ψυχῶν τὸν ἀγῶνα ἔχοντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: since we are engaged in a struggle on behalf of many souls
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀγών retains the image of a contest or struggle rather than merely denoting responsibility.

passages.text: “We hear that Simon the magician, after being defeated in the debate at Caesarea with our lord Peter, immediately fled and is committing many evils here. For by reviling Peter with every kind of charge contrary to the truth, he sweeps away the souls of the multitude. Though he is a magician himself, he calls that man a magician; though he is a deceiver himself, he publicly denounces that man as a deceiver. And though he himself came off worse in the debates before everyone and fled, he claims to have won. He repeatedly instructs people not to listen to Peter, supposedly out of concern that they might be bewitched by a formidable magician.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ τῆς ἐν Καισαρείᾳ πρὸς τὸν κύριον ἡμῶν Πέτρον ζητήσεως
lexical_decisions.chosen: in the debate at Caesarea with our lord Peter
lexical_decisions.rationale: ζήτησις here denotes a formal dispute or debate. κύριος is retained as the honorific “lord” for Peter rather than being treated as a divine title.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πᾶσι γὰρ τοῖς ὑπεναντίοις παρὰ τὴν ἀλήθειαν λοιδορῶν τὸν Πέτρον
lexical_decisions.chosen: by reviling Peter with every kind of charge contrary to the truth
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative plural τοῖς ὑπεναντίοις is taken as substantivized neuter, referring to hostile allegations or means of abuse. A possible alternative is to take it as masculine recipients: “reviling Peter before all his opponents, contrary to the truth.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: deceiver
lexical_decisions.rationale: The word can mean a deceiver, impostor, or one who leads others astray; “deceiver” fits the reciprocal accusation here.

lexical_decisions.chosen: came off worse
lexical_decisions.rationale: This idiom means to emerge as the inferior or defeated party, not literally to carry away something lesser.

lexical_decisions.chosen: supposedly out of concern
lexical_decisions.rationale: δῆθεν marks the stated concern as pretended or merely alleged.

lexical_decisions.chosen: might be bewitched by a formidable magician
lexical_decisions.rationale: δεινός may mean formidable, terrible, or highly skilled; “formidable” preserves the threatening ability implied by Simon’s warning.

passages.text: “Having learned these things, our lord Peter sent us ahead to investigate what had been reported to him, so that, if matters were so, once we had written he himself might learn; and when he comes, he will expose Simon in the very presence of those before whom Simon had slandered him. Since, then, danger involving many souls lies before us, for this reason we have set aside our bodily rest for a little while and wish to learn truthfully from you, since you live here, whether what we have heard is in fact true. So now please tell us every detail.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: προἀπέστειλεν ἡμᾶς ἐξεταστὰς τῶν λεχθέντων αὐτῷ ἐσομένους
lexical_decisions.chosen: sent us ahead to investigate what had been reported to him
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐξεταστάς identifies them as investigators or examiners; the English verbalizes that role without adding a separate office.

lexical_decisions.chosen: once we had written he himself might learn
lexical_decisions.rationale: The Greek leaves the recipient and contents of the writing implicit, so neither a letter nor a formal report is specified.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he will expose Simon
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐλέγχω can mean expose, convict, or refute. “Expose” accommodates both the personal accusations and the anticipated public confrontation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐκείνων ἄντικρυς ἐφ’ ὧν αὐτὸν διέβαλλεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: in the very presence of those before whom Simon had slandered him
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐκείνων and ὧν are taken as referring to the people before whom Simon had spoken against Peter. The repeated αὐτόν has different contextual referents, made explicit in English to prevent confusion.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς τοῦ σώματος ἡμῶν ἀναπαύσεως πρὸς βραχὺ ἀμελήσαντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: we have set aside our bodily rest for a little while
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀμελέω literally means to neglect or disregard; “set aside” expresses the temporary, deliberate forgoing of rest indicated by πρὸς βραχύ.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to learn truthfully
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverb denotes learning without falsehood or deception; “reliably” would be another contextual rendering.

passages.text: Having been called upon, Berenice said, “These matters are as you heard. But listen to the other things concerning Simon himself, which perhaps you do not know. For by making apparitions and phantom-images appear in the middle of the marketplace in broad daylight, he astonishes the whole city. When he goes out, statues move and many shadows go before him, which he himself says are the souls of the dead. Having soon afterward won over to himself many who were trying to expose him as a sorcerer, he sacrificed an ox under the pretext of a banquet and feasted them, then beset them with various diseases and subjected them to demons. And—to keep from saying too much—after harming many, he has been regarded as a god; besides being fearsome, he has also been held in special honor.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: Having been called upon, Berenice said
lexical_decisions.rationale: Although the passive of ἀξιόω can literally mean “having been deemed worthy,” it can contextually introduce someone who has been requested or invited to speak.

lexical_decisions.chosen: apparitions and phantom-images
lexical_decisions.rationale: The paired nouns both concern visual manifestations; the differentiated rendering preserves the source’s two terms rather than collapsing them into one.

lexical_decisions.chosen: When he goes out
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle can describe going out, coming forward, or proceeding in public; the surrounding moving statues and preceding shadows suggest a public appearance or procession.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Having soon afterward won over to himself
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαλλάσσω denotes reconciling or winning people over. εὐθύστερον is taken temporally as indicating prompt succession; it could instead qualify the manner as “more directly” or “more readily.” The supplied reading is retained without emendation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: beset them with various diseases
lexical_decisions.rationale: περιβάλλω literally evokes surrounding or enveloping; with diseases as its instrument, “beset” preserves more of that image than the generic “afflicted.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: subjected them to demons
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑποβάλλω here presents the victims as being placed under the power or influence of demons.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς τῷ φοβερὸν εἶναι καὶ προτετίμηται
lexical_decisions.chosen: besides being fearsome, he has also been held in special honor
lexical_decisions.rationale: φοβερός actively means fear-inspiring, while the perfect προτετίμηται indicates an established state of exceptional esteem or preference.

passages.text: “Therefore I do not think anyone will be able to extinguish so great a fire that has been kindled. For no one doubts what that man claims; rather, each person emphatically maintains that it is so.
