Therefore, so that you may not be put in danger, I urge you not to attempt anything against him before Peter comes, who alone will be able to contend against so great a power (being the most proven disciple of our Lord Jesus Christ). For I have become so afraid of the man that, if he had not on another occasion also debated with my lord Peter and come off worse, I would have advised you to persuade even Peter himself not to attempt a counter-debate with Simon.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: extinguish so great a fire that has been kindled
lexical_decisions.rationale: The attributive participle describes the fire as already kindled; the rendering retains both that existing state and the explicit fire metaphor.

lexical_decisions.chosen: what that man claims
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπαγγέλλομαι may mean promise, profess, or claim; here it concerns Simon’s asserted powers and representations.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀλλὰ τοῦτο οὕτως ἔχειν διαβεβαιοῦται ἕκαστος
lexical_decisions.chosen: rather, each person emphatically maintains that it is so
lexical_decisions.rationale: With its accusative-and-infinitive complement, διαβεβαιοῦται expresses emphatic affirmation. This preserves a distinction from the preceding οὐδὲ ἐνδοιάζει τις: the people not only do not doubt but positively maintain the claim.

lexical_decisions.chosen: against so great a power
lexical_decisions.rationale: δυναστεία can denote power, dominion, or potent authority; “power” best fits Simon’s feared magical capacity in context.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ δοκιμώτατος ὑπάρχων μαθητής
lexical_decisions.chosen: being the most proven disciple of our Lord Jesus Christ
lexical_decisions.rationale: δοκιμώτατος is formally superlative and can be comparative, “the most proven disciple,” or elative, “a highly approved” or “well-proven disciple,” without ranking Peter above every other disciple. The main rendering adopts the comparative force because the surrounding clause says that Peter alone can contend with Simon, but the elative reading remains viable.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς τὸν κύριόν μου Πέτρον διαλεχθεὶς τὸ ἧττον ἀπηνέγκατο
lexical_decisions.chosen: debated with my lord Peter and came off worse
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαλέγομαι denotes discussion or debate here, and τὸ ἧττον ἀπηνέγκατο is the idiom for emerging as the defeated or inferior party. “Lord” is lowercased because κύριος is an honorific for Peter in this clause.

lexical_decisions.chosen: not to attempt a counter-debate with Simon
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀντεξετάζομαι denotes engaging in examination or disputation in opposition to another; “counter-debate” preserves that reciprocal adversarial force.

passages.text: And I said, “If our lord Peter did not know that he alone can prevail over that man’s power, he would not have sent us ahead with instructions to learn in detail, without attracting notice, what concerned Simon and to write it to him.” All the same, since evening had overtaken us, we partook of salt and slept. In the morning, someone acquainted with Bernice came and said that Simon had sailed away to Sidon but had left behind some of his disciples: Appion the many-times victor, an Alexandrian man and a grammarian by training, whom I recognized as a friend of mine through my father; Annubion the Diospolitan, a certain astrologer; and Athenodorus the Athenian, who approved of the teaching of Epicurus. After learning what concerned Simon, we wrote everything down at dawn and sent it on to Peter, and then went off for a walk.

source_issues.issue: The printed accentuation gives ὁμῶς, ordinarily associated with “alike,” while the context supports the concessive force of ὅμως, “nevertheless” or “all the same.” The supplied form can still be represented contextually as “All the same.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: our lord Peter
lexical_decisions.rationale: The human honorific κύριος is retained as “lord” rather than recast as a theological title.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to learn in detail, without attracting notice, what concerned Simon
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαμανθάνω conveys thorough learning, while λανθανόντως indicates that it was to be done secretly or unnoticed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: we partook of salt
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording literally invokes sharing salt and can idiomatically denote taking food; the concrete image is preserved.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Appion the many-times victor
lexical_decisions.rationale: πλειστονίκης is treated as an epithet meaning one who has won very many victories; it could alternatively be presented as the title or name “Pleistonikes.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὃν πρὸς πατρός μοι φίλον ὄντα ἐπέγνων
lexical_decisions.chosen: whom I recognized as a friend of mine through my father
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρὸς πατρός indicates a paternal connection. Possible nuances include “a paternal family friend” or “my father’s friend.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: who approved of the teaching of Epicurus
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀρεσκόμενον expresses being pleased with or approving Epicurus’s λόγος; “approved of” avoids implying the stronger allegiance suggested by “devoted.”

passages.text: And Appion met us, not only with the two companions already mentioned but also with about thirty other men. As soon as he saw me, he greeted me, kissed me warmly, and said, “This is Clement, about whose noble birth and freeborn dignity I have spoken to you at length, telling you that, although he is a man of the family of Tiberius Caesar and has been trained in every branch of Greek education, he has been deceived by a certain barbarian named Peter into doing and saying the things of the Jews. I therefore ask you to join me in the effort to correct him. And in your presence I question the man himself. Let him tell me this: since he thinks he has devoted himself to being pious, how is he not committing the gravest impieties by abandoning his ancestral customs and turning aside to barbarian ways?”

source_issues.issue: The raised apostrophe after ἑτέρων is syntactically inert and appears to be anomalous editorial punctuation. It does not affect the sentence’s meaning.
The apostrophe beside the comma after πάτρια appears to be an extraneous editorial mark. The participial construction remains clear.

lexical_decisions.chosen: met us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The imperfect can describe Appion encountering or coming to meet the group.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς τε εὐγενείας καὶ τῆς ἐλευθεροπρεπείας
lexical_decisions.chosen: his noble birth and freeborn dignity
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὐγένεια concerns distinguished birth, while ἐλευθεροπρέπεια denotes dignity or conduct befitting a free person; “generosity” or “magnificence” is also possible for the latter.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I have spoken to you at length, telling you that
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὅτι is taken as introducing the content of Appion’s prior account and is therefore explicitly connected to λόγον. It could alternatively be causal—“I spoke at length because …”—but the reporting attachment provides a natural transition into what Appion had said about Clement.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he is a man of the family of Tiberius Caesar
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase presents Clement as related to or descended from Tiberius Caesar’s family.

lexical_decisions.chosen: doing and saying the things of the Jews
lexical_decisions.rationale: The elliptical τὰ Ἰουδαίων is preserved broadly rather than narrowed to particular Jewish rites or doctrines.

lexical_decisions.chosen: And in your presence I question the man himself
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐφ’ ὑμῶν means “before/in the presence of you,” and the genitive αὐτοῦ is naturally taken with πυνθάνομαι as the person questioned.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he thinks he has devoted himself to being pious
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀποδίδωμι with the reflexive expresses giving or devoting oneself to an undertaking.

passages.text: And I answered, “I welcome your good intention toward me, but I reject your ignorance. The intention is good, because you want me to be among those things you regard as good; but your understanding, being unsound, strives under the pretext of friendship to set an ambush for me.” Appion said, “Does it seem to you to be ignorance for someone who observes his ancestral customs to hold the beliefs of the Greeks?” And I answered, “One who chooses to be pious need not invariably observe ancestral customs. He should observe them if they are pious, but cast them off if they prove impious. For someone born of an impious father may wish to be pious and therefore not wish to follow the object of his father’s worship.” Appion replied, “What then? Are you saying that your father lived a wicked life?” And I said, “His life was not wicked, but his belief was.” Appion said, “What was this wicked notion of his? I want to hear.” And I said, “He believed the false and wicked myths of the Greeks.” Appion asked, “Which are these myths of the Greeks that are both false and wicked?” And I said, “The wrong conception of gods, which, if you are patient, you will hear about together with those who are eager to learn.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: but I reject your ignorance
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀποσείω literally suggests shaking something off and here expresses firm rejection.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ δὲ γνῶσις οὐκ ὀρθῶς ἔχουσα
lexical_decisions.chosen: but your understanding, being unsound
lexical_decisions.rationale: γνῶσις contrasts with ἀγνωσία and denotes Appion’s understanding or judgment, which Clement considers incorrectly disposed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: strives under the pretext of friendship to set an ambush for me
lexical_decisions.rationale: The martial image of lying in ambush is retained; “for me” supplies the contextually evident target.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ πάτρια ἔθη φυλάττοντα τὰ Ἑλλήνων φρονεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: for someone who observes his ancestral customs to hold the beliefs of the Greeks
lexical_decisions.rationale: τὰ Ἑλλήνων is elliptical, literally “the things of the Greeks,” and in this argumentative context denotes Greek beliefs or opinions.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to follow the object of his father’s worship
lexical_decisions.rationale: σέβασμα can denote an object of reverence or worship; “his father’s religion” is a broader possible rendering.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Κακοῦ μὲν οὐκ ἦν βίου, κακῆς δὲ ὑπολήψεως
lexical_decisions.chosen: His life was not wicked, but his belief was
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compact nominal contrast between βίος and ὑπόληψις is expressed idiomatically while preserving the repeated evaluation as wicked.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἡ περὶ θεῶν οὐκ ὀρθὴ δόκησις
lexical_decisions.chosen: The wrong conception of gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: δόκησις denotes an opinion or conception; the phrase does not itself specify one particular doctrine about the gods.

passages.text: “Therefore, before the discussions, let us now withdraw to some quieter place; there I will converse with you. This is the reason I have wished to speak in private: neither the many nor even all those who practice philosophy approach the judgment of things that exist sincerely. For we know many, even among those who take great pride in philosophy, who seek empty glory or have put on the coarse cloak for the sake of making money rather than for virtue itself. If they do not find what they practice philosophy for, they turn to scoffing. Because of such people, then, let us choose a place suitable for being by ourselves.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: I have wished to speak in private
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἰδιολογέομαι denotes holding a private or separate conversation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the judgment of things that exist
lexical_decisions.rationale: The philosophical expression may also be rendered “the examination of realities”; the more source-transparent wording preserves τὰ ὄντα.

lexical_decisions.chosen: who seek empty glory
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compound describes vainglorious conduct or pursuit of baseless prestige.

lexical_decisions.chosen: have put on the coarse cloak for the sake of making money
lexical_decisions.rationale: The τρίβων is the worn cloak conventionally associated with philosophers; the image is retained rather than replaced with a general reference to pretending to be philosophers.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐὰν μὴ εὕρωσιν δι’ ὃ φιλοσοφοῦσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: If they do not find what they practice philosophy for
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording leaves the desired objective implicit; it may refer to empty prestige, financial gain, or either motive just mentioned.

lexical_decisions.chosen: suitable for being by ourselves
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἰδιάζω here means withdrawing from the public or remaining in private, in parallel with the preceding wish for private conversation.

passages.text: And a certain wealthy man among them, who also always possessed around himself a certain tract of all-accomplished leaves, said, “Since the heat is blazing fiercely, let us withdraw a short distance from the city, into my gardens.” And so, after going on, they seated themselves where there were clear streams of cool spring water and a green canopy of trees of every kind. There I gladly sat down, with the rest around me. As they remained silent, in place of the voice that was about to make a request of me, they showed by staring at me that they were demanding the fulfillment of the promise. And so I began to speak in this way.

source_issues.source_quote: καὶ διὰ παντὸς χῶρόν τινα περὶ ἑαυτὸν κεκτημένος παμμούσων φύλλων
source_issues.issue: The image-checked supplied reading literally describes the man as continually possessing around himself “a certain tract of all-accomplished leaves.” The application of παμμούσων, denoting accomplishment in all the arts, to φύλλων, “leaves,” is contextually anomalous and may reflect corruption, but that possibility is not established. The main text therefore preserves a defensible literal representation of the selected edition. A possible conjecture is χορόν, “company,” for χῶρόν and φίλων, “friends,” for φύλλων, yielding a company of friends accomplished in every art; this conjecture has not been substituted into the translation.
source_issues.proposed_reading: καὶ διὰ παντὸς χορόν τινα περὶ ἑαυτὸν κεκτημένος παμμούσων φίλων

lexical_decisions.chosen: the heat is blazing fiercely
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιφλέγω presents the heat as burning or blazing upon them, and σφόδρα supplies the intensity.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a short distance from the city
lexical_decisions.rationale: The accusative βραχύ expresses a small extent of distance.

lexical_decisions.chosen: clear streams of cool spring water
lexical_decisions.rationale: νάματα denotes flowing or spring water, while ῥεύματα emphasizes its streams or currents.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a green canopy of trees of every kind
lexical_decisions.rationale: σκέπη is shelter or covering; in the garden setting, “canopy” conveys the trees’ green overhead cover.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀντὶ τῆς μελλούσης ἀξιοῦν με φωνῆς
lexical_decisions.chosen: in place of the voice that was about to make a request of me
lexical_decisions.rationale: The voice is personified as about to appeal to Clement. The wording is elliptical about the requested action, which the following clause identifies as fulfillment of the promise.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the fulfillment of the promise
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀπόδειξις literally denotes demonstration or proof; here it is the promised exposition whose delivery the listeners demand.

passages.text: There is a great difference, men of Greece, between truth and custom. Truth, when genuinely sought, is found; but a custom, whatever form it has when received, whether true or false, is uncritically reinforced by itself. The person who has received it neither delights in it because it is true nor is distressed because it is false. For such a person has believed not through judgment but through preconception, entrusting his own hope, with the outcome uncertain, to the opinion of those before him. And it is not easy to strip off the ancestral garment, even if it is shown to him quite plainly to be foolish and ridiculous.

lexical_decisions.chosen: truth and custom
lexical_decisions.rationale: συνήθεια can denote familiarity, habit, or customary practice; the ensuing discussion of inherited ἔθος supports “custom.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ δὲ ἔθος, ὁποῖον ἂν παραληφθῇ
lexical_decisions.chosen: but a custom, whatever form it has when received
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves both the indefinite quality of ὁποῖον and the idea of receiving an established custom.

lexical_decisions.chosen: is uncritically reinforced by itself
lexical_decisions.rationale: The reflexive agent is retained rather than assigning the reinforcement to an unstated external authority.

lexical_decisions.chosen: not through judgment but through preconception
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόληψις here is a belief accepted in advance rather than a conclusion reached by critical judgment; “presupposition” or “prejudice” are possible alternatives.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the ancestral garment
lexical_decisions.rationale: The concrete clothing image of περιβολή is preserved rather than flattened to “ancestral tradition.”

passages.text: For example, then, I say that the entire education of the Greeks is a most pernicious scheme of an evil demon. Some of them introduced many gods, and these evil and subject to every passion, so that anyone wishing to do similar things might not even feel shame—shame being characteristic of a human being—since he has as his example the evil and indecent lives of the gods spoken of in myth. And by not even feeling shame, such a person does not even show hope of reorientation. Others introduced fate, the so-called nativity, contrary to which no one can experience or do anything. So this too is likewise the same as the first position. For when someone has come to believe that no one is able either to experience or to do anything contrary to nativity, he readily comes to sin—and after sinning he does not regret what he has done impiously, offering as a defense that he was forced by nativity to do these things—and, since he is unable to correct his nativity, he is not even capable of feeling shame for the ways in which he sins.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν πᾶσαν Ἑλλήνων παιδείαν κακοῦ δαίμονος χαλεπωτάτην ὑπόθεσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the entire education of the Greeks is a most pernicious scheme of an evil demon
lexical_decisions.rationale: παιδεία denotes the Greek system of education or culture, while ὑπόθεσις here is understood as an underlying scheme or design; “most grievous undertaking” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: subject to every passion
lexical_decisions.rationale: The word characterizes the gods as undergoing or being governed by every kind of passion, not merely as suffering greatly.

lexical_decisions.chosen: shame being characteristic of a human being
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὅπερ is taken as referring to the immediately relevant act of feeling shame; reference to the broader preceding clause is grammatically possible but less fitting in context.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ δὲ μηδὲ αἰδεῖσθαι οὐδὲ ἐλπίδα μετανοίας ὁ τοιοῦτος ἐμφαίνει
lexical_decisions.chosen: And by not even feeling shame, such a person does not even show hope of reorientation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The paired μηδέ and οὐδέ are represented by the repeated “not even.” μετάνοια denotes prospective moral redirection here; the traditional alternative is “repentance,” and no Godward destination is added because the clause does not specify one.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the so-called nativity
lexical_decisions.rationale: In this argument γένεσις is the astrologically determined condition associated with one’s birth, not simply the event of birth; “birth-destiny” is an explanatory alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: παρ’ ἣν μηδένα πάσχειν τι ἢ ποιεῖν δύνασθαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: contrary to which no one can experience or do anything
lexical_decisions.rationale: παρά with the accusative is read as “contrary to” or “outside the determination of”; “apart from which” is a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: since he is unable to correct his nativity
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατορθόω can mean set right, correct, or successfully master. “Correct” preserves the text’s deliberately impossible task without replacing it with an explanatory paraphrase.

passages.text: Others propose a motion devoid of providence, as though all things revolved spontaneously, with no master presiding over them. To think this way about these matters, as we have said, is in fact the most pernicious of all beliefs. For, as though there were no one presiding, exercising providence, and assigning to each person what is deserved, someone will readily do everything he can because of his lack of fear. Hence those who think such things are not easily—or perhaps not at all—brought to self-restraint, for they do not foresee the danger that would turn them back. But the teaching of the barbarian Jews, as you call them, is most pious, proposing one Father and Creator of this universe, good and just by nature: good, in that he forgives the sins of those who regret them; and just, in that after the reorientation he proceeds against each person according to what the things done deserve.

source_issues.issue: The image-checked printed period after ὡς interrupts a construction in which ὡς appears to introduce the following description. The translation provisionally treats the stop as editorial punctuation rather than as the end of an independent sentence.

source_issues.source_quote: ταῦτα δὲ οὕτω νομίζειν, ὡς εἰρήκαμεν, πασῶν δοξῶν τυγχάνει οὖσα χαλεπωτάτη
source_issues.issue: The feminine forms οὖσα χαλεπωτάτη do not formally agree with the neuter infinitival clause ταῦτα ... νομίζειν. The sentence remains intelligible as an anacoluthon or as attraction to an understood feminine δόξα, “belief,” but no unique grammatical repair is certain.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a motion devoid of providence
lexical_decisions.rationale: φορά can denote motion, course, or movement; the following description of everything revolving spontaneously favors cosmic “motion.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: because of his lack of fear
lexical_decisions.rationale: This avoids the potentially positive connotations of English “fearlessness” and expresses the absence of deterrent fear intended by the argument.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the danger that would turn them back
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιστρέφοντα is taken transitively, with the affected persons understood. “The returning danger” or “the danger coming back upon them” is also grammatically possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he forgives the sins of those who regret them
lexical_decisions.rationale: χαρίζομαι with sins means freely remit or forgive them. μεταμέλομαι is rendered with regret rather than the distinct reorientation terminology used for μετάνοια.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after the reorientation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The temporal force of μετά is retained, even though this wording creates tension with the preceding statement about forgiveness. Alternatives include “after the change of mind” and the traditional “after repentance”; it is not rewritten as “if there is no reorientation.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἑκάστῳ ... κατ’ ἀξίαν τῶν πεπραγμένων ἐπεξιόντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: he proceeds against each person according to what the things done deserve
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπεξέρχομαι with the dative can mean proceed against, pursue, or call someone to account. “Proceeds against” retains its judicial and potentially punitive force without supplying a different verb such as “reward.”

passages.text: This teaching, even if it happens to be a myth, would nevertheless, since it is at least pious, not be unprofitable for life. For each person, in expectation of being judged by the all-seeing God, receives a stronger impulse toward self-restraint. And if the teaching should also be true, it has delivered the one who has lived with self-restraint from eternal punishment and has additionally benefited him through the everlasting and ineffable good things provided by God.

source_issues.issue: The image-checked printed period separates the passive infinitive κριθήσεσθαι from its apparent agent phrase ὑπὸ τοῦ παντεπόπτου θεοῦ. The syntax supports construing them together, so the translation provisionally does not reproduce the disruptive stop.

lexical_decisions.chosen: this teaching
lexical_decisions.rationale: λόγος here denotes the religious account or doctrine described in the preceding section, not merely a spoken word.

lexical_decisions.chosen: since it is at least pious
lexical_decisions.rationale: γε gives concessive emphasis: even if the teaching were a myth, its pious character would still make it beneficial.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the all-seeing God
lexical_decisions.rationale: παντεπόπτης describes one who observes everything; “all-observing God” is a close alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: toward self-restraint
lexical_decisions.rationale: σωφρονεῖν here concerns morally disciplined conduct. “Sound-mindedness” or “temperance” would preserve other aspects of the term.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: προσευεργέτηκεν δὲ τοῖς ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ ἀιδίοις τε καὶ ἀπορρήτοις γιγνομένοις ἀγαθοῖς
lexical_decisions.chosen: has additionally benefited him through the everlasting and ineffable good things provided by God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative τοῖς ... ἀγαθοῖς is taken instrumentally, and the beneficiary is supplied from the preceding τὸν σωφρόνως βεβιωκότα. “Has further bestowed benefit on him with” is a more formal alternative.

passages.text: Nevertheless, I return to the first belief of the Greeks, the one that tells the myth that there are many gods subject to every passion. And so that I may not spend much time on settled matters by setting out the impious deeds of each of the so-called gods, I would not, for my part, recount all their love affairs: those of Zeus and Poseidon, Pluto and Apollo, Dionysus and Heracles, and of every one of them individually. Not even you yourselves are ignorant of their lives, since you proceed from a Greek education—the lives in which you were instructed so that, as emulators of the gods, you might do similar things,

source_issues.issue: The image-checked printed reading πράττοτε is morphologically unexpected in this ἵνα purpose clause and is not the regular subjunctive or optative form ordinarily anticipated here. The intended action remains contextually defensible from ἵνα, the πράττ- stem, and the surrounding syntax, but whether the printed form is a typographical irregularity and what correction, if any, should be adopted remain uncertain.

source_issues.source_quote: ἵνα ὡς ζηλωταὶ τῶν θεῶν τὰ ὅμοια πράττοτε,
source_issues.issue: The selected section ends with a printed comma and therefore closes while the larger sentence or rhetorical sequence is still continuing. The English retains an open-ended close and supplies no continuation from outside the requested passage.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the first belief of the Greeks
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρωτίστην is read contextually as the first position previously listed, namely belief in many gods. “Foremost belief” or “earliest belief” is also lexically possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν πολλοὺς καὶ παντοπαθεῖς θεοὺς εἶναι μυθολογοῦσαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the one that tells the myth that there are many gods subject to every passion
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle μυθολογοῦσαν characterizes the belief as narrating or asserting through myth, while παντοπαθεῖς retains the gods’ subjection to every passion.

lexical_decisions.chosen: on settled matters
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀσφαλής here describes matters treated as certain or already established, not physically safe things.

lexical_decisions.chosen: all their love affairs
lexical_decisions.rationale: In the context of the gods’ indecent lives, ἔρωτες denotes their erotic involvements rather than love in a general sense.

lexical_decisions.chosen: since you proceed from a Greek education
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὁρμάομαι ἐκ marks one’s starting point or basis. “Being grounded in Greek education” is a smoother alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the lives in which you were instructed
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compressed construction can describe lives or ways of life received as the content of education. Alternatives include “the lives you were taught” and “the ways of life in which you were trained.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἵνα ὡς ζηλωταὶ τῶν θεῶν τὰ ὅμοια πράττοτε
lexical_decisions.chosen: so that, as emulators of the gods, you might do similar things
lexical_decisions.rationale: The purpose force comes from ἵνα, while the recognizable πράττ- stem supplies the action. The modal “might” expresses the purpose clause without claiming that the irregular printed πράττοτε is a regular subjunctive or optative form.

passages.text: I will begin with Zeus himself, the most royal of all. His father Cronus, by swallowing his own children, as you say, and harvesting the private parts of his father Uranus with an adamantine sickle, showed those zealous for the gods' mysteries the pattern of reverence toward parents and love toward children. Zeus himself bound his own father and imprisoned him in Tartarus, and he punishes the other gods. For those who wish to do unspeakable things, he begot Metis and swallowed her. Metis was semen, for it is impossible to swallow an infant. To provide a defense for lovers of boys, he abducts Ganymede. Coming to the aid of adulterers on behalf of adultery, he himself is often found to be an adulterer. He encourages the seduction of sisters, having had relations with his sisters Hera, Demeter, and heavenly Aphrodite, whom some call Didone. For those who wish to have relations with daughters, he becomes an evil example from the myths by having had relations with Persephone. Indeed, he has committed countless acts of impiety, so that the impious might pronounce this abomination a god because of his excessive lack of self-control.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ δὲ τοῦ βασιλικωτάτου Διὸς
lexical_decisions.chosen: with Zeus himself, the most royal of all
lexical_decisions.rationale: The superlative describes Zeus as supremely kingly or royal. The rendering preserves its degree rather than replacing it with an unexpressed formal title.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῇ ἐξ ἀδάμαντος ἅρπῃ τοῦ πατρὸς Οὐρανοῦ τὰ μόρια θερίσας
lexical_decisions.chosen: harvesting the private parts of his father Uranus with an adamantine sickle
lexical_decisions.rationale: The harvesting verb and sickle image are retained, while private parts follows the source's euphemistic noun in this context. Adamant denotes the mythic hard material; steel or diamond would be more specific than the supplied wording.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῖς τὰ μυστικὰ τῶν θεῶν ζηλοῦσιν τὸν ὑπογραμμὸν ἔδειξεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: showed those zealous for the gods' mysteries the pattern
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun can denote mysteries, secret rites, or secret practices, and the verb can express zeal for or emulation of them. The main text retains the mysteries language without deciding whether specific initiation rites are intended. The favorable-sounding pattern of filial reverence and parental love is preserved as the speaker's irony, not replaced by an explanatory moral label.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῖς δὲ ἀρρητουργεῖν θέλουσιν τὴν Μῆτιν γεννήσας κατέπιεν· ἦν δὲ ἡ Μῆτις γονή· βρέφος γὰρ καταπιεῖν ἀδύνατον
lexical_decisions.chosen: For those who wish to do unspeakable things, he begot Metis and swallowed her. Metis was semen, for it is impossible to swallow an infant
lexical_decisions.rationale: The active participle explicitly says begot, not impregnated. Γονή can refer to reproductive seed, generation, or offspring; semen best fits the stated contrast with an infant and the surrounding accusation. This preserves the ancient speaker's explanation without substituting a more familiar myth or adding physical detail.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὲρ δὲ ἀπολογίας παιδεραστῶν Γανυμήδην ἁρπάζει
lexical_decisions.chosen: To provide a defense for lovers of boys, he abducts Ganymede
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase states the apologetic purpose attributed to the mythic act. Lovers of boys renders the historical sexual category without embellishment, and abducts retains the force of seizing or carrying off.

lexical_decisions.chosen: He encourages the seduction of sisters, having had relations with his sisters
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compound verb carries a morally condemnatory sexual sense, while the participle supplies Zeus's own conduct as the inducement. Sexual corruption of sisters is a more literal alternative; the rendering does not specify coercion where the verb alone does not establish it.

lexical_decisions.chosen: whom some call Didone
lexical_decisions.rationale: The printed name is transliterated as Didone. It is not silently changed to Dione or equated with Dido on the basis of a more familiar name.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἵν’ ὑπὸ τῶν δυσσεβῶν διὰ τὴν ὑπερβάλλουσαν ἀκρασίαν θεὸς εἶναι τὸ μύσος δογματισθῇ
lexical_decisions.chosen: so that the impious might pronounce this abomination a god because of his excessive lack of self-control
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contemptuous neuter noun calls Zeus an abomination. The purpose construction and the stated reason for treating him as divine are retained as the speaker's polemical claim, rather than recast as a neutral statement about Greek belief.

passages.text: You might reasonably be moderately indignant with the uneducated over such beliefs. But as for those whose starting point is education, what does one even need to say? Some of them claim to be grammarians and sophists and affirm that such acts are worthy of gods. For, lacking self-control themselves, they seize on this mythical pretext and are bold in committing indecent acts, supposedly imitating those superior to them.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἰδιώταις ἔχοις περὶ τῶν τοιούτων ὑπολήψεων ἀγανακτεῖν μετρίως εὔλογον
lexical_decisions.chosen: You might reasonably be moderately indignant with the uneducated over such beliefs
lexical_decisions.rationale: The potential expression is retained. The main text attaches moderately to be indignant, giving restrained indignation in the contrast between uneducated and educated people. A material alternative attaches μετρίως to εὔλογον: You might be moderately justified in being indignant with the uneducated over such beliefs. That limits the justification rather than the intensity of indignation. Ἰδιῶται can mean ordinary people or non-specialists; uneducated follows the contrast without implying low intelligence.

lexical_decisions.chosen: claim to be grammarians and sophists
lexical_decisions.rationale: The claim to professional learned status is retained. Grammarians here are literary-language scholars as well as teachers of grammar; sophists denotes the historical learned profession rather than simply deceptive arguers.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰς τοιαύτας πράξεις θεῶν ἀξίας. εἶναι βεβαιοῦσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: affirm that such acts are worthy of gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: The infinitive construction is read across the printed punctuation: acts is the subject of being worthy, and affirm is the governing verb. No surviving wording is omitted or a missing clause supplied.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς δὴ μιμηταὶ τῶν κρειττόνων ἄσεμνα διαπραττόμενοι παρρησιάζονται
lexical_decisions.chosen: are bold in committing indecent acts, supposedly imitating those superior to them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb expresses confident openness or boldness, here accompanying conduct. Speak freely is a more speech-specific alternative. The qualification supposedly reflects ὡς δή, and the superior beings are not renamed in the main text where this clause leaves them implicit.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῖς δὲ ἐκ παιδείας ὁρμωμένοις τί δεῖ καὶ λέγειν;
lexical_decisions.chosen: But as for those whose starting point is education, what does one even need to say?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rhetorical question preserves δεῖ as need or necessity rather than ability. The preceding contrast with the uneducated remains explicit. What must one even say is a more compact alternative; the chosen wording retains the question about what needs saying without replacing it with what can be said.

passages.text: For this reason, those who live in the countryside sin much less than they do. They have not been wickedly instructed through the things used to instruct those who dare such deeds, who learned from a bad education to act impiously. For those who learn their letters through such myths from childhood, while their souls are still tender, ingrain the impious deeds of the so-called gods in their own minds. As a result, when they grow older, these deeds bear fruit like bad seeds sown in the soul. Worst of all, these deeply rooted acts of impiety cannot even be cut out easily when, as grown men, they recognize them as harmful. For everyone delights in remaining in the things to which they have been accustomed from childhood. Thus, since habit has almost as much power as nature, it becomes hard for them to change toward the good things that were not sown in their souls from the beginning.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκ εἰσηγμένοι πονηρῶς δι’ ὧν εἰσήχθησαν οἱ ταῦτα τολμῶντες, ἐκ παιδείας κακῆς ἀσεβεῖν μεμαθηκότες
lexical_decisions.chosen: They have not been wickedly instructed through the things used to instruct those who dare such deeds, who learned from a bad education to act impiously
lexical_decisions.rationale: The countryside dwellers are contrasted with those who dare the acts, and the final learned participle describes the latter. The repeated verb of introduction is rendered consistently as instruction; initiation is possible, but need not imply formal mystery initiation in this educational context.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰς τῶν λεγομένων θεῶν ἀσεβεῖς πράξεις εἰς τὸν αὑτῶν συνφύουσι νοῦν
lexical_decisions.chosen: ingrain the impious deeds of the so-called gods in their own minds
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb depicts the deeds growing together with or into the learner's mind. Ingrain conveys deep incorporation, while the following English retains the explicit seed, fruit, and root images. A more literal alternative is cause the deeds to grow into their own minds.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅθεν ἐπαυξηθείσης τῆς ἡλικίας ὡς κακὰ σπέρματα καταβληθέντα τῇ ψυχῇ τελεσφοροῦσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: As a result, when they grow older, these deeds bear fruit like bad seeds sown in the soul
lexical_decisions.rationale: The preceding impious deeds supply the contextually inferred subject of bear fruit, with seeds as the explicit comparison. The learners' increasing age is retained. An alternative foregrounds the learners as producing the fruit, but the seed comparison favors the ingrained deeds as what comes to fruition.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁπόταν ἀνδρωθεῖσιν αὐτοῖς χαλεπὰ εἶναι νοῆται
lexical_decisions.chosen: when, as grown men, they recognize them as harmful
lexical_decisions.rationale: The impious practices remain the things recognized, and the grown men the persons doing the recognizing. Grievous or troublesome is a material alternative to harmful for χαλεπά. The main rendering does not turn this into recognition merely that uprooting the practices is difficult.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς συνηθείας οὐ πολὺ ἔλαττον πρὸς τὴν φύσιν δυναμένης
lexical_decisions.chosen: since habit has almost as much power as nature
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source says habit's power is not much less than nature's, rather than identical to it or greater. Almost as much preserves that comparison in accessible English.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δυσμετάβλητοι γίνονται πρὸς τὰ μὴ ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς αὐτοῖς καταβληθέντα τῇ ψυχῇ καλά
lexical_decisions.chosen: it becomes hard for them to change toward the good things that were not sown in their souls from the beginning
lexical_decisions.rationale: Their resistance concerns a change toward goods not planted from the outset. The rendering retains the direction of change and the planting image without claiming that such change is impossible.

passages.text: Therefore, young people should not be trained in corrupting lessons, and those in their prime should carefully refrain from listening to Greek mythology. For their teachings are far worse than ignorance, as we demonstrated from those who live in the countryside, who sin less because they have not been educated in Greek teachings. One must therefore avoid their myths of this kind, their theaters, and their books—if only it were possible, their cities too. For they are full of evil teachings and breathe what is like a frenzy upon their associates; they pass on to those nearby what they themselves have suffered. Worst of all, whoever has received more education among them has strayed far from thinking in accordance with nature.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοὺς ἐπὶ τῆς ἀκμῆς ὄντας ἐπιμελῶς ὑποστέλλεσθαι τῆς Ἑλλήνων ἐπακούειν μυθολογίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: those in their prime should carefully refrain from listening to Greek mythology
lexical_decisions.rationale: Those at their prime are distinguished from the young people just mentioned. Refrain preserves the caution or withdrawal expressed by the middle verb without adding an external enforcer or extending the statement to all Greek learning.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἴθε δυνατὸν ἦν καὶ τὰς πόλεις
lexical_decisions.chosen: if only it were possible, their cities too
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase is a wish that avoiding even the cities were possible, not an unqualified claim that it is possible. Avoid is understood from the preceding obligation and is not repeated in Greek.

lexical_decisions.chosen: breathe what is like a frenzy upon their associates
lexical_decisions.rationale: The breath and contagion-like comparison are retained. Λύσσα can mean raging madness or rabies; frenzy avoids specifying a medical condition, while what is like preserves ὥσπερ rather than making the comparison a literal diagnosis.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅστις παρ’ αὐτοῖς πλεῖον πεπαίδευται, πολλῷ τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν οὗτος φρονεῖν ἐκτέτραπται
lexical_decisions.chosen: whoever has received more education among them has strayed far from thinking in accordance with nature
lexical_decisions.rationale: The greater extent of education and the great extent of deviation are both retained, without turning them into a precise proportional scale. The measure is the speaker's thinking in accordance with nature, not an added claim about a particular modern concept of normality.

passages.text: Some among them, even claiming to be philosophers, treat such sins as morally indifferent and call those who are angry at such acts foolish. For, they say, such things are not sins by nature: they were prohibited by laws enacted by the wise men who lived in the beginning because those men knew that people, with their easily swayed souls, are greatly distressed over such things and start wars against one another. For these reasons, the wise men established a law and prohibited such acts as sins. But it is ridiculous to think this way. For how are things that cause disturbances, murders, and every kind of turmoil not sins? Do not defrauding people of their livelihoods, the ruin of households, sorcery, deceit, hardship, and many other evils arise from adultery?

lexical_decisions.chosen: treat such sins as morally indifferent
lexical_decisions.rationale: Indifferent is used in the philosophical sense of neither morally good nor morally bad, not a lack of emotional interest. The speaker's own description of the acts as sins is retained even though the reported philosophers deny that description by nature.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ γὰρ ἔστιν (φασί) τὰ τοιαῦτα τῇ φύσει ἁμαρτήματα, ὅσα θετοῖς ἀπηγόρευται νόμοις ὑπὸ τῶν κατ’ ἀρχὰς γενομένων σοφῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: For, they say, such things are not sins by nature: they were prohibited by laws enacted by the wise men who lived in the beginning
lexical_decisions.rationale: The relative description identifies the acts prohibited by established law, contrasting enacted law with nature. The colon divides the long construction for English readability without changing the prohibition into a natural one. Those in the beginning is retained without specifying a historical period or identifying particular lawmakers.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εὐριπίστῳ ψυχῇ ἐπὶ τοῖς τοιούτοις μεγάλως ἀχθόμενοι πρὸς ἀλλήλους πόλεμον αἴρονται
lexical_decisions.chosen: with their easily swayed souls, are greatly distressed over such things and start wars against one another
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective describes a soul readily tossed or shifted about; fickle or unstable are material alternatives. The rendering preserves both the strong distress and the resulting interpersonal warfare rather than treating the claim as merely disagreement.

lexical_decisions.chosen: defrauding people of their livelihoods
lexical_decisions.rationale: Βίος can denote livelihood or property as well as life, and περιγραφή can denote fraudulent deprivation. The economic sense fits the ensuing household ruin and hardship. Cutting short of lives or loss of property are material alternatives if life or possessions, respectively, are foregrounded. The main text does not add a specific legal or financial mechanism.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the ruin of households, sorcery, deceit, hardship
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source lists the overturning of households, magical practices, deception, and want or difficulty. Hardship preserves the breadth of ἀπορίαι rather than restricting it to financial destitution; household ruin preserves the destructive force of ἀναστάσεις.

passages.text: “But why,” he says, “if a man does not know that his own wife is committing adultery, does he not become jealous, grow angry, cause an uproar, or wage war? Thus such things are not evils by nature; rather, irrational human opinion makes them terrible.” But I say that, even if these terrible things do not happen, it is possible for the wife, through her intimacy with the adulterer, either to abandon her husband, or, even while living with him, to plot against him, or to give the adulterer what her husband acquired through toil. And while her husband is away, she may conceive by the adulterer and, because she is ashamed of being exposed, wish to destroy what is in her womb and become a child-killer, or, while destroying it, perish along with it. But if she conceives by an adulterer while her husband is living with her and then gives birth, the child, once reared, does not know his father but takes the man who is not his father to be his father. And so, when the man who is not his father dies, he leaves his own estate to someone else’s child. And how many other evils naturally tend to spring from adultery! We do not know the hidden things belonging to these evils. For just as a rabid dog kills those whom it touches by transmitting its utterly unseen rabies, so also the hidden evil of adultery, even when it remains unknown, brings about the severing of succession.

source_issues.issue: The printed form has unassimilated συν- before φ. It remains intelligible as an orthographic form of the compound meaning “to be destroyed together,” so no content is uncertain.

The prefixed hyphen is present in the supplied image-checked reading but has no evident syntactic or morphological function. It is provisionally treated as a typographical feature rather than as part of the noun.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κἂν μὴ τὰ δεινὰ ταῦτα συμβαίνῃ
lexical_decisions.chosen: even if these terrible things do not happen
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase may refer particularly to the husband’s jealousy, anger, uproar, and conflict, or more generally to the harmful consequences just discussed; the English preserves that breadth.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through her intimacy with the adulterer
lexical_decisions.rationale: συνήθεια can denote familiarity, association, or intimacy; the adulterous context supports “intimacy,” while the wife remains the understood subject of the following infinitives.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to destroy what is in her womb
lexical_decisions.rationale: The idiom τὸ κατὰ γαστρός denotes what is in the womb. “Destroy” preserves φθείρω without replacing the author’s wording with a modern technical term.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he leaves his own estate
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here βίος most naturally means one’s means of living or property left at death, rather than biological life; “livelihood” or “possessions” are possible alternatives.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the severing of succession
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαδοχή may denote succession, inheritance, or continuation of a family line. The context of misidentified paternity and inheritance favors “succession” while leaving the precise dimension open.

passages.text: But let that now be passed over by us. This, however, we all know: as a rule, men are uncontrollably indignant over it; wars have been stirred up over it, households have been overthrown, cities have been captured, and countless other things have occurred. For this reason I took refuge with the Jews’ holy God and their law, having placed my confidence in the firm judgment that, from God’s just judgment, both law has been laid down and the soul, wherever it may be, certainly receives what its deeds deserve.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as a rule
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression indicates what happens generally or for the most part, not an exceptionless claim.

lexical_decisions.chosen: are uncontrollably indignant
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀνεπισχέτως conveys lack of restraint, while δυσχεραίνω can mean to be displeased, distressed, or indignant; the ensuing wars and destruction support the stronger contextual wording.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀποδεδωκὼς τὴν πίστιν ἀσφαλεῖ τῇ κρίσει
lexical_decisions.chosen: having placed my confidence in the firm judgment
lexical_decisions.rationale: πίστις here denotes confidence or credence given to a conclusion. An alternative is “having entrusted my faith to the sure judgment,” but that can suggest a more technical religious use than the construction requires.

lexical_decisions.chosen: what its deeds deserve
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally, the soul receives “what is according to the worth of the things it did”; the rendering expresses proportionate recompense without specifying reward or punishment beyond the Greek.

passages.text:
After I said this, Appion added to the argument, saying, “What then? Do not the laws of the Greeks also forbid base acts and punish adulterers?”

I said, “Then the gods of the Greeks, since they have acted contrary to the laws, owe a penalty. Moreover, how will I be able to discipline myself if I suppose that the gods themselves were the first to commit every grievous act along with adultery and have paid no penalty, although they owe it all the more for this very reason, since they are not enslaved to desire? But if they were subject to it, how could they be gods?”

Appion said, “Then let our objects of attention no longer be gods, but the judges; with our eyes on them, we will be afraid to sin.”

I replied, “The cases are not alike, Appion. A person who keeps a human being in view will dare to sin in the hope of escaping notice. But one who has settled in his own mind that God sees everything, knowing that he cannot escape God’s notice, will refrain even from sinning in secret.”

source_issues.issue: The image-checked edition prints a middle dot between πῶς and the postpositive δέ. That punctuation interrupts what is otherwise a coherent question, so the translation provisionally construes the words together without altering the supplied Greek wording.

lexical_decisions.chosen: added to the argument
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression means to bring or add something to the ongoing discourse; “responded to the argument” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they owe it all the more for this very reason
lexical_decisions.rationale: ταύτῃ points forward to their not being enslaved to desire: freedom from compulsion makes the gods, on the speaker’s reasoning, more accountable.

lexical_decisions.chosen: let our objects of attention be
lexical_decisions.rationale: σκοποί can mean goals, marks, or objects kept in view. The following εἰς οὓς ἀφορῶντες supports the visual and exemplary sense rather than “goals” alone.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: θεὸν παντεπόπτην τῇ ἑαυτοῦ ψυχῇ ὁρισάμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: one who has settled in his own mind that God sees everything
lexical_decisions.rationale: The construction can be rendered more formally as “one who has defined God in his soul as all-seeing.” The chosen wording gives a defensible modern English expression of the internal conviction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: will refrain even from sinning in secret
lexical_decisions.rationale: παραιτέομαι here means to decline, avoid, or refrain from an action; καί adds the force “even” in context.

passages.text:
When Appion heard this, he said, “Ever since I heard that you were associating with Jews, I knew that your outlook had changed. For someone has aptly said, ‘Bad associations corrupt good character.’”

I replied, “Then good associations correct worthless character.”

Appion said, “Today I had fully resolved to ascertain your position; that is why we allowed you to speak first. But tomorrow—here, if it pleases you—when the same friends have assembled, I will demonstrate that our gods are neither adulterers nor murderers nor destroyers of children, and that they did not have sexual relations with sisters or daughters. Rather, the ancients, wishing only lovers of learning to know the mysteries, veiled them in myths of the kind you have described. For in their account of nature they say that Zeus is the boiling substance, Cronus is time, and Rhea is the ever-flowing nature of water. Nevertheless, as I promised, tomorrow at dawn, when you have assembled, I will interpret each particular form allegorically and reveal to you the truth about what exists.”

In response I said, “Tomorrow do just as you have promised. But now, beginning from this point, listen also to what bears on the very things you are going to say.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: your outlook had changed
lexical_decisions.rationale: γνώμη can denote mind, judgment, opinion, or outlook. The passive ἠλλοιῶσθαι indicates that it had been altered.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Bad associations corrupt good character
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὁμιλίαι denotes associations or company, and ἤθη denotes habits, morals, or character. The wording preserves the maxim and its reversal in the next sentence without making a familiar rendering from another work controlling.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Σήμερον πεπληροφορήμην τὴν σὴν ἐπιγνῶναι ἔνστασιν, διὸ σοὶ πρώτῳ εἰπεῖν συνεχωρήσαμεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Today I had fully resolved to ascertain your position; that is why we allowed you to speak first
lexical_decisions.rationale: The pluperfect πεπληροφορήμην places the settled resolve before the permission expressed by συνεχωρήσαμεν, while ἐπιγνῶναι can denote learning or ascertaining the position. This sequence favors a prospective reading: Appion had resolved to ascertain the position and therefore let the other speaker go first. A materially possible alternative is “Today I had become fully assured that I understood your objection,” taking πεπληροφορήμην as achieved assurance and ἐπιγνῶναι as recognition already attained; ἔνστασις may mean “objection,” “position,” or “contention.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: destroyers of children
lexical_decisions.rationale: φθορεύς can denote a destroyer or corrupter. In a list with adultery and murder and in the context of myths about the gods, “destroyers” is the more direct choice, though “corrupters of children” is lexically possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they did not have sexual relations with sisters or daughters
lexical_decisions.rationale: πλησιάζω literally means to approach or associate closely, but with these dative objects and the surrounding accusations of sexual misconduct it has a sexual sense.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ζῆνα γὰρ τὴν ζέουσαν οὐσίαν εἶναι φυσιολογοῦσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: in their account of nature they say that Zeus is the boiling substance
lexical_decisions.rationale: φυσιολογοῦσιν introduces a natural-philosophical explanation. The Greek also makes an etymological sound association between Ζῆνα and ζέουσαν that cannot be reproduced naturally in English.

lexical_decisions.chosen: each particular form
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase may refer to each divine figure, each mythic form, or each individual feature of the allegory. “Form” preserves the expression without selecting one referent too narrowly.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐντεῦθεν καὶ πρὸς αὐτὰ ἃ μέλλεις λέγειν, ἄκουσον
lexical_decisions.chosen: beginning from this point, listen also to what bears on the very things you are going to say
lexical_decisions.rationale: The Greek elliptically commands Appion to hear something directed toward or bearing upon his forthcoming claims. “Listen to a reply to the very things you are going to say” is another possible way to supply the English relation.

passages.text:
If the deeds of the gods, though good, were veiled in evil myths, great wickedness is revealed in the one who covered them, because he hid honorable things beneath evil narratives so that no one might become an imitator of them. But if they truly committed impious acts, those acts should instead have been covered with good narratives, so that people, looking up to them as their superiors, would not attempt sins like theirs.

After I said this, those present were plainly beginning to feel love for the arguments I had made. Indeed, after repeatedly and earnestly urging me to come without fail on the following day, they departed.

source_issues.source_quote: τῆς πρὸς τοὺς ὑπ’ ἐμοῦ λεχθέντας λόγους · ἀγάπης
source_issues.issue: The image-checked edition prints a middle dot between λόγους and ἀγάπης, although the surrounding words support the continuous genitive construction “love for the arguments spoken by me.” The translation provisionally adopts that defensible syntax while preserving disclosure of the printed punctuation.
source_issues.proposed_reading: τῆς πρὸς τοὺς ὑπ’ ἐμοῦ λεχθέντας λόγους ἀγάπης

lexical_decisions.chosen: great wickedness is revealed in the one who covered them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive identifies the person responsible for concealing the deeds; “is demonstrated on the part of the one who covered them” is a more formal alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: honorable things
lexical_decisions.rationale: σεμνός can mean venerable, august, solemn, or honorable. Here it describes supposedly good divine deeds that would merit imitation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those acts should instead have been covered with good narratives
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπισκέπειν is understood here in the sense of covering over, corresponding to the earlier language of veiling. The substantival ἀγαθοῖς takes its contextual content from the preceding “myths” and “narratives.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: looking up to them as their superiors
lexical_decisions.rationale: κρείττονας may mean those who are better, stronger, or superior. The gods function here as supposedly higher examples whom humans observe and imitate.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀρχὴν λαμβάνοντες τῆς πρὸς τοὺς ὑπ’ ἐμοῦ λεχθέντας λόγους · ἀγάπης
lexical_decisions.chosen: beginning to feel love for the arguments I had made
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀρχὴν λαμβάνειν with the genitive means to make a beginning of something. λόγοι may be words, statements, or arguments; the argumentative setting favors “arguments,” while the printed middle dot is provisionally treated as editorial punctuation that does not prevent ἀγάπης from completing the construction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: me to come without fail on the following day
lexical_decisions.rationale: πάντως expresses insistence that the visit occur in any event or by all means.

passages.text: So, on the following day in Tyre, I went to the quiet place as we had arranged. After seeing and greeting the others, together with some additional people, but not seeing Appion, I asked why he was not present. Someone said that he had been physically unwell since that very evening. When I said that it was reasonable for us to set out immediately and visit him, almost everyone requested that I first hold a discussion with them and that then, in that way, I would be able to visit him as well. Once everyone had come to a single decision, I began to speak:

source_issues.issue: The main rendering analyzes κἀκεῖνον as the object of ἐπισκέψασθαι and αὐτόν as the accusative subject of δύνασθαι, contextually referring to Clement with a shift from the preceding first-person με to the participants’ third-person perspective. Alternatively, κἀκεῖνον and αὐτόν may be understood as an emphatic or resumptive double reference to Appion, yielding the sense “visit that man himself.” The construction is unusual but does not require deleting either accusative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δυσαρρώστως αὐτὸν ἀπ’ αὐτῆς ἑσπέρας ἐσχηκέναι τὸ σωμάτιον
lexical_decisions.chosen: he had been physically unwell since that very evening
lexical_decisions.rationale: The idiom describes the poor condition of his body. The diminutive σωμάτιον need not imply literal smallness and is represented naturally by “physically,” while “that very evening” preserves the intensive force of αὐτῆς.

lexical_decisions.chosen: that I first hold a discussion with them
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαλέγομαι can mean converse, discourse, or debate; “hold a discussion” suits the requested address without predetermining its degree of formality.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἶθ’ οὕτως κἀκεῖνον ἐπισκέψασθαι δύνασθαι αὐτόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: and that then, in that way, I would be able to visit him as well
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering takes κἀκεῖνον as the object of ἐπισκέψασθαι and αὐτόν as the accusative subject of δύνασθαι, referring to Clement from the participants’ perspective. English naturally returns that third-person reference to the narrator’s first person.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Once everyone had come to a single decision
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally, “when one opinion of all had come about”; the rendering expresses their resulting unanimity.

passages.text: “Yesterday, when I left this place, friends, I admit that I could not get to sleep, because I was deeply preoccupied with the discussion that was going to take place with Appion. As I lay awake, the stratagems I had devised against him in Rome rushed into my mind. They were as follows. From childhood I, Clement, had loved truth, had sought the things that matter to the soul, and had spent my time on refutations and demonstrations; but because I could find nothing definitive, under the strain of my thoughts I ran aground in illness. And indeed, while I lay ill, Appion arrived in Rome. He was a friend of my father and stayed as my guest. When he learned that I was bedridden, he came in to see me, since he was not unversed in medicine, and asked why I had taken to bed. I was well aware that the man held Jews in deep hatred—so much so that he had written many books against them—and that he had now taken Simon himself as a friend, not out of a love of learning, but because he knew him to be a Samaritan, a Jew-hater, and someone who had come forward against the Jews. For that reason he had drawn him close, so that he could learn from him something to use against the Jews—

source_issues.source_quote: ἵνα δύνατο κατὰ Ἰουδαίων τι παρ’ αὐτοῦ μανθάνειν
source_issues.issue: The form δύνατο after ἵνα is morphosyntactically unusual by classical standards but can be understood as late or nonclassical use of a past indicative in a purpose clause. The proposed optative is only a possible normalization, not the supplied reading.
source_issues.proposed_reading: ἵνα δύναιτο κατὰ Ἰουδαίων τι παρ’ αὐτοῦ μανθάνειν

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς πρὸς Ἀππίωνα μελλούσης ἔσεσθαι ζητήσεως
lexical_decisions.chosen: the discussion that was going to take place with Appion
lexical_decisions.rationale: ζήτησις can denote an inquiry, dispute, or debate. “Discussion” leaves its precise character open while the wider narrative supplies its adversarial aspect.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ ἐν Ῥώμῃ πρὸς αὐτόν μοι μεμηχανημένα
lexical_decisions.chosen: the stratagems I had devised against him in Rome
lexical_decisions.rationale: μηχανάομαι denotes contriving or devising, while πρὸς αὐτόν is contextually adversarial rather than merely relational.

lexical_decisions.chosen: on refutations and demonstrations
lexical_decisions.rationale: The paired terms denote arguments that respectively dismantle and establish a position; alternatives include “disproofs and proofs” or “negative and positive arguments.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὸ τῆς συνοίας ἐξώκειλα εἰς νόσον
lexical_decisions.chosen: under the strain of my thoughts I ran aground in illness
lexical_decisions.rationale: σύνοια can denote intense thought, anxiety, or distress arising from reflection. The rendering “strain of my thoughts” preserves that range, while “ran aground” retains the nautical image in ἐξώκειλα rather than reducing it to a generic transition into illness.

lexical_decisions.chosen: He was a friend of my father
lexical_decisions.rationale: πατρικὸς φίλος can mean a paternal or inherited family friend. The immediate first-person construction most naturally indicates a friend connected with Clement’s father.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: σαμαρέα αὐτὸν οἶδεν μισοϊουδαῖόν τε ὄντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: he knew him to be a Samaritan, a Jew-hater
lexical_decisions.rationale: The ethnic designation and the compound μισοϊουδαῖος are retained distinctly rather than treating Samaritan identity itself as equivalent to hatred of Jews.

passages.text: Knowing these things beforehand about Appion, as soon as he asked the cause of my illness, I answered in pretense, “I suffer what young men suffer, and my soul aches.” He replied, “Child, trust me as you would a father and tell me: what is the illness of your soul?” Once again I sighed in pretense, as though ashamed to speak about being in love. By my silence and by lowering my head, I gave him grounds to suspect what I wanted to suggest. Convinced that I was truly in love with a woman, he said, “There is nothing in life that cannot receive help. For when I myself was young, I fell in love with a most distinguished woman. Not only did I consider it impossible to obtain her; I did not even hope ever to address her. Nevertheless, I happened to meet an Egyptian who was highly accomplished in the practices of magicians. After he befriended me, I disclosed my passion, and he not only placed himself at my disposal for everything I wanted, but, endeavoring to be even more lavish toward me, did not begrudge teaching me also the incantation through which I obtained her. Persuaded by that secret instruction of his and by the unstinting generosity of the man who taught me, after I had succeeded once, I stopped being in love.”

source_issues.issue: The confirmed print has μὲ with a grave accent. The context provisionally supports understanding it as the pronoun με, “me,” rather than as an incomplete μέν; the proposed reading regularizes the accent but is not the supplied text.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I suffer what young men suffer
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compact expression literally refers to “the things of young men.” The rendering preserves Appion’s intended inference of youthful erotic distress without adding it directly to Clement’s words.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διά γε τῆς σιωπῆς καὶ τοῦ κάτω νεύειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: By my silence and by lowering my head
lexical_decisions.rationale: κάτω νεύειν describes the visible gesture of inclining or lowering the head, here conveying affected embarrassment.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ δὲ ἐρᾶν με γυναικὸς ἀληθῶς ἀναπεισθεὶς ἔφη
lexical_decisions.chosen: Convinced that I was truly in love with a woman, he said
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀληθῶς can qualify either ἐρᾶν (“truly in love”) or ἀναπεισθείς (“truly convinced”). The main rendering attaches it to the supposed love because Appion interprets Clement’s affected behavior as evidence of a real passion; the alternative is “Truly convinced that I was in love with a woman.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ μόνον αὐτῆς τυχεῖν ἡγούμην ἀδύνατον εἶναι, ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ προσαγορεῦσαί ποτε ἤλπιζον
lexical_decisions.chosen: Not only did I consider it impossible to obtain her; I did not even hope ever to address her
lexical_decisions.rationale: The coordinated clauses express an escalation from regarding possession of her as impossible to lacking even the hope of ever speaking to her.

lexical_decisions.chosen: highly accomplished in the practices of magicians
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀκριβόω here signifies exact mastery or thorough knowledge; τὰ μάγων denotes the matters or practices belonging to magicians.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ φιλωθεὶς ἐκφαίνω μου τὸν ἔρωτα
lexical_decisions.chosen: After he befriended me, I disclosed my passion
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive φιλωθείς can mean being loved or treated as a friend. “Befriended” fits the ensuing disclosure, while ἐκφαίνω is represented according to the sense of its vivid historical present.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the incantation through which I obtained her
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπαοιδή is a sung spell or incantation. Although the object of ἔτυχον is implicit here, the earlier αὐτῆς τυχεῖν supplies the woman as its contextual object; an alternative is “through which I succeeded.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐκ δὲ τῆς ἐκείνου λαθραίας ὑποδείξεως πεισθεὶς τῇ τοῦ διδάξαντος ἀφθονίᾳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: Persuaded by that secret instruction of his and by the unstinting generosity of the man who taught me
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative τῇ … ἀφθονίᾳ is taken instrumentally alongside ἐκ τῆς … ὑποδείξεως. An alternative is “persuaded by that secret instruction of his to trust in the teacher’s unstinting generosity.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ἅπαξ ἐπιτυχών, ἐπαυσάμην τοῦ ἔρωτος
lexical_decisions.chosen: after I had succeeded once, I stopped being in love
lexical_decisions.rationale: Placing “once” after “succeeded” explicitly preserves the numerical force of ἅπαξ rather than reducing it to a temporal conjunction meaning merely “after.”

passages.text: “Therefore, if you too have suffered something of this kind, as humans do, put your confidence in us and set your mind at ease, for within seven days I will make you obtain her without fail.” When I heard this, I kept my own purpose in view and said, “Forgive me for not fully believing that magic is real, for I have already had experience of many people making many promises and then failing to fulfill them. Still, your promise presses me and leads me to hope. Yet I am afraid when I consider whether demons may sometimes fail to obey magicians in the things they are commanded to do.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ καὶ σὺ τοιοῦτόν τι πέπονθας ἀνθρωπίνως
lexical_decisions.chosen: if you too have suffered something of this kind, as humans do
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀνθρωπίνως marks the experience as human or natural to humanity, not as morally commendable.

lexical_decisions.chosen: put your confidence in us and set your mind at ease
lexical_decisions.rationale: The text has the plural ἡμῖν, “in us,” although Appion is speaking. It may be an inclusive or self-referential plural; the translation preserves it rather than silently changing it to “me.” πρὸς τὸ ἀμέριμνον expresses the intended freedom from worry.

lexical_decisions.chosen: that magic is real
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑφίστημι in this construction concerns actual existence or reality, not merely the practice of magic.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πολλῶν γὰρ πολλὰ ἐπαγγελλομένων καὶ διαψευσαμένων ἤδη πεπείραμαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: I have already had experience of many people making many promises and then failing to fulfill them
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαψεύδομαι can denote proving false, disappointing expectations, or failing in a claim. “Failing to fulfill them” makes the relation to the promises explicit without alleging a particular motive.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δυσωπεῖ με καὶ εἰς ἐλπίδας ἄγει ἡ σὴ ὑπόσχεσις
lexical_decisions.chosen: your promise presses me and leads me to hope
lexical_decisions.rationale: δυσωπέω may mean shame, constrain, move, or win someone over. “Presses me” retains Clement’s affected reluctance without implying that he already believes Appion.

passages.text: Appion said, “Concede that I know more about these matters than you do. Yet, so that you may not think you have heard nothing from me in answer to what you said, learn how it is that demons are compelled to submit to magicians in the matters about which they receive commands. Just as it is impossible for a soldier to contradict his commander, and the commanders themselves cannot disobey a king—for if anyone contradicts those set over him, he is certainly judged deserving of punishment—so it is impossible for demons not to serve their angelic commanders. When adjured by appeal to those angels, they shudder and yield, knowing well that if they disobey, they will certainly be punished. But even the angels themselves, when magicians adjure them by the one who is superior, obey, for fear that they may be judged guilty of disobedience and perish. For if all beings that possess life and reason did not foresee the punishment coming from the superior one, confusion would have arisen, with all of them rebelling against one another.”

source_issues.issue: The confirmed edition prints a high stop after φρίττοντες. The translation provisionally reads the participle with εἴκουσιν as a continuous construction, while preserving the marked editorial break in this disclosure; no replacement wording is required for a defensible translation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ταῦτα ἐμοὶ σοῦ μᾶλλον συγχώρει εἰδέναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: Concede that I know more about these matters than you do
lexical_decisions.rationale: συγχωρέω here asks Clement to concede or grant Appion’s asserted superior knowledge, not to give Appion permission to acquire knowledge.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πῶς ἀνάγκην ἔχουσιν οἱ δαίμονες τοῖς μάγοις ὑπείκειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: how it is that demons are compelled to submit to magicians
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally, the demons “have necessity” to yield. “Are compelled” expresses the asserted necessity without introducing a distinct external agent.

lexical_decisions.chosen: their angelic commanders
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participial noun ἡγουμένοις identifies angels who lead or command the demons; the phrase need not imply that the demons possess the angels.

lexical_decisions.chosen: When adjured by appeal to those angels, they shudder and yield
lexical_decisions.rationale: In adjuration language, κατά with the genitive identifies the authority invoked. The participle φρίττοντες is rendered together with εἴκουσιν despite the printed high stop. An alternative is “being adjured by them, they yield with trembling.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κατὰ τοῦ κρείττονος ὑπὸ μάγων ὁρκιζόμενοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: when magicians adjure them by the one who is superior
lexical_decisions.rationale: κρείττων is comparative and may mean the greater, stronger, or higher-ranking one. “The one who is superior” preserves the hierarchy without identifying the referent beyond what the passage states.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the punishment coming from the superior one
lexical_decisions.rationale: δίκη can denote justice, judgment, or penalty. The repeated warnings of punishment and destruction favor “punishment” here, while κρείττων is rendered consistently with the preceding clause.

passages.text: And I said, “Then are the things said by poets and philosophers correct: that in Hades the souls of the impious, after being judged for what they dared to do, are punished—such as the souls of Ixion, Tantalus, Tityus, Sisyphus, the daughters of Danaus, and all the others who ever acted impiously here? And if these things are not so, how could magic have any reality?” When he said that matters in Hades were indeed so, I asked, “Why, then, have we ourselves not feared magic, since we are convinced of the punishment in Hades for adultery? For I do not agree that it is right to use magic to force a woman who is unwilling. But if someone promises to persuade her, I am quite ready for that and to acknowledge my gratitude as well.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: how could magic have any reality
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑφεστάναι has an existential sense here: magic could not subsist or be real if the premises about Hades were false.

lexical_decisions.chosen: have we ourselves not feared magic
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first-person plural is retained as an inclusive rhetorical question; αὐτοί adds emphasis, ‘we ourselves.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ μοιχείας πεπεισμένοι τὴν ἐν ᾅδου δίκην
lexical_decisions.chosen: since we are convinced of the punishment in Hades for adultery
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπὶ μοιχείας identifies adultery as the ground for the punishment; πεπεισμένοι governs the conviction expressed by τὴν ... δίκην.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς τοῦτο μετὰ τοῦ καὶ χάριν ὁμολογεῖν ἑτοίμως ἔχω
lexical_decisions.chosen: I am quite ready for that and to acknowledge my gratitude as well
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἑτοίμως ἔχω expresses readiness, while χάριν ὁμολογεῖν means to acknowledge gratitude or indebtedness.

passages.text: And Appion said, “Do you not think it amounts to the same thing whether you obtain her by magic or by persuading her with words?” I said, “They are not at all alike; each is far removed from the other. The man who compels an unwilling woman by magic’s force incurs the harshest punishment as one who has schemed against a chaste woman. But the man who persuades her by speech and makes his appeal depend on her own freedom and choice has used no force. Still, I think the persuader will be punished less than the man who used force. So if you can persuade her, I will be grateful if I succeed; otherwise, I would rather die than forcibly compel a woman who does not consent.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: you obtain her
