lexical_decisions.rationale: With a person as the genitive object in this erotic context, ἐπιτυγχάνω means to attain or succeed in obtaining that person.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ τῇ αὐτῆς ἐξουσίᾳ καὶ βουλῇ ποιησάμενος τὴν παράφασιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: makes his appeal depend on her own freedom and choice
lexical_decisions.rationale: παράφασις can denote an appeal, exhortation, or persuasion. The ἐπί phrase makes her own authority and will the basis on which the appeal succeeds; the defensible alternative ‘makes the persuasion subject to her own freedom and will’ preserves the same contrast with force.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἧττον δὲ οἶμαι κολασθήσεσθαι τὸν πεπεικότα τοῦ βιασαμένου
lexical_decisions.chosen: I think the persuader will be punished less than the man who used force
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive τοῦ βιασαμένου supplies the standard of comparison after ἧττον.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I will be grateful if I succeed
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally, the speaker will ‘have gratitude’ upon succeeding; English expresses this naturally as being grateful.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I would rather die than
lexical_decisions.rationale: The comparative wording is emphatic in Greek; idiomatic English expresses the preference with ‘rather ... than.’

passages.text: And Appion, genuinely at a loss, said, “What am I to say to you? At one moment, as a man tormented by love, you wish to obtain her; at another, as if you were not in love, you put fear before desire. You imagine that after persuading her you will be free from liability as though sinless, but that if you obtain her by the force of magic, you will incur punishment. Yet you fail to understand that what is judged in every action is its outcome—the fact that it happened—not how it happened. And if you commit adultery, surely you will not be judged to have acted impiously if you manage it by magic, yet be absolved of the sin involved in adultery if you persuade her.” I said, “Because I am in love, obtaining the woman I love is in any case my settled aim. I must therefore choose one of the two, and, if possible, I will choose to flatter rather than use magic. But it is not easy to persuade her even with flattery, for the woman is thoroughly a philosopher.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: genuinely at a loss
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαπορέω conveys serious perplexity or uncertainty about how to proceed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you put fear before desire
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive marks the thing over which fear is preferred; ‘prefer fear to desire’ is an equivalent alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you will be free from liability as though sinless
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀνεύθυνος means not liable or not accountable, while ὡς ἀναμάρτητος presents the supposed basis for that exemption.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ τέλος παντὸς πράγματος κρίνεται ὅτι γέγονεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: what is judged in every action is its outcome—the fact that it happened
lexical_decisions.rationale: τέλος denotes the resulting end or outcome. The following ὅτι γέγονεν clarifies that the occurrence itself, rather than its manner, is in view.

lexical_decisions.chosen: if you manage it by magic
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle δυνηθείς leaves the action implicit; the context supplies succeeding in the adultery through magic.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πάνυ γὰρ ἐστὶν ἡ γυνὴ φιλόσοφος
lexical_decisions.chosen: the woman is thoroughly a philosopher
lexical_decisions.rationale: πάνυ intensifies the predicate φιλόσοφος; ‘very much a philosopher’ is more literal but less idiomatic.

passages.text: And Appion said, “For that very reason I am more confident that I will be able to persuade her as you yourself wish, if indeed we can speak with her.” I answered, “Impossible.” Appion asked whether it was possible to write to her. I said, “That is possible.” Then Appion said, “Before this night is over, I will compose a book, an encomium to adultery. You will take it from me and send it on to her, and I hope that, once persuaded, she will consent.” Appion composed that book and gave it to me. It was about this book that I thought during this night, and at just the right time I was reminded that I had it among the other books I carry with me. After relating these things, I showed the book to those present and read it aloud when they wished to hear it. And then, after reading it, I said, “Gentlemen, this is the education of the Greeks, with a noble theme for sinning without fear.” The book ran as follows:

source_issues.issue: The confirmed printed wording has the third-person reflexive ἑαυτοῦ with the first-person verb ἐπιφέρομαι. Later Greek can extend ἑαυτοῦ beyond strict third-person reference, so the supplied wording remains intelligible as ‘with me’; the classically expected first-person reflexive would be ἐμαυτοῦ. The proposed reading is therefore only a conjectural normalization, not a correction to the selected edition.

lexical_decisions.chosen: For that very reason I am more confident
lexical_decisions.rationale: Ταύτῃ is taken causally as referring to the woman’s being a philosopher. It could more formally be rendered ‘in this respect,’ but the causal connection is contextually stronger.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Before this night is over
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔτι with the temporal dative indicates that the composition will occur while the present night still lasts; ‘this very night’ is an equivalent alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: once persuaded, she will consent
lexical_decisions.rationale: συντίθεμαι here means to agree or consent to the proposed relationship.

lexical_decisions.chosen: at just the right time I was reminded that I had it
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὐκαίρως is taken with the act of being reminded. A possible alternative attachment is ‘I was reminded that I conveniently had it,’ but the temporal reading is more natural in context.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: σὺν ἄλλοις βιβλίοις οἷς μεθ’ ἑαυτοῦ ἐπιφέρομαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: among the other books I carry with me
lexical_decisions.rationale: The relative οἷς is understood by case attraction to βιβλίοις, and the reflexive phrase is interpreted contextually with the first-person verb.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the education of the Greeks
lexical_decisions.rationale: παιδεία may also mean Greek culture or intellectual formation; ‘education’ preserves the immediate connection with the philosophical book just read.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: γενναίαν ὑπόθεσιν ἔχουσα πρὸς τὸ ἀδεῶς ἐξαμαρτάνειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: with a noble theme for sinning without fear
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording is ironic: γενναίαν calls the book’s ὑπόθεσις ‘noble,’ while the purpose or tendency expressed by πρός is fearless wrongdoing.

passages.text:
The Lover to His Beloved
(Anonymously, because of the laws originating from foolish people)

At the commands of Love—the oldest of all—for the sake of a child. I have learned that you devote yourself to philosophy and, for virtue’s sake, emulate the life of those who are superior. And who among all beings could be superior to the gods, and who among human beings could be superior to the philosophers? For philosophers alone know which actions are evil or good by nature, and which, though they are not so, are regarded as such through the enactment of laws. Take, for example, the act called adultery: some have supposed it to be evil, although it is good in every respect, for it takes place at Love’s commands for the multiplication of life. Love is the oldest of all gods. For without Love no mingling or generation can take place—of elements, of gods, of human beings, of irrational animals, or of all the remaining things. Indeed, we are all instruments of Love. But the craftsman himself, working through us and present in the souls of every being that is generated, is Mind. Consequently, it is not of our own volition that we desire to do his will, but when we are commanded by him. And if, while desiring by his will, we attempt for the sake of so-called self-control to restrain our desire, how will we not commit the greatest acts of impiety by opposing the oldest of all gods and human beings?

lexical_decisions.chosen: The Lover to His Beloved
lexical_decisions.rationale: The nominative sender and dative recipient form an epistolary heading. ἐρωμένη denotes the woman loved or desired.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀνωνύμως διὰ τοὺς ἐκ τῶν ἀνοήτων ἀνθρώπων νόμους
lexical_decisions.chosen: Anonymously, because of the laws originating from foolish people
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐκ marks the foolish people as the source of the laws; ‘because of the laws made by foolish people’ is an equivalent contextual rendering.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπιταγαῖς Ἔρωτος τοῦ πάντων πρεσβυτάτου παιδὸς χάριν
lexical_decisions.chosen: At the commands of Love—the oldest of all—for the sake of a child
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering takes Ἔρωτος with ἐπιταγαῖς, treats τοῦ πάντων πρεσβυτάτου as describing Love, and construes παιδὸς χάριν as the separate phrase ‘for the sake of a child.’ Because the compressed heading permits competing attachment, τοῦ πάντων πρεσβυτάτου παιδός could alternatively be understood together as ‘the oldest child of all,’ though that leaves the function of χάριν less clear.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τίνες δὲ ἂν εἶεν κρείττονες ἢ θεοὶ μὲν ἁπάντων, ἀνθρώπων δὲ οἱ φιλόσοφοι;
lexical_decisions.chosen: And who among all beings could be superior to the gods, and who among human beings could be superior to the philosophers?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering takes ἤ after comparative κρείττονες as ‘than’ and understands ἁπάντων and ἀνθρώπων partitively, expanding the elliptical second half to preserve the parallel rhetorical comparison. A viable alternative takes ἤ as ‘except’ or ‘other than’: ‘And who could be superior except the gods among all and the philosophers among human beings?’ Another possible construal treats the genitives comparatively, making the gods superior to all and philosophers superior to other humans.

lexical_decisions.chosen: For philosophers alone know
lexical_decisions.rationale: The demonstrative most naturally resumes the immediately preceding philosophers, who possess the claimed philosophical discernment. It could grammatically encompass both gods and philosophers, but the argument is directed to the recipient’s philosophical learning.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ποῖα δὲ τῇ τῶν νόμων θέσει (οὐκ ὄντα) νομίζεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: which, though they are not so, are regarded as such through the enactment of laws
lexical_decisions.rationale: The omitted predicate is supplied from ‘evil or good’; the parenthetical οὐκ ὄντα denies that the actions possess by nature the qualities assigned by law.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς γὰρ τὴν τοῦ βίου πολυγονίαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: for the multiplication of life
lexical_decisions.rationale: πολυγονία denotes abundant generation or production of offspring. ‘For life’s abundant procreation’ is a more literal alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: of irrational animals
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἄλογος contrasts nonhuman animals as lacking reason; ‘non-rational living creatures’ is an equivalent alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: present in the souls of every being that is generated
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιδημέω literally denotes residing, sojourning, or being present among; here it describes Mind’s presence in the souls of generated beings.

lexical_decisions.chosen: is Mind
lexical_decisions.rationale: νοῦς is capitalized because the passage identifies it as the craftsman operating through all beings; ‘intellect’ or lowercase ‘mind’ would preserve the lexical sense but less clearly convey the personified cosmic role.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ κελευσθῶμεν, τὸ ἐκείνου βούλημα
lexical_decisions.chosen: we are commanded by him ... his will
lexical_decisions.rationale: The pronouns immediately follow the identification of the craftsman as Mind, while the argument also closely identifies that craftsman with Love’s activity. The English preserves the masculine referent without forcing a sharper distinction between Love and Mind than the passage supplies.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: χάριν τῆς λεγομένης σωφροσύνης κρατεῖν τῆς ἐπιθυμίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: for the sake of so-called self-control to restrain our desire
lexical_decisions.rationale: σωφροσύνη can mean self-control, moderation, or chastity. ‘Self-control’ suits the immediately following attempt to master sexual desire, while ‘so-called chastity’ remains a viable context-specific alternative.

passages.text: But let every door be opened to him, and let all the wretched, enacted laws be dissolved, laws laid down for jealous people. Dominated by folly and unwilling to understand what is reasonable, and also looking suspiciously at the so-called adulterers, these people are reasonably made sport of by Zeus himself through Minos and Rhadamanthys, by means of enacted laws. For Love cannot be restrained once he has taken up residence in souls. The passion of lovers is not voluntary. Indeed, Zeus himself, the lawgiver of these people, had relations with countless women. Some wise men praise him as a benefactor in childbearing, granting human beings union with himself. But among those who, he knew, did not recognize him in connection with the favor, he changed his appearance, so that he would neither distress them nor seem to act against the laws he himself had established. Therefore, for the sake of a good life, you must devote yourself to philosophy and imitate those acknowledged to be superior, whose unions have been countless.

lexical_decisions.chosen: enacted
lexical_decisions.rationale: The laws are instituted or laid down, contrasting humanly established prohibition with the speaker's account of irresistible love. Arbitrary is a possible evaluative reading, but enacted does not add that judgment to the adjective itself.

lexical_decisions.chosen: are reasonably made sport of ... by means of enacted laws
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive verb describes the jealous people as being played with or mocked, not as themselves playing. The positive judgment reasonably is the letter writer's, and is not silently reversed to match the surrounding narrative's moral position.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: παρ’ οἷς δὲ ἐπὶ τῷ χάριτι ἠπίστατο ἀγνοούμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: among those who, he knew, did not recognize him in connection with the favor
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive participle describes Zeus himself as unrecognized or misunderstood, not the favor as unrecognized. The main text takes the former sense while retaining the respect in which he was unrecognized. A material alternative is among those by whom he knew he was misunderstood with respect to the favor; both leave the personal recipients general rather than naming a particular husband or woman.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you must devote yourself to philosophy
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine participle addresses the female recipient. The main English does not need a gendered pronoun, but retains the instruction to attend to philosophy rather than treating philosophy as an external agent.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ Ζεὺς αὐτὸς ὁ τούτων, νομοθέτης
lexical_decisions.chosen: Zeus himself, the lawgiver of these people
lexical_decisions.rationale: These is taken as referring to the jealous people just discussed, since the laws are said to have been laid down for them. The lawgiver of these laws is a material alternative, taking the genitive as referring to the previously mentioned enacted laws. The main wording does not claim this referent is grammatically unique.

passages.text: And so as not to waste time needlessly on further proofs, I will begin with Zeus himself, the father of gods and humans, and disclose some of his unions; recalling them all is impossible because of their number. Listen, then, to the unions of great Zeus himself that were concealed through changes of form because of foolish men's jealousy. First, wishing to remove for the wise the supposed sin of adultery arising from different unions, when he was about to marry, and knowing that, as at a first bed, he was not becoming an adulterer according to most people, he obtained a sinless marriage through the supposed sin, as I said. For he marries Hera, his own sister, having made himself resemble the plumage of a cuckoo. From her Hebe and Eileithyia were born. For he gives birth to Metis without union with anyone, just as Hera gives birth to Hephaestus.

lexical_decisions.chosen: different unions
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective can indicate differing or varied unions. The context presents the writer's attempt to remove the charge of adultery from multiple unions, but the phrase is not expanded to specify particular partners not named here.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ὡς ἐπὶ πρώτῃ εὐνῇ κατὰ τοὺς πολλοὺς μοιχὸς εἰδὼς οὐ γινόμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: and knowing that, as at a first bed, he was not becoming an adulterer according to most people
lexical_decisions.rationale: The unusual first-bed comparison and the appeal to most people's judgment are both preserved. Bed is a sexual or marital union here. The nominative participles are read as Zeus's knowledge of his own not becoming an adulterer; an alternative takes knowing and not becoming as parallel descriptions. The main text does not resolve the argument into an unstated rule about either partner's previous marital status.

lexical_decisions.chosen: having made himself resemble the plumage of a cuckoo
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative literally names a cuckoo's feather or plumage. Plumage preserves that expressed image rather than simply replacing it with the whole bird; a cuckoo's feather is a narrower alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν Μῆτιν γὰρ χωρὶς τῆς πρὸς τινὰ μίξεως ἀποκυΐσκει
lexical_decisions.chosen: For he gives birth to Metis without union with anyone
lexical_decisions.rationale: The active verb assigns the birth to Zeus. The supplied name and unusual parentage are retained rather than harmonized with other versions of the myth.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ τοῦ Διὸς τοῦ πατρὸς θεῶν τε καὶ ἀνθρώπων ἄρξομαι τὰς ἐνίων μηνύειν κοινωνίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: I will begin with Zeus himself, the father of gods and humans, and disclose some of his unions
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive some has an unexpressed referent. The main text follows the immediate focus on Zeus and the next sentence about his hidden unions, treating the selection as unions with some partners. A more source-literal alternative is I will begin with Zeus himself and disclose the unions of some of them, with some potentially referring to the divine beings under discussion. Unions with some partners is another explicit alternative; the English selection of his unions is contextual rather than a claim that the genitive uniquely modifies Zeus.

passages.text: He also has relations with a sister born to him from Uranus and Sea through Cronus's castration, .... Eros and Cypris, whom they also call Didone. He also has relations with Antiope, daughter of Nycteus, having made himself like a satyr; from her Amphion and Zethus were born. He unites with Alcmene, Amphitryon's wife, resembling Amphitryon her husband; from her Heracles was born. He also approaches Aegina, daughter of Asopus, becoming an eagle; from her Aeacus is born. He lies with Amalthea, daughter of Phocus, resembling a bear. He flowed down upon Danae, daughter of Acrisius, as gold; from her Perseus flew forth. For Callisto, daughter of Lycaon, he became a fierce lion, and she bears another, Arcas. He united with Europa, daughter of Phoenix, through a bull; from her Minos, Rhadamanthys, and Sarpedon sprang forth. With Eurymedusa, daughter of Achelous, he became an ant; from her came Myrmidon. With the nymph of Hersaeus he became a vulture; from her came the Palici in Sicily. He united with earth-born Himalia in Rhodes through rain; from her came Spartaeus, Cronius, and Cytus. He took Cassiopeia as a bride, resembling Phoenix her husband; from her Atymnius sprang forth for him. With Nemesis, daughter of Thestius, who was also considered Leda, he became a swan or a goose and fathered Helen; and again, becoming a star, he brought forth Castor and Polydeuces. For Lamia he changed into a hoopoe.

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a four-dot gap. The English retains exactly four dots and the following fragment Eros and Cypris, without inventing the lost connection or restoring a missing birth statement. The surviving passage is not represented as an unbroken original.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through Cronus's castration
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive can describe a castration associated with Cronus as agent or as the person castrated. Castration carried out by Cronus is a material alternative. The possessive English preserves the association without supplying an otherwise unnamed victim in this clause.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἔρως καὶ Κύπρις, ἣν καὶ Διδώνην λέγουσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Eros and Cypris, whom they also call Didone
lexical_decisions.rationale: The two names after the printed gap remain a fragment, without an invented verb or genealogical connection. The feminine relative refers to Cypris. Didone transliterates the printed name rather than silently correcting it to Dione.

lexical_decisions.chosen: from her Perseus flew forth
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb's flight image is retained. Sprang forth would be a more idiomatic birth expression but would conceal the explicit flying verb.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Καλλιστοῖ τῇ Λυκάονος ἠγριώθη λέων, καὶ ἄλλον τίκτει Ἀρκάδα
lexical_decisions.chosen: For Callisto, daughter of Lycaon, he became a fierce lion, and she bears another, Arcas
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied lion form and the word another are retained without harmonizing other accounts. The main text infers Callisto as the subject of bears from the childbearing context, assuming an unmarked change of subject. Continuing Zeus as subject is also viable, since τίκτω can describe male begetting: and he begets another, Arcas. The masculine name identifies the child but does not itself determine which parent is the verb's subject.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the nymph of Hersaeus
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive relationship is left broad. Νύμφη can also mean bride or young wife, so bride of Hersaeus is a material alternative. The text is not expanded into a specific genealogy or a different familiar myth.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Νεμέσει τῇ Θεστίου, τῇ καὶ Λήδᾳ νομισθείσῃ, κύκνος ἢ χὴν γενόμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: With Nemesis, daughter of Thestius, who was also considered Leda, he became a swan or a goose
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both the alternative bird forms and the source's identification of Nemesis with Leda are preserved rather than choosing a single familiar version.

passages.text: Resembling a shepherd, he makes Mnemosyne the mother of the Muses. He marries Semele, daughter of Cadmus, while blazing, and from her brings forth Dionysus. He himself takes his daughter Persephone as a bride, having made himself like a serpent; she was also considered the wife of his brother Pluto. He has relations with many other women even without changing form, their husbands feeling no jealousy as though over a sin, but knowing well that by freely sharing in union with their wives he fathers children, granting them Hermeses, Apollos, Dionysuses, Endymions, and all the others we have mentioned, outstanding in beauty from union with him.

lexical_decisions.chosen: while blazing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle describes Zeus as flaming or blazing. The translation does not supply a specific material body or explain the event using a different familiar account.

lexical_decisions.chosen: He himself takes his daughter Persephone as a bride
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb can concern marrying off or taking in marriage. The reflexive emphasis and the sexual sequence favor Zeus himself as the participant taking his daughter as a bride; the alternative of his giving her in marriage remains lexically possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Hermeses, Apollos, Dionysuses, Endymions
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source prints these names in the plural. The English preserves that conspicuous pattern rather than normalizing them to singular named children; it can characterize children of the named divine types.

lexical_decisions.chosen: freely
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverb may express abundance or the absence of jealousy or grudging. Freely keeps both generosity and lack of restraint available without adding the claim that every husband consented.

passages.text: So that I do not spend my time on an endless account, you will find ungrudging unions among all the gods along with Zeus—unions that foolish people call adulteries of the gods. The gods do not even avoid unions with males as shameful, but practice this too as something becoming. Thus Zeus himself loves Ganymede; Poseidon, Pelops; Apollo, Cinyras, Zacynthus, Hyacinthus, Phorbas, Hylas, Admetus, Cyparissus, Amyclas, Troilus, Branchus, Atymnius, Parus, Potnieus, and Orpheus; Dionysus, Adonis, Ampelus, Hymenaeus, Hermaphroditus, and Achilles; Asclepius, Hippolytus; Hephaestus, Peleus; Pan, Daphnis; Hermes, Perseus, Chrysus, Thersus, and Odrysus; and Heracles, Abderus, Dryops, Iocastus, Philoctetes, Ilas, Polyphemus, Haemon, Diomus, and Pirithous.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πάντων μετὰ Διὸς θεῶν ἀφθόνους εὑρήσεις κοινωνίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: ungrudging unions
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source separates this adjective and noun with the verb. The adjective can mean abundant or free from jealousy and grudging; the argument against jealousy supports ungrudging, while abundant unions is a material alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Zeus himself loves Ganymede
lexical_decisions.rationale: The stated erotic love supplies the understood verb for the ensuing series of gods and their named male beloveds. The English preserves every listed person and does not add ages or acts beyond the source.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Hylas
lexical_decisions.rationale: This name in Apollo's list begins with upsilon and a rough breathing. It is distinguished in transliteration from the printed Ἴλα in Heracles' list rather than silently treating the two spellings as identical.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Ilas
lexical_decisions.rationale: The printed iota spelling in Heracles' list is retained as Ilas. Identification with the Hylas in Apollo's list is possible but is not imposed on the source text.

passages.text: I have therefore set before you some of the loves of all the more prominent gods, dearest, so that you may know that only foolish human beings experience jealousy over this. That is also why they are mortal and pass their lives in sorrow: because, through their own jealousy, they have declared evil the things that seemed good to the gods. From now on, then, you will be blessed if you imitate gods rather than humans. For when people see you preserving what is considered chastity, they praise you because of their own passion, but do not benefit you. But when the gods see you becoming like themselves, they will both praise and benefit you.

lexical_decisions.chosen: some of the loves
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase signals partial coverage of each set of loves, not an exhaustive account. Loves can also be rendered love affairs in this context.

lexical_decisions.chosen: what is considered chastity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The qualifier marks the letter writer's skeptical treatment of conventional sexual restraint. It is not removed to make the writer endorse chastity, nor does the English adopt his skepticism as the translator's own judgment.

lexical_decisions.chosen: because of their own passion
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun can indicate emotion or a condition of suffering; the surrounding jealousy makes a possessive passion the likely reference. The main text leaves its precise emotional identity implicit rather than inserting a new named motive.

passages.text: For consider for me how many beloved women they rewarded: some they made into constellations, and they benefited both the children and the helpers of some of them. Thus Zeus made Callisto into a constellation, the one called the Little Bear, which some also call the Dog's Tail. Poseidon placed Dolphin in heaven because of Amphitrite, and counted Orion, born of Euryale daughter of Minos, worthy of the stars because of Euryale his mother. Dionysus did so with Ariadne's crown. Zeus assigned the eagle that helped in the abduction of Ganymede, and Ganymede himself, a place with the honor of Aquarius; and he honored the bull because of Europa. Moreover, as a favor to Leda, he made Castor, Polydeuces, and Helen into stars; Perseus because of Danae; Arcas because of Callisto; the Maiden, also called Justice, because of Themis; and Heracles because of Alcmene. I will not go on any longer. It would take a long time to detail how many others the gods have benefited because of their many beloved women, through their unions with humans. Foolish people forbid these unions as evil acts, not knowing that pleasure is the great enjoyment among humans.

source_issues.issue: The selected print places a full stop between the possessive Ganymede and the noun abduction. The English follows their grammatical relationship continuously. This is disclosed editorial punctuation treatment, not a lacuna, restoration, or allegation of OCR error; the supplied Greek remains unchanged.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν λεγομένην ἄρκτον μικράν, ἣν καὶ κυνὸς οὐρὰν προσαγορεύουσίν τινες
lexical_decisions.chosen: the one called the Little Bear, which some also call the Dog's Tail
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both constellation designations and their attribution to Callisto are retained exactly, without harmonizing the passage with a different astronomical identification.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Dionysus did so with Ariadne's crown
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source is an elliptical clause, carrying over the preceding placement among the stars. Did so supplies only that established predicate, not a new celestial act.

lexical_decisions.chosen: assigned ... a place with the honor of Aquarius
lexical_decisions.rationale: Aquarius translates the constellation title Water-Pourer by its conventional English name. The wording attaches the honor to Zeus's assignment; the extent to which the eagle shares the Aquarius description is not resolved by adding a different constellation for it.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the Maiden, also called Justice
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine designation is translated as the Maiden, with Justice retaining the meaning of Dike. The source's stray full stop is not treated as a lost-word marker or expanded into an extra gap.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡδονή ἐστιν ἡ μεγάλη ἐν ἀνθρώποις ἀπόλαυσις
lexical_decisions.chosen: pleasure is the great enjoyment among humans
lexical_decisions.rationale: The near repetition of pleasure and enjoyment belongs to the source's maxim. It is retained rather than replaced by a stronger claim that pleasure is the only good or purpose of human life.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ Ὠρίωνα τὸν ἐξ Εὐρυάλης τῆς Μίνω δι’ Εὐρυάλην τὴν μητέρα τῶν ἄστρων κατηξίωσεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: and counted Orion, born of Euryale daughter of Minos, worthy of the stars because of Euryale his mother
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text attaches stars as the genitive complement of deemed worthy, a verb that can govern what someone is worthy of. The mother refers to Orion's mother, supported by the preceding identification of him as born of Euryale. A material alternative attaches the genitive stars to mother: he deemed Orion worthy because of Euryale, the mother of the stars. That reading leaves the celestial object of worthiness implicit in the context. The main attachment is defensible but not grammatically unique.

passages.text: What then? Do not even the celebrated wise men prefer pleasure, and did they not have relations with whichever women they wished? First among them is the teacher of Greece, about whom Phoebus himself said, ‘Of all men, Socrates is wisest.’ Does he not propose that women be held in common in the best-governed city, Lacedaemon, and cover the handsome Alcibiades beneath his cloak? The Socratic Antisthenes also writes that one should not reject so-called adultery. And does not his pupil Diogenes openly have relations with Lais, in return for carrying her publicly on his shoulders? Does not Epicurus prefer pleasure? Does not Aristippus, after being perfumed, give his whole self to Aphrodite? Does not Zeno, hinting at treating things as indifferent, say that the divine is present through everything, so that intelligent people may recognize that, with whomever someone has relations, he has relations as with himself, and that forbidding so-called adulteries or unions with a mother, daughter, sister, or children is superfluous? Chrysippus, in his love letters, also mentions the image in Argos, placing Hera's face at Zeus's genitals.

lexical_decisions.chosen: propose that women be held in common
lexical_decisions.rationale: The claim is assigned to Socrates in the source and retained as the letter writer's claim. It is not silently reassigned to another philosopher or rewritten into a historically corrected account.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ μισθῷ τοῦ φέρειν αὐτὴν ἐπ’ ὤμων δημοσίᾳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: in return for carrying her publicly on his shoulders
lexical_decisions.rationale: The infinitive specifies the payment or recompense as carrying Lais. The rendering does not add money, identify a fee amount, or reverse who carries whom.

lexical_decisions.chosen: hinting at treating things as indifferent
lexical_decisions.rationale: Indifference is the philosophical treatment of the acts as morally neither good nor bad, not simply emotional unconcern. The source presents this as an indirect implication, retained as hinting rather than an explicit quotation from Zeno.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μίξεις μητρὸς ἢ θυγατρὸς ἢ ἀδελφῆς ἢ παίδων
lexical_decisions.chosen: unions with a mother, daughter, sister, or children
lexical_decisions.rationale: Children preserves the broad age and relationship range of παῖδες. Boys is possible in this sexual context, but the adjacent family categories also support children; the source does not name particular ages.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς τῷ τοῦ Διὸς αἰδοίῳ φέρων τῆς Ἥρας τὸ πρόσωπον
lexical_decisions.chosen: placing Hera's face at Zeus's genitals
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle concerns the writer's description of the image. The precise position is retained without adding an act not expressly named in the supplied wording.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκ Ἀρίστιππος μυρισθεὶς ὅλον αὐτὸν Ἀφροδίτῃ χαρίζεται;
lexical_decisions.chosen: Does not Aristippus, after being perfumed, give his whole self to Aphrodite?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering takes whole self with the finite giving verb, foregrounding his complete self-dedication to Aphrodite after perfuming. The alternative Does not Aristippus, perfumed all over, give himself to Aphrodite takes whole self as an accusative of respect with perfumed and foregrounds the extent of perfuming. Both attachments are viable; the chosen one keeps the full accusative expression as what is given rather than leaving the giving object to inference alone.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἵνα γνώριμον τοῖς συνετοῖς γένηται ἵνα ᾧ ἂν τις μιγῇ, ὡς ἑαυτῷ μίγνυται
lexical_decisions.chosen: so that intelligent people may recognize that, with whomever someone has relations, he has relations as with himself
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied wording repeats ἵνα. The first clause is purposive; the main text reads the second clause loosely as the content of the intended recognition, which the phrase become known calls for in this context. A material alternative preserves the repeated purpose force, so that it may become known to the intelligent ... so that, with whomever someone has relations, he has relations as with himself. Their exact syntactic relationship remains uncertain. No substitution of an unprinted ὅτι or other Greek emendation has been supplied.

passages.text: I know that these things appear terrifying and utterly shameful to those uninitiated in the truth, but not to the gods and philosophers of the Greeks, nor to the mysteries of Dionysus and Demeter. But, after all this, so that I do not waste time recounting the lives of every god and philosopher, let two be your greatest models: Zeus among gods, and Socrates among human philosophers. Having understood the rest from what I have reminded you of in writing, take care never to distress a lover of yours. For if you act against gods and lovers, you will be judged impious and undergo the appropriate punishment. But if you offer yourself to every lover, then, as an imitator of the gods, you will obtain their beneficence. For the rest, dearest, remember the mysteries I have disclosed to you and show me your decision in writing. Farewell.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those uninitiated in the truth
lexical_decisions.rationale: The initiation image is explicit and continues into the reference to mysteries. Uninformed would be smoother but would erase the writer's claim to privileged initiatory knowledge.

lexical_decisions.chosen: let two be your greatest models
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun can mean marks, aims, or objects of attention. The two exemplary figures and the subsequent imitation argument favor models; the rendering does not make them legal authorities or assign a new office.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐὰν δὲ παντὶ ἐραστῇ ἑαυτὴν παράσχῃς
lexical_decisions.chosen: if you offer yourself to every lover
lexical_decisions.rationale: The universal every and reflexive yourself are retained as the letter writer's demand. The translation reports his coercive argument without adopting it or adding detail.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ δὲ λοιπὰ ἐξ ὧν σοι γράψας ὑπέμνησα συνεῖσα ἔπεχε, μήποτε ἐραστήν σου λυπήσῃς
lexical_decisions.chosen: Having understood the rest from what I have reminded you of in writing, take care never to distress a lover of yours
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes the rest as the object of understanding and the written reminders as its basis, explicitly preserving ἐξ as from. An alternative treats the rest adverbially, for the rest, while still requiring an understanding drawn from those reminders. The prior wording made the reminders themselves the direct object and has been corrected.

passages.text: So I took this document from Apion as though I really intended to send it to the beloved woman. I fabricated a reply as though she had written back to these things, and when Apion came the next day, I gave it to him as her supposed reply. It read as follows:

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπλασάμην ὡς ἐκείνης πρὸς ταῦτα ἀντιγραψάσης
lexical_decisions.chosen: I fabricated a reply as though she had written back to these things
lexical_decisions.rationale: The narrator explicitly claims authorship of the fictional response. It is not presented as an authentic letter from the woman or as a mere transcription of one.

lexical_decisions.chosen: this document
lexical_decisions.rationale: The object is the preceding written letter, not necessarily a codex or full-length book. Document preserves the written artifact without imposing a modern book format.

passages.text: Copy of a letter to Apion, supposedly from the beloved woman. I am amazed that, after praising me for wisdom, you write to me as though I were foolish. For, wishing to persuade me into your passion, you drew your examples from myths about the gods, not afraid to blaspheme Love—the oldest of all, as you said, and above all gods and humans—so that you might corrupt my soul and outrage my body. For the love involved in desires is not the originator of the gods. If he desires willingly, he himself is his own passion and punishment, and one who suffers willingly would not be a god. But if he unwillingly desires union and, passing through our souls, is carried through our bodies as through instruments into unions with intelligible beings, the one who makes him love and carries him is greater than he is. And again, if that very one who carries him is carried by another longing, another, greater one is found who carries that one, and an endless regress of lovers results, which is impossible. Thus there is neither one who carries nor one who is carried; rather, it is the lover's own desiring passion, increasing through hope and diminishing through despair.

source_issues.issue: The former Lagarde phrase is exactly ἐπὶ τῆς πάντων θεῶν καὶ ἀνθρώπων. The selected phrase ἐπὶ πάντων θεῶν καὶ ἀνθρώπων is Dressel's independently image-read main print, not a newly collated manuscript. It is not the separate marginal proposal ἐπιθεὶς, and no participle from that proposal has been adopted or silently added. The main interpretation and its alternative attachment are explained in the lexical note; no unique original wording is claimed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἀντίγραφον ἐπιστολῆς πρὸς Ἀππίωνα ὡς παρὰ τῆς ἐρωμένης
lexical_decisions.chosen: Copy of a letter to Apion, supposedly from the beloved woman
lexical_decisions.rationale: The heading's supposedly marks the letter's presented rather than certified authorship. It is retained without turning the heading into an authentic attribution.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἔρωτα τὸν πάντων πρεσβύτατον (ὡς ἔφης) ἐπὶ πάντων θεῶν καὶ ἀνθρώπων
lexical_decisions.chosen: Love—the oldest of all, as you said, and above all gods and humans
lexical_decisions.rationale: The selected ἐπὶ with the genitive is read as a relation of superiority, above or over all, describing Love alongside oldest of all. English and links the two descriptors without supplying a Greek participle meaning set or place. A material alternative attaches the prepositional phrase to blaspheme: before or in the presence of all gods and humans. The age and universal scope are retained in either reading; the superiority interpretation fits the ensuing denial that desire-based love originates the gods but is not claimed as uniquely established.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἔρως γὰρ θεῶν οὐκ ἔστιν ἀρχηγέτης ὁ ἐν ταῖς ἐπιθυμίαις
lexical_decisions.chosen: For the love involved in desires is not the originator of the gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: The qualification limits this denial to love associated with desires. Originator preserves the founding or originating force of ἀρχηγέτης; leader is a viable alternative stressing rule rather than origin.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς τὰς τῶν νοητῶν φέρεται συνουσίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: is carried ... into unions with intelligible beings
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied adjective concerns beings or things apprehensible to thought. With intelligible beings takes the genitive as partners of union; unions of intelligible beings is a material alternative leaving their relation broader. The unusual wording is not silently replaced with mortal or bodily partners.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς ἀπέραντον ἐπαναφορὰ τῶν ἐρώντων γίνεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: an endless regress of lovers results
lexical_decisions.rationale: The argument repeatedly seeks a greater bearer behind each bearer. Regress denotes that unending backward sequence rather than a finite recurring cycle.

passages.text: Those unwilling to master shameful desire tell lies about the gods, so that, by pointing to the gods as having done first the things they themselves do, they may escape blame. For if the so-called gods committed adulteries for the sake of having children and not sexual excess, why did they also have relations with males? ‘But,’ he says, ‘as a favor to their beloved women, they made them into constellations.’ So were there no stars before this, until heaven was adorned with stars by adulterers on the pretext of sexual excess? And how is it that the descendants of those made into constellations are punished in Hades: Atlas weighed down, Tantalus tormented by thirst, Sisyphus pushing a rock, Tityus having his entrails dug into, and Ixion rolling endlessly around a wheel? And how is it that the lovers, being gods, made those whom they defiled into constellations, without granting this favor to themselves?

lexical_decisions.chosen: sexual excess
lexical_decisions.rationale: The term describes unrestrained or shameless sexual conduct in this argument. The same rendering is maintained in the two occurrences rather than replacing the second by an invented account of how constellations were formed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the descendants of those made into constellations
lexical_decisions.rationale: The relationship and direction of descent are retained as the speaker's claim. They are not changed to ancestors or to the constellated figures themselves to harmonize the list with other myths.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Tityus having his entrails dug into
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive suffering and the body part are retained. No animal, instrument, or additional violent detail absent from this clause is supplied.

passages.text: They were not gods, then, but veiled representations of tyrants. For a tomb of Cronus is shown in the Caucasian mountains—not in heaven but on earth—the tomb of a savage man who devoured his children. A tomb of the sexually unrestrained Zeus of myth, who likewise swallowed his daughter Metis, is also seen in Crete. There is also Pluto's tomb at the Acherusian lake, Poseidon's on Tenos, the Sun's at Atroi and the Moon's at Carrhae, Hermes' at Hermopolis, Ares' in Thrace, Aphrodite's on Cyprus, Dionysus' at Thebes, and those of others in other places. In any case, the tombs of the very gods mentioned are visible. For they were humans, and wicked ones and sorcerers at that. They could not otherwise have become absolute rulers—I mean the Zeus of myth and Dionysus—unless, through transformation into whatever they themselves wished, they held sway over whomever they wished.

lexical_decisions.chosen: veiled representations of tyrants
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun denotes enigmatic or figurative representations. The claim identifies the mythic gods as disguised presentations of human tyrants, not merely difficult riddles that tyrants posed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἡλίου δὲ ἐν Ἄτροις καὶ Σελήνης ἐν Κάρραις
lexical_decisions.chosen: the Sun's at Atroi and the Moon's at Carrhae
lexical_decisions.rationale: The divine names are rendered by their transparent celestial meanings; Helios and Selene are conventional name alternatives. Atroi follows the supplied place-name spelling without silently identifying it with another city.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ μὴ τῇ μεταμορφώσει ὧν ἤθελον ἐπεκράτουν εἰς ὅπερ αὐτοὶ ἤθελον
lexical_decisions.chosen: unless, through transformation into whatever they themselves wished, they held sway over whomever they wished
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text attaches into whatever they themselves wished to transformation, retaining the explicit changing-form image that matches the preceding accounts of assumed forms. The material alternative unless through transformation they gained control over whomever they wished for whatever purpose they themselves wished takes the final phrase as the intended end of domination. The source does not expressly settle whose form changes, so no otherwise unnamed magical mechanism is supplied.

passages.text: If we must emulate their lives, let us imitate not only their adulteries but also their tables. For Cronus swallowed his own children, and Zeus likewise his own daughter. And what need is there to say more? Pelops became a dinner for all the gods. So let us too, before our unlawful marriages, hold a dinner like the gods'. Then the dinner would be worthy of the marriages. But you would never bear to do this, just as I would never bear to commit adultery. Besides all this, you threaten me with the wrath of Love as though he were a powerful god. Love is not a god such as he is thought to be, but a desire arising from the constitution of the living being for the succession of life, according to the providence of the one who brought everything into being. This is so that the whole race may never fail, but, on the pretext of pleasure, another may again come into being from the substance of the one who is going to die, sprung from a lawful marriage, so that he may know his own father in order to support him in old age. Those born from adultery would not be able to do this, lacking a natural affection toward those who begot them.

lexical_decisions.chosen: And what need is there to say more?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rhetorical question concerns what needs saying, not what one is able to say. More is supplied from the movement toward the final example, rather than changing the question into an appeal to ability.

lexical_decisions.chosen: from the constitution of the living being
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun refers to the mixture or constitution of the organism. Animal is another literal rendering of ζῷον, but living being preserves its applicability to humans in this explanation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: on the pretext of pleasure
lexical_decisions.rationale: The same pretext language used in the polemic is retained in the positive account of generation. For the sake of pleasure would flatten the distinction between the reproductive purpose and the pleasure that provides its occasion.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅπως πρὸς τὸ γηροτροφεῖν τὸν αὐτοῦ πατέρα γνώσῃ
lexical_decisions.chosen: so that he may know his own father in order to support him in old age
lexical_decisions.rationale: The child is the inferred subject of knowing, with the father its expressed object and support in old age the purpose. The source's ensuing assertion about children born from adultery is retained as the fictional letter writer's claim, not presented as an established psychological fact.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅθεν καὶ ἡμεῖς πρὸ τῶν ἀθεμίτων γάμων ὅμοιον δεῖπνον τοῖς θεοῖς ἐπιτελέσωμεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: So let us too, before our unlawful marriages, hold a dinner like the gods'
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative gods is read comparatively because the preceding instruction explicitly calls for imitation of the gods' tables. A material alternative reads it as beneficiaries: let us too, before our unlawful marriages, hold a similar dinner for the gods. That alternative would propose a banquet offered to them rather than only a banquet modeled on theirs; the main text does not claim to exclude it grammatically.

passages.text: Since, then, erotic desire arises for the sake of succession and legitimate increase, as I said, parents should take thought for chastity and educate their children in advance, before desire arises, through books that teach self-restraint. They should accustom them beforehand to better teachings, because habit is a second nature. In addition, they should frequently remind them of the punishments imposed by the laws, so that, using fear like a bridle, they do not rush along with improper pleasures. It is also fitting to satisfy through marriage the natural passion of their age before desire reaches its height, having first persuaded them not to fix their eyes on the figure of a courtesan.

lexical_decisions.chosen: legitimate increase
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective concerns legitimate descent in the contrast with adultery. Genuine growth is a more literal lexical alternative, but would obscure the explicitly marital context.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: σωφροσύνης προνοουμένους, τοὺς αὐτῶν παῖδας πρὸ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας διὰ τῶν σωφρονιζόντων βιβλίων
lexical_decisions.chosen: take thought for chastity ... through books that teach self-restraint
lexical_decisions.rationale: The shared word-family concerns restraint, here especially sexual chastity. The English varies the cognate forms for natural readability while disclosing their connection; books that teach chastity is a narrower alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸ τοῦ τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν ἐπακμάσαι γάμῳ τὸ φυσικὸν τῆς ἡλικίας πληροφορεῖν πάθος
lexical_decisions.chosen: satisfy through marriage the natural passion of their age before desire reaches its height
lexical_decisions.rationale: The ancient recommendation and its timing are retained without turning them into present-day guidance or adding an age not stated in the source. The verb denotes filling or satisfying the passion, not merely recognizing it.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς εἶδος ἑταίρας γυναικὸς μὴ ἀτενίζειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: not to fix their eyes on the figure of a courtesan
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied ἑταίρας is read as the noun courtesan, not silently changed to ἑτέρας, another. Figure renders visible form or appearance without adding the adjective beautiful.

passages.text: For our mind, whenever at the outset it takes an impression of the beloved woman’s appearance under the influence of pleasure, is tormented through memory, as though always gazing at her form in a mirror; and when it does not attain its desire, it devises the paths to attainment, but when it does attain it, it grows still more, like a fire amply supplied with fuel, and especially when fear has not already been impressed on the lover’s soul before the passion. For just as water extinguishes fire, so fear too is an extinguisher of irrational desire. Therefore, since I learned from a certain Jew both to think and to do what befits God, I am not made easy prey to adultery by false myths. But may God help you, as you wish and strive to be self-controlled while your soul is inflamed with erotic passion, and may he provide the cure.

lexical_decisions.chosen: takes an impression of the beloved woman’s appearance
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀπομάσσομαι can describe taking or receiving an impression, fitting the following mirror image; “copies” or “imprints upon itself” are also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: but when it does attain it, it grows still more
lexical_decisions.rationale: The English pronouns preserve the referential tension: νοῦς is the formal subject, while the context may make the growing element the desire or passion.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a fire amply supplied with fuel
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὕλη can mean material or wood; in the fire image it denotes available fuel.

lexical_decisions.chosen: easy prey to adultery
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὐάλωτος literally describes what is easily captured, so the rendering preserves the predatory image rather than merely saying “easily persuaded.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: while your soul is inflamed with erotic passion
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔρως here denotes erotic love or desire, while φλεγμαίνω continues the preceding fire imagery.

passages.text: On hearing the feigned written reply, Appion said, “Do I hate Jews without reason? Now, at any rate, a certain Jew once encountered this woman, brought her over to his religion, and persuaded her to be self-controlled; and from now on it is impossible for her to enter into intimacy with anyone else, because such people, having set God before themselves as the all-seeing observer of actions, steadfastly persist in strict self-control, since they are unable to go unnoticed.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: the feigned written reply
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀντιγραφή is a written response, while ὑπόκριτος marks it as assumed, acted, or feigned.

lexical_decisions.chosen: brought her over to his religion
lexical_decisions.rationale: μετάγω expresses transfer to another position, and θρησκεία may denote religion, worship, or religious observance. The possessive is contextually supplied by the preceding Jewish agent, though it is not explicit in Greek.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to enter into intimacy with anyone else
lexical_decisions.rationale: κοινωνία can mean association or participation, but the surrounding discussion of adultery supports sexual intimacy or union here.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν θεὸν ὡς παντεπόπτην τῶν πράξεων προθέμενοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: having set God before themselves as the all-seeing observer of actions
lexical_decisions.rationale: παντεπόπτης presents God as seeing everything; προτίθημι depicts placing that awareness before oneself.

lexical_decisions.chosen: since they are unable to go unnoticed
lexical_decisions.rationale: The infinitive λαθεῖν means escaping notice; the one from whom they cannot remain hidden is implicit from the preceding reference to God.

passages.text: Having heard this, I said to Appion, “Now I will confess the truth to you. I did not fall in love with a woman, nor with any other person, because my soul was entirely expended upon other longings and upon the discovery of true doctrines. And up to the present, after scrutinizing many opinions of philosophers, I inclined toward none of them except only that of the Jews, when a certain merchant of theirs, who sold linen cloths and was staying here in Rome, through a fortunate encounter set before me in simpler terms the belief in one sovereign.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: nor with any other person
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive form can be masculine, “anyone else,” or neuter, “anything else.” The personal sense fits the statement about falling in love, but the broader alternative remains grammatically possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: because my soul was entirely expended
lexical_decisions.rationale: δαπανάω conveys spending or consuming resources; here the soul is portrayed as having its energies consumed or devoted elsewhere.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς οὐδένα αὐτῶν ἔνευσα ἢ πρὸς τὸ Ἰουδαίων μόνον
lexical_decisions.chosen: I inclined toward none of them except only that of the Jews
lexical_decisions.rationale: νεύω literally means nodding or inclining toward something and here denotes assent. The neuter τὸ Ἰουδαίων leaves the Jewish opinion, position, or doctrine implicit.

lexical_decisions.chosen: who sold linen cloths
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὀθόνη denotes a linen cloth, sheet, or similar piece of fabric; “linen cloths” retains the commercial object without narrowing its use.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the belief in one sovereign
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally a “monarchic conviction,” the phrase in this theological context concerns sole sovereignty, commonly understood as the sole rule of God; “monotheism” would flatten its wording.

lexical_decisions.chosen: set before me in simpler terms
lexical_decisions.rationale: παρατίθημι means placing or presenting something before another, while the comparative ἁπλούστερον can mean “more simply” or, idiomatically, “quite simply.”

passages.text: But when Appion heard the truth from me—he who irrationally hates what is Jewish and neither knows nor wishes to know what their belief actually is—he grew angry without examination and, in silence, at once departed from Rome itself. And now, having met him for the first time since then, I reasonably suspect that his anger dates from that time. Nevertheless, in your presence I will ask him what he might have to say about the so-called gods, whose lives—mythologized as subject to every passion—are deliberately sung in public to encourage imitation of such things, and whose tombs are also pointed out in their respective places, in addition to their human passions, as I said.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: what is Jewish
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantivized neuter expression can denote the Jewish position, doctrine, cause, or way; the broad rendering avoids replacing it with the Jewish people themselves.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τί ποτε ἐστὶν αὐτῶν τὸ πιστὸν
lexical_decisions.chosen: what their belief actually is
lexical_decisions.rationale: τὸ πιστόν may denote their belief, faith, or what they hold as trustworthy; the interrogative τί ποτε adds the force of “what exactly” or “actually.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: he grew angry without examination and, in silence
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀκρίτως indicates acting without judgment or examination. The dative τῇ σιωπῇ is read as manner, “silently,” though attachment as anger “at the silence” is grammatically conceivable but contextually less natural.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Nevertheless, in your presence I will ask him
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐφ᾽ ὑμῶν means “before you” or “in your presence,” while αὐτοῦ is taken as the genitive personal complement of πεύσομαι, supplying “him.” This is syntactically straightforward and identifies Appion as the person questioned. Alternatively, αὐτοῦ may be adverbial, “there” or “on the spot,” with “him” inferred from context.

lexical_decisions.chosen: mythologized as subject to every passion
lexical_decisions.rationale: παντοπαθής can describe undergoing every kind of passion, experience, or suffering; the repeated πάθεσιν and the moral context favor “every passion.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς τὴν τοῦ ὁμοίου μίμησιν ἐπίτηδες ᾄδονται δημοσία
lexical_decisions.chosen: are deliberately sung in public to encourage imitation of such things
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπίτηδες makes the singing purposeful, and πρὸς with μίμησις expresses its intended movement toward imitation of like conduct.

lexical_decisions.chosen: their tombs are also pointed out in their respective places
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατὰ τόπον can mean place by place, locally, or in the respective locations; the rendering preserves the claim that identifiable tombs are shown.

passages.text: The others, having heard these things from me beforehand and longing to learn what came next, joined me, intending to visit Appion. And indeed we found him already bathed at a table that had been made ready; therefore . we went into only a few details concerning the discussion about gods. But he, I think, perceived our purpose and promised that on the following day he would have something to say about gods; and he indicated the same place to us in advance, intending to converse there. With that promise, after expressing our thanks to him, we each departed for home.

source_issues.issue: The selected image-checked edition prints one isolated dot after διόπερ as a gap marker. The content represented by the gap is unavailable; the translation retains exactly one dot and supplies no restoration. This faithful representation of the selected edition’s printed lacuna does not itself block publication.

lexical_decisions.chosen: having heard these things from me beforehand
lexical_decisions.rationale: The prefix in προακούω indicates hearing in advance, and the genitive identifies the narrator as the source.

lexical_decisions.chosen: intending to visit Appion
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὡς with the future participle expresses the companions’ purpose or intention.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: λελουμένον αὐτὸν ἤδη κατελαμβάνομεν ἐφ᾽ ἑτοίμῳ τραπέζῃ
lexical_decisions.chosen: we found him already bathed at a table that had been made ready
lexical_decisions.rationale: λελουμένον depicts Appion as having bathed, while ἐφ᾽ ἑτοίμῳ τραπέζῃ places him at a prepared or ready table.

lexical_decisions.chosen: we went into only a few details
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀκριβολογέομαι denotes speaking or discussing with precision; ὀλίγα limits the discussion to a few matters or a small amount.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he indicated the same place to us in advance
lexical_decisions.rationale: προδηλόω marks advance indication or notification, and τὸν αὐτὸν τόπον most directly means “the same place.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: σὺν τῇ ὑποσχέσει, χάριν ὁμολογήσαντες αὐτῷ
lexical_decisions.chosen: With that promise, after expressing our thanks to him
lexical_decisions.rationale: χάριν ὁμολογεῖν means acknowledging or expressing gratitude; σύν retains the promise as the circumstance accompanying their departure.

passages.text: On the third day I went with my closest companions to the appointed place in Tyre. There I found Apion sitting between Anubion and Athenodorus, waiting for us with many other educated men. Nevertheless, I was not at all intimidated. I greeted him and sat down opposite Apion, who soon began to speak: ‘I want to begin first and move quickly from here to the question at issue. Before you joined us, my child Clement, this Anubion and Athenodorus, who heard you speaking yesterday along with the others, told me how, when I associated with you in Rome on the assumption that you were in love, I told many lies about the gods. I said they were lovers of boys, sexually unrestrained, having relations with mothers, sisters, and daughters, and involved in countless adulteries. But you should have known, my child, that I did not write these things because I held such views about the gods. Rather, out of affection for you, I held back from telling the truth. If you now wish, hear that truth from me.’

source_issues.issue: The first occurrence spells Anubion's name with doubled nu, while the same passage later has Ἀνουβίων. The English uses the conventional name Anubion for both occurrences; no second person is inferred.

lexical_decisions.chosen: on the assumption that you were in love
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative participle refers to Clement, with whom Apion associated. The phrase presents the supposition under which Apion acted; it does not name the object of Clement's supposed love. ‘As with someone in love’ is a closer but less natural alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: lovers of boys, sexually unrestrained
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first term names the gods' alleged sexual interest in boys, and the second their lack of sexual restraint in this context. The rendering preserves the historical accusation without adding details.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: στοργῇ τῇ πρὸς σὲ τὰ ἀληθῆ λέγειν ἀπεκρυπτόμην
lexical_decisions.chosen: out of affection for you, I held back from telling the truth
lexical_decisions.rationale: The middle verb and infinitive express Apion's concealment or withholding of his truthful account. ‘I concealed the truth from you out of affection’ is also possible, but loses the explicit reference to speaking.

passages.text: ‘The wisest men of old learned the whole truth themselves through hard work, but kept those who were unworthy and had no desire for divine teachings from receiving this knowledge. For twelve children were not born to Uranus and his mother Earth, as the myth lists them: the males Oceanus, Coeus, Crius, Hyperion, Iapetus, and Cronus; and the females Theia, Themis, Mnemosyne, Demeter, Tethys, and Rhea. Nor did Cronus cut off the genitals of his father Uranus with an adamantine sickle, as you say, and throw them into the depths. Nor did Aphrodite come into being from drops of blood that flowed from Uranus's severed part. Nor, again, did Cronus have relations with Rhea and, after fathering Pluto first, swallow him, fearing because of some pronouncement of Prometheus that a child born to him might prove nobler than he was and strip him of his kingship. He did not father Poseidon second and swallow him in the same way. After these, when Zeus was born, his mother Rhea did not hide him and give Cronus a stone instead when he demanded him to swallow. That stone did not, when swallowed, squeeze those swallowed earlier and force them out, so that Pluto, the first swallowed, came out first, Poseidon after him, and Zeus third. Nor, as they say, did Zeus, saved by his mother's foresight, ascend into heaven and depose his father from his kingship. He did not punish his father's brothers. He did not come down out of desire for mortal women. He did not have shameful relations with sisters or daughters, with brothers' wives, or with boys. Nor did he beget Metis and swallow her ...., so that he might cause Athena from Metis to grow out of his brain and give birth from his thigh to Dionysus, whom they say the Titans tore apart. He does not hold a feast at the wedding of Thetis and Peleus. He did not exclude Strife from the wedding. This Strife, dishonored, did not devise conflict and faction among the guests. She did not take a golden apple from the gardens of the Hesperides and inscribe on it, “A gift for the beautiful one.” Then they tell the myth that Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite find the apple and, quarreling over it, come to Zeus. He did not judge between them himself, but sent them through Hermes to the shepherd Paris to have their beauty judged. Yet the goddesses were not judged, nor did Paris award the apple to Aphrodite. Aphrodite, thus honored, did not honor him in return with marriage to Helen. For the goddess's honor would not have become the occasion for a war involving every people, and that to the destruction of the man who had received the honor and was closely related to Aphrodite's family. But, as I said, my child, such stories have an appropriate philosophical explanation, capable of being expressed through allegory, so that you will marvel when you hear it.’ I said, ‘Please do not torment me by delaying.’ He replied, ‘Have no fear. I will not put it off, but will begin speaking now.’

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a gap of four dots after ‘swallowed.’ The English retains exactly four dots at the corresponding point. Its unavailable content has not been restored, and the sentence must not be represented as an unbroken original.

source_issues.source_quote: ὡς προελθεῖν πρῶτον μὲν τὸν πρῶτον καταποθέντα Πλούτωνα, ἐπ’ αὐτῷ δὲ Ποσειδῶνα καὶ τρίτον τὸν Δία
source_issues.issue: This enumeration includes Zeus third among those coming out, although the preceding account has Rhea hide him. The translation retains the supplied names and order instead of reconciling the narrative with itself or with other versions of the myth.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with an adamantine sickle
lexical_decisions.rationale: Adamant names the exceptionally hard material of the mythic weapon. ‘A sickle of adamant’ is equally close; specifying steel or diamond would identify a material more precisely than the Greek warrants.

lexical_decisions.chosen: because of some pronouncement of Prometheus
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun can denote an ordinance or decree, here a pronouncement that supplies the reason for Cronus's fear. ‘Decree’ preserves its authoritative force more explicitly; ‘prophecy’ fits the story but narrows the noun beyond what is stated.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὃς οὐ καταποθεὶς τοὺς προκαταποθέντας θλίψας ἐξῶσεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: That stone did not, when swallowed, squeeze those swallowed earlier and force them out
lexical_decisions.rationale: The negative is taken with the finite verb, within Apion's repeated denials of mythic events, rather than as ‘not swallowed’ attached only to the participle. The swallowed participle and the stone as subject are both retained.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Nor did he beget Metis and swallow her
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied active participle says ‘having begotten,’ with Metis as its expressed object. The translation preserves that wording rather than substituting a familiar myth about impregnation or swallowing an already pregnant Metis.

lexical_decisions.chosen: A gift for the beautiful one
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective is positive, not superlative. ‘For the fairest’ would introduce a degree not expressed in this wording.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: λόγον τὰ τοιαῦτα οἰκεῖον καὶ φιλόσοφον, ἀλληγορίᾳ φρασθῆναι δυνάμενον
lexical_decisions.chosen: such stories have an appropriate philosophical explanation, capable of being expressed through allegory
lexical_decisions.rationale: The account is both fitting to its subject and philosophical, and allegory is the means of expressing it. ‘An explanation proper to them and philosophical in character’ is more explicit but heavier English.

passages.text: ‘There was once a time when nothing existed except chaos and an undifferentiated mixture of elements still heaped together without order. Nature itself acknowledges this, and great men have understood that this was so. I will give you Homer himself as a witness, the greatest in wisdom among great men. Speaking of the original confusion, he says, “But may you all become water and earth,” since everything originated from that state and, after the dissolution of its moist and earthy substance, is restored again to its first nature, which is chaos. Hesiod says in his Theogony, “Indeed, first of all chaos came into being.” Clearly, “came into being” signifies having originated, as things that come into being do, not always existing, as things without origin do. Orpheus, too, compares chaos to an egg, in which the first elements were mixed together. What Hesiod proposes as chaos, Orpheus calls an egg that came into being, brought forth from boundless matter. It came about in this way:’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: χάος καὶ στοιχείων ἀτάκτων ἔτι συντεφορημένων μίξις ἀδιάκριτος
lexical_decisions.chosen: chaos and an undifferentiated mixture of elements still heaped together without order
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering retains both the named chaos and the description of the mixture, including the elements' disorder and lack of differentiation. ‘An unseparated mixture’ is another possible rendering of the last adjective.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: γεγενῆσθαι ὡς γενητὰ σημαίνει, οὐ τὸ ἀεὶ εἶναι ὡς ἀγένητα
lexical_decisions.chosen: signifies having originated, as things that come into being do, not always existing, as things without origin do
lexical_decisions.rationale: The distinction concerns coming into existence versus existing without an origin. ‘Created’ and ‘uncreated’ could introduce a maker not specified in these terms; ‘begotten’ could imply biological generation too narrowly.

lexical_decisions.chosen: brought forth from boundless matter
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb describes the egg's being projected or brought forth, while the adjective qualifies matter as unlimited. The translation does not identify a personal agent where none is supplied.

passages.text: ‘The fourfold matter was alive, and an entire boundless deep was forever flowing and moving without differentiation, bringing up countless incomplete mixtures, now one and now another, and so dissolving them in its disorder. It gaped open, unable to be bound together so as to generate a living being. At some point, as the boundless sea itself was driven around by its own nature, it happened to flow in an orderly way, by a natural movement, from the same point back to that same point, like a whirlpool, and to mix the substances. Thus, from what was audible, the richest part of everything, which was particularly suited to generating a living being, flowed through the middle of the whole as through a funnel. Driven by the whirlpool that carried everything, it moved into the depths and drew in the surrounding breath; and, gathered together as into something supremely fertile, it formed a structure capable of differentiation. For just as a bubble tends to form in liquid, so a spherical cavity took shape, enclosed on every side. Then, having been gestated within itself and being lifted by the sulfurous breath that had received it, this enormous offspring emerged into the light: a living work brought forth, as it were, from the entire boundless deep, resembling the roundness of eggs and the swiftness of flight.’

source_issues.issue: The supplied wording literally supports ‘from what was audible’ or ‘from what was heard,’ but its role in this physical account is obscure. The English retains the audible sense openly rather than conjecturally replacing the printed Greek. This is not a claim that the cosmological referent has been identified; no alternative source wording has been supplied.

lexical_decisions.chosen: The fourfold matter was alive
lexical_decisions.rationale: The matter comprises four kinds and is described as possessing life or soul. ‘The matter of four kinds was ensouled’ is more technical; ‘alive’ keeps the assertion accessible without replacing it with a modern physical explanation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐξ ἀκουστοῦ τῶν πάντων τὸ νοστιμώτατον
lexical_decisions.chosen: from what was audible, the richest part of everything
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied ἀκουστοῦ is rendered according to its ordinary sense ‘audible’ or ‘heard’; the resulting unusual phrase is not silently changed to ‘from it’ or a different cosmological expression. The superlative νοστιμώτατον is read as the choicest or richest portion, clarified by the following statement of its suitability for generating life. See the separate source issue.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς εἰς γονιμώτατον συλληφθὲν ποιεῖν κριτικὴν σύστασιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: gathered together as into something supremely fertile, it formed a structure capable of differentiation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase ὡς εἰς is retained as an analogical qualification, “as into,” rather than reduced to an unqualified description of an actual condition. The neuter superlative γονιμώτατον is rendered substantivally as “something supremely fertile”; the Greek does not expressly name a state, mass, or receptacle. The participle can evoke conception as well as gathering. For κριτικὴν σύστασιν, “a discerning constitution” is a material alternative if the adjective points to a living being's discriminating faculty rather than physical differentiation. “A structure capable of differentiation” preserves a capacity to distinguish without importing a particular physiological mechanism.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a spherical cavity took shape, enclosed on every side
lexical_decisions.rationale: Κύτος can denote a hollow container, cavity, or enclosing body; the bubble analogy favors a cavity enclosed on all sides. The translation does not identify a shell material.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὸ τοῦ παρειληφότος θειώδους πνεύματος ἀναφερόμενον
lexical_decisions.chosen: being lifted by the sulfurous breath that had received it
lexical_decisions.rationale: The active perfect participle παρειληφότος agrees with πνεύματος: the breath is the agent that has received something. The developing body is supplied as its contextually inferred object, not made the receiving agent. Θειώδης can mean sulfurous; divine-like is a material lexical alternative. The physical account of the rising enclosed breath supports sulfurous here. Πνεῦμα is rendered breath in this physical account, with wind or spirit as alternatives. The following section's explicit θεῖον πνεῦμα is separately rendered divine spirit rather than automatically homogenized with this adjective.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῇ περιφερείᾳ τῶν ὠῶν προσεοικὸς καὶ τῷ τάχει τῆς πτήσεως
lexical_decisions.chosen: resembling the roundness of eggs and the swiftness of flight
