lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόδρομος explicitly calls Simon a forerunner, while προαπατάω presents the deception as prior; the translation does not specify whose forerunner he is.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through reorientation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The context concerns moral and spiritual redirection expressed by accepting what pleases God. “Through repentance” is the traditional alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ τὰ σώματα ἀναρρῶσαι καὶ τὰς ψυχὰς ἀναλαβεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: both restore your bodies to health and recover your souls
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀναρρωννύω denotes renewed bodily strength, while ἀναλαμβάνω here presents the souls as regained or recovered; “take up your souls again” would be more formally literal.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτὸν αἰτεῖν ὡς πάντα νόμῳ κριτικῷ διδόντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: to make requests of him as the one who gives everything according to a judicial law
lexical_decisions.rationale: κριτικός can mean discriminating or judicial. “According to a law of discernment” is possible, but the surrounding emphasis on consequences and punishment favors “judicial.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: not to taste dead flesh
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording directly prohibits tasting flesh that is dead; it has not been generalized to a familiar dietary formula.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐν πολλοῖς σώμασιν μίαν γνώμην ἀναλαβόντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: taking up one mind in many bodies
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering retains the author’s image of bodily plurality united in a single judgment or disposition.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ θέλεις τὴν σὴν ὑφ’ ἑτέρου μοιχευθῆναι γυναῖκα, τὴν ἑτέρου μὴ μοίχευε γαμετήν
lexical_decisions.chosen: You do not want another to commit adultery with your wife; do not commit adultery with another man’s wedded wife
lexical_decisions.rationale: The English changes the first clause from passive to active to avoid implying sexual coercion while preserving the participants and the repeated adultery terminology. The distinction between γυναῖκα, “wife,” and γαμετήν, “wedded wife,” is also retained.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπεὶ καὶ ἐν τῷ παρόντι αἰῶνι βασανισθήσεσθε
lexical_decisions.chosen: for otherwise you will be tormented in your bodies in the present age
lexical_decisions.rationale: After an exhortation or stated favorable outcome, ἐπεί can introduce the consequence that follows otherwise. The formally possible “since indeed you will be tormented” would obscure the warning contrast supplied by the context.

passages.text: After being instructed in such things by Peter over a few days and being healed, they were baptized. Then, all deeply grieved by his further wonders, they sat together as a whole populace in the middle of the marketplaces on ashes and sackcloth, reorienting themselves over the sins they had previously committed. When those in Sidon heard these things, they did the same and sent suppliants to Peter, since they themselves were unable to come to him because of their diseases. Peter, after staying in Tyre for not many days, instructing everyone in it, freeing them from every kind of affliction, forming a church, and appointing for them a bishop from among the elders who followed him, set out for Sidon. On learning that Peter was coming, Simon immediately fled to Beirut with Appion and his companions.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοιαῦτα ὑπὸ τοῦ Πέτρου ἐν ὀλίγαις ἡμέραις κατηχηθέντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: After being instructed in such things by Peter over a few days
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατηχέω here means to instruct orally; “catechized” would preserve the later technical term but would be less accessible in modern English.

lexical_decisions.chosen: deeply grieved by his further wonders
lexical_decisions.rationale: περίλυπος takes the dative as the cause or occasion of grief, and λοιπός can mean remaining, other, or further. “Deeply grieved at his other wonders” is a close alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πανδημεὶ ἐπὶ σποδοῦ καὶ σάκκου ἐκαθέζοντο
lexical_decisions.chosen: they sat together as a whole populace ... on ashes and sackcloth
lexical_decisions.rationale: πανδημεί means collectively or with the whole populace, while ἐπί with the genitive presents ashes and sackcloth as what they sat upon.

lexical_decisions.chosen: reorienting themselves over the sins they had previously committed
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle describes moral reorientation in response to earlier sins, while ἐπί identifies those sins as its occasion. “Repenting over their former sins” is the traditional alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: forming a church
lexical_decisions.rationale: In the context of appointing a bishop from among elders, ἐκκλησία denotes an organized congregation or church, and συνίστημι denotes forming or establishing it.

lexical_decisions.chosen: On learning that Peter was coming
lexical_decisions.rationale: In the narrative sequence Peter has just set out for Sidon, so the present participle is best understood as his approach. Because ἥκω can also have a perfect-like sense, “had arrived” remains grammatically possible.

passages.text: As Peter entered Sidon, people carried many in on beds and laid them before him. But he said to them, “Then do not suppose that I can do anything for your healing, since I am myself a mortal man capable of falling prey to many sufferings. But I do not begrudge showing you the way by which you will be able to be saved, for I myself learned from the prophet of truth the determinations of God, foreordained ‘before the foundation of the world.’ I mean the evil actions for which he appointed human beings to be afflicted by the ruler of wickedness, and likewise the good actions for which he determined that those who first believed in him as he healed the bodies would be saved, and afterward that their souls too would be restored to imperishability.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Μὴ τοίνυν νομίσητε ἐμέ τι δύνασθαι πρὸς ὑμετέραν ἴασιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Then do not suppose that I can do anything for your healing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The infinitive construction expresses what the hearers must not suppose; πρὸς ὑμετέραν ἴασιν indicates ability directed toward their healing.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοὺς προωρισμένους τοῦ θεοῦ „πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου“ ὁρισμούς
lexical_decisions.chosen: the determinations of God, foreordained ‘before the foundation of the world’
lexical_decisions.rationale: “Foreordained determinations” preserves the source’s repetition of the ὁρίζω word group rather than replacing it with unrelated English terms.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the evil actions for which
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here ἐπί with the dative introduces the actions or conditions on account of which the stated consequence was appointed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὥρισεν πρότερον πιστεύσαντας αὐτῷ ἰωμένῳ τὰ σώματα σώζεσθαι, ἔπειτα καὶ τὰς ψυχὰς ἐπανορθοῦσθαι πρὸς τὸ ἀνώλεθρον
lexical_decisions.chosen: he determined that those who first believed in him as he healed the bodies would be saved, and afterward that their souls too would be restored to imperishability
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering takes τὰ σώματα as the object of the immediately preceding ἰωμένῳ. Alternatively, τὰ σώματα may specify the bodily scope of σώζεσθαι: “he determined that, after first believing in him who heals, they should be saved in body, and afterward that their souls too should be restored to imperishability.” That attachment makes the parallel between bodies and souls explicit. The immediate position of τὰ σώματα after ἰωμένῳ supports the chosen attachment, but the alternative remains syntactically viable; αὐτῷ may likewise be represented as “in him” or “him.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: to imperishability
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantivized adjective denotes the imperishable or indestructible state toward which the souls are restored.

passages.text: Knowing, then, both these good and evil actions, I announce them to you beforehand as two roads, showing you along which one people perish as they walk and along which one they are saved as they travel, guided by God. The road of those who perish is broad and very smooth, but it brings destruction without toil; the road of those who are saved is narrow and rough, but at the end it saves those who have traversed it laboriously. At the head of these two roads sit unbelief and faith. Those who have preferred pleasures travel by way of unbelief; because of those pleasures . . . . they did not even continue to seek what is beneficial. Yet they do not know that God’s purposes are not like human purposes. For first of all, he knows everyone’s thoughts, and each person is held accountable not only for undertaking something but also for intending it. Those who try to think what is good and fail act far less impiously than those who do not attempt good things at all. For God himself saw fit that the person who lapses despite knowing what is good should, after being punished moderately in proportion to human transgressions, be saved. But those who have neglected even to begin to know what is better—even if they do countless other good things—but do not adopt the religious observance he himself prescribed will, having incurred a charge of negligence, be utterly extinguished by the greatest punishment.

source_issues.source_quote: δι’ ἃς . . . . οὐδὲ ζητεῖν τὸ συμφέρον οὐ διεφύλαξαν
source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints exactly four dots between the surviving opening causal phrase and the surviving negative clause. The unavailable wording leaves the complete causal statement fragmentary, and no restoration has been supplied. The image-checked transcription verifies the printed gap but does not recover its content. Under the selected-edition coverage scope, the translation preserves the exact gap marker and defensibly represents all surviving words, so the unavailable content does not itself block publication.
The article is printed as του without the expected circumflex. This is an accentual feature and does not affect the meaning.
The print has the orthographic form ἐνχειρῆσαι where the assimilated compound spelling ἐγχειρῆσαι is more usual. The supplied form remains intelligible as the aorist infinitive of “undertake.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: At the head of these two roads sit unbelief and faith
lexical_decisions.rationale: προκάθημαι depicts unbelief and faith as positioned before or at the head of their respective roads.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δι’ ἃς . . . . οὐδὲ ζητεῖν τὸ συμφέρον οὐ διεφύλαξαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: because of those pleasures . . . . they did not even continue to seek what is beneficial
lexical_decisions.rationale: δι’ ἃς refers back to the pleasures, while διαφυλάσσω with the infinitive is understood as maintaining or continuing an activity. The two negatives are treated as emphatic negative concord; a strictly logical double-negative reading is possible in isolation but is contextually less likely. The exact four-dot gap is preserved because its unavailable wording prevents recovery of the complete causal statement.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκ ἐν τῷ ἐνχειρῆσαι μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐν τῷ ἐννοῆσαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: not only for undertaking something but also for intending it
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contrast extends accountability from beginning an action to conceiving or intending it; “something” and “it” represent the implicit object shared by the two infinitives. “Conceiving it” is also possible for ἐννοῆσαι.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἱ ἐγχειροῦντες καλὰ νοεῖν καὶ ἀποτυγχάνοντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: Those who try to think what is good and fail
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves νοεῖν as mental activity rather than adding an action not explicitly stated; “try to understand good things” is a viable lexical alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κατὰ λόγον τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων παραπτωμάτων μετρίως κολασθέντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: after being punished moderately in proportion to human transgressions
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατὰ λόγον is attached to the punishment and expresses proportion. It could instead qualify the person’s lapse as occurring according to the measure or character of human transgressions, but its placement before μετρίως κολασθέντα permits the chosen attachment.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐν ᾗ δὲ αὐτὸς ὥρισεν θρησκείᾳ μὴ γένωνται
lexical_decisions.chosen: but do not adopt the religious observance he himself prescribed
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally, they do not “come to be in” the θρησκεία he determined. “Religious observance” preserves the practical cultic or devotional sense; “religion” or “worship” is also possible in this context.

lexical_decisions.chosen: will be utterly extinguished
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb retains the image of quenching or extinguishing rather than being generalized to “will be punished” or “will perish”; “utterly” represents παντελῶς.

passages.text: The religious observance appointed by him is this: to worship him alone; to believe the one prophet of truth; to be baptized “for forgiveness of sins” and thus, through the purest immersion, to be born anew to God through the water that saves; not to partake of “a table of demons” (I mean things sacrificed to idols, animals found dead, strangled animals, animals caught by wild beasts, and blood); not to live in impurity; to bathe after intercourse with a woman, while women themselves must also observe menstrual separation; for everyone to practice self-control, do good, and not act unjustly; and to await eternal life from the all-powerful God, asking through continual prayers and petitions to receive it. As Peter gave such exhortations also in Sidon, within a few days many there too reoriented themselves, believed, and were healed. He established a church, appointed one of the elders accompanying him as their overseer, and departed from Sidon.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ τῆς ἀληθείας μόνῳ πιστεύειν προφήτῃ
lexical_decisions.chosen: to believe the one prophet of truth
lexical_decisions.rationale: μόνῳ characterizes the prophet as the sole or one prophet of truth. The phrase could also be rendered “to believe only the prophet of truth,” with the exclusivity attached adverbially to believing.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through the purest immersion
lexical_decisions.rationale: βαφή denotes dipping or immersion and here refers to the preceding baptism; the superlative force of ἁγνοτάτης is retained.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀναγεννηθῆναι θεῷ διὰ τοῦ σώζοντος ὕδατος
lexical_decisions.chosen: to be born anew to God through the water that saves
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves both the God-directed dative θεῷ and the source’s direct description of the water as saving.

lexical_decisions.chosen: animals found dead, strangled animals, animals caught by wild beasts
lexical_decisions.rationale: These substantivized plurals occur in a list of prohibited foods. “Animals found dead” expresses νεκρῶν contextually; more literally it is simply “dead things.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: to bathe after intercourse with a woman
lexical_decisions.rationale: κοίτη γυναικός literally refers to a woman’s bed but in this purity context denotes sexual intercourse.

lexical_decisions.chosen: while women themselves must also observe menstrual separation
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἄφεδρος is a term for menstruation or the associated period of separation. The phrase may also be rendered “observe the menstrual period”; the source does not explicitly repeat the preceding command to bathe.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοιαῦτα καὶ ἐν τῇ Σιδῶνι τοῦ Πέτρου παραινοῦντος
lexical_decisions.chosen: As Peter gave such exhortations also in Sidon
lexical_decisions.rationale: The additive καί is preserved with “also,” explicitly stating that Peter gave such exhortations in Sidon as well. This is distinct from the later κἀκεῖ, rendered “there too,” which characterizes the people’s response.

lexical_decisions.chosen: reoriented themselves
lexical_decisions.rationale: The context describes moral and religious redirection accompanying belief; the traditional alternative is “repented.” No Godward phrase is added because the Greek does not state one here.

lexical_decisions.chosen: overseer
lexical_decisions.rationale: The word designates the supervisory office assigned to the elder; “bishop” is a possible institutional rendering but may imply a later fixed title.

passages.text: As soon as he set foot in Berytus, an earthquake occurred. The crowds approached Peter and said, “Help us! For we are afraid,” they declared, “that perhaps we may all be utterly destroyed.” Then Simon, taking courage, together with Appion, Anubion, Athenodorus, and the rest of his companions, publicly shouted to the crowds against Peter: “Flee from this man, men! He is a magician—believe it! He himself brought the earthquake upon us and stirred up the diseases, so that he might overawe you as though he himself were a god.” Simon’s party made many such false claims against Peter, alleging that he possessed power beyond human capacity. But when the crowds fell silent for him, Peter gave a slight smile and said with startling boldness, “Men, I acknowledge that, if God wills, I am able to do the very things these men say. What is more, if you do not heed me in what I say, I am ready to tear your entire city up from its foundations.”

source_issues.issue: The purpose clause is printed with the future indicative καταπλήξεται after ἵνα rather than the more classically expected subjunctive. The selected edition’s reading is construed provisionally as later Greek syntax supporting a purpose clause; no emendation is required for a defensible translation, and the feature is not treated as an OCR defect.

lexical_decisions.chosen: set foot in Berytus
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιβαίνω with the genitive can denote entering or setting foot in a place; “Berytus” preserves the ancient city name rather than modernizing it to Beirut.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ τὸν σεισμὸν αὐτὸς ἐποίησεν ἡμῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: He himself brought the earthquake upon us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative ἡμῖν presents the earthquake as something caused for or against the speakers; “upon us” conveys the hostile result.

lexical_decisions.chosen: so that he might overawe you
lexical_decisions.rationale: καταπλήσσω can denote terrifying, stunning, or overwhelming with amazement. “Overawe” fits the accusation that Peter is using wonders to induce a false perception of divinity. The purpose interpretation of the printed future indicative after ἵνα is contextually defensible but remains provisional.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as though he himself were a god
lexical_decisions.rationale: The anarthrous predicate θεός permits “a god,” while “God” is also possible in the work’s monotheistic setting. The chosen wording preserves the accusers’ comparison without identifying Peter with the supreme God unambiguously.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς ὑπὲρ δύναμιν ἀνθρωπίνην δυναμένου τοῦ Πέτρου
lexical_decisions.chosen: alleging that he possessed power beyond human capacity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The ὡς construction presents this superhuman ability as the content or guise of Simon’s party’s false allegations.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with startling boldness
lexical_decisions.rationale: παρρησία denotes open, confident speech, while καταπληκτική marks its astonishing or overwhelming effect.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to tear your entire city up from its foundations
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐκβαθρεύω evokes uprooting or razing down to the foundations, an image stronger than simply “destroy.”

passages.text: When the crowds became frightened and promised to act otherwise as they might be commanded by him, Peter said, “None of you is to associate with these sorcerers or mingle with them.” As soon as the crowds heard the brief command, they picked up sticks and pursued them until they had driven them completely out of the city. Then the sick and demon-possessed among them came in and threw themselves at Peter’s feet. But when he saw this and wished to dispel their consternation, he said to them:

source_issues.source_quote: ἑτέρως ποιήσειν ἐπαγγειλαμένων ὅπερ ἂν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ κελεύωνται
source_issues.issue: The printed adverb ἑτέρως (“differently” or “otherwise”) produces a compressed connection with the following relative clause, but it can defensibly mean that the crowds promised to change their conduct in conformity with his commands. The smoother ἑτοίμως (“readily”) is only a possible conjecture and has not been used in the translation.
source_issues.proposed_reading: ἑτοίμως ποιήσειν ἐπαγγειλαμένων ὅπερ ἂν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ κελεύωνται

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἑτέρως ποιήσειν ἐπαγγειλαμένων ὅπερ ἂν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ κελεύωνται
lexical_decisions.chosen: promised to act otherwise as they might be commanded by him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied ἑτέρως is taken in its normal sense, “differently” or “otherwise,” indicating a promised change of conduct in accordance with Peter’s commands. The connection with the following relative clause is compressed but yields a defensible contextual sense.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with these sorcerers
lexical_decisions.rationale: γόης can denote a sorcerer, charlatan, or impostor. “Sorcerers” fits the immediately preceding accusation of magic, though “charlatans” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the brief command
lexical_decisions.rationale: σύντομος characterizes the command as concise or terse; “brief” preserves its form without adding an emotional tone.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they picked up sticks
lexical_decisions.rationale: ξύλα literally denotes pieces of wood; in the pursuit scene, “sticks” expresses their likely use without specifying weapons more precisely than the source.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the sick and demon-possessed among them
lexical_decisions.rationale: αὐτῶν most naturally refers to the crowds, though grammatically it could be heard as a possessive “their.” “Among them” avoids implying that the crowds owned or controlled the afflicted people.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to dispel their consternation
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατάπληξις can be amazement, shock, or terror. In the aftermath of Peter’s threat and the people’s prostration, “consternation” preserves both alarm and astonishment.

passages.text: If I were able to cause earthquakes and to do anything at all I wish, I am not saying that I would annihilate Simon together with his companions—for I have not been sent to bring destruction on human beings—but I would make him my friend, so that, by slandering my true proclamation, he might not hinder many on their way to salvation. But if you believe me, he himself is a magician, he himself a slanderer, he himself a servant of evil against those who do not know the truth. And for this reason he can produce diseases in those who sin, having those who sin as partners in the power directed against them. But I am a servant of God, who made all things, and a disciple of his right-side prophet. Therefore, as that prophet’s apostle, I speak the truth. For in serving what is good, I also drive diseases away. For I was sent second, since disease goes first and healing follows. Thus, through that magician who does evil, having disbelieved God, you became ill; but through me, if you believe him, you will be healed. For in this way, having experienced power and turned to doing good, you might also be able to be saved in your souls.

source_issues.issue: The postpositive τε has no explicit correlative in the printed construction. It can provisionally be read as a weak connective whose force is absorbed into the coordinated contrast, so no correction is required.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Σίμωνα οὐ λέγω ὅτι μετὰ τῶν αὐτοῦ ἑταίρων ἐξωλόθρευον
lexical_decisions.chosen: I am not saying that I would annihilate Simon together with his companions
lexical_decisions.rationale: The imperfect ἐξωλόθρευον functions as the unreal result of the preceding condition; “annihilate” preserves its intensive destructive force.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he himself a slanderer
lexical_decisions.rationale: διάβολος can mean “slanderer” or “devil.” The nearby cognate διαβάλλων (“slandering”) supports the common-noun sense, while “he himself a devil” remains a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he can produce diseases in those who sin
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἁμαρτάνουσι is taken as a dative plural participle, anticipated by τοὺς ἁμαρτάνοντας. Morphologically it could instead be finite—“they sin”—with a sentence break after it.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: συνεργοὺς ἔχων τοὺς ἁμαρτάνοντας τῆς κατ’ αὐτῶν δυνάμεως
lexical_decisions.chosen: having those who sin as partners in the power directed against them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The sinners paradoxically cooperate in the power exercised against them; the rendering preserves both the partnership and the hostile direction of the power.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a disciple of his right-side prophet
lexical_decisions.rationale: δεξιοῦ modifies “prophet” and marks him as right or right-sided. “Right-hand prophet” is possible, but may suggest merely a trusted assistant; replacing it with “true prophet” would erase the printed wording.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as that prophet’s apostle
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐκείνου most naturally refers to the immediately preceding prophet. Reference to God is grammatically possible but less immediate.

lexical_decisions.chosen: For in serving what is good
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantival ἀγαθῷ may denote goodness or a good person, including “the Good One.” The neutral wording preserves the contrast with serving evil without fixing the referent.

lexical_decisions.chosen: For I was sent second
lexical_decisions.rationale: δεύτερος indicates his position in the sequence subsequently explained: disease precedes and healing follows.

lexical_decisions.chosen: if you believe him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The pronoun is retained in English. God is the most likely antecedent because this belief contrasts with τῷ θεῷ ἀπιστήσαντες, though the magician is grammatically nearer.

lexical_decisions.chosen: having experienced power
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantival δυνατοῦ can denote what is powerful or “the Powerful One.” The main rendering expresses the experience of power without fixing a personal referent; “having experienced the Powerful One” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you might also be able to be saved in your souls
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀνασωθῆναι is passive, so the addressees do not actively save their own souls. The rendering takes τὰς ψυχὰς as an accusative of respect—“as regards your souls”—and preserves the contrast with the preceding bodily healing; “you might also be able to have your souls rescued” is a possible but less direct English formulation.

passages.text: As he was saying these things, they all lay kneeling at his feet. He, however, raised his hands toward heaven, prayed to God, and healed them all by prayer alone. After remaining with the people of Beirut for quite a few days, accustoming many to monarchical worship and baptizing them, and appointing as their bishop one of the elders who followed him, he departed for Byblos. When he arrived there and learned that Simon had not stayed with them for even one day but had immediately hurried to Tripolis, he stayed with them for a few days, healed quite a few people, and trained them in the books; then he traveled to Tripolis in Simon’s tracks, having chosen to pursue him rather than flee from him.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: γονυπετεῖς πρὸ τῶν αὐτοῦ ἔκειντο ποδῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: they all lay kneeling at his feet
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording preserves both ἔκειντο, “lay,” and γονυπετεῖς, “kneeling” or “fallen on the knees.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: accustoming many to monarchical worship
lexical_decisions.rationale: θρησκεία can mean worship, religious observance, or religion, while μοναρχική evokes sole rule or sovereignty. “The religion of sole rule” is a possible more literal alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: appointing as their bishop one
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπίσκοπος literally denotes an overseer, but “bishop” fits the explicitly appointed community office in this historical narrative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with the people of Beirut
lexical_decisions.rationale: The Greek uses the civic demonym rather than the city name; the rendering makes that reference explicit in conventional English.

lexical_decisions.chosen: trained them in the books
lexical_decisions.rationale: The definite plural βίβλοις is retained as “the books”; the source does not explicitly identify them as Scripture.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in Simon’s tracks
lexical_decisions.rationale: This preserves the source’s physical trail or footprint image rather than reducing it to the abstract “after Simon.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: to pursue him rather than flee from him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contrast is between continuing the pursuit and withdrawing or slipping away; “flee from him” gives the natural English opposition.

passages.text: As Peter was entering Tripolis, many of those more eager to learn, from Tyre and Sidon as well as Beirut and Byblos and the neighboring districts, were entering with him. Especially, too, crowds from the city itself were converging, wishing to question him. So in the suburbs we were met by the brothers whom he had sent out to ascertain precisely both the other matters concerning the city and what Simon was doing, so that they might return and give an account. They welcomed him and led him to the house of Maroones.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those more eager to learn
lexical_decisions.rationale: The comparative describes people especially fond of learning; “the more inquisitive” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: wishing to question him
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἱστορεῖν with a personal object can mean to inquire of or question someone, rather than merely to learn about that person.

lexical_decisions.chosen: what Simon was doing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative may denote Simon's activities or affairs; “what was happening with Simon” is a viable broader rendering.

lexical_decisions.chosen: so that they might return and give an account
lexical_decisions.rationale: The motion is understood contextually as coming back to Peter after their fact-finding mission; more literally, “so that, having come, they might explain.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: led him to the house of Maroones
lexical_decisions.rationale: Μαροόνου is treated as the genitive of the personal name Μαροόνης, transliterated Maroones.

passages.text: When he had already reached the very gate of the guesthouse, he turned to the crowds and promised to speak with them about reverence for God after the coming night. When he entered, the advance party prepared lodging for those who had gathered. Nor did those who received and hosted them fall short of the eagerness of those asking to host them. Peter knew nothing of these arrangements, and when we invited him to partake of food, he said that he himself would not partake before those who had come with him had found rest. We answered, “This has already been accomplished as follows: making their affection for you their plea, people received all of them with such eagerness that those who had obtained no one to host were exceedingly grieved.” When Peter heard this, he was delighted; and after blessing them for their prompt kindness, he went out, bathed in the sea, came back inside, partook of food with the advance party, and, as evening came on, went to sleep.

source_issues.issue: The omitted noun creates a genuine temporal ambiguity. Supplying the conventional ἡμέραν gives “after the following day,” while the narrative sequence supports supplying νύκτα, “after the coming night.” No textual alteration is proposed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπ’ αὐτῷ τῷ τῆς ξενίας πυλῶνι
lexical_decisions.chosen: at the very gate of the guesthouse
lexical_decisions.rationale: ξενία can denote hospitality, lodging, or guest quarters; the mention of a gate favors a place of lodging.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after the coming night
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine adjective has an omitted noun. Although ἡ ἐπιοῦσα often means “the following day,” the subsequent evening, sleep, and expectation of an address “today” favor understanding an ensuing night here.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the advance party
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun denotes those sent ahead, identified later as the twelve who had gone in advance.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the eagerness of those asking to host them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The object of ἀξιούντων is unstated. The subsequent grief of people who obtained no guests supports understanding these as prospective hosts asking to receive travelers. Alternatively, the phrase may mean “the eagerness of those requesting hospitality or lodging,” referring to travelers or those arranging lodging for them; “those who considered it an honor” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those who had come with him had found rest
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative αὐτῷ is taken as associative with συνεληλυθότας, identifying those who had accompanied or joined Peter, rather than people assembled for his benefit.

lexical_decisions.chosen: making their affection for you their plea
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόφασις can mean a pretext, plea, or stated reason; “plea” preserves the expressed motive without necessarily implying insincerity.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for their prompt kindness
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally “keen” or “swift benevolence”; the context emphasizes the speed and eagerness of their hospitality.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as evening came on, went to sleep
lexical_decisions.rationale: The image is of evening overtaking or coming upon the situation; idiomatic English uses “came on.”

passages.text: At about the second crowing of the roosters, he awoke and found us awake. All of us with him numbered sixteen: Peter himself, I, Clement, Nicetas and Aquila, and the twelve who had gone ahead. After greeting us, he said, “Today, since we are not devoting our time to those outside, we are free for one another. Therefore I will recount to you what happened after the departure from Tyre, and you tell me what Simon has done here and explain it in greater detail.” After we had exchanged our accounts in turn, one of the companions presented a report to Peter, saying, “Simon, having learned that you had arrived, set out on the road toward Syria. The crowds have regarded this one night as a year's span and are unable to wait for the time appointed by you. They are standing before the doors in clusters and gatherings, talking with one another about Simon's slander. They say that after raising their expectations and promising that, when you came, he would expose you as guilty of many evils, he learned that you had arrived and fled by night. But as they long to hear you, a certain rumor—I do not know from where—has fallen upon them that you are going to speak with them today. Therefore, so that they do not wear themselves out for a long time only to disperse to no purpose, you yourself know what you ought to do.”

source_issues.source_quote: εἰσήγει τις τῶν συνήθων ἀπαγγέλλων Πέτρῳ
source_issues.issue: The verified print reads εἰσήγει. It is provisionally analyzed as the imperfect of εἰσηγέω, “introduce” or “present,” rather than silently normalized to εἰσῄει, “was coming in.” Because the object of εἰσήγει is implicit, “presented a report” is contextual; “introduced the matter, reporting to Peter” is a viable alternative.

The supplied print has a hyphen between the article and the name. It has no evident syntactic or lexical function and is provisionally treated as an editorial or line-division feature rather than as part of the name.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὸ δὲ τὰς δευτέρας τῶν ἀλεκτρυόνων φωνὰς
lexical_decisions.chosen: At about the second crowing of the roosters
lexical_decisions.rationale: The plural phrase refers to the second cockcrow or round of rooster calls; ὑπό here marks approximate time.

lexical_decisions.chosen: since we are not devoting our time to those outside
lexical_decisions.rationale: σχολάζω with the dative means to be occupied with or devote time to someone; τοῖς ἔξω may mean outsiders generally or, in context, the people physically outside.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀμειψαμένων οὖν ἀλλήλους ταῖς ἐν μέρει διηγήσεσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: After we had exchanged our accounts in turn
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐν μέρει indicates narration by turns, with each side giving its account.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰσήγει τις τῶν συνήθων ἀπαγγέλλων Πέτρῳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: one of the companions presented a report to Peter
lexical_decisions.rationale: The printed εἰσήγει is taken as an imperfect of εἰσηγέω, “introduce” or “present,” while ἀπαγγέλλων Πέτρῳ identifies the action as reporting to Peter. The object of εἰσήγει is implicit; “introduced the matter, reporting to Peter” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: set out on the road toward Syria
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπί with the accusative expresses direction toward Syria; ὁρμάω conveys setting out energetically.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Simon's slander
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαβολή can mean slander, accusation, or calumny; the ensuing claim against Peter supports “slander.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: raising their expectations
lexical_decisions.rationale: μετεωρίζω can mean to lift up, excite, or keep in suspense; the promised confrontation has heightened their expectations.

lexical_decisions.chosen: expose you as guilty of many evils
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐλέγχειν may mean expose, convict, or refute, while ἐπὶ πολλοῖς κακοῖς states the alleged wrongs on which the exposure would rest.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a certain rumor ... has fallen upon them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording preserves the source's image of a rumor falling upon or overtaking the crowd; “has reached them” would be more idiomatic.

lexical_decisions.chosen: disperse to no purpose
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀλόγως can mean unreasonably, pointlessly, or without due cause; the concern is that their prolonged waiting might prove futile.

passages.text: And Peter, marveling at the crowds' eagerness, answered, “See, brothers, how our Lord's words are visibly being fulfilled. For I remember him saying, ‘Many will come from east and west, north and south, and will recline in the bosoms of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob.’ But he also says, ‘Many are called, but few are chosen.’ Thus the part about their coming when called has been fulfilled. But since this is not their own doing, but God's—‘the one who called’ them and caused them to come—they have no reward for this alone, because it is not their own doing but belongs to the one who brought it about. But if, after being called, they do good deeds, which is their own doing, then they will have a reward for this.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἱ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν λόγοι ἐμφανῶς τελοῦνται
lexical_decisions.chosen: our Lord's words are visibly being fulfilled
lexical_decisions.rationale: τελοῦνται denotes being accomplished or fulfilled, while ἐμφανῶς stresses that the fulfillment is evident.

lexical_decisions.chosen: north and south
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἄρκτος, literally “the Bear,” denotes the north, while μεσημβρία, literally “midday,” denotes the south.

lexical_decisions.chosen: will recline in the bosoms
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves both the banquet image of reclining and the unusual plural κόλπους; “at the breastsides” or “in the embraces” would interpret the image more strongly.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ μὲν οὖν ἐλθεῖν αὐτοὺς κληθέντας πεπλήρωται
lexical_decisions.chosen: the part about their coming when called has been fulfilled
lexical_decisions.rationale: The articular infinitive identifies their coming in response to being called as the element already fulfilled.

lexical_decisions.chosen: this is not their own doing
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἴδιον marks what belongs distinctively to them; “doing” fits the contrast with God's action and their later good deeds.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who called
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source itself marks this phrase as a quotation, so the quotation is retained rather than absorbed into the surrounding clause.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who brought it about
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐνεργέω here refers to the agent who effected their coming, not merely one who was active in a general sense.

lexical_decisions.chosen: do good deeds
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase refers to performing morally good actions, in contrast with merely responding to the divine call.

passages.text: “For not even Hebrews who believe Moses while not keeping what was said through him are saved, unless they keep what was said to them. For even the fact that they believed Moses did not arise from their own decision, but from God, who said to Moses, ‘Look, I myself am coming to you in a pillar of cloud, so that the people may hear me speaking to you and may believe you forever.’ Therefore, since for both Hebrews and those called from the nations, believing teachers of truth has come from God, while good deeds have been left to each person to perform according to that person's own judgment, the reward is rightly paid to those who do good. For there would have been no need either for Moses or for Jesus's coming, if indeed they were willing to understand what is reasonable on their own; nor does salvation come about by believing teachers and calling them lords.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ δι’ αὐτοῦ ῥηθέντα μὴ φυλάσσοντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: while not keeping what was said through him
lexical_decisions.rationale: φυλάσσω here means to observe or obey what was spoken, while διά presents Moses as the one through whom it was communicated.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the fact that they believed Moses
lexical_decisions.rationale: The articular infinitive makes their belief in Moses the subject of the clause; πιστεύω with the dative can mean believe or trust someone.

lexical_decisions.chosen: did not arise from their own decision
lexical_decisions.rationale: βουλή may mean counsel, purpose, or decision; “decision” best expresses the contrast with God's initiative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in a pillar of cloud
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording specifically presents a pillar of cloud and is not replaced by a more familiar rendering from another textual form.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those called from the nations
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase identifies people called from among the nations; “Gentiles who were called” is a viable idiomatic alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: believing teachers of truth
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative construction denotes placing belief or trust in teachers characterized as teachers of truth.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν καλῶν πράξεων ἰδίᾳ κρίσει ἑκάστῳ ποιεῖν ἀπολελειμμένων
lexical_decisions.chosen: good deeds have been left to each person to perform according to that person's own judgment
lexical_decisions.rationale: The construction contrasts divinely produced belief with actions left to each individual's κρίσις, which may also be rendered “choice” or “decision.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: Jesus's coming
lexical_decisions.rationale: παρουσία can denote presence, arrival, or coming; the contrast with the need for Moses favors Jesus's historical coming, though “the presence of Jesus” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: what is reasonable
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective used substantivally denotes what accords with reason; “the reasonable course” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: calling them lords
lexical_decisions.rationale: The plural κυρίους may mean lords or masters. “Lords” preserves the source's title-like wording and its application to the teachers under discussion.

passages.text: For this reason, Jesus is concealed from the Hebrews who have received Moses as teacher, while Moses is hidden from those who have trusted Jesus; for since the teaching through both is one, God accepts the person who has trusted either of them. But trusting a teacher is for the sake of doing the things spoken by God. That this is so, our Lord himself says: “I praise you, Father of heaven and earth, because you hid these things from wise elders and revealed them to nursing infants.” Thus God himself hid a teacher from some, since they already knew what must be done, but revealed one to others, since they did not know what they ought to do.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those who have trusted Jesus
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect of πιστεύω with a personal object can denote placing trust in someone; “believed Jesus” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I praise you
lexical_decisions.rationale: In an address to God, ἐξομολογοῦμαι can express praise or thanksgiving rather than confession; “I give thanks to you” is a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: wise elders
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both terms are retained as printed rather than harmonized with a familiar form of the quotation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: since they already knew
lexical_decisions.rationale: The context contrasts prior knowledge of what to do with ignorance; the more formally temporal “since they had known beforehand” remains possible.

passages.text: Therefore, neither are the Hebrews condemned for not knowing Jesus, because of the one who hid him, provided that, while doing the things through Moses .... they do not hate the one they did not know; nor, in turn, are those from the nations who did not know Moses condemned because of the one who concealed him, provided that they too, while doing the things spoken through Jesus, do not hate the one they did not know. Nor do people gain any benefit by calling their teachers “lords” while not performing servants’ duties. For this reason, our Jesus said to someone who repeatedly called him Lord but did nothing that he commanded: “Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I say?” For saying will not benefit anyone, but doing will. In every way, therefore, good works are needed. Yet if anyone should be deemed worthy to recognize both of them as proclaiming one teaching, that man has been counted rich in God, having understood the ancient things to be new with respect to time and the new things to be old.

source_issues.source_quote: ἐάν γε πράττοντες τὰ διὰ Μωϋσέως .... ὃν ἠγνόησαν μὴ μισήσωσιν
source_issues.issue: The selected image-checked edition contains a confirmed four-dot printed lacuna after “the things through Moses.” Its lost content and precise syntactic contribution are unavailable, so the four dots are retained exactly and no restoration is supplied. This prevents recovery of the complete lost wording but does not block publication of a translation explicitly representing the selected edition’s surviving text and printed gap.

lexical_decisions.chosen: not performing servants’ duties
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantival phrase means the things characteristic of servants. In accordance with the reader-facing wording policy, δούλων is rendered “servants,” but it can denote slaves or owned or bonded servants; the contrast with “lords” invokes their subordinate status and obligations.

lexical_decisions.chosen: repeatedly
lexical_decisions.rationale: The comparative adverb can mean “more frequently” or, idiomatically, “rather frequently”; the context emphasizes repeated address.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοὺς ἀμφοτέρους ἐπιγνῶναι ὡς μιᾶς διδασκαλίας ὑπ’ αὐτῶν κεκηρυγμένης
lexical_decisions.chosen: to recognize both of them as proclaiming one teaching
lexical_decisions.rationale: This renders the teaching proclaimed by both as the basis or content of recognizing them together. The ὡς with the genitive absolute may alternatively be represented more explicitly as “to recognize both of them, inasmuch as one teaching has been proclaimed by them.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: In every way, therefore
lexical_decisions.rationale: The idiom stresses necessity by every consideration; “by all means” is an alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τά τε ἀρχαῖα νέα τῷ χρόνῳ καὶ τὰ καινὰ παλαιὰ ὄντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: the ancient things to be new with respect to time and the new things to be old
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the printed paradox. τῷ χρόνῳ may alternatively be understood as “with time” or “in relation to time.”

passages.text: As Peter was saying these things, the crowds entered the place where he was, as though summoned by someone. When he saw the large crowd flowing gently in like the quiet current of a river, he said to Maroones, “Where around here do you have a place better able to hold the crowds?” When Maroones led him on to an outdoor place laid out as a garden, the crowds followed. Peter took his stand on the not very high pedestal of a statue and, immediately upon greeting the crowd according to a devout custom, knowing that many among the crowds present had for many years been tormented by demons and numerous afflictions, gnashing their teeth amid wailing and falling down in supplication, he rebuked them and ordered them to remain quiet. Then, after promising healing once he had delivered his discourse, he began to speak as follows:

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὥσπερ ποταμοῦ ἥσυχον ῥεῦμα πράως προσρέοντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: flowing gently in like the quiet current of a river
lexical_decisions.rationale: The comparison presents the approaching crowd as a calm river current rather than as a violent rush.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Maroones
lexical_decisions.rationale: The name is transliterated from its dative form; the corresponding nominative is Μαροόνης.

lexical_decisions.chosen: an outdoor place laid out as a garden
lexical_decisions.rationale: κεκηπευμένον describes a place cultivated or arranged as a garden; “a cultivated open-air place” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: gnashing their teeth amid wailing
lexical_decisions.rationale: βρύχω commonly describes gnashing, though “roaring” or “growling” is lexically possible in this depiction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: once he had delivered his discourse
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive-form verb is used in the deponent sense of speaking or discoursing; “after he had spoken” is a less specific alternative.

passages.text: As I begin to deliver the discourse concerning reverence for God to people who know nothing at all and whose minds have been stained by the slanders of Simon, our opponent, I have thought it necessary first to deliver a discourse on why one must not blame God, who made everything. I begin nowhere else than from the very occasion that he himself providentially presented at the opportune moment, so that it may be known that with good reason many people have been held fast by many demons and overtaken by strange afflictions, in order that in this too God’s justice may become apparent; and so that those who blame him through ignorance, even now, after learning how they ought to think, may call themselves back from their former accusation by speaking well and doing good, offering ignorance—the cause of their wicked audacity—as grounds for pardon.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὸ τῶν τοῦ ἀντικειμένου ἡμῖν Σίμωνος διαβολῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: by the slanders of Simon, our opponent
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive construction identifies Simon as the one opposing the speakers and as the source of the slanders.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀπ᾽ αὐτῆς τῆς κατὰ πρόνοιαν ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ εὐκαίρως ὑποβληθείσης προφάσεως
lexical_decisions.chosen: from the very occasion that he himself providentially presented at the opportune moment
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόφασις here can denote an occasion or starting point, not necessarily a deceptive pretext; αὐτοῦ most naturally refers to God.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with good reason
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverb asserts that the demonic and physical afflictions occurred on reasonable or justifiable grounds, rather than merely describing them as intelligible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: may call themselves back from their former accusation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording can depict withdrawal from their prior accusation against God. Alternatively, ἔγκλημα may denote the charge or culpability they incurred, yielding “extricate themselves from their former charge.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: by speaking well and doing good
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the parallel between favorable speech and beneficial action; “through praise and good works” is also possible.

passages.text: The matter is as follows: when the only good God had made everything well and handed it over to the human being who had come into being according to his image, the one who had come into being, breathing the divinity of the one who made him, being a true prophet and knowing all things, in honor of the father who had given him everything and for the salvation of the sons who came from him, as a genuine father preserving his goodwill toward the children brought into being by him, and wishing them, for their own benefit, to love God and be loved by him, revealed the road that leads to friendship with him. He taught by what human actions the sole God and Master of all rejoices; and, after declaring the things pleasing to him, he established an eternal law for all, one that cannot be burned up by war, is not secretly adulterated by any impious person, and is not hidden in a single place, but can be read by everyone. Consequently, through obedience to the law, everything was abundant for them: the finest fruits, the full span of years free from pain and disease, all securely bestowed along with every temperate condition of the air.

source_issues.issue: The supplied print has smooth-breathing ἐνὶ, which can be the extended preposition “in,” giving “not hidden away in a place.” The main rendering provisionally takes it in the contextual numeral/locative sense “in a single place,” for which the usual numeral form would be ἑνὶ. The contrast with “but can be read by everyone” supports that interpretation, but does not make it certain. This is a disclosed printed orthographic and lexical ambiguity, not an asserted OCR defect or an unresolved loss of source content.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: παραδεδωκότος τῷ κατ᾽ εἰκόνα αὐτοῦ γενομένῳ ἀνθρώπῳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: handed it over to the human being who had come into being according to his image
lexical_decisions.rationale: παραδίδωμι here denotes handing over or entrusting the created order, while κατ᾽ εἰκόνα is retained as “according to his image.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς τοῦ πεποιηκότος αὐτὸν πνέων θειότητος
lexical_decisions.chosen: breathing the divinity of the one who made him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The unusual genitive construction is preserved without resolving whether πνέων means breathing in, breathing forth, or manifesting the maker’s divinity.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the sons who came from him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase uses ἐξ αὐτοῦ to express origin from him.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς τοὺς ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ γενομένους παῖδας
lexical_decisions.chosen: toward the children brought into being by him
lexical_decisions.rationale: Unlike the preceding ἐξ αὐτοῦ, ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ marks agency, so the observable distinction is retained without implying that the phrases necessarily identify different groups.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν πρὸς φιλίαν αὐτοῦ ἄγουσαν ἐξέφηνεν ὁδόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: revealed the road that leads to friendship with him
lexical_decisions.rationale: αὐτοῦ most naturally refers to God; “his friendship” is possible but less explicit about the direction of the road.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he established an eternal law for all
lexical_decisions.rationale: τοῖς ὅλοις may refer to all people or to the whole created order; the inclusive “for all” preserves that breadth.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μήτε πολέμῳ ἐμπρησθῆναι δυνάμενον μήθ᾽ ὑπὸ ἀσεβοῦς τινὸς ὑπονοθευόμενον μήτε ἐνὶ τόπῳ ἀποκεκρυμμένον, ἀλλὰ πᾶσιν ἀναγνωσθῆναι δυνάμενον
lexical_decisions.chosen: one that cannot be burned up by war, is not secretly adulterated by any impious person, and is not hidden in a single place, but can be read by everyone
lexical_decisions.rationale: The inability expressed by δυνάμενον is attached explicitly to being burned, while the next two participles describe separately negated states. The final δυνάμενον expressly states the law’s ability to be read by everyone.

lexical_decisions.chosen: is not secretly adulterated by any impious person
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπονοθεύω denotes covert falsification, adulteration, or interpolation; “is not covertly tampered with” is a broader alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in a single place
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering provisionally understands printed ἐνὶ in the numeral/locative sense associated with ἑνί, because concealment in one particular place contrasts directly with the law’s being readable by everyone. As printed, however, ἐνὶ can instead be the extended preposition “in,” yielding “in a place”; that alternative remains viable.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ τῶν ἐτῶν τέλεια καὶ ἄλυπα καὶ ἄνοσα
lexical_decisions.chosen: the full span of years free from pain and disease
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression is elliptical; it can denote complete years or a full lifetime, characterized as painless and healthy.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μετὰ πάσης τῆς τῶν ἀέρων εὐκρασίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: along with every temperate condition of the air
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὐκρασία denotes a favorable balance or temperateness, while the plural ἀέρων can encompass atmospheric or climatic conditions.

passages.text: But because they had not first experienced evils, they were insensible to the gift of good things and, through plentiful nourishment and luxury, were turning toward ingratitude, so that they thought there was no providence at all, since they had received the good things as a reward without first laboring for righteousness. For none of them had fallen under any affliction, sickness, or other necessity, so that—as people are inclined to do when distressed by grievous misfortune—they might look around for the God able to heal them. But in fact, immediately after the contempt born of their fearlessness and carefree luxury, a just punishment met them, as though following from a certain harmoniously ordered sequence: it thrust away the good things as having harmed them and brought in the evils in exchange as having benefited them.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπεὶ μὴ πρότερον καμόντες ἐπὶ δικαιοσύνης· ὡς μισθὸν τὰ ἀγαθὰ εἰλήφεσαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: since they had received the good things as a reward without first laboring for righteousness
lexical_decisions.rationale: The printed punctuation and word order favor taking μή with καμόντες: the good things were received without prior righteous labor. A broader scope for μή, “since they had not received the good things as a reward after first laboring for righteousness,” is also grammatically possible and likewise emphasizes that the benefits were unearned.

lexical_decisions.chosen: when distressed by grievous misfortune
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαμαρτία can denote a failure, reverse, or misfortune; “grievous misfortune” fits the affliction-and-healing context without specifying its nature more narrowly.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὥσπερ ἐξ ἁρμονίας τινὸς ἀκολούθως ἐφηρμοσμένης
lexical_decisions.chosen: as though following from a certain harmoniously ordered sequence
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording depicts punishment as emerging in due succession from an arrangement whose parts have been fitted together harmoniously.

passages.text: For among the spirits inhabiting heaven, the angels dwelling in the lowest region, distressed at humanity’s ingratitude toward God, ask to enter human life, so that, by becoming humans in reality and exposing through their higher way of life those who had been ungrateful to him, they might there and then subject each one to the punishment deserved. When, then, they received what they had asked for, they changed themselves into every kind of nature, since they were of a more divine substance and could readily turn themselves into anything. They became a precious stone, a much-admired pearl, perhaps the most beautiful purple, renowned gold, and every sort of costly material. They fell into the hands of some people and into the laps of others and willingly allowed themselves to be stolen by them. They also changed into four-footed animals, reptiles, swimming creatures, winged creatures, and anything else they wished. Your poets also sing of these things at random because they have no fear, attributing to a single being the many and varied deeds of them all.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν γὰρ τὸν οὐρανὸν ἐνοικούντων πνευμάτων
lexical_decisions.chosen: For among the spirits inhabiting heaven
lexical_decisions.rationale: The initial γάρ explicitly presents the angels’ intervention as an explanation of the punishment introduced in the preceding section.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through their higher way of life
lexical_decisions.rationale: πολιτεία here denotes conduct or a way of life, and the following section says that the angels intended to demonstrate the possibility of pious conduct. The comparative may alternatively mean “more extensive” rather than “higher.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: perhaps the most beautiful purple
lexical_decisions.rationale: πορφύρα may denote purple material or dye, while εἰ τύχοι introduces it as a possible example, literally “if it should happen.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: sing of these things at random because they have no fear
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀφοβία literally denotes fearlessness but can imply brazen audacity here; ὡς ἔτυχεν means without careful discrimination, “as it happens” or “at random.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐνὶ τοίνυν τὰς πάντων πολλὰς καὶ διαφόρους πράξεις ἀπονέμοντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: attributing to a single being the many and varied deeds of them all
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐνί means “to one”; “being” is supplied only to make the otherwise unspecified singular referent intelligible in English.

passages.text: However, when by becoming these things they had exposed as greedy those who seized them, they changed themselves into human nature so that, after living piously and showing that such conduct was possible, they might subject the ungrateful to an accounting. But because they truly became human in every respect and acquired human desire, they were overcome by it and slipped into intercourse with women. Once entangled with them, congealed by defilement, and completely emptied of their original power, they were not strong enough to recombine their limbs, which had been transformed from fire, into the original undefiled state of their own nature. For under the weight of their fire, which through desire had ended in flesh, they traveled the impious road downward. Fettered by bonds of flesh, they have been held down and tightly bound; for this reason they could no longer ascend into the heavens.

source_issues.source_quote: εἰς τὸ πρῶτον αὐτῶν τῆς ἰδίας φύσεως ἀμίαντον· μετασυγκρῖναι οὐκ ἐξίσχυσαν.
source_issues.issue: The supplied edition prints a high stop before the delayed infinitive μετασυγκρῖναι. The translation provisionally treats this as an editorial or rhetorical break rather than as a boundary preventing εἰς τὸ πρῶτον αὐτῶν τῆς ἰδίας φύσεως ἀμίαντον from expressing the state into which they could not recombine their limbs. The printed punctuation is verified and is not treated as an OCR defect.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπειδὴ ὄντως τὰ πάντα ἄνθρωποι ἐγίνοντο
lexical_decisions.chosen: because they truly became human in every respect
lexical_decisions.rationale: The accusative τὰ πάντα functions adverbially, indicating complete rather than merely apparent participation in human nature.

lexical_decisions.chosen: congealed by defilement
lexical_decisions.rationale: παγέντες evokes being fixed, congealed, or solidified. “Made fast by defilement” remains a viable less specific alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ ἐκ πυρὸς τραπέντα μέλη εἰς τὸ πρῶτον αὐτῶν τῆς ἰδίας φύσεως ἀμίαντον· μετασυγκρῖναι οὐκ ἐξίσχυσαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: they were not strong enough to recombine their limbs, which had been transformed from fire, into the original undefiled state of their own nature
lexical_decisions.rationale: The English makes restoration into the original state the unaccomplished result of μετασυγκρῖναι, not the result of the earlier transformation from fire. The supplied high stop before μετασυγκρῖναι makes the attachment visually unusual, so this interpretation remains provisional.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ γὰρ βάρει τῷ ὑπὸ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας εἰς σάρκα τελευτήσαντος αὐτῶν τοῦ πυρός
lexical_decisions.chosen: For under the weight of their fire, which through desire had ended in flesh
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive participle τελευτήσαντος qualifies τοῦ πυρός: their fire had ended in flesh through desire, and its resulting weight bears them downward. The repeated article links the genitive qualification to “weight”; the wording does not make that weight the cause of the transformation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: have been held down
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect middle-passive form is understood from κατέχω, “hold” or “restrain.” In context it parallels being fettered and tightly bound.

passages.text: For after intercourse, when they were asked for what they had become at first and were no longer able to furnish it—because after defilement they could not turn themselves into anything else—and because they wished to please their beloved women, they showed them, in place of themselves, the marrows of the earth, by which I mean the blooms from mines: gold, copper, silver, iron, and the like, together with all the most precious stones. So to those bewitched by these stones they also handed down the crafts for the operations relating to each one; they disclosed practices of magic, taught astronomy, the powers of roots, and whatever could never be discovered by human thought, and furthermore the casting of gold, silver, and similar materials, as well as the many-colored dyeing of garments. Simply put, everything that serves women’s adornment and pleasure is an invention of the demons bound in flesh.

lexical_decisions.chosen: For after intercourse
lexical_decisions.rationale: The initial γάρ explicitly presents this account as an explanation and elaboration of the loss of transformative power described in the preceding section.

lexical_decisions.chosen: when they were asked for what they had become at first
lexical_decisions.rationale: The request concerns their former transformations into precious materials, which they could no longer reproduce after their defilement.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the marrows of the earth
lexical_decisions.rationale: The literal anatomical image is retained and immediately explained by the author as metals and precious stones extracted from mines.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὖν τούτοις δὲ τοῖς μαγευθεῖσιν λίθοις
lexical_decisions.chosen: So to those bewitched by these stones
lexical_decisions.rationale: The article with μαγευθεῖσιν is taken substantivally for the recipients, while τούτοις λίθοις identifies the stones by which they were bewitched. A less likely alternative makes all the dative forms one phrase, “these enchanted stones,” but that leaves the dative’s relationship to “handed down” less clear.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰς τέχνας τῶν πρὸς ἕκαστα πραγμάτων
lexical_decisions.chosen: the crafts for the operations relating to each one
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compressed phrase refers to technical arts associated with working or using what had just been listed; “each one” may refer to each material or to each corresponding operation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πάνθ’ ἁπλῶς ὅσαπερ πρὸς κόσμου καὶ τέρψεώς ἐστι γυναικῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Simply put, everything that serves women’s adornment and pleasure
lexical_decisions.rationale: κόσμος here means ornament or adornment rather than the physical world.

passages.text: From their illegitimate union, illegitimate human beings came into existence, much taller than humans. Those who came afterward called them giants. They were not snake-footed beings who had raised war against God, as the blasphemous Greek myths sing, but beastlike in character, larger in size than humans because they came from angels, yet smaller than angels because they had been born of women. God knew that they had grown savagely beastlike and that the world was not sufficient to satisfy them, for it had been created in proportion to humans and for human use. So, lest through lack of food they turn to the unnatural eating of animals and seem free from responsibility, as though having dared this from necessity, almighty God rained manna upon them in response to their varied desire, and they enjoyed whatever they wished. But because of their illegitimate nature they were not pleased with the purity of the food and longed only for the taste of blood. That is why they were also the first to taste flesh.

source_issues.issue: The former Lagarde reading is exactly ἐγλίχοντα. The selected independently image-read Dressel main-print reading is ἐγλίχοντο, a finite verb translated longed. This is a documented print-variant choice, not personal manuscript collation or recovery of an autograph.

The selected text retains a full stop between eating and the participle turning. The English follows their surviving grammatical relationship as one construction. The point is not treated as an established lacuna, and no missing wording is supplied.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς νόθου μίξεως αὐτῶν ἄνθρωποι ἐγένοντο νόθοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: From their illegitimate union, illegitimate human beings came into existence
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated adjective is preserved in both union and offspring. Hybrid or mixed-lineage captures a material aspect of the angel-human parentage, while illegitimate retains the ancient author's evaluative designation; it is not a modern legal or medical classification supplied by the translator.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πολλῷ γε τῶν ἀνθρώπων κατὰ κορυφὴν μείζους
lexical_decisions.chosen: much taller than humans
lexical_decisions.rationale: The head or crown phrase identifies the comparison as height or stature. It does not specify a fixed difference of exactly one head; the considerable difference expressed by πολλῷ is retained.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ δρακοντόποδες ὄντες καὶ πρὸς θεὸν πόλεμον ἀράμενοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: They were not snake-footed beings who had raised war against God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The negative rejects the combined mythic characterization. The unusual snake-footed form is preserved rather than converted into an unnamed species or omitted.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μάννα αὐτοῖς ὁ παντοδύναμος θεὸς ἐπώμβρισεν ἐκ ποικίλης ἐπιθυμίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: almighty God rained manna upon them in response to their varied desire
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase from varied desire is read causally as responding to their differing desires, supported by their immediately ensuing enjoyment of whatever they wished. A more literal alternative is rained manna upon them from varied desire, which leaves whose desire it is broader. The main text does not specify flavors or turn manna into animal flesh.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μόνης τῆς τῶν αἱμάτων γεύσεως ἐγλίχοντο
lexical_decisions.chosen: longed only for the taste of blood
lexical_decisions.rationale: The selected finite verb denotes craving or longing, with only governing the taste desired. The plural bloods is rendered idiomatically as blood without introducing separate victims or an act not supplied here.

passages.text: The humans, then, first became eager at that time to do the same as they did. Thus we are not born either good or evil, but become so, and once we have grown accustomed to it, we find it hard to break away. When the irrational animals ran out, the humans of mixed parentage tasted human flesh as well. For it was no longer a long step for them to destroy their own flesh, since they had previously tasted it in other forms.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἱ δὲ οὖν αὐτοῖς ἄνθρωποι τὸ ὅμοιον τότε πρῶτον ποιεῖν ἐζήλωσαν.
lexical_decisions.chosen: The humans, then, first became eager at that time to do the same as they did.
lexical_decisions.rationale: Takes αὐτοῖς with τὸ ὅμοιον, expressing imitation of the previously mentioned beings; the supplied passage does not name them here. ἐζήλωσαν expresses emulation or eagerness, not merely the fact of imitation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: and once we have grown accustomed to it, we find it hard to break away.
lexical_decisions.rationale: Represents acquired habit and the difficulty of detachment. The Greek leaves the object of that habitual attachment implicit; the English does not identify a new object.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the humans of mixed parentage
lexical_decisions.rationale: νόθοι can be rendered illegitimate or bastard-born. Mixed parentage makes the ancestry category intelligible without introducing a modern insult; 8.18 explicitly describes the mixture as angelic fire and women’s blood.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκέτι γὰρ αὐτοῖς ἦν μακρὰν τὴν ἰδίαν διαφθεῖραι σάρκα, πρότερον ἐν ἑτέραις μορφαῖς αὐτῆς γευσαμένοις.
lexical_decisions.chosen: For it was no longer a long step for them to destroy their own flesh, since they had previously tasted it in other forms.
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the source’s own-flesh/other-forms wording and its causal comparison. Their own flesh can refer to flesh of their own kind rather than self-mutilation; the text does not require English to settle the underlying account of flesh in different forms.

passages.text: With so much blood flowing, the pure air was polluted by an impure vapor and became diseased, making those who breathed it diseased, so that people now died before their time. The earth, severely polluted by these things, then for the first time cast up venomous and destructive animals. Since everything had taken a turn for the worse because of the beastlike demons, God resolved to remove them like bad leaven, lest, from evil seed, each successive generation should become like the one before it and, behaving just as impiously, leave the age to come empty of people being saved. For this reason, having told one righteous man beforehand to survive in an ark, with his three offspring and their wives, together with the rest, he poured forth water as a flood. This was so that, once all had been destroyed, the world, thoroughly cleansed, might be given back in purity to that very man who had survived in the ark, for a second beginning of life. And that is what happened.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ καθαρὸς ἀὴρ ἀκαθάρτῳ ἀναθυμιάσει μιανθεὶς καὶ νοσήσας τοὺς ἀναπνέοντας αὐτὸν νοσώδεις ἀπειργάζετο
lexical_decisions.chosen: the pure air was polluted by an impure vapor and became diseased, making those who breathed it diseased
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the repeated disease language and the historical author’s explanation of contaminated air. Vapor renders ἀναθυμίασις, also exhalation or rising fumes, without modernizing the causal claim.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ ἰοβόλα καὶ λυμαντικὰ ζῷα ἐξέβρασεν.
lexical_decisions.chosen: cast up venomous and destructive animals.
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἰοβόλα indicates venom-bearing or venom-darting creatures. Cast up preserves the vivid expulsion image of ἐξέβρασεν, also disgorged or spewed out. The earth is the subject, and the rendering retains the author’s image without replacing it with a generic statement of emergence.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἵνα μὴ ἀπὸ σπορᾶς κακῆς κατ’ ἀκολουθίαν ἑκάστη γενεὰ τῇ πρὸ αὐτῆς ἐξομοιουμένη, ὁμοίως ἀσεβοῦσα τὸν ἐσόμενον αἰῶνα σωζομένων ἀνδρῶν κενώσῃ.
lexical_decisions.chosen: lest, from evil seed, each successive generation should become like the one before it and, behaving just as impiously, leave the age to come empty of people being saved.
lexical_decisions.rationale: Keeps the generational sequence, evil seed, repeated impiety, future age, and salvation language. σωζομένων is present passive, here rendered being saved rather than assigning a particular doctrine or stage of salvation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἑνί τινι δικαίῳ μετὰ τῶν ἐξ αὐτοῦ τριῶν σὺν ταῖς αὐτῶν γυναιξὶν ἅμα τοῖς λοιποῖς ἐν λάρνακι διασώζεσθαι προαγγείλας
lexical_decisions.chosen: having told one righteous man beforehand to survive in an ark, with his three offspring and their wives, together with the rest
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐξ αὐτοῦ denotes those sprung from him; offspring preserves this without adding the unprinted noun sons. Their wives retains the Greek pronoun rather than independently enumerating all spouses. The rest remains unspecified. λάρναξ literally denotes a chest or coffer, here functioning as the flood vessel, hence ark. διασώζεσθαι is preservation through danger, rendered survive; the same preservation vocabulary recurs later in the section.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ κόσμος κατεκκαθαρισθεὶς αὐτῷ τῷ ἐν λάρνακι διασωθέντι εἰς δευτέραν βίου ἀρχὴν καθαρὸς ἀποδοθῇ.
lexical_decisions.chosen: the world, thoroughly cleansed, might be given back in purity to that very man who had survived in the ark, for a second beginning of life.
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the cleansing and clean-state repetition, the emphatic beneficiary, and a second beginning of life. Thoroughly reflects the compounded cleansing verb, not a new theological intensifier.

passages.text: Since, then, the souls of the dead giants were larger than human souls—because they also surpassed them in bodily size—they were called by a new name as well, as a new race. For them, as newcomers to the world, God established through an angel a law prescribing how they must live. For, being of mixed parentage by descent, from the fire of angels and the blood of women, and therefore going to desire something of a kind peculiar to themselves, they were restrained in advance by a just law. For God sent an angel to them, making his will known and saying:

source_issues.issue: The desired kind is not specified here. The phrase can mean that they would desire a particular kind proper to themselves; their own particular kind is another close rendering. The main text deliberately leaves that kind unidentified rather than supplying a specific appetite or object.

source_issues.source_quote: ἅτε δὴ καὶ τοῖς σώμασιν ὑπερέχουσαι
