source_issues.issue: The feminine participle agrees grammatically with souls, although the bodily comparison naturally concerns the giants. The main text retains the pronoun they and the causal connection, leaving this source-level metonymic subject relationship visible rather than silently substituting an explicit subject. Exceeded them in body is a closer but less idiomatic alternative to surpassed them in bodily size.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αἱ τῶν τεθνεώτων γιγάντων ψυχαὶ τῶν ἀνθρωπείων ψυχῶν μείζους ἦσαν, ἅτε δὴ καὶ τοῖς σώμασιν ὑπερέχουσαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: the souls of the dead giants were larger than human souls—because they also surpassed them in bodily size
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἅτε δή presents factual causal ground: the larger bodily size grounds the claim of larger souls, not merely an analogy alongside it. The feminine participle grammatically agrees with souls, while the bodily description concerns the giants whose souls are in view; the English preserves they rather than replacing this metonymic subject with a new explicit subject. In bodily size makes the quantitative force clear without implying moral superiority.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς καινὸν γένος καινῷ καὶ τῷ ὀνόματι προσηγορεύθησαν.
lexical_decisions.chosen: they were called by a new name as well, as a new race.
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the repeated new and the new classification/name connection. The supplied sentence does not give the name, so none is inserted.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἷς ἐπηλύτοις τῷ κόσμῳ ὡς δεῖ βιοῦν ὑπὸ θεοῦ δι’ ἀγγέλου νόμος ὡρίσθη.
lexical_decisions.chosen: For them, as newcomers to the world, God established through an angel a law prescribing how they must live.
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπήλυτος denotes one who has come from elsewhere, also a stranger or immigrant. Newcomers retains this without adding a place of origin. The law regulates their manner of life.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὄντες γὰρ νόθοι τῷ γένει ἐκ πυρὸς ἀγγέλων καὶ αἵματος γυναικῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: For, being of mixed parentage by descent, from the fire of angels and the blood of women
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the explicit components of the hybrid descent. As in 8.16, νόθοι could be rendered illegitimate or bastard-born; mixed parentage conveys the relevant ancestry contrast without a modern insult.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἰδίου τινὸς γένους ἐπιθυμεῖν μέλλοντες, δικαίῳ τινὶ προελήφθησαν νόμῳ.
lexical_decisions.chosen: and therefore going to desire something of a kind peculiar to themselves, they were restrained in advance by a just law.
lexical_decisions.rationale: Leaves the object of desire at the source’s general level of kind rather than supplying food, blood, sacrifice, or sexual partners. ἰδίου τινὸς γένους can be understood as a particular kind proper to them or their own particular kind; the chosen rendering preserves the former without asserting what it denotes. προελήφθησαν expresses preventive action, here their desires being forestalled by law.

passages.text: “This is the will of the all-seeing God: you are to rule over no human being and trouble no one, unless someone enslaves himself to you by worshiping you and sacrificing and pouring libations and sharing in your table, or by doing anything else that ought not to be done, or by shedding blood, or by tasting dead flesh, or by filling himself with the remains of a wild animal, or with something cut up, or with something strangled, or with any other impure thing. Those who take refuge in my law you will not even touch; instead, you will give them honor and flee from their presence. For whatever they, being righteous, decide against you, you will have to suffer. But if any of those devoted to me sin, whether by committing adultery, practicing magic, living impurely, or doing anything else that does not meet with my approval, then, at my command, they will have to suffer something at your hands or at the hands of others. And if they reorient, I will judge their reorientation, whether it is worthy of forgiveness or not, and make my decision. So you must remember and do these things, knowing well that not even your thoughts will be able to escape his notice.”

source_issues.issue: The genitive can refer to remains belonging to a wild animal or remains left by one. The main rendering retains the first defensible reading; the alternative is remains left by a wild animal, that is, its leavings. No lost wording is assumed.

The precise dietary category is not specified by this standalone substantivized adjective. Cut up preserves its cutting sense; mutilated is another possible rendering. It has not been expanded into a particular animal part or a specified method of slaughter.

lexical_decisions.chosen: This is the will of the all-seeing God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The decree formula literally states what seems good to God; will conveys its prescriptive force in this setting. παντεπόπτῃ is all-seeing.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐὰν μή τις ἑαυτὸν ὑμῖν καταδουλώσῃ
lexical_decisions.chosen: unless someone enslaves himself to you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb describes placing oneself under another’s ownership or domination, not merely voluntary service. The POB main-text servant convention concerns the noun δοῦλος; here enslaves preserves the explicit verbal subjugation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: or by tasting dead flesh
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves both flesh and dead without making the phrase exclusively human flesh. Flesh of the dead is a viable alternative if νεκρῶν is taken substantivally; the source here does not specify the species.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἢ θηρίου λειψάνου ἢ τμητοῦ ἢ πνικτοῦ ἢ ἄλλου τινὸς ἀκαθάρτου ἐμπιπλάμενος.
lexical_decisions.chosen: or by filling himself with the remains of a wild animal, or with something cut up, or with something strangled, or with any other impure thing.
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains all items and the filling/eating construction. θηρίου λειψάνου can describe a wild animal’s remains or remains left by a wild animal; the main text preserves the former grammatical reading. τμητοῦ literally denotes something cut, cut up, or mutilated; no specific unprinted slaughter rule is imposed. πνικτοῦ denotes something strangled or choked.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν δὲ νόμῳ ἐμῷ προσφευγόντων οὐ μόνον οὐ ψαύσετε, ἀλλὰ καὶ τιμὴν δώσετε, καὶ ἐκ προσώπου φεύξεσθε.
lexical_decisions.chosen: Those who take refuge in my law you will not even touch; instead, you will give them honor and flee from their presence.
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the refuge metaphor, the prohibition on touching, the additional requirement of honor, and flight from their presence. My is retained as the divine first-person speech, rather than normalizing the whole speech to third person.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅ,τι γὰρ ἂν αὐτοῖς δικαίοις οὖσι καθ’ ὑμῶν δοκῇ, τοῦθ’ ὑμᾶς δεήσει παθεῖν.
lexical_decisions.chosen: For whatever they, being righteous, decide against you, you will have to suffer.
lexical_decisions.rationale: Represents the open-ended decision against the demons and its compulsory consequence, with being righteous retained rather than expanded into an unprinted condition.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἷς καὶ μετανοήσασιν, τὴν μετάνοιαν κρίνας εἴτε ἀξία ἐστὶν συγγνώμης εἴτε καὶ οὔ, τὴν ἀπόφασιν ποιήσομαι.
lexical_decisions.chosen: And if they reorient, I will judge their reorientation, whether it is worthy of forgiveness or not, and make my decision.
lexical_decisions.rationale: Uses POB reorient/reorientation for moral-spiritual redirection, traditionally repent/repentance, without inventing an intensifier or adding a destination. The divine judgment, possibility of forgiveness, and possibility of non-forgiveness are all retained. The participial construction is expressed as an English conditional.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εὖ εἰδότες ὅτι οὐδὲ αἱ ἐνθυμήσεις ὑμῶν λαθεῖν αὐτὸν δυνήσονται.
lexical_decisions.chosen: knowing well that not even your thoughts will be able to escape his notice.
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the Greek’s return to third-person him at the end of speech otherwise containing divine first-person language; it is not silently harmonized to my notice.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: προσκυνῶν ὑμᾶς καὶ θύων καὶ σπένδων καὶ τῆς ὑμετέρας μεταλαμβάνων τραπέζης ἢ ἕτερόν τι ὧν οὐ χρὴ ἐκτελῶν ἢ αἷμα χέων ἢ σαρκῶν νεκρῶν γευόμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: by worshiping you and sacrificing and pouring libations and sharing in your table, or by doing anything else that ought not to be done, or by shedding blood, or by tasting dead flesh
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated and preserves the initial καί-linked ritual sequence, while the repeated or retains the subsequent ἤ-linked alternatives. This rendering represents the coordination without adding a claim that all initial acts must be performed jointly as a necessary condition of subjugation.

passages.text: After giving them these instructions, the angel departed. But you still do not know this law: anyone who worships demons, sacrifices, or shares a table with them becomes enslaved to them and will receive every punishment that comes from them, as from evil masters. Through this ignorance, corrupted through your attachment to their altars and filled with them, you have come under their authority; and, with your bodies being mistreated in every way, you fall ill. You must know that the demons have authority over no one unless someone first shares their diet, since not even their ruler can do anything contrary to the law God has laid down against them. Therefore he has no authority over anyone who has not worshiped him. Nor can anyone receive from them any of the things he wants, nor suffer any harm, as you can learn from what follows.

source_issues.issue: The deictic ἐκεῖθεν does not explicitly say whether it points forward or backward. The main text adopts a forward reference, what follows; a backward reference, from that, remains viable from the supplied sentence alone.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπόδουλος αὐτοῖς γενόμενος ὡς ὑπὸ κακῶν δεσποτῶν πάσης τῆς ἐξ αὐτῶν μεθέξει τιμωρίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: becomes enslaved to them and will receive every punishment that comes from them, as from evil masters
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves subjection, the comparison with evil masters, and the punishment coming from them. ὑπόδουλος describes an enslaved or subject condition, not merely being helpful; it is not the standalone noun δοῦλος governed by the POB servant gloss.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῖς αὐτῶν βωμοῖς προσφθαρέντες καὶ αὐτῶν ἐκπληρωθέντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: corrupted through your attachment to their altars and filled with them
lexical_decisions.rationale: προσφθαρέντες carries corruption through attachment or association, here with their altars. Filled with them retains the pronoun and does not replace it with unprinted sacrificial food; demons are the contextual antecedent, though association with what is offered at their altars can be heard in the phrasing.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ παντὶ τρόπῳ ὑβριζόμενοι τὰ σώματα νοσεῖτε.
lexical_decisions.chosen: and, with your bodies being mistreated in every way, you fall ill.
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the abuse/mistreatment of bodies and the ensuing illness without inventing symptoms or a modern medical explanation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐὰν μὴ πρότερόν τις αὐτοῖς ὁμοδίαιτος γένηται
lexical_decisions.chosen: unless someone first shares their diet
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὁμοδίαιτος can indicate sharing a diet or a way of life. The immediately preceding altar and table setting favors diet, while shared way of life is a viable broader rendering. First retains πρότερον.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁπότε οὐδὲ ὁ αὐτῶν ἄρχων παρὰ τὸν ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ κατ’ αὐτῶν κείμενον νόμον ποιεῖν τι δύναται
lexical_decisions.chosen: since not even their ruler can do anything contrary to the law God has laid down against them
lexical_decisions.rationale: Takes ὁπότε causally, since or seeing that, in the argument explaining the limit on demonic authority. Both not even and anything are retained, as is the law’s application against them.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ λαβεῖν τις παρ’ αὐτῶν δύναταί τι ὧν θέλει, ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ βλαβῆναι οὐδέν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Nor can anyone receive from them any of the things he wants, nor suffer any harm
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves both negative claims and their indefinite objects. The preceding worship/authority qualification provides context, but no extra conditional clause is inserted into this sentence.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as you can learn from what follows.
lexical_decisions.rationale: Takes the deictic from there as pointing forward to explanatory material. A backward reference, as you can learn from that, is also possible from the isolated wording; this does not alter the preceding claims.

passages.text: For the temporary king once approached the king of our piety, not using force (for that was not permitted), but exhorting and persuading, because being persuaded lies within each person’s own power. So he approached as king of present things and said to the king of things to come, “All the kingdoms of the present world are subject to me; moreover, the gold and the silver and all the luxury of this world are under my authority. Therefore, fall down and worship me, and I will give you all these things.” He said this knowing that, with that act of worship, he would also have authority over him, and so the latter would deprive himself of the glory and kingdom to come. Knowing these things, the latter not only did not worship him, but did not even wish to take any of the things that had been given by him. For he would thereby have pledged himself as security together with what was his own—that is, from then on he would no longer be permitted even to touch any of the things returned to him. He therefore answered, “It is written: ‘You shall fear the Lord your God and serve him alone.’”

source_issues.source_quote: ταῦτα δὲ ἔλεγεν εἰδὼς ὅτι μετὰ τοῦ προσκυνῆσαι καὶ τὴν κατ’ αὐτοῦ εἶχεν ἐξουσίαν καὶ οὕτως τῆς μελλούσης δόξης καὶ βασιλείας ἑαυτὸν ἀφῄρει
source_issues.issue: The unexpressed subject of ἀφῄρει is materially ambiguous. The main text takes it to be the future king, who would deprive himself of the coming glory and kingdom by worshiping; alternatively, the subject may continue to be the temporary king from εἶχεν, despite the resulting contextual difficulty. This is a provisional contextual interpretation, not a correction of the supplied text.

source_issues.source_quote: ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ τῶν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ δεδομένων λαβεῖν τι ἠθέλησεν
source_issues.issue: The perfect passive δεδομένων describes the things as already given by the temporary king, although his preceding direct speech promises, “I will give you all these things.” The translation preserves this shift in presentation rather than changing “given” to “offered.” The discourse relation is uncertain, but the printed wording is translatable without emendation.

source_issues.source_quote: ἑαυτὸν γὰρ σὺν τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ κατενεχύραζεν, ὅπερ ἐστὶν μὴ ἐξεῖναι τοῦ λοιποῦ τῶν αὐτῷ ἀποδοθέντων μηδὲ ψαῦσαι ἔτι
source_issues.issue: The subject of κατενεχύραζεν and the referent of αὐτῷ are not explicit. The translation continues the future king as the implied subject and takes αὐτῷ as referring to him; alternatively, one or both may refer to the temporary king. The substantival τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ may denote his own things, possessions, or those belonging to him. The supplied construction is translatable without emendation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ γὰρ τῆς εὐσεβείας ἡμῶν βασιλεῖ
lexical_decisions.chosen: the king of our piety
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the unusual genitive description rather than replacing it with a familiar Christological title.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the temporary king
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόσκαιρος marks limited duration and contrasts this ruler with the king of things to come.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μετὰ τοῦ προσκυνῆσαι καὶ τὴν κατ’ αὐτοῦ εἶχεν ἐξουσίαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: with that act of worship, he would also have authority over him
lexical_decisions.rationale: Takes the temporary king as the one who would have authority and the future king as the one placed under it; κατ’ αὐτοῦ can express authority directed against or over someone.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ οὕτως τῆς μελλούσης δόξης καὶ βασιλείας ἑαυτὸν ἀφῄρει
lexical_decisions.chosen: and so the latter would deprive himself of the glory and kingdom to come
lexical_decisions.rationale: Supplies the future king as the subject of ἀφῄρει because worship would cost him the coming glory and kingdom, although the Greek does not explicitly mark a change of subject.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ τῶν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ δεδομένων λαβεῖν τι ἠθέλησεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: but did not even wish to take any of the things that had been given by him
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the perfect passive gift-language of δεδομένων rather than replacing it with “offered,” despite the preceding promise being expressed in the future.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἑαυτὸν γὰρ σὺν τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ κατενεχύραζεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: For he would thereby have pledged himself as security together with what was his own
lexical_decisions.rationale: Renders the security or pledge imagery of κατενεχύραζεν while leaving τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ broad enough to include his own things or those belonging to him.

lexical_decisions.chosen: You shall fear
lexical_decisions.rationale: Follows the supplied Greek rather than harmonizing the quotation with a familiar temptation narrative using “worship.”

passages.text: Nevertheless, after the king of the impious had tried in many ways to draw the king of the devout toward his own will and was unable, he ceased his effort to ensnare him in the remaining areas of his way of life. But you, because you were ignorant of the law laid down beforehand, came under his authority through evil deeds. Therefore, you were defiled in body and soul, and in the present you are abused by both sufferings and demons, while in what is to come you will have souls destined to be punished. You are not the only ones who have suffered this through ignorance, but so have some from our own nation. Having been seized beforehand for evil deeds by the ruler of wickedness, they were then invited as though to a banquet by a father celebrating a wedding for his son, but they did not obey. In place of those who disobeyed because of that prior seizure, the father celebrating the wedding for his son commanded us through the prophet of truth, when we had gone to the outlets of the roads (that is, toward you), to put a clean wedding garment around you (which is baptism, performed for forgiveness of the evil deeds you have committed) and to bring into God’s banquet those who have become good through a change of heart, even if they had at first been left out of the feast.

source_issues.source_quote: ἐπαύσατο, πρὸς τὰ λοιπὰ τῆς πολιτείας θηρεύειν αὐτὸν ἐπιχειρῶν
source_issues.issue: The present participle ἐπιχειρῶν may describe the effort that ceased or an attendant attempt made before or while he ceased. The translation takes the attempt to ensnare him as the effort that ceased; the alternative attachment does not require a textual correction.

The person around whom the garment is to be placed is not expressed. The translation supplies “you” from the immediately preceding parenthesis and the following reference to deeds committed by the audience; “those encountered at the roads” is a broader possible referent.

source_issues.source_quote: καὶ τοὺς ἀγαθοὺς εἰς τὸ θεοῦ δεῖπνον εἰσάγειν ἐκ τῆς μεταμελείας
source_issues.issue: The attachment of ἐκ τῆς μεταμελείας is not explicit. The main text takes it with τοὺς ἀγαθούς, describing people who have become good through a change of heart. Alternatively, it may modify εἰσάγειν, so that their change of heart or regret provides the grounds for bringing the good into God’s banquet. Both readings are possible without altering the supplied Greek.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in the remaining areas of his way of life
lexical_decisions.rationale: πολιτεία here denotes conduct or manner of life, not a political constitution.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the law laid down beforehand
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the prior determination expressed by προορισθέντα without importing a later doctrinal sense of predestination.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὸ τοῦ τῆς κακίας ἡγεμόνος προληφθέντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: having been seized beforehand by the ruler of wickedness
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive verb depicts prior capture or preemption and prepares for the related noun πρόληψιν.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to put a clean wedding garment around you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The person being clothed is implicit; the parenthetical identification with baptism for the audience’s past deeds supports taking the audience as the recipient.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ τοὺς ἀγαθοὺς εἰς τὸ θεοῦ δεῖπνον εἰσάγειν ἐκ τῆς μεταμελείας
lexical_decisions.chosen: and to bring into God’s banquet those who have become good through a change of heart
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text relates ἐκ τῆς μεταμελείας to τοὺς ἀγαθούς, understanding the people as good through moral reconsideration. μεταμέλεια may denote change of heart, regret, or reconsideration. The phrase may instead modify εἰσάγειν, yielding “to bring the good into God’s banquet on account of their change of heart.”

passages.text: Therefore, if you wish to become a garment of the divine spirit, first make every effort to strip off the filthy hold already laid on you (which is an unclean spirit) and the defiled covering. You cannot strip this off in any other way unless you are first baptized on the basis of good deeds and in this way, having become clean in both body and soul, enjoy the eternal kingdom that is to come. Therefore, do not put your trust in idols or share a defiled table with them. Do not murder, do not commit adultery, do not hate those whom it is not right to hate, do not steal, and do not set yourselves to any evil deeds at all. Otherwise, deprived of the hope of the good things to come, in the present you will be beset by both evil demons and painful afflictions, while in the eternal age to come you will be punished with fire. What has been said to you today is sufficient. Now, those of you troubled by afflictions, remain for healing; among the others, those who wish may go in peace.

source_issues.issue: The force of ἐπί with the dative is contextually open: it may express basis or condition, association, or purpose. The main rendering selects basis, while “with a view to good deeds” remains viable. No alteration of the supplied text is required.

source_issues.source_quote: ἐν δὲ τῷ ἐσομένῳ αἰῶνι αἰδίῳ κολασθήσεσθε πυρί
source_issues.issue: The dative adjective αἰδίῳ can modify either αἰῶνι or πυρί because both nouns are dative singular forms compatible with it. The main text follows the immediate attachment to αἰῶνι: “in the eternal age to come you will be punished with fire.” Alternatively, αἰδίῳ may form an adjective–noun phrase with πυρί across the intervening verb: “in the coming age you will be punished with eternal fire.” This is an attachment ambiguity, not evidence of source corruption.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἔνδυμα οὖν εἰ βούλεσθε γενέσθαι θείου πνεύματος
lexical_decisions.chosen: if you wish to become a garment of the divine spirit
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the source’s image of people becoming the spirit’s garment rather than merely being clothed by the spirit.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the filthy hold already laid on you
lexical_decisions.rationale: In context πρόλημμα denotes a prior possession or seizure, identified immediately as an unclean spirit; “preconception” would obscure that contextual image.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you are baptized on the basis of good deeds
lexical_decisions.rationale: Takes ἐπί with the dative as expressing a basis or condition. Other viable nuances are “in connection with good deeds” or “with a view to good deeds.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ οὕτω καθαροὶ σώματί τε καὶ ψυχῇ γενόμενοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: and in this way, having become clean in both body and soul
lexical_decisions.rationale: Renders οὕτω as “in this way,” preserving its manner or result connection with the preceding statement that the covering cannot be removed in any other way.

lexical_decisions.chosen: do not hate those whom it is not right to hate
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the source’s qualification rather than broadening it into an unqualified prohibition of all hatred.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπό τε κακῶν δαιμόνων καὶ χαλεπῶν παθημάτων συνελασθήσεσθε
lexical_decisions.chosen: you will be beset by both evil demons and painful afflictions
lexical_decisions.rationale: συνελαύνω depicts being driven together, hemmed in, or hard-pressed; “beset” conveys that force naturally.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐν δὲ τῷ ἐσομένῳ αἰῶνι αἰδίῳ κολασθήσεσθε πυρί
lexical_decisions.chosen: while in the eternal age to come you will be punished with fire
lexical_decisions.rationale: Attaches αἰδίῳ to the immediately preceding αἰῶνι, with which it agrees, preserving the contiguous phrase “eternal age.” Because αἰδίῳ can also agree with πυρί, “with eternal fire” remains a viable alternative.

passages.text: When he had said these things, everyone remained—some for the sake of being healed, and others in order to observe those who obtained healing. Peter merely laid his hands on them and prayed, and he healed them, so that those who had been healed at once became overjoyed, while those who had observed were extraordinarily amazed and, after praising God, believed with assured hope. Together with those who had been healed, they went away to their own homes under instructions to gather early the next day. After they had left, Peter remained there with his companions, partook of food, and gave himself rest in sleep.

source_issues.issue: The genitive βεβαίας ἐλπίδος has more than one defensible relation to πιστεύειν. The translation takes it as characterizing the hope accompanying their belief; an alternative is “believed in a sure hope.” The construction remains intelligible without conjecture.

πρωΐτερον is comparative in form. The translation understands it absolutely or elatively as “early,” while “to gather earlier the next day,” with an implicit comparison point, is also defensible. This is an interpretive ambiguity, not evidence of source corruption.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦ ἱστορῆσαι τοὺς τῆς θεραπείας ἐπιτυγχάνοντας
lexical_decisions.chosen: in order to observe those who obtained healing
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἱστορέω can mean to inquire into or observe closely; remaining at the scene to witness the healings supports “observe.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰς χεῖρας αὐτοῖς ἐπιθεὶς μόνον καὶ εὐξάμενος ἰάσατο
lexical_decisions.chosen: merely laid his hands on them and prayed, and he healed them
lexical_decisions.rationale: μόνον emphasizes the simplicity of Peter’s actions accompanying the healing.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοὺς μὲν παραχρῆμα θεραπευθέντας γενέσθαι περιχαρεῖς
lexical_decisions.chosen: those who had been healed at once became overjoyed
lexical_decisions.rationale: The placement of παραχρῆμα within the participial phrase marks the healing as immediate rather than the subsequent becoming overjoyed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: believed with assured hope
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive phrase is taken as characterizing the hope accompanying their belief; “believed in a sure hope” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to gather early the next day
lexical_decisions.rationale: Although πρωΐτερον is morphologically comparative, it is taken here in an absolute or elative sense, referring to an early time. The formally comparative alternative is “to gather earlier the next day,” with the point of comparison left implicit.

lexical_decisions.chosen: gave himself rest in sleep
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves both the reflexive expression and the explicit reference to sleep rather than reducing the phrase simply to “slept.”

passages.text: On the following day, then, Peter went out with his companions, came to the place where they had been the day before, stood there, and began to say: “God destroyed with water all the people of old who had acted impiously. Yet, finding among them all one godly man, he caused him to be saved in an ark together with his three sons and the women. From this one can perceive his nature: it takes no account of a crowd of people acting impiously, but it does not neglect the salvation of one godly person. The greatest impiety of all, then, is to abandon the sole Master of all and revere many nonexistent gods as though they existed.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: in an ark
lexical_decisions.rationale: λάρναξ can denote a chest or coffer; the flood setting supports “ark.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μετὰ τριῶν αὐτοῦ υἱῶν καὶ γυναικῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: together with his three sons and the women
lexical_decisions.rationale: γυναικῶν can mean “women” or “wives.” The rendering avoids specifying whose wives they were, since the Greek does not make that relationship explicit.

lexical_decisions.chosen: it takes no account of a crowd of people acting impiously
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine participle refers back to God’s “nature”; the collective construction is represented naturally in English.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πολλοὺς τοὺς οὐκ ὄντας ὡς ὄντας σέβειν θεούς
lexical_decisions.chosen: revere many nonexistent gods as though they existed
lexical_decisions.rationale: This preserves both the denial that these gods exist and the contrast introduced by ὡς ὄντας.

passages.text: “If, then, while I am instructing you and showing that this is the greatest sin, one that can destroy you all, the thought should steal into your mind that you will not be destroyed because you are many crowds, you have been deceived. For you have the example of the world that was flooded long ago. And yet their sin was much less than yours: they acted impiously against those like themselves, either by murdering or by committing adultery, but you act impiously against the God of all by revering lifeless images instead of him, or even alongside him, and by casting his divine name upon all insentient matter. In the first place, then, you have suffered misfortune by failing to recognize the difference between rule by one and rule by many: rule by one produces concord, whereas rule by many produces wars. For the one does not fight itself, but the many have occasion to launch a fight against another.”

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a period between ὑποδράμῃ and νοῦν, interrupting the phrase containing “your mind.” It appears to be extraneous editorial punctuation rather than a lacuna marker; the construction remains intelligible when the period is disregarded. This interpretation is provisional, but the printed dot is not treated as unavailable wording.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the thought should steal into your mind
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑποτρέχω here depicts the content of the following ὅτι clause slipping or stealing into the mind; the printed period is treated separately as a source issue.

lexical_decisions.chosen: because you are many crowds
lexical_decisions.rationale: The deliberately unusual plural image is retained rather than reduced to the smoother but less exact “because you are numerous.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ θεῖον αὐτοῦ ὄνομα πάσῃ ἀναισθήτῳ ὕλῃ ἐπιρρίψαντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: by casting his divine name upon all insentient matter
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the concrete image of ἐπιρρίπτω, “cast upon,” and takes ὕλη as physical matter rather than merely “material.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: rule by one and rule by many
lexical_decisions.rationale: These expressions convey the contrast without importing the narrower modern political associations of “monarchy” and “polyarchy.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: have occasion
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόφασις may mean a pretext, ground, or occasion; “occasion” fits the claim that plurality creates an opening for conflict.

passages.text: “Indeed, immediately after the flood, Noah lived on for three hundred fifty years and continued in concord with the multitudes descended from him, being a king in the likeness of the only God. But after his death, many of his descendants desired kingship, and in their eagerness to reign, each devised how he might be able to do so. One sought it by war, another by deceit, another by persuasion, and another in some other way. One of them was a certain man from the lineage of Ham, who fathered Mestrem, from whom indeed the tribes of the Egyptians, Babylonians, and Persians multiplied.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: lived on for three hundred fifty years
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιζάω denotes continuing to live or surviving beyond an event, here the flood.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦ μόνου θεοῦ κατ’ εἰκόνα ὑπάρξας βασιλεύς
lexical_decisions.chosen: being a king in the likeness of the only God
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατ’ εἰκόνα expresses correspondence or likeness; the wording preserves the author’s comparison between Noah’s kingship and God.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀπὸ γένους ὢν Χάμ, τοῦ ποιήσαντος τὸν Μεστρέμ
lexical_decisions.chosen: from the lineage of Ham, who fathered Mestrem
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive participle τοῦ ποιήσαντος most naturally describes Ham as the one who produced or fathered Mestrem. The edition’s forms Χάμ and Μεστρέμ are preserved as names rather than harmonized with another form.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐξ οὗπερ τὰ Αἰγυπτίων καὶ Βαβυλωνίων καὶ Περσῶν ἐπλήθυνε φῦλα
lexical_decisions.chosen: from whom indeed the tribes of the Egyptians, Babylonians, and Persians multiplied
lexical_decisions.rationale: The nearest antecedent of οὗπερ is Mestrem, which is therefore followed in the main text; reference to Ham remains grammatically possible. The singular verb with the neuter plural φῦλα is an ordinary Greek agreement pattern.

passages.text: “From this lineage there arose in succession a certain man named Nimrod, who had inherited magical arts. Like a giant, he chose to set his mind against God. The Greeks called him Zoroaster. After the flood, this man desired kingship and, being a great magician, used magical arts to compel the star of the evil one now reigning—the star that astrologically observes the world—to bestow kingship upon him. But the star, since it was a ruler and had authority over the one using force, angrily poured down the fire of kingship, so that it might both comply with the adjuration and punish the one who had first compelled it.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: who had inherited magical arts
lexical_decisions.rationale: παραλαμβάνω can describe receiving something through transmission or succession; μαγικά is a substantive expression for magical practices or lore.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Like a giant
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase most naturally characterizes Nimrod, though it could also color the manner in which he opposed God.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he chose to set his mind against God
lexical_decisions.rationale: φρονεῖν concerns thought or disposition, while ἐναντία marks opposition; the rendering preserves both volition and mental hostility.

lexical_decisions.chosen: The Greeks called him Zoroaster
lexical_decisions.rationale: The relative clause identifies Nimrod as the person to whom the Greeks gave the name Zoroaster; it is retained in its source position before the account of his post-flood pursuit of kingship.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦ νῦν βασιλεύοντος κακοῦ τὸν ὡροσκοποῦντα κόσμον ἀστέρα
lexical_decisions.chosen: the star of the evil one now reigning—the star that astrologically observes the world
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὡροσκοπέω belongs to astrological observation and literally evokes watching an hour or ascendant. Alternatives include “watches the world’s hour” and “governs the world’s horoscope”; the chosen wording is intelligible without resolving the astrological mechanism more precisely than the Greek permits.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς τὴν ἐξ αὐτοῦ βασιλείας δόσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: to bestow kingship upon him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase expresses the intended result, a grant of kingship proceeding from the star; the recipient is contextually Nimrod.

lexical_decisions.chosen: But the star
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both ἀστήρ, “star,” and the substantival κακός, “evil one,” are masculine possible antecedents. The star is nearest and is supported by the following section’s description of the star’s stream being directed against Nimrod.

lexical_decisions.chosen: poured down the fire of kingship
lexical_decisions.rationale: The unusual source image is retained without replacing it with the later explanation that the fire was lightning.

lexical_decisions.chosen: comply with the adjuration
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὁρκισμός is an adjuration or binding invocation, and εὐγνωμονέω here indicates responding favorably or compliantly to it; “honor the oath” is another possible rendering.

passages.text: “By this lightning, then, which fell from heaven to earth, the magician Nimrod was killed and, because of what had happened, was renamed Zoroaster, since the star’s living stream had been borne against him. But the foolish among the people of that time thought that his soul had been summoned by a thunderbolt because of his love for God. After burying what remained of his body, they honored the tomb with a temple among the Persians, where the descent of the fire had occurred, and worshiped him as a god. Following this example, the others there also bury those who die by a thunderbolt as people dear to God, honor them with temples, and erect statues representing the dead in their own forms. From this, those who held power in the various regions similarly imitated the practice. Most of them honored with temples and carved images the tombs of people dear to them even when those people had not died by a thunderbolt; they also kindled altars and commanded that the dead be worshiped as gods. Much later, because so much time had passed, later generations came to believe that they really were gods.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐκ ταύτης οὖν τῆς ἐξ οὐρανοῦ χαμαὶ πεσούσης ἀστραπῆς
lexical_decisions.chosen: By this lightning, then, which fell from heaven to earth
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀστραπή is rendered “lightning,” preserving its distinction from the recurring κεραυνός, rendered “thunderbolt” below.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διὰ τὸ τὴν τοῦ ἀστέρος κατ’ αὐτοῦ ζῶσαν ἐνεχθῆναι ῥοήν
lexical_decisions.chosen: since the star’s living stream had been borne against him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the source’s proposed wordplay explaining the name Zoroaster through a “living” flow or stream associated with a star.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς διὰ τὴν εἰς θεὸν φιλίαν κεραυνῷ μεταπεμφθεῖσαν τὴν ψυχὴν νομίσαντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: thought that his soul had been summoned by a thunderbolt because of his love for God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive of μεταπέμπω commonly means “be sent for” or “be summoned.” The phrase εἰς θεὸν φιλίαν directs the love or friendship toward God, while κεραυνῷ is consistently represented here as “by a thunderbolt.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν μὲν τάφον ναῷ ἐτίμησαν ἐν Πέρσαις
lexical_decisions.chosen: they honored the tomb with a temple among the Persians
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐν Πέρσαις literally locates the action among the Persian people; “in Persia” would be a smoother geographical alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those who die by a thunderbolt as people dear to God
lexical_decisions.rationale: θεοφιλεῖς most naturally describes people dear or beloved to God here, presenting death by a thunderbolt as evidence of divine favor. “God-loving” is a possible formal alternative, but “friends of God” would blur the distinction from the preceding love directed toward God.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν τεθνεώτων ἰδίων μορφῶν ἱστᾶσιν ἀγάλματα
lexical_decisions.chosen: erect statues representing the dead in their own forms
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase describes images corresponding to the individual forms or likenesses of the deceased.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ τῶν κατὰ τόπους οἱ δυναστεύσαντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: those who held power in the various regions
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression τῶν κατὰ τόπους is elliptical; the rendering takes it as referring to people or communities distributed place by place.

lexical_decisions.chosen: even when those people had not died by a thunderbolt
lexical_decisions.rationale: The negation is retained, and κεραυνός receives the same rendering as in the preceding descriptions of this manner of death. καί has the contextual force “even.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: with temples and carved images
lexical_decisions.rationale: ξόανα are carved cult images, often specifically wooden, but the material is not made explicit here.

lexical_decisions.chosen: commanded that the dead be worshiped as gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: The infinitive lacks an explicit accusative subject. The deceased people whose tombs were honored are the contextual referent; taking the tombs or images themselves as the object is less likely but grammatically conceivable.

passages.text: Nevertheless, although the origin was one, many divisions of kingship arose in this way. The Persians were the first to take coals from the lightning that had fallen from heaven and preserve them with fuel of their own. They gave the fire special honor as a heavenly god, and because they were the first to worship it, they were the first to be honored with kingship by that very fire. After them, the Babylonians stole coals from the fire there, brought them safely into their own lands, and worshiped it; they too reigned next in succession. The Egyptians acted likewise and in their own language called the fire Phthae, which is interpreted “Hephaestus”; the one who first reigned among them is also called by his name. Thus those who reigned in each locality followed this practice, made an image, and kindled altars in honor of the fire. Most of them were extinguished from kingship;

lexical_decisions.chosen: although the origin was one
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπαρχή can denote an origin, beginning, underlying basis, or established state. “Origin” fits the following account of how multiple divisions of kingship arose, though “although the underlying basis was one” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: preserve them with fuel of their own
lexical_decisions.rationale: τροφή ordinarily denotes nourishment or sustenance; in relation to coals, “fuel” conveys what feeds and preserves the fire.

lexical_decisions.chosen: into their own lands
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantivized neuter plural is elliptical and could refer to their own places, territory, or possessions. “Lands” contextually expresses the transfer from the Persian fire to Babylonia.

lexical_decisions.chosen: called the fire Phthae, which is interpreted “Hephaestus”
lexical_decisions.rationale: The Egyptian designation is transliterated, while the author’s Greek identification introduced by ἑρμηνεύεται is translated rather than harmonized with another naming tradition.

lexical_decisions.chosen: made an image
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἵδρυμα can denote an erected sacred image, a shrine, or a sacred establishment. “Image” is chosen in view of the ξόανα mentioned immediately afterward, while “made a shrine” remains a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς μὲν βασιλείας οἱ πλεῖστοι ἀπεσβέσθησαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Most of them were extinguished from kingship
lexical_decisions.rationale: The marked extinguishing metaphor is retained because it echoes the preceding fire imagery. The sense is that most lost their kingship, but that smoother wording would erase the wordplay.

passages.text: Yet they did not cease reverencing the carved images, because of the wicked contrivance of the Magi, who devised for them pretexts capable of holding them fast to futile worship. For, after installing the images with magical rites, they appointed festivals for them consisting of sacrifices, libations, flutes, and clapping. Deceived under cover of these things, the senseless—even though their kingship had been taken away—do not abandon the accumulated religious observances. To such an extent, because of their love of pleasure, did they prefer error to truth. These people also, after becoming drunk, raise a ritual cry beside the altar, while their soul, from its depths as if through dreams, foretells to them the punishment that is to come for such deeds of theirs.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the wicked contrivance of the Magi
lexical_decisions.rationale: μάγοι can denote Magi or magicians. “Magi” preserves the historically specific designation, while the magical rites in the context make the polemical sense clear.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εὑρόντων αὐτοῖς προφάσεις κρατεῖν αὐτοὺς πρὸς τὴν ματαίαν λατρείαν δυναμένας
lexical_decisions.chosen: who devised for them pretexts capable of holding them fast to futile worship
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὑρίσκω here concerns finding or devising pretexts, and κρατεῖν conveys keeping the worshipers under control or holding them fast.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἱδρύσαντες γὰρ αὐτὰ μαγικαῖς τελεταῖς ἑορτὰς αὐτοῖς ὥρισαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: For, after installing the images with magical rites, they appointed festivals for them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The explanatory γάρ is represented by “For.” The participle is read temporally, while ἱδρύω can denote setting up, installing, or ritually establishing an image.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐκ τε θυμάτων, σπονδῶν, αὐλῶν τε καὶ κρότων
lexical_decisions.chosen: consisting of sacrifices, libations, flutes, and clapping
lexical_decisions.rationale: κρότοι can denote clapping, striking sounds, noisy applause, or clashing. “Clapping” supplies a concrete festival sound, though “clashing sounds” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the accumulated religious observances
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally, these are religious observances that have “come together.” “Accumulated” treats them as observances combined in the festivals; “combined religious observances” or “assembled rites” are alternatives.

lexical_decisions.chosen: raise a ritual cry beside the altar
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὀλολύζω denotes a loud ritual cry or ululation, while παραβώμιον locates the action beside the altar.

passages.text: Therefore, with many forms of worship having passed through the world, we—the good merchants—are here bringing you the form of worship handed down to us from our ancestors and preserved, like a pearl, displaying it and placing it before your judgment and at your disposal. Choose what seems good to you. If, then, you choose what is ours, you will not only be able to escape demons and the sufferings caused by demons, but, as you yourselves put them to flight and are implored by them, you will also enjoy the good things that will exist forever.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πολλῶν οὖν ἐν βίῳ παρελθουσῶν θρησκειῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Therefore, with many forms of worship having passed through the world
lexical_decisions.rationale: “Therefore” explicitly represents the inferential οὖν. The genitive absolute is rendered circumstantially; it could also be understood concessively, “Therefore, although many forms of worship have passed through the world.” The phrase ἐν βίῳ may mean “in life” or, contextually, “in the world.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πάρεσμεν φέροντες ὑμῖν (οἱ ἀγαθοὶ ἔμποροι) ἐκ προγόνων ἡμῖν παραδοθείσης καὶ φυλαχθείσης θρησκείας ὥσπερ μαργαρίτην
lexical_decisions.chosen: we—the good merchants—are here bringing you the form of worship handed down to us from our ancestors and preserved, like a pearl
lexical_decisions.rationale: The presentation by the speakers is retained before the description of the inherited worship, following the supplied clause order. The genitive θρησκείας is represented idiomatically as what is brought and compared to a pearl; a more formally genitival interpretation is “bringing you, like a pearl, something from or of the worship handed down to us.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: we—the good merchants
lexical_decisions.rationale: The nominative phrase is appositional to the implied subject of πάρεσμεν and continues the pearl-merchant image.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ τῇ ὑμετέρᾳ κρίσει καὶ ἐξουσίᾳ τιθέντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: placing it before your judgment and at your disposal
lexical_decisions.rationale: κρίσις denotes judgment or evaluation, while ἐξουσία can denote authority, freedom of action, or power of disposal. The rendering preserves both the evaluation and the hearers’ freedom to choose.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Choose what seems good to you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantivized participle denotes what appears good or suitable to the hearers without asserting that their choice is objectively correct.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you choose what is ours
lexical_decisions.rationale: The neuter plural leaves the referent broad enough to include the speakers’ teaching, worship, and practices.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτοὶ αὐτὰ φυγαδεύοντες καὶ ἱκετευόμενοι ὑπ’ αὐτῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: as you yourselves put them to flight and are implored by them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The neuter αὐτά may refer to the sufferings or may collect both the demons and the demonic sufferings just mentioned. The genitive plural αὐτῶν is formally compatible with every gender, so its morphology does not identify its referent; although reference to the sufferings or the preceding collection is grammatically possible, the act of imploring contextually favors the demons as the agents. The English pronouns retain the contextual reference without introducing a gender distinction absent from the Greek form.

passages.text: For otherwise, while in the present life you are abused by demons with strange afflictions, upon release from the body you will also have your souls punished forever—in truth, not because God condemns them, but because evil deeds carry such a judgment. For the demons, having authority through the food rendered to them, are admitted by your own hands into your own bodies. For, after dwelling in the innermost recesses for a long time, they also become blended with the soul. And because of the negligence of those who do not think to help themselves, or are even unwilling to do so, the soul of these very people, united to the demon when the body is dissolved, must be carried by it to whatever places it wishes. Worst of all, when, at the consummation of all things, the demon is first handed over to the purifying fire, the soul blended with it must itself be punished inexpressibly, while the demon takes pleasure. For the soul, since it comes from light, cannot bear the flame of the fire, which is foreign to its kind, and is tormented; but the demon, being within the substance of its own kind, takes immense pleasure, having become a bond hard to break for the soul that, under its influence, shares its condition.

source_issues.source_quote: οἱ γὰρ δαίμονες, διὰ τῆς αὐτοῖς ἀποδοθείσης τροφῆς ἐξουσίαν ἔχοντες, ὑπὸ τῶν ὑμετέρων χειρῶν εἰς τὰ ὑμέτερα εἰσκρίνεται σώματα
source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints the singular verb εἰσκρίνεται with the plural subject οἱ δαίμονες and plural participle ἔχοντες. The English represents the contextually clear plural sense, but a plural Greek form would be a conjectural grammatical normalization rather than the supplied reading.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you are abused by demons with strange afflictions
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐνυβρίζω conveys abusive or outrageous treatment, while ἀλλόκοτος denotes what is strange, alien, or extraordinary.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ τῇ ἐκ τοῦ σώματος ἀπαλλαγῇ καὶ τὰς ψυχὰς εἰσαεὶ κολασθησομένας ἕξετε
lexical_decisions.chosen: upon release from the body you will also have your souls punished forever
lexical_decisions.rationale: The future passive participle κολασθησομένας states that punishment will actually be inflicted on the souls, not merely that they will face its possibility. The construction with ἕξετε is retained rather than recast as a wholly impersonal prediction.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ ἀληθῆ οὐ θεοῦ καταδικάζοντος, ἀλλὰ κακῶν πράξεων τοιαύτην ἐχουσῶν κρίσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: in truth, not because God condemns them, but because evil deeds carry such a judgment
lexical_decisions.rationale: τὰ ἀληθῆ functions adverbially as “in truth.” The contrasting genitive constructions deny that God’s condemnation is the cause and attribute the judgment to the character of evil deeds; the object “them” is supplied from the souls just mentioned.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through the food rendered to them
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀποδίδω can mean give back, render, or deliver what is due. “Rendered” preserves the implication of food presented to demons rather than ordinary eating alone.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐνδομυχήσαντες γὰρ πολλῷ τῷ χρόνῳ καὶ τῇ ψυχῇ ἀνακίρνανται
lexical_decisions.chosen: For, after dwelling in the innermost recesses for a long time, they also become blended with the soul
lexical_decisions.rationale: “For” represents the explanatory γάρ, and “also” represents καί. ἐνδομυχέω depicts dwelling or making a lair deep within, while ἀνακίρναμαι denotes becoming mixed or blended.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν ἑαυτοῖς βοηθεῖν μὴ νοούντων ἢ καὶ μὴ βουλομένων
lexical_decisions.chosen: those who do not think to help themselves, or are even unwilling to do so
lexical_decisions.rationale: νοέω with an infinitive can concern thinking of, considering, or intending an action. “Do not think to help themselves” avoids narrowing the phrase to ignorance about how to help; “do not intend to help themselves” is also viable.

lexical_decisions.chosen: be punished inexpressibly
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀπορρήτως can mean unspeakably, indescribably, or in a manner that cannot be disclosed. “Inexpressibly” preserves this uncertainty without reducing the punishment to something merely secret.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the flame of the fire, which is foreign to its kind
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀλλόφυλος literally describes something belonging to another race or kind. The flame is represented as foreign to the soul that comes from light, in contrast to the demon’s affinity with the fire.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a bond hard to break
lexical_decisions.rationale: δύσρηκτος describes something difficult to break or rupture without necessarily asserting absolute impossibility.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for the soul that, under its influence, shares its condition
lexical_decisions.rationale: συμπαθέω can mean sharing a condition, being affected together, suffering together, or having affinity, while ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ may express agency or causal influence. The rendering takes the soul as sharing the demon’s joined condition under its influence, not necessarily its pleasurable response to the fire. Alternatives include “for the soul that suffers together with it because of it” and “for the soul affected along with it under its power.”

passages.text: As for the demons’ eagerness to slip into human bodies, this is the cause. Being spirits and having desire for foods, drinks, and intercourse, yet being unable to partake because they are spirits and need instruments suited to their use, they enter human bodies so that, obtaining them as instruments that serve them, they may be able to obtain what they want—whether foods through the person’s teeth or intercourse through that person’s genitals. Consequently, to put demons to flight, deprivation, fasting, and hardship are the most fitting aid. For if they enter a human body for the sake of partaking, it is clear that hardship drives them out. But since some are more formidable and, having persisted obstinately, remain in the body undergoing punishment even while they themselves are being punished, it is therefore necessary to take refuge in God with prayers and supplications, while abstaining from every occasion of impurity, so that God’s hand may be able to touch that person for healing, as one who is pure and believes.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοὺς δαίμονας γλίχεσθαι εἰς τὰ ἀνθρώπων εἰσδύειν σώματα
lexical_decisions.chosen: the demons’ eagerness to slip into human bodies
lexical_decisions.rationale: γλίχομαι expresses eager desire or striving, while εἰσδύω depicts entering or slipping into something.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς βρωτὰ καὶ ποτὰ καὶ συνουσίαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: for foods, drinks, and intercourse
lexical_decisions.rationale: Although συνουσία can denote association generally, the later reference to the genitals establishes sexual intercourse here.

lexical_decisions.chosen: obtaining them as instruments that serve them
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπουργέω describes rendering subordinate service; the human bodies function as instrumental agents through which the demons satisfy their desires.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ ἔνδεια καὶ ἡ νηστεία καὶ ἡ κακουχία
lexical_decisions.chosen: deprivation, fasting, and hardship
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔνδεια denotes lack or deprivation, while κακουχία denotes harsh treatment, bodily hardship, or privation; the separate terms are retained rather than collapsed into fasting.

lexical_decisions.chosen: having persisted obstinately
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compound conveys continued contentious resistance or stubborn persistence; “persisted obstinately” fits demons that remain despite punishment.

lexical_decisions.chosen: while abstaining from every occasion of impurity
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόφασις can mean pretext, occasion, or ostensible cause. “Occasion” best fits practical abstention, though “every impure pretext” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ τοῦ θεοῦ χεὶρ εἰς ἴασιν αὐτοῦ ἐπιψαῦσαι δυνηθῇ ὡς ἁγνοῦ καὶ πιστεύοντος
lexical_decisions.chosen: God’s hand may be able to touch that person for healing, as one who is pure and believes
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιψαύω takes the genitive αὐτοῦ. Although the pronoun could grammatically look back toward the body, the accompanying “pure and believing” identifies the intended referent as the afflicted person.

passages.text: And in prayers one must also confess that one has taken refuge in God and solemnly affirm that, on the demon’s part, it is not disobedience but delay. For everything comes to pass for the one who believes, but nothing for the one who does not believe. Hence the demons themselves, knowing the quantity of faith possessed by those whom they overpower, allot a proportionate measure of their own persistence. For this reason they persist with those who do not believe, linger with those who have difficulty believing, but cannot remain even for an instant with those who have believed completely and act well. For the soul, having been turned by faith toward God as though into the nature of water, extinguishes the demon like a spark of fire. It is therefore difficult for each person to recognize the flight of the demon within them. For the demons, blending themselves with souls so that a person may neglect their own salvation, suggest to each person’s mind thoughts directed toward whatever they wish.

lexical_decisions.chosen: that one has taken refuge in God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect infinitive presents recourse to God as an accomplished act with a continuing state.

lexical_decisions.chosen: not disobedience but delay
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contrast concerns the demon’s delayed departure rather than outright refusal.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the quantity of faith
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording explicitly presents faith as possessing a measurable degree or amount.

lexical_decisions.chosen: linger with those who have difficulty believing
lexical_decisions.rationale: δύσπιστος denotes difficulty or reluctance in believing, distinguished here from outright unbelief.

lexical_decisions.chosen: It is therefore difficult
lexical_decisions.rationale: κάματος literally denotes labor or weariness and here characterizes recognition as laborious or difficult.

passages.text: Hence many, not knowing where the power acting on them comes from, assent to the evil notions suggested by demons as though they were the reasoning of their own soul. Therefore they become more reluctant to go to those capable of saving them; and while being consumed by the very demons lying in wait for them, they fail to recognize those people. The demons lurking in the innermost recesses of their souls prompt them to suppose that it is not a demon troubling them but a bodily disease—such as acrid matter, bile, phlegm, an imbalance of blood, inflammation of the meninges, or something else—. . . . But even if this were so, not even that is exempt from being a form of demon. For the universal and earthy soul, which extends through all foods as their cause, when taken in to a greater extent through more abundant food, itself unites with the spirit as something kindred to it—the spirit being the soul of a human being—while the material portion of the food, once united with the body, is smeared upon it like a terrible poison. Therefore self-sufficiency is good in everything.

source_issues.source_quote: καὶ τοὺς ὑπ’ αὐτῶν τῶν ἐνεδρευόντων δαιμόνων ἀναλισκόμενοι ἀγνοοῦσιν
source_issues.issue: The placement of the accusative τοὺς before the intervening participial phrase is marked, but it can defensibly function as an anaphoric object of ἀγνοοῦσιν, referring back to τοὺς σώζειν αὐτοὺς δυναμένους. The main text follows that reading. If τοὺς is not anaphoric, the construction becomes irregular and deletion might be conjectured, but no correction is adopted.

source_issues.source_quote: ἢ ἄλλου τινός) . . . . εἰ δὲ καὶ τοῦτο ἦν
source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a lacuna marked by exactly four dots. Its content is unavailable, and no restoration has been supplied; the same four-dot gap remains explicit in the translation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: where the power acting on them comes from
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive verb describes an agency or power operating upon them, while πόθεν asks its source.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ τοὺς ὑπ’ αὐτῶν τῶν ἐνεδρευόντων δαιμόνων ἀναλισκόμενοι ἀγνοοῦσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: and while being consumed by the very demons lying in wait for them, they fail to recognize those people
lexical_decisions.rationale: The accusative τοὺς is taken anaphorically as the object of ἀγνοοῦσιν, referring to the people capable of saving them; ἀναλισκόμενοι describes those who fail to recognize their prospective helpers.

lexical_decisions.chosen: demons lurking in the innermost recesses
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐνδομυχέω depicts dwelling or hiding deep within an interior recess.

lexical_decisions.chosen: acrid matter
lexical_decisions.rationale: In the medical list ὕλη denotes bodily matter or material; “acrid humor” is possible but would impose a more specific technical sense.

lexical_decisions.chosen: being a form of demon
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase categorizes the proposed bodily condition as a manifestation or kind of demon within the author’s framework.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ γὰρ καθόλου καὶ γεώδης ψυχή
lexical_decisions.chosen: For the universal and earthy soul
lexical_decisions.rationale: καθόλου and γεώδης characterize this soul as universal and earth-associated; “general terrestrial soul” is a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: self-sufficiency
lexical_decisions.rationale: In this dietary context αὐτάρκεια may imply contentment, sufficiency, or moderation, but the main rendering retains its broader sense.

passages.text: Some of the wicked demons lie in wait in another way. At first they do not even reveal that they exist, so that no effort against them may arise; but at an opportune moment, under the pretext of anger, erotic passion, or something else, they suddenly assault the body by a sword, a noose, a precipice, or some other means. And they bring it about that the deceived souls of those who have been mingled with them will be punished to the end, as we said, after they—the demons—have entered the purifying fire. Others, being ambushed in another way, do not approach us, because they are deceived by the thoughts of the wicked demons into supposing that they suffer these things from their own gods because of their neglect toward them, that they can reconcile those gods through sacrifices, and that they must not approach us but, on the contrary, must flee and hate us. And they likewise hate and flee those who have greater compassion for them and pursue them in order to benefit them.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν ἀρχὴν οὐδὲ ὅτι εἰσὶν ἐνφαίνοντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: At first they do not even reveal that they exist
lexical_decisions.rationale: τὴν ἀρχήν can mean “at the beginning” or idiomatically “at all”; the subsequent reference to an opportune occasion favors a temporal contrast.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὀργῆς προφάσει, ἔρωτος ἢ ἄλλου τινὸς
lexical_decisions.chosen: under the pretext of anger, erotic passion, or something else
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔρως here denotes passionate or erotic desire, while πρόφασις presents these emotions as pretexts or occasions.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they suddenly assault the body
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐνυβρίζω conveys violent mistreatment or outrage against the body.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they bring it about that ... will be punished to the end
lexical_decisions.rationale: The future passive participle κολασθησομένας gives the punishment prospective force. εἰς τέλος may mean “to the end,” “completely,” or, in some contexts, “forever”; the source-transparent wording leaves its extent unresolved.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after they—the demons—have entered the purifying fire
lexical_decisions.rationale: χωρήσαντες is nominative masculine plural and most directly resumes the demons as grammatical subject. A contextual association with the people mingled with them is possible despite the case difference.

lexical_decisions.chosen: And they likewise hate and flee
lexical_decisions.rationale: The selected print reads ὁμῶς, ordinarily alike, equally, or likewise. Likewise preserves that sense. The prior English all the same was concessive in context, corresponding to the different customary Greek accentuation ὅμως, nevertheless; that interpretation is not silently imposed or presented as the printed form. No Greek accent correction or OCR defect is claimed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν ἀνακεκραμένων τὰς ἠπατημένας αὐτοῖς ψυχάς
lexical_decisions.chosen: the deceived souls of those who have been mingled with them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main wording attaches αὐτοῖς to the more distant mingling participle, supported by the blending of demons with souls described immediately before in9.11. A material alternative attaches it to the nearer deceived participle: the souls deceived by them, belonging to those who have been mingled. The main text does not claim its longer-distance attachment is uniquely established, and no correction to the supplied Greek is proposed.

passages.text: Thus, by hating and fleeing us, they are ensnared, not knowing from what source it comes about that they think things contrary to their own salvation. For neither can we compel them, when they are unwilling, to incline toward salvation—since we do not now have such authority over them—nor can they by themselves recognize the demon’s evil thought, for they do not know from where the thoughts of evil are suggested to them. These are the people whom the demons terrify by appearing in whatever forms they wish. Sometimes they also prescribe treatments for the sick, and in this way they gain among those already deceived a reputation as gods and conceal from most people that they are demons—but not from us, who know their secret, the reason why they do such things, transforming themselves in dreams against those over whom they have authority. Some they terrify; to others they issue oracles, demand sacrifices, and command them to share a feast, so that they may drink down their souls along with them.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to incline toward salvation
lexical_decisions.rationale: νεύω depicts leaning, inclining, or signaling assent rather than merely moving physically.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the demon’s evil thought
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐνθύμησις can denote a thought, consideration, or inward suggestion; the genitive identifies the demon as its source.

lexical_decisions.chosen: prescribe treatments
lexical_decisions.rationale: συντάσσω can mean arrange or prescribe, and θεραπεία here refers to treatment or care for the sick.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they gain ... a reputation as gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: δόξα here is reputation or estimation, while θεῶν expresses the status attributed to them.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἑαυτοὺς κατ’ ὄναρ καθ’ ὧν τὴν ἐξουσίαν ἔχουσι μεταμορφοῦντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: transforming themselves in dreams against those over whom they have authority
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first κατά marks the dream setting; the second can bear the adversative sense “against.” It may alternatively refer more generally to those subject to their power.

lexical_decisions.chosen: so that they may drink down their souls along with them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The souls are the accusative object of συνπίνωσιν. The compound evokes drinking together at the feast while portraying the demons as consuming the participants’ souls.

passages.text: For just as fearsome snakes draw sparrows to themselves by their breath, so these beings draw those who share their table toward their own will, having mingled with their minds through food and drink. In dreams they transform themselves according to the forms of carved images, in order to increase deception. For the carved image is neither alive nor possessed of a divine spirit; the demon that appeared made use of its form. To how many other people have they similarly appeared in dreams—and, when those people met one another while awake and compared their dream experiences, did those people not agree? Thus it is no longer a dream; that is a manifestation—but either a demon's or the soul's, the soul reproducing as images the effects arising from present fears and desire. Or, indeed, struck by fear in its mind, it gives birth to images through dreams. If you think carved images, being possessed of breath, can perform such things, set them on a balance. With the beam level, place the counterweight on the other pan and ask them to become either heavier or lighter. If that happens, they have breath. But it does not happen. But if it does happen, is such a thing thereby a god? For this can happen even by a demon's finger. Worms move too, and are not called gods.

source_issues.issue: The former Lagarde reading is exactly παρίᾳ. The selected Dressel main-print reading παροῦσι was independently read from the primary image. Dressel's apparatus identifies it as Cotelerius's conjecture: its printed attestation is not a claim of directly newly attested manuscript wording. It is translated as present while the remaining sentence-level interpretation is separately disclosed; no unique original recovery is claimed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by their breath
lexical_decisions.rationale: The snake comparison refers to breath or exhalation, not a separately named snake spirit. It is retained as the speaker's ancient analogy rather than corrected into modern animal behavior.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὥστε οὐκέτι ὄναρ ἐπιφανείη ἐκεῖνό ἐστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Thus it is no longer a dream; that is a manifestation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes ὄναρ nominally as the denied dream, with an elliptical copula, followed by the positive predication that it is a manifestation. The preceding assent-seeking question about agreement supports distinguishing a corroborated experience from a mere dream, while the next clause qualifies whose manifestation it is. A materially different nominal reading takes ὄναρ adverbially and denies the whole dream-apparition predicate: Thus that is no longer an apparition in a dream. This changes what is denied and affirmed and remains viable if the preceding question concerns disagreement. The unusual ἐπιφανείη is read as a noun; an optative verbal reading might appear is another morphological alternative but fits the copular sequence less readily. English interpretive punctuation does not alter the supplied spelling or punctuation of the Greek, and no missing Greek word has been restored.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ψυχῆς τὰ ἐπιγενήματα τοῖς παροῦσι φόβοις καὶ ἐπιθυμίᾳ ἀποδιδούσης τὰς ἰδέας
lexical_decisions.chosen: the soul's, the soul reproducing as images the effects arising from present fears and desire
lexical_decisions.rationale: The effects and images are taken as two expressions of the dream products, with present fears and desire as the circumstances generating them. A material alternative foregrounds the returning of images in response to those fears and desire: the soul giving back images of their ensuing effects. The main text preserves both the effects and the images rather than collapsing the first accusative into the fears themselves. The selected present adjective directly agrees with fears, while desire is coordinated with them.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἢ γὰρ φόβῳ τὸν νοῦν πληγεῖσα
lexical_decisions.chosen: Or, indeed, struck by fear in its mind
lexical_decisions.rationale: The initial or is retained as another explanatory turn rather than silently deleted. The feminine participle continues the soul, and mind expresses the respect in which fear strikes it.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ δὲ ἔσται, οὕτω τὸ τοιοῦτο θεός ἐστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: But if it does happen, is such a thing thereby a god?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The next demon-finger and worm examples support a rhetorical question denying that movement alone establishes divinity. The source has a full stop, so the question punctuation is interpretive. An assertion such a thing is then a god is a formal alternative, but runs against the ensuing counterexamples; the Greek words have not been changed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πόσοις κατ’ ὄναρ ὁμοίως ἄλλοις ὤφθησαν καὶ ὕπαρ συναντήσαντες ἀλλήλοις πρὸς τὸ κατ’ ὄναρ ἀντιβάλλοντες οὐ συνεφώνησαν;
lexical_decisions.chosen: To how many other people have they similarly appeared in dreams—and, when those people met one another while awake and compared their dream experiences, did those people not agree?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The appearing beings are the subject of appeared; the subsequent meeting, comparing, and agreement are read with their human recipients as an understood changed subject. The main text makes that change explicit. The negative question is taken rhetorically to invite assent that the recipients agreed. A material alternative asks how many recipients did not agree, treating οὐ as actual disagreement rather than an assent-seeking question. Neither rhetorical interpretation nor the unmarked subject shift is presented as grammatically unique.

passages.text: That each person’s soul, in accordance with its preconceptions, depicts forms of demons, and that the so-called gods do not appear, is clear from the fact that they do not appear to Jews. But someone will say, “How, then, do they deliver oracles foretelling the future?” This too is false. Yet grant that it is true: does that therefore make such a thing a god? For something is not a god merely because it foretells the future. Python mediums also foretell the future, but when adjured by us as demons, they are driven away. But someone will say, “They prescribe treatments for some people.” That is false. Yet grant that this is so: does that therefore make such a thing a god? Physicians also heal many people, and they are not gods. “But,” someone says, “physicians do not invariably heal those for whom they care, whereas these both deliver an oracle and heal.” Demons, however, know the remedies actually suited to each particular ailment. Consequently, they are knowledgeable physicians capable of healing—even these ailments that human beings are capable of healing—but they are also divinatory beings and know when each ailment is cured spontaneously; at that time they prescribe the treatments, so that they may claim the credit for themselves.

source_issues.issue: The printed text shifts to neuter plural participial forms after the masculine subjects οἱ δαίμονες and ἰατροὶ ... δυνάμενοι. This may be an anacoluthon or may reflect an implicit neuter referent such as δαιμόνια. The translation follows the demons as the continuing semantic subject, but that interpretation remains provisional.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in accordance with its preconceptions
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρός with the accusative indicates correspondence to each soul’s prior conceptions, according to which it depicts the demonic forms.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Python mediums
lexical_decisions.rationale: The term denotes persons or agencies associated with a Python spirit and divination. Alternatives include “Python spirits” and “those possessed by Python.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δεδόσθω δὲ ἀλήθειαν εἶναι, οὕτω τὸ τοιοῦτο θεός ἐστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Yet grant that it is true: does that therefore make such a thing a god?
lexical_decisions.rationale: Although the last clause is printed as a statement, the immediately following denial supports taking it as a rhetorical question: even genuine prediction would not establish divinity.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ταῦτα τὰ ὑπὸ ἀνθρώπων ἰαθῆναι δυνάμενα
lexical_decisions.chosen: even these ailments that human beings are capable of healing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The neuter ταῦτα is understood as referring to the ailments under discussion and emphasizes that they also fall within the reach of human medicine.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ εἰδότα πότε ἕκαστον ἐξ αὐτομάτου θεραπεύεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: and know when each ailment is cured spontaneously
lexical_decisions.rationale: The neuter ἕκαστον most naturally resumes the earlier ἕκαστον πάθος, “each ailment.” A patient-focused alternative, “when each person recovers spontaneously,” is contextually possible but less directly reflects the grammatical gender and antecedent.

lexical_decisions.chosen: so that they may claim the credit for themselves
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally, they seek to “inscribe” themselves upon the cure, idiomatically attaching their own name or credit to it.
