passages.text: For why do they announce healings by oracle only after a long time? Why, if they can do everything, do they not bring about healing without an offering? Why do they prescribe treatments for some who pray, but sometimes deliver no oracle to others who are even more closely connected with them? It is in this way: whenever a spontaneous recovery is about to occur, they make a promise so that they may claim the credit for themselves. Others fell ill and prayed, and when they recovered spontaneously, they credited those whom they had invoked and made votive offerings. Those who died after prayer, however, cannot dedicate their failures. Yet if the relatives of the dead, or some from among them, had jointly investigated the failures, you would have found the failures more numerous than the successes. But no one already prepossessed in their favor wants to expose the case against them, being ashamed or afraid. On the contrary, they join in concealing their well-attested absurdities.

source_issues.issue: The image-checked print has the unassimilated compound spelling συνκρύβουσιν, where συγκρύβουσιν would be the standard assimilated spelling. The printed form still yields the clear sense “conceal together” or “join in concealing.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: without an offering
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantivized infinitive means presenting something, naturally an offering in this cultic context. The more literal alternative is “without presenting anything.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: who are even more closely connected with them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The comparative describes a closer relationship or affiliation, though whether familial, cultic, or generally intimate is not specified.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἱ μέντοι γε μετὰ εὐχὴν διαφωνήσαντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: Those who died after prayer, however
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαφωνέω ordinarily denotes disagreement, discrepancy, or an outcome contrary to expectation, so a broader rendering would be “those whose cases turned out otherwise after prayer.” The following reference to “the relatives of the dead” strongly supports understanding it here as a euphemistic reference to those whose failed treatment ended in death.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πλὴν εἰ οἱ συγγενεῖς τῶν τεθνεώτων ἢ ἐξ αὐτῶν τινὲς συνεζήτησαν τὰς ἀποτυχίας, πλείονας ἂν εὑρήκειτε τὰς ἀποτυχίας τῶν ἐπιτευγμάτων
lexical_decisions.chosen: Yet if the relatives of the dead, or some from among them, had jointly investigated the failures, you would have found the failures more numerous than the successes
lexical_decisions.rationale: The aorist indicative in the condition and the pluperfect with ἄν in the result form a retrospective contrary-to-fact construction. The referent of ἐξ αὐτῶν remains open; it may indicate some among the unsuccessful supplicants or among a broader previously mentioned group.

lexical_decisions.chosen: had jointly investigated the failures
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb can mean jointly examine, investigate, or discuss. “Had compiled the failures” is possible in view of the subsequent numerical comparison, but “jointly investigated” more directly preserves the verb.

lexical_decisions.chosen: already prepossessed in their favor
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect participle describes someone whose judgment has already been captured or prejudiced by them. “Previously taken in by them” is an alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: their well-attested absurdities
lexical_decisions.rationale: πιστά can mean credible, reliable, or firmly established. Here it presents the absurdities as attested evidence rather than as conduct worthy of trust.

passages.text: How many also falsely claim oracular responses and cures accomplished by these images, and confirm them with oaths? How many have hired themselves out, undertaking through certain contrivances to suffer something and proclaiming it in that way, then, having been restored from their affliction by a counteracting treatment, say that the cure was revealed by an oracle, so that they may label the unfeeling thing an object of worship? How many of these objects were consecrated from the beginning by magical art, so that they might dream and give oracles? Yet over a long time these too proved discordant. How many now practice sorcery, wishing to strengthen such things? Nevertheless, if something has powers of divination or healing, that does not make it a god.

source_issues.issue: The former Lagarde reading is exactly ὑνερπολῇ. The selected independently image-read Dressel main-print reading is ὀνειροπολῇ, concerning dreaming or dream activity, not the unresolved former form. This is an explicitly documented public-domain primary-print variant; it is not adopted or relicensed upstream XML, a new manuscript collation, or an autograph claim. The contextual lexical alternatives remain disclosed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: having been restored from their affliction by a counteracting treatment
lexical_decisions.rationale: The restoration concerns the people in respect of their affliction, not a strengthening or restoration of the affliction itself. The counteraction opposes the contrived suffering; the text does not identify a substance, remedy, or procedure, so none is supplied.

lexical_decisions.chosen: so that they may label the unfeeling thing an object of worship
lexical_decisions.rationale: The insensate thing is what is labeled, and object of worship is its assigned designation. The translation does not add a physical inscription or a particular dedication text.

lexical_decisions.chosen: so that they might dream and give oracles
lexical_decisions.rationale: The selected first verb concerns dreaming or dealing in dreams; the second concerns giving oracular responses. Dream preserves the lexical activity as attributed to the consecrated objects without inventing a mechanism. Deal in dreams or provide dream manifestations is a material contextual alternative in the preceding account of images appearing to dreamers. The source's singular verbs with the neuter plural things are rendered by normal English plural agreement.

lexical_decisions.chosen: over a long time these too proved discordant
lexical_decisions.rationale: The lack of agreement or consistency is retained, without inventing a specific prediction, date, or measurable error rate.

passages.text: For God can do everything. He is good and just, showing patience toward everyone now, so that those who are willing, after regretting the evil deeds they committed and living accordingly, may, on the day when everything is judged, receive what they deserve. Therefore begin now, obeying God, the cause of good knowledge, to oppose your evil desires and thoughts, so that you may recover for yourselves the original saving religion handed down to humanity. In this way good things will immediately spring up for you; once you have received them, you will thereafter leave behind your experience of evils. But give thanks to the one who gave them, reigning forever with the King of Peace over the inexpressible good things. At present, after washing yourselves in an ever-flowing river or spring, or indeed even in the sea, with the thrice-blessed invocation, you will not only be able to drive away the spirits lurking in your innermost recesses, but—if you yourselves no longer sin and believe God without wavering—you will drive out other people’s evil spirits and fierce demons, together with their dreadful afflictions. Sometimes, however, they will flee when you merely yield. For they recognize those who have given themselves to God, and therefore, showing them honor, they flee in fear. Just as yesterday you saw how, when I had put off praying for those who were suffering until after the discourse, the afflictions themselves cried aloud because of the honor paid to the religion, unable to endure for even a short time.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after regretting
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb denotes regret or a changed concern regarding the evils committed. It is kept distinct from the μετανοέω terminology governed by the reorientation policy.

lexical_decisions.chosen: and living accordingly
lexical_decisions.rationale: πολιτεύομαι concerns conducting one’s life. “Accordingly” expresses the contextual connection with regret; the more formally literal alternative is “and having conducted their lives.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: obeying God, the cause of good knowledge
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative αἰτίᾳ is taken in apposition to θεῷ, identifying God as the cause of good knowledge. Other possible attachments are “because of good knowledge, obeying God” and “for the sake of good knowledge, obeying God.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν πρώτην τῇ ἀνθρωπότητι παραδοθεῖσαν σωτήριον θρησκείαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the original saving religion handed down to humanity
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρώτην characterizes the religion as first or original, while σωτήριον describes it as saving. The wording preserves the author’s historical claim without harmonization.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἅτινα λαβόντες πεῖραν τῶν κακῶν τοῦ λοιποῦ καταλείψετε
lexical_decisions.chosen: once you have received them, you will thereafter leave behind your experience of evils
lexical_decisions.rationale: The chosen attachment takes ἅτινα, referring to the good things, as the object of λαβόντες and πεῖραν τῶν κακῶν as the object of καταλείψετε. A grammatically possible alternative joins λαβόντες πεῖραν τῶν κακῶν, “having experienced evils,” and takes ἅτινα as the object of καταλείψετε: “which, after experiencing evils, you will thereafter leave behind.” That alternative would make the promised good things what is abandoned and is therefore contextually difficult.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with the thrice-blessed invocation
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπονομασία can mean naming, designation, or invocation. In the washing context, “invocation” conveys an enacted naming formula without supplying words not quoted in the source.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ μόνον τὰ ἐνδομυχοῦντα ὑμῖν πνεύματα ἀπελάσαι δυνήσεσθε, ἀλλ᾽ αὐτοὶ μηκέτι ἁμαρτάνοντες καὶ θεῷ ἀνενδοιάστως πιστεύοντες τὰ ἄλλων κακὰ πνεύματα καὶ δαιμόνια χαλεπὰ σὺν τοῖς δεινοῖς πάθεσιν ἀπελάσετε
lexical_decisions.chosen: you will not only be able to drive away the spirits lurking in your innermost recesses, but—if you yourselves no longer sin and believe God without wavering—you will drive out other people’s evil spirits and fierce demons, together with their dreadful afflictions
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first member explicitly expresses ability with ἀπελάσαι δυνήσεσθε, whereas the second uses the direct future ἀπελάσετε. The English therefore does not extend “be able” over the second expulsion.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the spirits lurking in your innermost recesses
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐνδομυχέω depicts dwelling or hiding deep within and preserves the source’s spatial image.

lexical_decisions.chosen: when you merely yield
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive absolute uses ἐνδίδωμι in the intransitive sense “yield” or “give way.” In context it may mean yielding oneself to God, as the following clause about self-dedication suggests; “when you merely consent” or “when you merely permit it” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτὰ τὰ πάθη τῇ πρὸς τὴν θρησκείαν τιμῇ ἀνέκραγεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the afflictions themselves cried aloud
lexical_decisions.rationale: The neuter plural subject takes a singular verb, a regular Greek construction. The personification, or identification of the afflictions with their spiritual agents, is preserved rather than explained away.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐμοῦ ἀναθεμένου μετὰ τὴν προσομιλίαν εὔξασθαι ὑπὲρ τῶν πασχόντων
lexical_decisions.chosen: when I had put off praying for those who were suffering until after the discourse
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes ἀναθεμένου as postponing or reserving the prayer and attaches after the discourse to its intended time. This fits the following inability of the afflictions to endure even the brief delay. A material alternative takes the verb as undertaking: when after the discourse I undertook to pray for those who were suffering. That places the undertaking after the discourse rather than depicting the prayer as deferred. Both lexical and temporal choices are disclosed; the verified Greek has not been corrected.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτὰ τὰ πάθη τῇ πρὸς τὴν θρησκείαν τιμῇ ἀνέκραγεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the afflictions themselves cried aloud because of the honor paid to the religion
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main causal dative leaves the source of the honor unexpressed. A material alternative is cried aloud out of respect for the religion, taking the afflictions or their spiritual agents themselves as showing reverence, supported by the immediately preceding demons showing honor. Neither identifies a new explicit honor-giver, and the personification of the afflictions remains intact.

passages.text: Therefore, do not suppose that we are unafraid of demons because we are of a different nature. For we are of the same nature as you, though not of the same religion. Consequently, being superior to you not merely by much but altogether, we do not begrudge your becoming such people; on the contrary, we counsel you to do so, knowing that all these beings, in an uncomprehending way, hold in special regard and fear those who have become closely allied with God.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡμεῖς ἄλλης φύσεως ὄντες κατὰ τοῦτο δαίμονας οὐ φοβούμεθα
lexical_decisions.chosen: we are unafraid of demons because we are of a different nature
lexical_decisions.rationale: The warning rejects a proposed explanation of their fearlessness, not necessarily the claim that they are unafraid: their freedom from fear comes from religion rather than a different nature.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς γὰρ αὐτῆς ὑμῖν ἐσμὲν φύσεως, ἀλλ᾽ οὐ θρησκείας
lexical_decisions.chosen: For we are of the same nature as you, though not of the same religion
lexical_decisions.rationale: The second genitive is elliptical, contrasting shared human nature with differing religion or worship.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ πολύ, ἀλλὰ τὸ πᾶν κρείττονες
lexical_decisions.chosen: superior to you not merely by much but altogether
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compressed expression is literally “not much, but the whole/altogether.” The rendering treats it as a rhetorical escalation beyond superiority by degree to comprehensive superiority. “Not by much, but in every respect superior” is a more formally literal but potentially contradictory-sounding alternative; no correction of the printed πολύ is warranted.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ὑμᾶς τοιούτους γενέσθαι οὐ φθονοῦμεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: we do not begrudge your becoming such people
lexical_decisions.rationale: τοιούτους refers to becoming people of the religious standing just described, while φθονέω means begrudging or envying another’s acquisition of that standing.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those who have become closely allied with God
lexical_decisions.rationale: προσοικειόω denotes being brought into close relationship or affinity. Alternatives include “those made God’s own” and “those who have drawn near to God.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ταῦτα πάντα ἀγνώστως προτιμᾷ καὶ φοβεῖται
lexical_decisions.chosen: all these beings, in an uncomprehending way, hold in special regard and fear
lexical_decisions.rationale: The neuter plural collectively refers to the demonic beings or powers under discussion and takes singular Greek verbs. ἀγνώστως may mean “unknowingly,” “without understanding,” or “in an inexplicable manner.” The chosen wording allows the beings to recognize God’s people, as stated previously, without necessarily understanding their standing or authority.

passages.text: For just as the soldiers subordinate to one of Caesar’s commanders of a thousand know, because of the authority of the one who granted it, to honor the person who received it—so fully that those set over them can say to one, “Come,” and he comes, and to another, “Go,” and he goes—so also the person who has given himself to God—faithful as he is—merely speaks to demons and afflictions and is obeyed; and demons withdraw, though they are much stronger than those commanding them. For by an inexpressible power God subjects each person’s mind to whomever he wishes. For just as many governors, together with all their camps and cities, have feared Caesar, although he is a man, while each person’s heart hastens to give precedence to the image of all things (for all things, enslaved by God’s will, do not know the cause because of fear), so all the spirits that produce affliction honor and flee the person who takes refuge in God and carries righteous faith in his own heart as though it were God’s image, having become afraid through some natural way.

source_issues.source_quote: (πιστὸς ὢν δαίμοσίν τε καὶ πάθεσιν) μόνον λέγων ἀκούεται
source_issues.issue: The printed parentheses group δαίμοσίν τε καὶ πάθεσιν with πιστός, which could yield the contextually difficult sense “faithful/trustworthy to demons and afflictions.” The translation instead construes those datives with λέγων across the editorial parenthesis: the faithful person speaks to demons and afflictions and is obeyed. Another possible reading is that he is recognized as trustworthy by them.
source_issues.proposed_reading: πιστὸς ὢν, δαίμοσίν τε καὶ πάθεσιν μόνον λέγων, ἀκούεται

lexical_decisions.chosen: one of Caesar’s commanders of a thousand
lexical_decisions.rationale: χιλίαρχος literally denotes a commander of a thousand; the expanded rendering translates the office rather than merely transliterating it.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those set over them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle can denote people placed in authority; “those standing by” is also lexically possible, but the command structure favors the former.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀφράστῳ γὰρ δυνάμει τὸν ἑκάστου νοῦν ὁ θεὸς ὑποτάσσει ᾧ βούλεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: For by an inexpressible power God subjects each person’s mind to whomever he wishes
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative relative ᾧ is taken personally as “whomever”; “to whatever he wishes” remains grammatically possible but fits the comparison with delegated personal authority less well.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the image of all things
lexical_decisions.rationale: The referent of the image is not explicitly identified. The genitive may also be represented as “of the whole” or “of the universe,” so the translation does not identify the image specifically with Caesar or with God.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: θεοῦ γὰρ βουλῇ τὰ πάντα δεδουλωμένα φόβῳ τὴν αἰτίαν οὐκ οἶδεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: for all things, enslaved by God’s will, do not know the cause because of fear
lexical_decisions.rationale: θεοῦ βουλῇ is taken instrumentally with δεδουλωμένα and φόβῳ causally with οὐκ οἶδεν. Alternatively, φόβῳ could mean that all things are “enslaved to fear.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: the spirits that produce affliction
lexical_decisions.rationale: πάθος can denote suffering, illness, or passion. “Affliction” retains a range broad enough for the surrounding healing and demonic context.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὥσπερ εἰκόνα αὐτοῦ ἐν τῇ αὐτοῦ βαστάζοντα καρδίᾳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: carries righteous faith in his own heart as though it were God’s image
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first αὐτοῦ is understood as referring to God and the second reflexively to the person taking refuge in God; the Greek itself uses the same pronoun for both.

passages.text: But nevertheless, even if all demons together with all afflictions flee from you, you must not rejoice in this alone, but in the fact that, because you have proved pleasing, your names have been inscribed in heaven as those of people who live forever. Thus the divine Holy Spirit too rejoices because a human being has conquered death; for the expulsion of demons takes place for someone else’s healing. We say these things, however, not as people who deny the claim that there is no need to help others, but because one must not grow conceited over this and neglect oneself. Sometimes demons flee some lawless men because of an honored name, and both the one who drove them away and the one who witnessed what happened are ambushed. The one who drove them away is ambushed as though he had been favored because of righteousness, not knowing the demon’s villainy (for the demon has both honored the name and, by its flight, wrapped the impious man in a conceit of righteousness and deceived him into not reorienting); but the one who witnessed what happened, having associated with the one who drove them away as with a devout man and having hastened toward the same way of life, perishes. At times they also pretend to flee oaths not connected with God, so that, after deceiving them, they may destroy them whenever they wish.

source_issues.issue: The printed period separates the elided conjunction ἀλλ᾽ from ὅμως, leaving ἀλλ᾽ abruptly isolated. The translation reads the two together as “But nevertheless” while retaining both words.

source_issues.source_quote: οὐχ ὡς ἀρνούμενοι τὸ μὴ δεῖν ἄλλοις βοηθεῖν
source_issues.issue: As printed, the nested negatives mean “not as denying the claim that there is no need to help others,” and that sense is retained in the translation. It is contextually awkward because the following clause warns only against neglecting oneself, and an intrusive μή may be suspected. The surviving wording nevertheless permits a defensible literal translation.
source_issues.proposed_reading: οὐχ ὡς ἀρνούμενοι τὸ δεῖν ἄλλοις βοηθεῖν

lexical_decisions.chosen: because you have proved pleasing
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὐαρεστία denotes being pleasing or acceptable. God is the likely implied evaluator, but the Greek does not state the referent explicitly.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the divine Holy Spirit
lexical_decisions.rationale: The article and paired adjectives present the spirit as the divine holy spirit in view; capitalization reflects the personal theological referent without adding a title absent from the wording.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who witnessed what happened
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἱστορέω can mean to observe, investigate, inquire about, visit, or recount. Here it denotes the person who learns of or observes the expulsion and consequently treats the exorcist as devout.

lexical_decisions.chosen: wrapped the impious man in a conceit of righteousness
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the clothing or enveloping image of περιβάλλω; οἴησις may mean an opinion, supposition, or conceited belief.

lexical_decisions.chosen: deceived him into not reorienting
lexical_decisions.rationale: The articular infinitive expresses the outcome sought by the deception. “Reorienting” follows the supplied terminology policy; “repenting” is the traditional alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: oaths not connected with God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle grammatically modifies ὅρκους and describes oaths not attached or devoted to God. Context may imply “oaths used by people not devoted to God,” but those people are not explicitly named in this phrase.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἵν’ ἀπατήσαντες αὐτοὺς ὅτε θελήσωσιν ἀνέλωσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: so that, after deceiving them, they may destroy them whenever they wish
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated masculine pronoun is preserved without supplying an explicit antecedent. It most plausibly concerns the people relying on the oaths, though grammatically it can refer back to the masculine plural ὅρκους.

passages.text: So then, we want you to know this too: unless someone willingly gives himself over as a servant to demons (as I said earlier), the demon has no authority against him. Therefore, having chosen to worship one God, having abstained from the “table of demons,” having embraced self-control together with benevolence and righteousness, and having been baptized with the thrice-blessed invocation for the forgiveness of sins, by devoting yourselves as much as you can toward the perfection of purity, you can, once rescued from everlasting punishment, become heirs of eternal good things. After saying this, he ordered those troubled by afflictions to come forward. And so many, having gathered together on the evidence of those who had been healed the day before, came forward. He laid his hands on them and prayed, healing them at once; then, after instructing them and the others to assemble earlier in the morning, he himself bathed, took food, and went to sleep.

lexical_decisions.chosen: gives himself over as a servant to demons
lexical_decisions.rationale: δοῦλος is rendered “servant” under the supplied policy, while ἐκδίδωμι conveys voluntary surrender into the demons’ ownership and control.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as I said earlier
lexical_decisions.rationale: The comparative adverb τάχιον can mean “more quickly,” but in references to prior speech it naturally means “earlier” or “a little while ago.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: self-control together with benevolence and righteousness
lexical_decisions.rationale: σωφροσύνη can include sound-minded restraint, temperance, or chastity; φιλανθρωπία denotes humane love or benevolence; δικαιοσύνη can also be rendered “justice.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: the thrice-blessed invocation
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπονομασία can denote an invocation, naming, or appellation. “Invocation” fits baptismal use, but the Greek does not spell out the invoked wording.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ ὅσον δύνασθε ἐπὶ τὸ τέλειον τῆς ἁγνείας ἑαυτοὺς ἐπιδιδόναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: by devoting yourselves as much as you can toward the perfection of purity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The articular infinitive is taken instrumentally with δύνασθε. ἁγνεία may denote purity generally or chastity specifically.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κολάσεως αἰδίου ῥυσθέντες αἰωνίων ἀγαθῶν κληρονόμοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: once rescued from everlasting punishment, become heirs of eternal good things
lexical_decisions.rationale: Different English terms preserve the source’s distinction between ἀΐδιος, “everlasting,” and αἰώνιος, “eternal,” without asserting that the author intended sharply different durations.

lexical_decisions.chosen: on the evidence of those who had been healed the day before
lexical_decisions.rationale: πείρᾳ can refer to experience, proof, or the evidentiary effect of what was experienced; the healed people supplied the reason others gathered.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to assemble earlier in the morning
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὀρθριαίτερον is a comparative referring to an earlier morning hour, while συνεδρεύω literally means to sit together and can denote meeting or assembling.

passages.text: On the third day in Tripolis, then, Peter rose from sleep rather early and entered the garden, where there was a large reservoir into which abundant water flowed continuously. There he bathed; then, after praying in this way, he sat down. Realizing that we were sitting around him and gazing intently at him as though we wanted to hear something, he said:

lexical_decisions.chosen: rather early
lexical_decisions.rationale: The comparative adverb indicates an earlier-than-usual or notably early hour; “earlier in the morning” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a large reservoir
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun denotes a receptacle or reservoir for water; “large water basin” is a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: then, after praying in this way
lexical_decisions.rationale: οὕτως most naturally qualifies the praying as “thus/in this way,” though it may function more loosely as a sequential “thereupon.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: we were sitting around him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle portrays the group seated around Peter; the object “him” is supplied from the immediate context.

passages.text: “There seems to me to be a great difference between the ignorant and those who have gone astray. For the ignorant person seems to me to resemble a man who chose not to set out for a flourishing city because he did not know the good things there, whereas the person who has gone astray resembles one who learned of the city’s good things but, while setting out along the road, turned aside from the path and therefore wanders. In the same way, then, there seems to me to be a great difference between those who worship idols and those who wander in the worship of God. For those who worship idols are ignorant of eternal life (and for that reason they do not even desire it, since they cannot love what they do not know); but those who have chosen to worship the one God and have learned that eternal life is given to the good, if they either believe or do anything contrary to what God approves, resemble those who have left the city of punishment but to come to the flourishing city ... and who, while on the road, have strayed from the straight way.”

source_issues.issue: The selected image-checked edition prints exactly three dots here, marking a lacuna that disrupts the construction after “to come to the flourishing city.” The unavailable content has not been restored, and the three printed dots are retained in the translation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: between the ignorant and those who have gone astray
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contrast is between lack of knowledge and deviation after acquiring knowledge; “those who have been misled” is also grammatically possible for the perfect passive form.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for a flourishing city
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle describes a city prospering or thriving; “prosperous city” is an alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: turned aside from the path
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase depicts deviation from or missing the traveled track; “passed by the path” is more formally possible but less suitable to the ensuing wandering.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those who wander in the worship of God
lexical_decisions.rationale: θεοσέβεια can denote worship of God, reverence for God, or piety; “worship of God” best preserves the contrast with idol worship.

lexical_decisions.chosen: what God approves
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression denotes what seems right or acceptable to God; “what seems right to God” is a more formally transparent alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ τῆς εὐθείας πλανηθεῖσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: who, while on the road, have strayed from the straight way
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive τῆς εὐθείας is taken with πλανηθεῖσιν as what they strayed from, while ἐν τῇ ὁδῷ supplies the setting. An attachment yielding “on the road of the straight way” is possible but less idiomatic.

passages.text: While he was discussing these things with us, one of our people came in—the man appointed to report such matters to him—and said, “Large crowds, my lord Peter, are standing before the doors.” When he gave permission, a large crowd came in. Peter rose, took his place on the platform used the day before, greeted them according to the custom of reverence for God, and said: “The human being, having come into being in the image and likeness of God—the God who created heaven and earth and made everything in them, as the true prophet told us—was appointed to rule and exercise dominion. I mean over the things in the air, on the earth, and in the waters. From the fact itself one can perceive that by his own intelligence he brings down the things in the air, brings up the things in the depths, and captures the things on the earth, even though they are far stronger than he is—I mean elephants, lions, and things like them.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ ἐπὶ τῷ ἀπαγγέλλειν αὐτῷ τὰ τοιαῦτα καθεστηκὼς
lexical_decisions.chosen: the man appointed to report such matters to him
lexical_decisions.rationale: καθεστηκώς indicates that this person had been assigned or established in the reporting role.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the platform used the day before
lexical_decisions.rationale: βάσις may denote a base, stand, or raised platform; the context of public speaking favors “platform.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: greeted them according to the custom of reverence for God
lexical_decisions.rationale: προσαγορεύω denotes addressing or greeting, while θεοσέβεια may also be rendered “piety” or “worship of God.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κατ’ εἰκόνα καὶ καθ’ ὁμοίωσιν γεγονὼς
lexical_decisions.chosen: having come into being in the image and likeness of God
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατά expresses correspondence to an image and likeness; “according to the image and likeness” is a more formally literal alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κατ’ ἀλκὴν αὐτοῦ πολλῷ μείζονα ὄντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: even though they are far stronger than he is
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally, the animals are “much greater than he in strength”; the chosen wording gives that comparison idiomatic English without reducing its force.

passages.text: “Yet when he was righteous, he was also above every suffering, since, with an immortal body, he was incapable of experiencing pain. But when he sinned (as we showed yesterday and the day before), he became a servant of sin and fell under every suffering, deprived by a just judgment of all good things. For it was not reasonable that, when the giver had been abandoned, the things given should remain with the ungrateful. Therefore, out of his surpassing compassion, so that, along with the original good things, we might also receive the eternal good things to come, he sent his prophet. The prophet commanded us to speak to you—to tell you what you must think and do. Make your choice, then; that lies within your power. What you must think, then, is this: to worship the God who made everything. If you apprehend him with your mind, you will receive from him, along with the original good things, the eternal good things to come.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: above every suffering
lexical_decisions.rationale: πάθημα here denotes suffering or affliction, as the following reference to pain indicates; “beyond all sufferings” is an alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he became a servant of sin
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording portrays subjection and belonging to sin. “Slave of sin” makes the ownership nuance more explicit, while the stipulated default renders δοῦλος as “servant.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: along with the original good things
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantivized adjective refers to the former or first good things of which humanity had been deprived; “the former good things” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐλέσθε οὖν, ὃ ἐπὶ τῇ ὑμετέρᾳ κεῖται ἐξουσίᾳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: Make your choice, then; that lies within your power
lexical_decisions.rationale: The relative clause is taken as referring to the act of choosing. It could instead be construed as “choose what lies within your power.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: to worship the God who made everything
lexical_decisions.rationale: The delayed θεόν is taken with the substantival participle. The syntax can also be represented as “to worship as God the one who made everything.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὃν ἂν ἀπολάβητε τῷ νῷ, ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ ἀπολήψεσθε
lexical_decisions.chosen: If you apprehend him with your mind, you will receive from him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first ἀπολαμβάνω is understood as mentally grasping or apprehending because of τῷ νῷ, while the second means receiving from God. “When you take hold of him with your mind” is a viable alternative.

passages.text: “You will therefore be able to persuade yourselves to do what benefits you if, as though chanting an incantation to the fearsome serpent nesting in your heart, you say, ‘You shall fear the Lord God, and you shall serve him alone.’ By every line of reasoning, then, it is beneficial to fear him alone, not as unjust, but as just. For one fears an unjust person lest one be unjustly killed, and the just one lest, after being caught in sin, one be punished. Through fear of him, then, you can be freed from many harmful fears. For if you do not fear the one Lord and Maker of all, you will be servants of all evils, to your own harm—I mean demons, sufferings, and everything capable of causing harm in any way whatever.”

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints this as a single, unusually accented and undivided sequence. In context it is defensibly understood as the relative-plus-particle expression meaning “in any way whatever”; this is an orthographic or word-division issue rather than an unreadable construction.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πεῖσαι οὖν ἑαυτοὺς πρὸς τὰ συμφέροντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: persuade yourselves to do what benefits you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The πρός phrase expresses movement toward beneficial things. “Bring yourselves around to what is beneficial” is a closer structural alternative but less direct in English.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ ἐμφωλεύοντι ἐν τῇ ὑμετέρᾳ καρδίᾳ δεινῷ ὄφει
lexical_decisions.chosen: the fearsome serpent nesting in your heart
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐμφωλεύω depicts making a lair or dwelling within, while δεινός here conveys the serpent’s fearsome or terrible character.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as though chanting an incantation
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπᾴδω refers to singing or reciting a charm over or to someone or something; “casting a spell” is a possible but less source-transparent rendering.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the just one
lexical_decisions.rationale: In context this most naturally refers to God as the just one, contrasting him with an unjust person. Grammatically, “a just person” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: servants of all evils
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase expresses subjection to every evil. “Slaves of all evils” would foreground the ownership and bondage force of δοῦλοι.

lexical_decisions.chosen: demons, sufferings
lexical_decisions.rationale: πάθημα continues the sense of suffering or affliction found in the preceding section; “passions” is lexically possible but less consistent with the immediate discussion of harmful experiences.

passages.text: Take courage, then, and approach God—you who were made at the beginning to rule and exercise lordship over everything, who have his image in the body and likewise possess in the mind the likeness of will. Since, then, by doing things resembling irrational animals you lost from your soul the soul of a human being, you became like pigs and became what demons ask for. If, then, you accept God’s law, you become human beings. For it is not possible to say to irrational animals, “You shall not murder; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal,” and the rest. Therefore, do not begrudge yourselves entering your original nobility when you are called back to it. For it is possible. If you become like God through good deeds, then, having been reckoned his sons because of the likeness, you will be able to be restored as masters of everything.

source_issues.source_quote: ἐκ τῆς ψυχῆς τὴν ἀνθρώπου ψυχὴν ἀπωλέσατε
source_issues.issue: The repetition of ψυχή produces the semantically unusual statement “you lost from your soul the soul of a human being.” The supplied reading is translatable and has been preserved rather than silently changed, though rhetorical paradox or textual disturbance remains possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν ἀρχὴν ἐπὶ τῷ πάντων ἄρχειν καὶ κυριεύειν γεγενημένοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: made at the beginning to rule and exercise lordship over everything
lexical_decisions.rationale: Treats τὴν ἀρχήν temporally and preserves the distinction between ἄρχειν and κυριεύειν.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐν τῷ νῷ τῆς γνώμης τὴν ὁμοιότητα
lexical_decisions.chosen: possess in the mind the likeness of will
lexical_decisions.rationale: γνώμη can denote will, disposition, purpose, or judgment. “Will” fits the contrast between bodily image and mental or volitional likeness without adding an explicit possessive absent from the phrase.

lexical_decisions.chosen: became what demons ask for
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally, “became requests of demons.” The contextual rendering treats αἰτήματα as the objects requested, likely invoking demons’ request concerning pigs; “became demons’ demands” is another possible rendering.

lexical_decisions.chosen: do not begrudge yourselves
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the reflexive force and the sense of withholding a good from oneself.

lexical_decisions.chosen: be restored as masters of everything
lexical_decisions.rationale: Takes πάντων with δεσπόται and retains the restoration motif established earlier in the section.

passages.text: Begin, then, to strip off the harmful fears of empty idols, so that you may escape unjust slavery. For they have become your masters, though they are useless to you even as servants. I mean the material of the lifeless statues, which are of no use even in serving you. For it neither hears nor sees nor perceives; indeed, it cannot even move. Or does any of you wish to see as it sees, to hear as it hears, and to perceive and move? But far be it to insult any human being at all with such an insult, one who carries God’s image around, even if he has lost the likeness.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀποδύεσθαι τῶν κενῶν εἰδώλων τοὺς ἐπιβλαβεῖς φόβους
lexical_decisions.chosen: strip off the harmful fears of empty idols
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the clothing metaphor in ἀποδύεσθαι and allows the genitive to identify the idols that occasion or receive the fears.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἳ καὶ εἰς δούλους ὑμῖν ἄχρηστοι τυγχάνουσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: though they are useless to you even as servants
lexical_decisions.rationale: The idols are contrasted with the mastery wrongly granted to them: they would be useless even in the subordinate role of servants.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I mean the material
lexical_decisions.rationale: The singular pronouns in the following sentence naturally refer to ὕλη, the statue’s inert material, rather than to the preceding plural statues.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὕτως ὁρᾶν ὡς ὁρᾷ καὶ ἀκούειν ὡς ἀκούει
lexical_decisions.chosen: to see as it sees, to hear as it hears
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the deliberately absurd comparison with the sight and hearing of insensible material.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀπείη τοιαύτῃ λοιδορίᾳ λοιδορεῖν πάνθ’ ὁντινοῦν ἄνθρωπον
lexical_decisions.chosen: far be it to insult any human being at all with such an insult
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the emphatic repudiation, the repetition of the λοιδορία word group, and the comprehensive force of πάνθ’ ὁντινοῦν.

passages.text: Restore, at any rate, your gods—those of gold and silver, or those made from any other material—to their original nature: to bowls, I mean, and basins and all the other things that can be useful in serving you. And these good things, given to you from the beginning, will be able to be restored to you. But perhaps you will say, “The laws of those in authority do not permit us to do this.” Good! It is laws, and not the nonexistent power of the vain objects of worship themselves. How, then, have you regarded as gods those who are defended by human laws, guarded by dogs, and secured by bars? And this is so if they are of gold, silver, or bronze; for the stone or earthenware ones are protected by their lack of value, because no human being desires to steal a stone or earthenware god. Thus your gods made from more costly material are exposed to great danger. How, then, are they even gods when they are stolen, melted down, weighed, and hammered?

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς τὴν πρώτην αὐτῶν φύσιν ἀποκαταστήσατε
lexical_decisions.chosen: restore ... to their original nature
lexical_decisions.rationale: The statues’ materials are to be returned to their prior, useful forms, preserving both φύσις and the restoration language.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἴς τε φιάλας λέγω καὶ λεκάνας
lexical_decisions.chosen: to bowls, I mean, and basins
lexical_decisions.rationale: φιάλη denotes a broad or shallow bowl, while λεκάνη denotes a basin; λέγω marks the author’s clarification.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the laws of those in authority
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐφεστῶτες are those standing over others, hence rulers or authorities; the less specific rendering preserves the source’s formulation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καλῶς ὅτι Νόμοι, καὶ οὐκ αὐτῶν τῶν εἰκαίων σεβασμάτων ἡ μὴ οὖσα δύναμις
lexical_decisions.chosen: Good! It is laws, and not the nonexistent power of the vain objects of worship themselves
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compressed retort contrasts the actual restraint of civil laws with the nonexistent power of the objects being revered. εἰκαῖος can mean vain, idle, or groundless.

lexical_decisions.chosen: defended by human laws
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐκδικέω in the passive can mean avenged, vindicated, or protected. “Defended” best fits laws preventing the statues’ destruction or removal.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the stone or earthenware ones
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὀστράκινος denotes material made from fired clay or earthenware, not merely an object shaped like a shell.

lexical_decisions.chosen: stolen, melted down, weighed, and hammered
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves all four passive participles and the sequence of actions to which valuable metal images are subjected.

passages.text: Ah, the minds of wretched human beings, afraid of things deader than corpses! For I cannot even call things that have never lived dead—unless, that is, they are tombs of ancient people. Sometimes someone arriving in unfamiliar places does not know whether the temples he sees are memorials of dead men or of the so-called gods. But after asking and hearing that they belong to gods, he worships, without being ashamed that, if he had not learned by inquiry, he would have passed one by as a dead man’s monument because of the exact resemblance. Still, I need not contribute toward an extensive demonstration concerning superstition of this kind. For anyone willing to understand can easily grasp that it is nothing—unless someone does not see. Nevertheless, at least now hear that it does not hear, and understand that it does not understand. For the hands of a man who died “made” it. And if the one who made it came to his end, how will what came into being through him not be dissolved? Why, then, do you worship a mortal’s work, when it is entirely without sensation and people who possess reason do not even worship animals or pay court to the elements made by God—I mean heaven, sun, moon, stars, earth, sea, and everything in them—but correctly judge that they should not worship the things made by him, but should revere God, the creator and provider of these things? For these things themselves also rejoice in this: that no one has attached to them the honor belonging to the one who made them.

source_issues.source_quote: εἰ μὴ ἐκτὸς τάφοι ἀρχαίων ἀνθρώπων εἰσίν
source_issues.issue: The combination εἰ μὴ ἐκτός is unusually redundant as an exceptive expression. A defensible emphatic reading is available, so the supplied text is retained without conjectural correction.

source_issues.source_quote: πλὴν οὐ χρή με πρὸς τὴν τῆς τοιαύτης δεισιδαιμονίας πολλὴν παρέχειν ἀπόδειξιν
source_issues.issue: The printed order places πρός before an accusative phrase extending through ἀπόδειξιν, although παρέχειν can elsewhere take ἀπόδειξιν directly as its object. The translation provisionally takes παρέχειν absolutely, “contribute,” with the πρός phrase expressing the goal. The syntax is compressed and alternative construals such as “contribute toward an extensive exposition concerning this kind of superstition” remain possible, but no correction of the supplied text is required for a defensible translation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: deader than corpses
lexical_decisions.rationale: The comparative image is retained; νεκροί here naturally denotes dead persons or corpses rather than abstractly “the dead.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ μὴ ἐκτὸς τάφοι ἀρχαίων ἀνθρώπων εἰσίν
lexical_decisions.chosen: unless, that is, they are tombs of ancient people
lexical_decisions.rationale: Treats the stacked exceptive wording εἰ μὴ ἐκτός as emphatic. The alternative “unless perhaps” gives a similar contextual sense.

lexical_decisions.chosen: because of the exact resemblance
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally referring to the equality of the likeness, the phrase stresses that a temple and a tomb are indistinguishable in appearance.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πλὴν οὐ χρή με πρὸς τὴν τῆς τοιαύτης δεισιδαιμονίας πολλὴν παρέχειν ἀπόδειξιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Still, I need not contribute toward an extensive demonstration concerning superstition of this kind
lexical_decisions.rationale: Takes παρέχειν absolutely as “contribute” and πρὸς with the accusative phrase ending in ἀπόδειξιν as expressing the goal. The genitive τῆς τοιαύτης δεισιδαιμονίας identifies the demonstration’s subject matter. “Contribute toward an extensive exposition of superstition of this kind” is a viable alternative; the construction does not explicitly express proof “against” superstition.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Nevertheless, at least now hear
lexical_decisions.rationale: In this exhortation κἄν has the concessive-minimal force “at least,” rather than introducing a full conditional clause.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the hands of a man who died “made” it
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the source’s quotation marking around the rendering of ἐποίησαν alone, while rendering the singular object αὐτό outside the quotation marks.

lexical_decisions.chosen: when ... people who possess reason
lexical_decisions.rationale: The clause is attached to the preceding rhetorical question as a contrasting circumstance. It could instead be presented as a loosely independent “seeing that” or “whereas” sentence; the edition’s punctuation does not require emendation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐδὲ στοιχεῖα τὰ ὑπὸ θεοῦ γεγενημένα κολακεύουσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: do not ... pay court to the elements made by God
lexical_decisions.rationale: στοιχεῖα denotes cosmic elements or constituent parts of the world, while κολακεύω literally evokes flattering or courting them.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν τούτων δημιουργὸν καὶ πάροχον σέβειν θεόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: revere God, the creator and provider of these things
lexical_decisions.rationale: πάροχος can denote a provider, supplier, or giver. “Provider” preserves its distinction from δημιουργός, “creator.”

passages.text: For glory worthy of honor belongs to him alone, the only unoriginated one, since everything else has come into being. Just as being God, then, belongs uniquely to the unoriginated one, so anything at all that has come into being is not truly God. Above all, therefore, you must understand the malicious scheme of the serpent that is deceiving you from within. It cleverly deceives you with the promise of better reasoning, crawling from your brain into your spinal marrow and regarding your being deceived as a great gain.

lexical_decisions.chosen: glory worthy of honor
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔντιμος describes something honored, esteemed, or worthy of honor. The rendering avoids turning the adjective and noun into two separate source claims.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the only unoriginated one
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀγένητος is contrasted here with γενητός and γενόμενον, so “unoriginated” preserves the coming-into-being contrast more precisely than “unbegotten.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πᾶν ὁτιοῦν γενόμενον θεὸς τῷ ὄντι οὐκ ἔστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: anything at all that has come into being is not truly God
lexical_decisions.rationale: πᾶν ὁτιοῦν is emphatically comprehensive, while τῷ ὄντι means “in reality” or “truly.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν τοῦ ἐν ὑμῖν ἀπατῶντος ὄφεως κακοῦργον ἐπίνοιαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the malicious scheme of the serpent that is deceiving you from within
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐν ὑμῖν may describe either the serpent’s location or the sphere of its deception. “From within” preserves both possibilities without identifying the serpent with a specific anatomical structure.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: φρονίμως ὑμᾶς ἀπατᾷ ὑποσχέσει κρείττονος λογισμοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: cleverly deceives you with the promise of better reasoning
lexical_decisions.rationale: φρονίμως is ironic here and means intelligently or shrewdly; λογισμός may mean reasoning, calculation, or thought.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἕρπων ὑμῶν ἐκ τοῦ ἐγκεφάλου εἰς τὸν νωτιαῖον μυελὸν
lexical_decisions.chosen: crawling from your brain into your spinal marrow
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the anatomical image and the serpent’s downward movement from the brain into the spinal cord or marrow.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μέγα κέρδος ἡγούμενος τὴν ὑμετέραν ἀπάτην
lexical_decisions.chosen: regarding your being deceived as a great gain
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑμετέραν ἀπάτην could formally mean “your deception,” including deception practiced by you, but the repeated claim that the serpent deceives the audience favors the objective sense, their being deceived.

passages.text: For, knowing the law from the beginning—that if he merely brings you to entertain the notion of any beings called gods, so that you sin against the good of sole rule, your destruction becomes gain for him (and this is because, having been condemned to eat earth, he has authority to eat the person who through sin has dissolved into earth and become earth, while your souls pass into the belly of his fire)—he therefore, so that you may suffer these things, suggests to you every notion directed against you.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the law from the beginning
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the temporal phrase; “the original law” is possible but would make its characterization less explicit.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς ὑπόνοιαν ὡνδήποτε λεγομένων θεῶν ἐνέγκῃ
lexical_decisions.chosen: brings you to entertain the notion of any beings called gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπόνοια denotes a notion or supposition here, while λεγομένων marks them as beings designated or said to be gods.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the good of sole rule
lexical_decisions.rationale: μοναρχία refers contextually to the rule of one God; “sole rule” preserves that claim without importing a familiar theological formula.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς τὴν τοῦ πυρὸς αὐτοῦ γαστέρα
lexical_decisions.chosen: into the belly of his fire
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the source’s unusual image and possessive attachment rather than replacing it with the smoother “fiery belly.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πᾶσαν τὴν καθ’ ὑμῶν ὑμῖν ὑποβάλλει οἴησιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: suggests to you every notion directed against you
lexical_decisions.rationale: καθ’ ὑμῶν describes the notions as working against their recipients; οἴησις may also be rendered “opinion” or “supposition.”

passages.text: For all the deceptive suppositions opposed to sole rule are sown by him into your mind for your harm. First, so that after hearing the words concerning reverence for God you may not drive away ignorance, the cause of evils, he lies in ambush under the pretext of false knowledge. At first he uses one preconception applied to everyone: the idea that one has decided wisely because, if someone does not hear the message concerning reverence for God, he is not “liable to judgment.” Therefore some, deceived in this way, do not wish to listen, so that they may remain ignorant, not knowing that ignorance is itself, on its own, enough of a deadly poison. For it is not the case that, if someone takes deadly poison unknowingly, he does not die. In the same way, sins by their nature destroy the sinner, even if in ignorance he does what he ought not to do.

source_issues.issue: The supplied ἁμαρτία is singular in form, while the article αἱ and verb ἀναιροῦσιν are plural. The English follows the plural agreement required by the surrounding construction; the proposed reading adds the expected final iota but is not the supplied reading.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αἱ κατὰ τῆς μοναρχίας ἀπατηλοὶ ... ὑπολήψεις
lexical_decisions.chosen: the deceptive suppositions opposed to sole rule
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπολήψεις are received notions or suppositions, and κατὰ marks their opposition to divine sole rule.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he lies in ambush under the pretext of false knowledge
lexical_decisions.rationale: ψευδοῦς grammatically modifies γνώσεως; “under the pretext” conveys the instrumental dative προφάσει.

lexical_decisions.chosen: one preconception applied to everyone
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατὰ πάντων may indicate universal application or direction against everyone; the rendering adopts universal application in this context.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the idea that one has decided wisely because
lexical_decisions.rationale: The middle perfect βεβουλεῦσθαι can describe having formed a supposedly wise resolution; alternatively, the phrase may be understood impersonally as “thinking it has been wisely determined that.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ γάρ, εἴ τις προσλάβοι θανασίμου φαρμάκου ἀγνοῶν, οὐκ ἀποθνήσκει
lexical_decisions.chosen: For it is not the case that, if someone takes deadly poison unknowingly, he does not die
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expanded English preserves the emphatic negative construction and the analogy between unknown poison and unwitting sin.

passages.text: But if judgment comes on account of disobedience to words, much more will God destroy those who have refused to accept the worship directed toward him. For the one who does not wish to learn in order not to be liable is already judged as one who knows. For the one who does not wish to listen has understood; thus no contrivance can serve as a defense before God, the “knower of hearts.” Therefore flee the crafty thought that the serpent insinuates into your mind. But even if someone actually ends the present life in ignorance, he will face the charge that, though he lived for a time, he did not know who had been his benefactor and the source of the provisions supplied to him, and that he is rejected from the kingdom of God as an insensible, ungrateful, and very unworthy servant.

source_issues.source_quote: ἔγνω γὰρ ὁ μὴ ἀκοῦσαι θέλει
source_issues.issue: In the supplied reading, ὁ precedes the finite verb θέλει rather than a participle, producing an irregular construction under standard Greek syntax. The main text adopts a contextually defensible subject-reading in parallel with the preceding sentence. An orthographic normalization of ὁ to the neuter relative ὃ would instead yield the object-reading “For he has come to know what he is unwilling to hear.” The normalization is conjectural, not the supplied reading.
source_issues.proposed_reading: ἔγνω γὰρ ὃ μὴ ἀκοῦσαι θέλει

lexical_decisions.chosen: on account of disobedience to words
lexical_decisions.rationale: παρακοή can denote failure to hear or disobedience; the context concerns a culpable refusal to listen, so “disobedience” preserves that moral force.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to accept the worship directed toward him
lexical_decisions.rationale: θρησκεία denotes religious observance or worship, while εἰς αὐτόν explicitly supplies its direction.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἔγνω γὰρ ὁ μὴ ἀκοῦσαι θέλει
lexical_decisions.chosen: For the one who does not wish to listen has understood
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering treats the supplied ὁ as introducing the person characterized by the finite clause, in contextual parallel with the preceding ὁ μὴ θέλων. If ὁ is instead normalized to the neuter relative ὃ, the materially different rendering would be “For he has come to know what he is unwilling to hear.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: before God, the “knower of hearts”
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering retains the source’s quotation marks around the descriptive compound καρδιογνώστης.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἵνα δὲ καὶ ὄντως ἀγνοήσας τις τὸν παρόντα βίον τελευτήσει
lexical_decisions.chosen: But even if someone actually ends the present life in ignorance
lexical_decisions.rationale: The unusual ἵνα with the future indicative is understood as introducing an argumentative concession or supposition; “suppose that someone actually ends” is a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τίς αὐτῷ τε καὶ τῶν αὐτῷ ἐπιχορηγηθεισῶν τροφῶν ὑπῆρξεν εὐεργέτης
lexical_decisions.chosen: who had been his benefactor and the source of the provisions supplied to him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The Greek coordinates the personal beneficiary and the supplied provisions unevenly. “Source” conveys the beneficent provision without positing a second benefactor.

lexical_decisions.chosen: servant
lexical_decisions.rationale: The policy-default rendering is used; the term still presents the person as belonging to and accountable to a superior.

passages.text: Again, the formidable serpent suggests to you that you should think this and say this very thing, which, roughly speaking, most of you say: “We too know that the Lord of all is one, but these also are gods. For just as Caesar is one but has administrators under him—consular officials, prefects, commanders of a thousand, commanders of a hundred, and commanders of ten—in the same way, since the great God is one, like Caesar, they too are gods by analogy with the subordinate authorities: they are subject to him but administer us.” Listen, then, you who have been smeared by him with this supposition as with a terrible poison—I mean the evil implication of the example—so that you may know what is good and what is evil. For you have not yet regained your sight, since you do not even look closely into the things you yourselves put forward.

source_issues.issue: The supplied print reads οὕπω, with rough breathing and an acute; the negative adverb is conventionally written οὔπω, with smooth breathing and an acute. The English renders the contextual negative sense “not yet.” The proposed form is an orthographic normalization, not the supplied reading.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the formidable serpent
lexical_decisions.rationale: δεινός can mean formidable, terrible, or fearsome; “formidable” fits the serpent’s dangerous cunning without weakening the description.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὃ σχεδὸν οἱ πλεῖστοι ὑμῶν λέγουσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: which, roughly speaking, most of you say
lexical_decisions.rationale: σχεδόν explicitly qualifies the attribution with approximation. Its position permits the sense “roughly speaking, most of you”; “which nearly all of you say” is another possible idiomatic rendering of the combined expression.

lexical_decisions.chosen: consular officials, prefects, commanders of a thousand, commanders of a hundred, and commanders of ten
lexical_decisions.rationale: The transparent numerical renderings preserve the descending administrative or military hierarchy; ὑπατικοί denotes persons of consular standing rather than necessarily serving consuls.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κατὰ τὸν τῶν ὑποκειμένων ἐξουσιῶν λόγον
lexical_decisions.chosen: by analogy with the subordinate authorities
lexical_decisions.rationale: λόγος here expresses the proposed correspondence or analogy, though “according to the status of the subordinate authorities” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: smeared ... as with a terrible poison
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the physical image of ὑπαλείφω, “smear” or “anoint,” and the comparison of the supposition to poison.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the evil implication of the example
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here ὑπόνοια is understood as the underlying implication carried by the Caesar analogy; “evil supposition arising from the example” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐδὲ τοῖς προβαλλομένοις ὑφ’ ὑμῶν ἐνορᾶτε
lexical_decisions.chosen: you do not even look closely into the things you yourselves put forward
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording preserves the distinction between advancing an argument and discerning what lies within or follows from it.

passages.text: For if you say that God, on the analogy of Caesar, has subordinate authorities—the beings called gods—even so you do not follow your own example. For if you did follow it, you ought to know this: just as it is not permissible to give Caesar’s name to another—I mean, to a consul, a prefect, a commander of a thousand, or anyone else—because the giver will not live and the receiver will be put to death, so, by your own example, it is not permissible for the name “God” to be given to another, since even the person persuaded either to receive it or to give it perishes. And if an affront in a human case incurs punishment, much more will those who call others gods, as people who have insulted God, be subject to eternal punishment. And rightly so, because you have subjected the name entrusted to you to honor with regard to his sole rule to every insult of which you were capable. For “God” is not his true name. Rather, having received it for the present, you insulted what was given to you for this purpose: that however you might use it, it might be reckoned as treatment of his true name; but you subjected it to every insult.

lexical_decisions.chosen: on the analogy of Caesar
lexical_decisions.rationale: λόγος refers to the proposed correspondence between divine and imperial administration; “according to Caesar’s model” is a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Caesar’s name
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὄνομα may also mean title or designation here, but “name” is retained because the passage explicitly compares it with the name “God.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ πεισθεὶς εἴτε λαβεῖν εἴτε δοῦναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: the person persuaded either to receive it or to give it
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive participle is preserved; the unnamed object is contextually the disputed name or designation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: an affront in a human case
lexical_decisions.rationale: The ἀπό phrase is compact and may describe an insult involving a human being, an insult committed by one, or punishment at human hands. The contextual rendering preserves the human-versus-divine comparison without deciding the phrase’s exact direction.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ εἰς τὴν αὐτοῦ μοναρχίαν παραδοθὲν ὑμῖν τιμᾶν ὄνομα
lexical_decisions.chosen: the name entrusted to you to honor with regard to his sole rule
lexical_decisions.rationale: The name remains the object of τιμᾶν: it was entrusted to the recipients for them to honor. The phrase εἰς τὴν αὐτοῦ μοναρχίαν may qualify either the entrusting or the honoring; “with regard to his sole rule” preserves that attachment uncertainty.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ γὰρ τὸ ὄντως ἐστὶν αὐτοῦ ὄνομα θεός
lexical_decisions.chosen: For “God” is not his true name
lexical_decisions.rationale: The clause distinguishes the designation θεός from God’s actual or true name; quotation marks clarify that the designation itself is under discussion.

lexical_decisions.chosen: having received it for the present
lexical_decisions.rationale: τέως may mean “for the present” or “up to now.” The former suits the contrast between the provisionally received designation and the true name, while the temporal alternative remains possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὃ ἐδόθη ὑμῖν, ἵνα ὡς ἂν αὐτῷ χρήσῃσθε, εἰς τὸ ὄντως αὐτοῦ ὄνομα λογισθῇ
lexical_decisions.chosen: what was given to you for this purpose: that however you might use it, it might be reckoned as treatment of his true name
lexical_decisions.rationale: The purpose clause is understood as explaining why the designation was given: its use would count as treatment of the true name it represents. Attachment of ἵνα to ὑβρίσατε is syntactically possible, yielding “you insulted what was given to you so that ...,” but that would make the reckoning the purpose of their insult and is less suitable contextually.

passages.text: For example, the leaders among your Egyptians—those who boasted of their study of phenomena aloft and professed to distinguish the natures of the stars—because of an evil suspicion lurking deep within them, subjected it to every dishonor, as far as lay in their power. For some of them handed down the worship of an ox called Apis, others of a male goat, others of a cat, others of a serpent, and even of a fish, onions, winds from bellies, sewers, and limbs of irrational animals, along with countless other utterly shameful absurdities.

lexical_decisions.chosen: For example
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here the phrase introduces the Egyptians as an immediate illustrative case rather than asserting that their conduct occurred at once; a temporal rendering such as “immediately, then” is possible in other contexts.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the leaders among your Egyptians
lexical_decisions.rationale: This takes the adjacent τῶν Αἰγυπτίων ὑμῶν together as “your Egyptians.” Alternatively, ὑμῶν can qualify ἀρχηγέται, yielding “your leaders from among the Egyptians.” The noun ἀρχηγέται can denote leaders, originators, or founders; “leaders” preserves their authoritative role without specifying that they were historical founders.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those who boasted of their study of phenomena aloft
lexical_decisions.rationale: μετεωρολογία denotes inquiry or discourse concerning phenomena aloft, including astronomical and atmospheric matters. “Study of phenomena aloft” preserves both the field-of-study sense and its broader ancient scope, which modern “meteorology” would narrow.

lexical_decisions.chosen: because of an evil suspicion lurking deep within them
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐνδομυχέω depicts something dwelling or lurking in the innermost recesses, while ὑπό expresses cause or agency.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πάσῃ αὐτὸ ἀτιμίᾳ ὅσον τὸ κατ’ αὐτοὺς ὑπέβαλαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: subjected it to every dishonor, as far as lay in their power
lexical_decisions.rationale: The neuter αὐτό has no explicit antecedent within this section, so the translation retains the pronoun rather than identifying its referent in the main text; in the preceding context it most naturally refers to the name under discussion.

lexical_decisions.chosen: others of a male goat
lexical_decisions.rationale: τράγος specifically denotes a male goat; the elliptical English continues “handed down the worship” from the preceding clause.

lexical_decisions.chosen: winds from bellies, sewers
lexical_decisions.rationale: πνεύματα preserves the bodily-wind image, while ὀχετοί denotes drains or sewers in this deliberately degrading list.

passages.text: When Peter had said these things, the crowd standing there laughed. In response to their laughter Peter said, “You laugh at their practices, not knowing that you yourselves are being laughed at far more by them. Yet you laugh at one another’s practices, for you do not see your own, having been led into deception by evil custom. I agree that you do indeed rightly ridicule the Egyptians, since, although they are rational beings, they worship irrational animals—things certain to die. But hear how those people in turn speak while ridiculing you: ‘Although we worship things that die,’ they say, ‘they at least were once alive, whereas you venerate things that have never been alive.’ In addition, they say, ‘Wanting to honor the form of the one God, and not discovering what it is like, we chose to honor every form.’ Similarly, by saying certain things of this sort, they suppose that their thinking is sounder than yours.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: You laugh at their practices
lexical_decisions.rationale: Γελᾶτε can be indicative or imperative. The accompanying participle “not knowing” supports describing the audience’s conduct, though “Laugh at their practices” remains grammatically possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πλὴν τὰ ἀλλήλων γελᾶτε· τὰ γὰρ ἴδια ὑπὸ συνηθείας κακῆς εἰς ἀπάτην ἀχθέντες οὐ βλέπετε
lexical_decisions.chosen: Yet you laugh at one another’s practices, for you do not see your own, having been led into deception by evil custom
lexical_decisions.rationale: The explanatory γάρ connects their reciprocal ridicule with their failure to perceive their own practices; the participial phrase identifies evil custom as what led them into deception.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅτι δὲ ὄντως ὀρθῶς καταγελᾶτε τῶν Αἰγυπτίων, σύνφημι
lexical_decisions.chosen: I agree that you do indeed rightly ridicule the Egyptians
lexical_decisions.rationale: “Do indeed” preserves the explicit emphasis of ὄντως, “rightly” renders ὀρθῶς, and “I agree” represents σύνφημι.

lexical_decisions.chosen: ‘Although we ...,’ they say
lexical_decisions.rationale: The singular parenthetical φησίν functions as a quotation formula within a response introduced as what the Egyptians say, even though the quoted speakers use the plural.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to honor every form
lexical_decisions.rationale: Although προτιμάω can mean “prefer” or “honor especially,” “honor” fits the claim that every form was selected as an object of reverence.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Similarly
lexical_decisions.rationale: The printed ὁμῶς is the adverb “alike” or “similarly,” not the more familiar ὅμως, “nevertheless.”

passages.text: “Therefore you too should answer them: ‘You are lying, for it is not out of honor directed toward the God who truly is that you venerate these things. For then all of you would be worshiping every form, which is not what you have been doing. Some of you, having supposed the divine to be an onion and venerating winds from a belly, wage war; and similarly all of you, having singled out one thing for honor, fault the objects of others. With divergent judgment, one person venerates one limb of the same animal and another person another.’ Yet some of them, still breathing sentiments of sound reason and ashamed of the manifest disgrace, attempt to turn these things into allegories, wishing through another kind of weakness to fortify what is deadly in their deception. Nevertheless, we would have refuted the allegories as well, had we been there—the allegories of those whom so foolish a passion has mastered as to produce the greatest sickness in their imagination. For the plaster must not be applied to the healthy part of the body, but to the part that is suffering. Since, then, by laughing at the Egyptians’ practices you showed that you had not suffered what they suffer, it was reasonable, regarding the condition from which you yourselves suffer, for me, being here, to provide you with a cure for the condition within you.”

source_issues.issue: The selected print places a high stop between the preposition πρὸς and its object αὐτούς. The syntax requires the words to be construed together; this is treated provisionally as an editorial punctuation anomaly, not as missing wording.

The selected print has the unassimilated compound spelling ἐνποιῆσαι, where the normalized assimilated spelling ἐμποιῆσαι is common. The printed form remains intelligible and has not been silently normalized.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τιμῇ τῇ πρὸς τὸν ὄντως θεὸν
lexical_decisions.chosen: out of honor directed toward the God who truly is
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase describes honor oriented toward the genuinely existing God; “the true God” is possible but would make the existential wording less visible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: which is not what you have been doing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The imperfect ἐποιεῖτε points to their established conduct, which contradicts their claim to honor every form.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἱ μὲν γὰρ ὑμῶν κρόμμυον ὑπονοήσαντες εἶναι τὸ θεῖον καὶ γαστρὸς πνεύματα σέβοντες πολεμοῦσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Some of you, having supposed the divine to be an onion and venerating winds from a belly, wage war
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering takes both participles as describing the shared subject introduced by οἱ μὲν. A material alternative distributes them between rival groups: “Some among you—the ones supposing the divine to be an onion and the ones venerating winds from a belly—wage war.” The ensuing account of each group preferring one object supports that distributive possibility. The Greek does not state an object for “wage war,” so none is supplied.

lexical_decisions.chosen: having supposed the divine to be an onion
lexical_decisions.rationale: The construction presents τὸ θεῖον as the subject of the infinitive and κρόμμυον as its predicate.

lexical_decisions.chosen: having singled out one thing for honor
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves both selection or preference and the religious honor implied by προτιμάω.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διαφόρῳ δὲ γνώμῃ τοῦ αὐτοῦ ζῴου μελῶν ὃς μὲν ἄλλο σέβει, ἕτερος δὲ τὸ ἕτερον
lexical_decisions.chosen: With divergent judgment, one person venerates one limb of the same animal and another person another
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive μελῶν is represented partitively through “one limb ... another,” while διαφόρῳ γνώμῃ marks the worshipers’ differing judgments.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πλὴν αὐτῶν ἔτι τὰ τοῦ ὀρθοῦ λογισμοῦ πνέοντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: Yet some of them, still breathing sentiments of sound reason
lexical_decisions.rationale: The partitive αὐτῶν is understood with an omitted “some,” while πνέοντες retains the metaphor of breathing or exuding what belongs to sound reasoning.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δι’ ἑτέρας ἀτονοίας τὰ τῆς ἀπάτης αὐτῶν θανάσιμα κρατύνειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: through another kind of weakness to fortify what is deadly in their deception
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀτονία denotes weakness or lack of strength, while the substantival τὰ ... θανάσιμα refers generally to the deadly features or effects belonging to their deception.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὧν τὸ τοσοῦτον μωρὸν ἐπεκράτησεν πάθος
lexical_decisions.chosen: those whom so foolish a passion has mastered
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὧν is taken as the genitive object of ἐπεκράτησεν. It could alternatively be possessive—“whose exceedingly foolish passion became strong enough”—without materially changing the accusation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the plaster
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression supplies the image of a medicinal plaster being applied specifically to the diseased part.

passages.text: The one who chooses to worship God ought first of all to know what alone is distinctive of God’s nature, something that cannot belong to another, so that, by looking to his distinctive property and not finding it in anyone else, he may never be deceived into assigning to another the status of being God. God’s distinctive property is that he alone, as maker of all things, is also superior to all. With respect to power, what makes is greater than what is made; with respect to magnitude, the infinite is greater than the finite; with respect to form, what is most beautiful; with respect to blessedness, what is most blessed; and with respect to intellect, what is most perfect.
