Likewise, in all other respects he himself possesses superiority beyond comparison. Since, then, as I said, it is distinctive of God that he is superior to all things, and since the world that contains everything has come into being through him, it is absolutely necessary to say that nothing that has come into being through him can stand in equal comparison with him.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τί μόνον τῆς θεοῦ φύσεως ἴδιόν ἐστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: what alone is distinctive of God’s nature
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἴδιον denotes a uniquely proper or distinguishing characteristic, not merely a common attribute.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἑτέρῳ τὸ θεῷ εἶναι μὴ ἀπατηθῇ δοῦναί ποτε
lexical_decisions.chosen: he may never be deceived into assigning to another the status of being God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The infinitive phrase literally concerns giving “being God” to another; “status” makes the construction intelligible without reducing it to a divine quality.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦτον μόνον εἶναι, ὡς πάντων ποιητήν, οὕτως καὶ κρείττονα
lexical_decisions.chosen: that he alone, as maker of all things, is also superior to all
lexical_decisions.rationale: κρείττονα is the predicate of the infinitive, while πάντων explicitly accompanies “maker” and is contextually carried into the comparison. A more structurally literal alternative is “that he alone is, just as maker of all, so also superior.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: what makes is greater than what is made
lexical_decisions.rationale: τοῦ ποιητοῦ is read as the substantivized verbal adjective ποιητός, “made,” rather than the identically formed genitive of ποιητής, “maker,” since the resulting maker-made contrast fits the argument and the parallel comparisons.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with respect to form, what is most beautiful
lexical_decisions.rationale: The comparative idea “is greater” is carried forward elliptically from κρείττόν ἐστιν, while the Greek supplies no explicit second term for this comparison.

lexical_decisions.chosen: stand in equal comparison
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression denies that anything created can bear a comparison that places it on equal terms with God.

passages.text: But if one who does not possess incomparability, unsurpassability, and freedom from need in every way and on every side cannot himself be God, and if the whole world cannot be this insofar as it has come into being, would it not be all the more irrational for its parts to be called God? By “parts” I mean those you call gods, made from gold and silver, bronze and stone, or indeed from any other material whatsoever—and these fashioned by a mortal hand. Nevertheless, in answer to these points, let us see what kinds of poison the terrible serpent, through a human mouth, administers with his hissings to those who are being deceived.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ ἀπαράβλητον καὶ ἀνυπέρβλητον καὶ πάντῃ πάντοθεν ἀνενδεὲς
lexical_decisions.chosen: incomparability, unsurpassability, and freedom from need in every way and on every side
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantivized adjectives name qualities required of God; πάντῃ πάντοθεν emphatically expresses completeness from every direction or standpoint.

lexical_decisions.chosen: cannot himself be God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The predicate “God” is supplied from the surrounding argument and is stated explicitly later in the same sentence; “cannot himself be” would be unintelligibly incomplete in English.

lexical_decisions.chosen: insofar as it has come into being
lexical_decisions.rationale: καθό gives the respect or ground on which the world fails the stated criterion: it is something generated.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πόσῳ γε μᾶλλον τὰ μόρια αὐτοῦ οὐκ ἂν ἀλόγως κληθείη θεός;
lexical_decisions.chosen: would it not be all the more irrational for its parts to be called God?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering takes οὐκ as framing a rhetorical negative question and ἀλόγως as characterizing the act of calling the parts God. The sequence οὐκ ἂν ἀλόγως can alternatively be parsed as “would not unreasonably,” but that reading would reverse the argument developed in the surrounding sentences. The neuter plural subject can take the singular verb κληθείη in Greek.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ταῦτα ὑπὸ θνητῆς χειρὸς δεδημιουργημένα
lexical_decisions.chosen: and these fashioned by a mortal hand
lexical_decisions.rationale: καὶ ταῦτα adds emphatic indignation: the alleged gods are not merely material but are manufactured by mortal agency.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἷα δι’ ἀνθρώπου στόματος ὁ δεινὸς ὄφις φαρμάσσει τοῖς συριγμοῖς τοὺς ἐξαπατωμένους
lexical_decisions.chosen: what kinds of poison the terrible serpent, through a human mouth, administers with his hissings to those who are being deceived
lexical_decisions.rationale: φαρμάσσω can mean to drug, poison, or bewitch. “Administers poison” preserves the serpent’s venom image and the instrumental hissings; a less imagistic alternative is “how the terrible serpent drugs or bewitches those who are being deceived.”

passages.text: For most people say, “In our objects of worship, we venerate not the gold, nor the silver, nor wood or stone (for we too know that these are nothing other than lifeless matter and the craftsmanship of a mortal human), but the spirit dwelling in them; this is what we call a god.” See, then, the dishonesty of those who say this. For since what is visible is easily exposed as nothing, they have fled for refuge to the invisible, as though they could not be refuted about something uncertain. Nevertheless, such people agree with us in part that one half of the cult images among them is not a god but unfeeling matter. It remains for them to show how we are to believe that it has a divine spirit. Yet such a person cannot demonstrate to us that it exists, since it does not—and we do not believe that they have seen it themselves. We will provide them with proofs that it does not have a divine spirit, so that lovers of truth, on hearing the refutation of this rabid supposition, may turn away from thinking that these things are animate.

lexical_decisions.chosen: In our objects of worship
lexical_decisions.rationale: σεβάσματα denotes things treated as sacred or worthy of veneration; “objects of worship” preserves the cultic sense without assuming that they are divine.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ ἥμισυ τῶν παρ’ αὐτοῖς ἱδρυμάτων
lexical_decisions.chosen: one half of the cult images among them
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἱδρύματα refers here to erected cult objects. “One half” preserves the argument that their alleged material-and-spirit composite is already conceded to be partly mere matter.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: λοιπὸν δὲ περιλείπεται δεῖξαι αὐτοῖς πῶς πιστεύομεν ὅτι· θεῖον ἔχει πνεῦμα.
lexical_decisions.chosen: It remains for them to show how we are to believe that it has a divine spirit.
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering construes αὐτοῖς with περιλείπεται and the infinitive as identifying those responsible for demonstrating the claim. Alternatively, αὐτοῖς may be the recipient of δεῖξαι: “it remains to show them how we believe that it has a divine spirit.” The main reading better anticipates the demand that follows for an opponent to demonstrate the spirit’s existence. πῶς πιστεύομεν could also be rendered indicatively as “how we believe,” but “how we are to believe” gives it deliberative or challenging force consistent with the speaker’s stated disbelief.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀλλ’ ἐπιδεῖξαι ἡμῖν οὐ δύναται ὅτι ἔστιν, ἐπεὶ μὴ ἔστιν — καὶ αὐτοῖς ἑωρακέναι οὐ πιστεύομεν.
lexical_decisions.chosen: Yet such a person cannot demonstrate to us that it exists, since it does not—and we do not believe that they have seen it themselves.
lexical_decisions.rationale: The singular δύναται is taken as referring to a representative opponent, while the following αὐτοῖς resumes the opposing group in the plural. Because the subject of δύναται is unstated, an image or the alleged spirit could instead be understood as the subject: “Yet it cannot demonstrate to us that it exists.” The confirmed singular has not been regularized as a plural.

lexical_decisions.chosen: this rabid supposition
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπόνοια can mean suspicion, notion, or supposition; here it is the hostile characterization of the belief that the images are animate. λυσσώδης supplies the forceful image of rabid madness.

lexical_decisions.chosen: animate
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective means possessing breath or life, in contrast with the objects’ lifeless material.

passages.text: First, then, if you venerate them as animate, why do you also bow down before the tombs of ancient people, who admittedly did not even possess a divine spirit? Thus you are not telling the truth in this respect either. Yet if your objects of worship really were animate, they would move by themselves, would have a voice, would shake off the cobweb on them, would repel those who wish to plot against them and who steal from them, and would easily seize those stripping away the votive offerings. But now they do none of these things. Instead, like condemned prisoners—and especially the more valuable among them—they are kept under guard, as we said at the outset. Again, do not the rulers demand taxes and duties from you on their account, on the ground that you derive great profit from the things there? And have they not often been plundered by enemies and, after being smashed, divided up? And do not the priests themselves, even more than those who worship from outside, having passed judgment against themselves over their useless worship, secretly remove many of the votive offerings?

source_issues.source_quote: τί καὶ ἀνθρώπων; ἀρχαίων τάφους προσκυνεῖτε
source_issues.issue: The selected edition’s question mark separates ἀνθρώπων from the agreeing genitive adjective ἀρχαίων, although the surviving words form the coherent phrase “tombs of ancient people” when read continuously. This is treated provisionally as an editorial-punctuation irregularity, not as missing wording.
source_issues.proposed_reading: τί καὶ ἀνθρώπων ἀρχαίων τάφους προσκυνεῖτε;

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints both a Greek question mark and a period at the end of the question. The duplicated punctuation does not affect the recoverable syntax or wording.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the tombs of ancient people
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀρχαίων agrees with ἀνθρώπων in the genitive plural; together they identify whose tombs are meant. The English reads the wording continuously across the selected edition’s question mark, as disclosed in the punctuation note.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοὺς αὐτοῖς ἐπιβουλεῦσαι θέλοντας καὶ κλέπτοντας
lexical_decisions.chosen: those who wish to plot against them and who steal from them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first participle expresses hostile intent and the second actual theft. The object of κλέπτοντας is unstated; “from them” fits the surrounding discussion of images and their offerings, while “who steal them” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the more valuable among them
lexical_decisions.rationale: τίμιος can mean honored or costly. The need to guard the objects from theft makes material value the more immediate sense, though “the more honored” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: on the ground that you derive great profit from the things there
lexical_decisions.rationale: καρπίζομαι denotes enjoying or reaping proceeds. τῶν ἐκεῖ is elliptical, referring to the things or resources located at the cult sites.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those who worship from outside
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase distinguishes the priests from worshipers outside the priestly group; “lay worshipers” is a contextual alternative but is more interpretive.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ τῇ ἀχρήστῳ θρησκείᾳ ἑαυτῶν κατεγνωκότες
lexical_decisions.chosen: having passed judgment against themselves over their useless worship
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect participle presents the priests as having reached, or as standing in, an adverse judgment against themselves concerning their worship before or while they secretly remove the offerings. It does not state that the theft itself produces that judgment.

passages.text: “Yes,” he says, “but they were detected through the gods’ providence.” This is false. For how many of them have gone undetected? If, because some have been caught, they say that those gods possess power, they are mistaken. Some tomb robbers too are discovered, while others escape notice, and surely those who are caught were not detected by the power of the dead. We can understand something similar about the gods that are stolen and despoiled. “But,” he says, “the gods within them have no concern for their own carved images.” Why, then, do you yourselves tend them—scrubbing, washing, and cleaning them, crowning them, and offering sacrifices to them? Therefore recognize from this that you are not acting with sound reasoning either. For just as you weep over the dead, so you also offer sacrifices and pour libations to your gods.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ναί φησιν, ἀλλὰ προνοίᾳ αὐτῶν ἐφωράθησαν.
lexical_decisions.chosen: “Yes,” he says, “but they were detected through the gods’ providence.”
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first plural referent is the thieves, while αὐτῶν refers contextually to the gods or cult images credited with providential action. The nouns are made explicit in English to prevent the two pronouns from being confused.

lexical_decisions.chosen: that those gods possess power
lexical_decisions.rationale: The accusative αὐτούς resumes the gods credited with detecting thieves, not the thieves who were caught.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοιοῦτόν τι καὶ περὶ τοὺς κλεπτομένους καὶ συλωμένους θεοὺς ἔστιν ἡμῖν νοεῖν.
lexical_decisions.chosen: We can understand something similar about the gods that are stolen and despoiled.
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔστιν with the dative and infinitive expresses the possibility or availability of understanding the analogous situation, rather than an obligation or recommendation. Both passive participles modify the gods themselves.

lexical_decisions.chosen: their own carved images
lexical_decisions.rationale: ξόανον originally denotes a carved, especially wooden, cult image and can more broadly denote an idol or statue. “Carved images” preserves that material sense without requiring that every object be wooden.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τημελεῖτε σμήχοντες καὶ πλύνοντες καὶ καθαίροντες, στεφανοῦντες, ἐπιθύοντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: tend them—scrubbing, washing, and cleaning them, crowning them, and offering sacrifices to them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The sequence lists the physical and ritual care supplied by the worshipers. ἐπιθύω here means to offer sacrifice, not merely to desire.

passages.text: Yet calling them administrators no longer accords even with the analogy of Caesar and the authorities under him, when you yourselves take all care of them, as I said before, tending your cult images in every respect. For, capable of nothing, they do nothing. So tell us: what do they administer? What do they do comparable to what the rulers in each locality do? What do they accomplish comparable to God’s stars? Unless perhaps they shine like the sun—the very ones for whom you yourselves light lamps? Can they, just as the clouds bring rains, also bring downpours—they who cannot even move themselves unless people take hold of them? Or do they provide fruits in the same way as the earth—they for whom you supply sacrifices? Thus they can do nothing.

lexical_decisions.chosen: calling them administrators
lexical_decisions.rationale: διοικητής denotes one who manages, governs, or administers. “Administrators” maintains the comparison with Caesar’s subordinate authorities.

lexical_decisions.chosen: cult images
lexical_decisions.rationale: The erected objects are the material images being tended, illuminated, and physically moved; “cult images” conveys this setting better than the broader “institutions” or “establishments.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: the rulers in each locality
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase denotes leaders or governors assigned to particular places, continuing the administrative analogy.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ μήτι φαίνουσιν ὡς ὁ ἥλιος, οἷς λύχνους ὑμεῖς ἅπτετε;
lexical_decisions.chosen: Unless perhaps they shine like the sun—the very ones for whom you yourselves light lamps?
lexical_decisions.rationale: εἰ μήτι introduces an ironic possible exception. The emphatic ὑμεῖς sharpens the contrast between supposedly shining gods and worshipers who must provide their light.

lexical_decisions.chosen: unless people take hold of them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The middle verb means to grasp or take hold of something; here people must handle the immobile images before they can move.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in the same way as the earth
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative τῇ γῇ marks the earth as the standard of comparison for providing fruit.

passages.text: And even if they were able to do something, you would not rightly call them gods, since even the elements, through which good things are supplied, may not be called gods. But only the one who ordered them to carry out everything for our use and commanded them to serve humankind—him alone do we rightly call God. Unaware of his beneficence, you proclaimed that the elements assigned to you as servants were to rule over human beings. And why is there any need to speak about the elements, when you even make lifeless statues and not only bow down before them but also think it proper to be subjected to them in every respect as servants? For this reason, you yourselves, through the things by which you lost your senses, have become subject to demons. Nevertheless, through recognition of God himself, you can by good deeds become masters again, give orders to demons as servants, and, as sons of God, be established as heirs of an eternal kingdom.

source_issues.source_quote: τὰ ὑμῖν δοῦλα ἀπονεμηθέντα στοιχεῖα καθ’ αὐτῶν δεσπόζειν ἀνηγορεύσατε
source_issues.issue: The plural αὐτῶν has no nearby plural human antecedent; its nearest explicit plural antecedents are the elements or the good things, neither of which gives the expected contrast. The translation defensibly treats it as a notional resumption of generic ἀνθρώπῳ, but καθ’ ὑμῶν, “over you,” is a plausible conjecture and is not the supplied reading.
source_issues.proposed_reading: τὰ ὑμῖν δοῦλα ἀπονεμηθέντα στοιχεῖα καθ’ ὑμῶν δεσπόζειν ἀνηγορεύσατε

source_issues.source_quote: διὰ τοῦτο ἑαυτοὺς δι’ ὧν παρεφρονήσατε, δαίμοσιν ὑποχείριοι γεγόνατε.
source_issues.issue: The accusative ἑαυτούς does not formally agree with the nominative predicate ὑποχείριοι and the second-person subject of γεγόνατε. It can be read as a pendent accusative emphasizing the people addressed, which supports the main rendering; nominative αὐτοί would be a possible conjectural regularization.
source_issues.proposed_reading: διὰ τοῦτο αὐτοὶ δι’ ὧν παρεφρονήσατε, δαίμοσιν ὑποχείριοι γεγόνατε.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the elements
lexical_decisions.rationale: The term denotes the constituent powers or elements of the natural order through which benefits are supplied; the argument denies that their usefulness makes them gods.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν μόνον τάξαντα αὐτὰ πρὸς τὴν ἡμετέραν χρῆσιν ἐκτελεῖν τὰ πάντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: only the one who ordered them to carry out everything for our use
lexical_decisions.rationale: τάσσω expresses appointing or ordering the elements to perform their assigned functions for human use.

lexical_decisions.chosen: commanded them to serve humankind
lexical_decisions.rationale: The singular ἀνθρώπῳ is generic, referring to humanity rather than one particular man.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ ὑμῖν δοῦλα ἀπονεμηθέντα στοιχεῖα καθ’ αὐτῶν δεσπόζειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: that the elements assigned to you as servants were to rule over human beings
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering takes αὐτῶν as a notional plural resumption of the preceding generic ἀνθρώπῳ, “humankind.” Taking it as referring to the elements themselves or to the good things would produce a much less coherent claim.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς δοῦλοι κατὰ πάντα αὐτοῖς ὑποτετάχθαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: to be subjected to them in every respect as servants
lexical_decisions.rationale: δοῦλοι marks complete subordinate status. “Servants” follows the supplied wording policy, while “slaves” would more explicitly foreground ownership and coercive subjection.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διὰ τοῦτο ἑαυτοὺς δι’ ὧν παρεφρονήσατε, δαίμοσιν ὑποχείριοι γεγόνατε
lexical_decisions.chosen: For this reason, you yourselves, through the things by which you lost your senses, have become subject to demons.
lexical_decisions.rationale: The accusative ἑαυτούς is treated as a pendent emphatic expression resumed by the second-person verb. δι’ ὧν refers to the cult objects as the means or occasion of their loss of reason.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διὰ τῆς εἰς αὐτὸν τὸν θεὸν ἐπιγνώσεως ἐκ τῶν καλῶν πράξεων
lexical_decisions.chosen: through recognition of God himself, you can by good deeds
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering attaches ἐκ τῶν καλῶν πράξεων to becoming masters again, while διὰ τῆς ... ἐπιγνώσεως gives the broader means. It could alternatively describe recognition of God as arising from good deeds.

lexical_decisions.chosen: give orders to demons as servants
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative phrase identifies the demons as the servants being commanded, reversing the preceding subjection to them.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς υἱοὶ θεοῦ αἰωνίου βασιλείας κληρονόμοι καταστῆναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: as sons of God, be established as heirs of an eternal kingdom
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering attaches αἰωνίου to βασιλείας. Grammatically it could instead modify θεοῦ, yielding “as sons of the eternal God, be established as heirs of a kingdom,” but the chosen attachment gives the more natural division of the two genitive phrases.

passages.text: After saying these things, he ordered those possessed by demons and those gripped by diseases to be brought to him. When they had been brought, he laid his hands on them and prayed, then sent them away in good health, reminding them and the rest of the crowds to remain there in attendance for however many days he might stay there and speak. After the others had withdrawn, Peter bathed in the reservoir there together with those who wished to do so. He ordered the meal to be laid out on the ground beneath a dense canopy of trees for the sake of the shade, and had each person recline according to his rank; and so we partook of food. Then, after offering a blessing and further thanking God for the refreshment received, in accordance with the Hebrews’ customary faith, while much time still remained, he allowed us to ask about whatever we wished. And although there were twenty of us, he answered each one as each asked in turn. When evening had now come upon us, we all entered the most spacious room of the lodging together with him and slept there.

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a high stop between αὐτοὺς and ὑγιαίνοντας. The accusative participle naturally construes with αὐτούς, yielding “sent them away in good health.” The punctuation is editorial and does not require alteration of the Greek wording.

The wording does not explicitly identify what was spread on the ground. The banquet context supports “the meal to be laid out,” while “couches or coverings to be spread” and “the table to be set” remain viable alternatives. This is ordinary contextual ellipsis, not evidence of omitted text.

Both the attachment of the phrase and the contextual range of πίστις admit alternatives. It is rendered as describing the manner of the blessing and thanksgiving, with πίστις retained as “faith”; “according to the Hebrews’ customary observance/practice” is also defensible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those possessed by demons and those gripped by diseases
lexical_decisions.rationale: The coordinated participles are rendered as two contextually natural classes. Grammatically, they could instead describe a single group suffering both conditions.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to remain there in attendance
lexical_decisions.rationale: παρεδρεύω denotes staying close by or waiting in attendance, not merely sitting.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for however many days he might stay there and speak
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιδημέω describes remaining in a place, while διαλέγομαι may mean speak, converse, or deliver discourse.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in the reservoir there
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑδροχοεῖον denotes a place where water is collected or held; “reservoir” fits the bathing context.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the meal to be laid out on the ground
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive infinitive leaves what was spread unstated. The meal context supports this rendering, though couches, coverings, or a table setting are also possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὸ τινὰ πυκνὴν τῶν δένδρων κόμην
lexical_decisions.chosen: beneath a dense canopy of trees
lexical_decisions.rationale: κόμη literally denotes hair or foliage and here forms an image of the trees’ thick leafy canopy.

lexical_decisions.chosen: had each person recline according to his rank
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατ’ ἀξίαν indicates arrangement according to worth, dignity, status, or rank.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπευχαριστήσας τῷ θεῷ ἐπὶ τῷ εὐφρανθῆναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: further thanking God for the refreshment received
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording denotes additional thanksgiving for being gladdened or refreshed; “for having enjoyed the meal” is another contextually possible expression.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in accordance with the Hebrews’ customary faith
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering retains πίστις as “faith” and attaches the phrase to the blessing and thanksgiving. In this context πίστις could alternatively denote customary religious observance or practice.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he answered each one as each asked in turn
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐν μέρει means “in turn,” and ἐπιλύω here means to resolve or explain what each person asked.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the most spacious room of the lodging
lexical_decisions.rationale: οἶκος can denote a room or chamber, and ξενία here refers to the place of lodging or guest accommodation.

passages.text: On the fourth day in Tripolis, then, Peter got up and found us awake. After greeting us, he went out to the water basin to wash and pray, and we followed his example. After we had prayed together and sat down before him, he spoke about the need to keep pure. When it was now daylight, he allowed the crowds to enter. Once the crowd had come in, he greeted many of them as usual and began to speak:

lexical_decisions.chosen: water basin
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun denotes a place or vessel supplying water, not necessarily a modern bathroom. Washing precedes prayer.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν περὶ τοῦ δεῖν ἁγνεύειν ἐποιεῖτο λόγον.
lexical_decisions.chosen: he spoke about the need to keep pure
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἁγνεύειν can concern ritual or moral purity; the discourse develops both and neither is excluded here.

passages.text: “Because of your great neglect of yourselves, your mind has sprouted the many harmful notions associated with religious worship, and you have become like land left uncultivated for lack of a farmer. You need much time for cleansing, so that your mind, receiving the true word imparted to you like good seed, may not choke it with evil thoughts and make it fruitless in the deeds that can save. Therefore those concerned for their own salvation must listen more continually, so that the wrongs multiplied over long periods may be brought into proportion, for cleansing, with the short time remaining through sustained .. effort. Since each person does not know the end of his own time, hurry to pull out the many thorns from your hearts, not little by little. For you will not be able to be cleansed that way, since you have lain uncultivated for so long.

source_issues.issue: The supplied text contains exactly two dots between the adjective and noun. They remain as two dots in English; no unavailable wording is reconstructed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰς πολλὰς καὶ βλαβερὰς τῶν θρησκειῶν ὑπονοίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: the many harmful notions associated with religious worship
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains religious practices in the plural conceptual background; notions can also be suspicions or suppositions.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through sustained .. effort
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied edition has two consecutive dots after συνεχεῖ. Exactly two dots remain in the main text; unavailable content is not restored.

lexical_decisions.chosen: may be brought into proportion, for cleansing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The proportionality concerns accumulated errors and the short remaining time, with sustained effort as means; the wording is not replaced by a claim of automatic cleansing.

passages.text: You will not otherwise endure undertaking the great effort needed for your cleansing unless you become angry with them and rebuke them for the ways in which, like useless servants, you were ambushed by agreeing with your evil desires, so that you may be able to apply your righteous anger to your mind like fire to a field left uncultivated. So if you do not have righteous fire—I mean anger against evil desires—learn what good things you have been ambushed and deprived of, what punishment you have been prepared for, and by whom you have been deceived. In this way your mind, becoming clear-minded and kindled to anger like fire by the teaching of the one who sent us, may be able to consume the things that are against desire. Believe me: if you are willing, you will be able to set everything right.

source_issues.source_quote: τὰ κατὰ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας ἀναλῶσαι δυνηθῇ.
source_issues.issue: The formal grouping the things that are against desire is defensible from the supplied article and genitive construction, but its fit with the surrounding fire-and-desire argument is difficult. This translation does not claim to resolve that difficulty or emend the Greek. The previous adverbial attachment is not retained, because an independent object for τὰ was not adequately established.

lexical_decisions.chosen: like useless servants
lexical_decisions.rationale: Uses the POB servant gloss; the comparison retains the underlying bonded-status and master-accountability sense of δοῦλοι.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ κατὰ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας ἀναλῶσαι δυνηθῇ.
lexical_decisions.chosen: may be able to consume the things that are against desire.
lexical_decisions.rationale: τὰ substantivizes the following prepositional phrase, and κατά with the supplied genitive τῆς naturally means against. The formal grouping preserves that syntax without silently replacing the genitive with an accusative or moving opposition to qualify the consuming action. Its precise intended sense remains difficult in the surrounding fire-and-desire argument; things belonging to desire would require a textual or syntactic account not established by this wording.

lexical_decisions.chosen: become angry with them and rebuke them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied αὐτοῖς is third-person them, not reflexive αὑτοῖς. The English retains the anaphoric pronoun without independently naming its antecedent. The prior self-directed rendering is not retained because the supplied spelling and context do not establish it; a reflexive reading would require separate grammatical or textual support, not silent accent alteration.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἵνα τὴν δικαίαν ὑμῶν ὀργὴν τῷ νῷ ὡς πῦρ χερσευσάσῃ ἀρούρῃ ἐπαφεῖναι δυνηθῆτε.
lexical_decisions.chosen: so that you may be able to apply your righteous anger to your mind like fire to a field left uncultivated
lexical_decisions.rationale: So that explicitly keeps the purpose or intended-result link of ἵνα with the preceding anger and rebuke, not an independent assured future result. The fire/uncultivated-field comparison remains intact.

passages.text: You are an image of the invisible God. Therefore those who wish to practice reverence must not say that idols are an image of God and that they must therefore be revered. For the human being is God’s image. Whoever wishes to show reverence toward God does good to a human being, because the human body bears God’s image. But not everyone bears the likeness: that belongs to the pure mind of a good soul. Nevertheless, since we know that the human being was made “according to the image and according to the likeness” of God, we tell you to show reverence toward this human being, so that the gratitude may be credited to God, whose image he is. You must therefore offer honor to God’s image—that is, the human being—in this way: food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the unclothed, care to the sick, shelter to the stranger, and visits and whatever help is possible to the prisoner. Not to speak item by item: whatever good things someone wishes for himself, let him likewise provide for another who needs them. Then a good reward can be credited to him for having shown reverence toward God’s image. By the same reasoning, if he does not undertake to do these things, he will be punished for having neglected the image.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν δὲ ὁμοιότητα οὐκέτι πάντες, ἀλλὰ ἀγαθῆς ψυχῆς ὁ καθαρὸς νοῦς.
lexical_decisions.chosen: But not everyone bears the likeness: that belongs to the pure mind of a good soul.
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the author’s image/likeness distinction rather than harmonizing them.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἵνα εἰς θεόν, οὗπέρ ἐστιν εἰκών, ἡ χάρις λογισθῇ.
lexical_decisions.chosen: so that the gratitude may be credited to God, whose image he is
lexical_decisions.rationale: χάρις can be gratitude, favor, or the benefit; gratitude is preferred in the transfer of honor to the one represented. The benefaction being reckoned as directed to God is another viable construal.

passages.text: What can it mean, then, to say that you revere every form for the sake of reverence toward God, when in every way you abuse the human being who truly is God’s image—murdering, committing adultery, stealing, and dishonoring him in many other ways? You ought not to do any evil that causes a person grief. But now you do everything that makes a person lose heart. For injustice and discouragement come through being murdered, having one’s property taken away, and all the other things you know you do not want to suffer. But you, deceived into evil by a certain malicious serpent through a notion of knowledge of many gods, show irreverence toward the true image—that is, the human being—while imagining that you show reverence toward insensible things.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a certain malicious serpent
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἑρπετόν is a creeping creature; serpent follows the recurring figure explicitly called ὄφις nearby without adding its identity as a name.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through a notion of knowledge of many gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: Keeps the claim to knowledge and its many-gods qualification; it is not presented as the translator’s own true knowledge.

passages.text: Some say, “If he did not want them to exist, they would not exist, but would have been destroyed.” I too say that this certainly will happen when everyone has displayed his own choice toward him; then the present world will be changed. Yet even if you wanted him to act in this way, so that none of the things worshiped existed, tell us: which existing thing have you not worshiped? Do not some of you worship the sun, others the moon, others water, others earth, others mountains, others plants, others seeds, and others even a human being, as in Egypt? Then God would have had to leave nothing, not even us, so that there would be neither anything worshiped nor anyone worshiping. Truly, this is what the terrible serpent lurking within you wants to happen; he does not spare you. But it will not be so. For the thing worshiped commits no sin: it suffers violence at the hands of the person who wants to worship it. Even if all human beings judge unjustly, God does not. For it is not just for the one who suffers and the one who inflicts it to receive the same punishment—unless the former himself willingly accepts the honor belonging to the one who alone is most worthy of honor.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν αὐτῶν πρὸς αὐτὸν δείξωσιν προαίρεσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: has displayed his own choice toward him
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains human choice and its orientation toward God without inserting a doctrine of predestination.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐκτὸς εἰ μὴ αὐτὸς ἑκὼν ἀναδέξηται τὴν τοῦ μόνου τιμιωτάτου τιμήν.
lexical_decisions.chosen: unless the former himself willingly accepts the honor belonging to the one who alone is most worthy of honor
lexical_decisions.rationale: The exception concerns a recipient of worship willingly accepting divine honor. No named example is added.

passages.text: “But,” someone says, “the worshipers themselves ought to be destroyed by the true God, so that no one else does this.” But you are not wiser than God, so as to offer him advice as someone more intelligent. He knows what he is doing. For he is patient with all who live in impiety, like a merciful father who loves humanity, knowing that even impious people become reverent. Many of the very people who revere shameful and insensible things have become clear-minded, stopped revering them and sinning, and taken refuge in the true God; through prayers and good deeds they have been saved.

lexical_decisions.chosen: have become clear-minded
lexical_decisions.rationale: Uses the POB clear-minded rendering for awakening from religious error, not an exclusively literal sobriety claim.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through prayers and good deeds they have been saved
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the author’s explicit linkage of salvation, prayers, and good deeds without imposing a denominational explanation.

passages.text: “But from the beginning he ought to have made us not even think about such things at all.” In saying this, you do not know what freedom of choice is or how it is possible to be truly good. For the person who is good by his own choice is truly good; the person made good by someone else’s compulsion is not truly so, because he is not what he is by his own choice. Since each person’s freedom produces what is truly good and reveals what is truly evil, God has arranged, through the circumstances, for becoming an enemy or a friend to lie within each person. “No,” someone says, “rather, he himself makes us think everything that we think.” Stop! What further blasphemy are you speaking when you say this? For if, in everything we may think, we are moved by him, you are calling him the cause of sexual immoralities, shameless acts, greed, and every blasphemy. Stop speaking ill of him, you who ought to speak well of him and assign him every honor. And do not say, “God does not claim honor.” Even if he claims nothing, we still ought, with an eye to what is just, to repay with a thankful voice the one who has benefited us in every way.

lexical_decisions.chosen: freedom of choice
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally self-determination or being in one’s own power; the paragraph explicitly contrasts personal choice and external compulsion.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through the circumstances
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑποθέσεις can denote situations, underlying conditions, or proposed matters; circumstances fits the arrangements in which choice operates without specifying their exact mechanism.

lexical_decisions.chosen: sexual immoralities, shameless acts, greed
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves distinct vice categories without embellishing sexual content or reducing all three to a generic evil.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ γὰρ πᾶν ὅ,τι ἂν ἐνθυμηθῶμεν, ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ ἐνεργούμεθα
lexical_decisions.chosen: For if, in everything we may think, we are moved by him
lexical_decisions.rationale: We remains the subject of ἐνεργούμεθα. Moved or actuated concerns the alleged divine agency in our thinking; it does not make thoughts into actions implemented by God.

passages.text: “But,” someone says, “we do better by thanking him and everyone else together.” In saying this, you do not know the plot against you. For suppose many physicians promise to treat one sick person but can do nothing, while one who really can heal does not administer his remedy, reasoning that if he heals the patient, others will take the credit. In the same way, when God is esteemed along with many who can do nothing, he does not bestow benefits. “What then?” someone says. “Is God indignant about this, if someone else gets the credit when he heals?” I say that even if he is not indignant, he still does not wish to become an accomplice in deception. For when he does good, the idol that has done nothing is also confirmed as having power. I too say that if the person infatuated with insensible things were not harmed in his nature, perhaps God would have put up even with this. So become clear-minded for the sake of salvation and think what is reasonable. For God, being without need, himself needs nothing and is not harmed. It is we who benefit or are harmed. Just as Caesar is neither harmed when he is reviled nor benefited when he is thanked, but safety belongs to the one who thanks him and destruction to the one who reviles him, so those who speak well of God do not benefit him at all but save themselves. Likewise, those who blaspheme do him no injury but are themselves destroyed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ μὴ φυσικῶς ἠδίκητο πρὸς ἀναίσθητα ἐπτοημένος, ἴσως ἂν καὶ τοῦτο ὑπομεμενήκει
lexical_decisions.chosen: if the person infatuated with insensible things were not harmed in his nature, perhaps God would have put up even with this
lexical_decisions.rationale: The subject of being harmed and infatuated is understood as the worshiper, while the subject of putting up with this is God, who immediately afterward is explicitly said not to suffer harm. φυσικῶς can also mean naturally. The Greek leaves these subjects implicit, so this contextual subject differentiation is disclosed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Caesar
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the imperial name/title without identifying a particular emperor.

passages.text: “But,” someone says, “it is not the same with a human being and God.” I agree that it is not the same. For the punishment is greater for having shown irreverence toward one who is greater, and less for the one who has sinned against someone lesser. Thus, just as God is greater than all, the person who has shown irreverence toward him will undergo greater punishment for having sinned against someone greater. It is not that God retaliates with his own hand; rather, all creation is indignant at this and pursues the offender by its nature. For neither will the sun give the blasphemer light, nor the earth its fruits, nor a spring its water, nor the ruler established in Hades give the soul there rest, since even now, while the world’s allotted term still stands, all creation shares in the indignation. Therefore neither does heaven provide rain in full nor the earth its fruits, and most people are consequently brought to ruin. Even the air itself, inflamed with anger, changes to act as a pestilence. Yet whatever good things we enjoy, he compels creation by his mercy to act with love toward us. This is how all creation is angry with you who dishonor the maker of all.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκ ἐν ᾅδῃ τῇ ψυχῇ ὁ ἐκεῖ καθεστὼς ἄρχων τὴν ἀνάπαυσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: nor the ruler established in Hades give the soul there rest
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains Hades as the source’s named realm; it is not replaced by a later, more specific doctrine of hell.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ τῆς τοῦ κόσμου προθεσμίας ὑφεστώσης
lexical_decisions.chosen: while the world’s allotted term still stands
lexical_decisions.rationale: The stated time-limit belongs to the world; the text does not supply its length.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ αὐτοῦ ἐλέῳ εἰς τὴν ἡμετέραν φιλανθρωπίαν βιάζεται τὴν κτίσιν.
lexical_decisions.chosen: he compels creation by his mercy to act with love toward us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The reflexive/possessive references are retained contextually: God compels creation toward humane treatment of us. The active force of βιάζεται is not softened into permission.

passages.text: For even if you escape punishment through the dissolution of the body, how will you be able through destruction to escape your soul, which is indestructible? For even the soul of the impious is immortal; it would have been better for them not to have it indestructible. Punished by unquenchable fire with unending punishment and not dying, it cannot come to an end, to its own hurt. But perhaps one of you will say, “You frighten us, Peter.” Then teach us how we are to state things as they are while remaining silent, for we cannot make them known to you otherwise. If we remain silent, you are ambushed by evils through ignorance; if we speak, we are suspected of frightening you on a false premise. How, then, are we to examine the evil lurking within you and cunningly sowing in you notions hostile to God under the pretext of friendship with God? Be reconciled with yourselves: taking refuge in him with good deeds is for your salvation. Irrational desire within you is a kind of enmity toward God; for through supposed understanding, it strengthens ignorance.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ εἰς τὴν ὑμετέραν κακῷ ἐνδομυχοῦντι
lexical_decisions.chosen: the evil lurking within you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The possessive phrase τὴν ὑμετέραν has no expressed feminine noun in the supplied wording. Within you preserves the contextual location of the lurking evil without inventing a named organ or restoring Greek words.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ κακῷ τῷ αὐτῆς τέλος λαβεῖν οὐκ ἔχει.
lexical_decisions.chosen: it cannot come to an end, to its own hurt
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains endless survival as harmful to the punished soul; the author’s claim is not harmonized with annihilation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ πανούργως ὑποσπείροντι ὑμῖν τὰς θεῷ ἐχθραινούσας ὑπονοίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: and cunningly sowing in you notions hostile to God
lexical_decisions.rationale: In you explicitly preserves ὑμῖν as the recipients of the sowing, separately from the earlier location of the lurking evil.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπονοίᾳ γὰρ φρονήσεως τὴν ἄγνοιαν κρατύνει.
lexical_decisions.chosen: for through supposed understanding, it strengthens ignorance.
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπόνοια is a supposition, notion, or suspicion; supposed understanding preserves that cognitive claim rather than introducing a deliberate display or pretension. For retains the explanatory γάρ.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πῶς οὖν ἐτάσωμεν τῷ εἰς τὴν ὑμετέραν κακῷ ἐνδομυχοῦντι
lexical_decisions.chosen: How, then, are we to examine the evil lurking within you
lexical_decisions.rationale: Examine preserves the testing, scrutiny, or questioning force of ἐτάσωμεν instead of general deal with. Its dative complement is understood as the target or concern of the examination, with the lurking/sowing participles describing that evil. The English object construction makes this contextual relation readable without changing the printed dative or diagnosing an OCR defect. Question or put to the test are viable lexical alternatives.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Be reconciled with yourselves:
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text reads plural ἑαυτοῖς reflexively because the surrounding argument concerns evil, ignorance, and irrational desire within the hearers. Be reconciled with one another is the material reciprocal alternative, also possible with the plural reflexive. Neither reading is presented as uniquely established.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἔχθρα τις ἐστὶν θεῷ ἐν ὑμῖν ἄλογος ἐπιθυμία·
lexical_decisions.chosen: Irrational desire within you is a kind of enmity toward God;
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔχθρα is the noun enmity, not adjective ἐχθρά. A kind preserves the indefinite τις and the nominal classification of desire as enmity, rather than introducing only the existence of a hostile desire.

passages.text: Others say, “God has not cared about us.” This too is false. For if he truly did not care, he would not make his sun rise on good and evil people or send his rain on the righteous and unrighteous. Others say, “We are more reverent because we revere both him and the statues.” I do not think so—if someone who says this tells a king, “I assign you the same honor as I do the dead and discarded dung,” I do not think he will come off well. But someone will say, “Do you call our objects of reverence dung?” Yes, I say. For you made them useless to yourselves by counting them among objects of worship, although their substance might have served some other purpose, even the use of dung. But now it is not useful even for this, since you have reshaped it and worship it. How can you, the most impious of all, also claim to be more reverent? For this one incomparable sin alone you truly owe the destruction of your soul, if you persist. Just as a son who receives many benefits from his father and gives someone else, who is not his father, the honor owed to his father certainly becomes disinherited, so, when he lives according to his father’s judgment and gives thanks for the benefits, he reasonably becomes an heir.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς οὐσίας αὐτῶν ἴσως εἰς ἄλλο τι (εἰς χρῆσιν κόπρου) εὐχρηστησάσης.
lexical_decisions.chosen: although their substance might have served some other purpose, even the use of dung
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the parenthetical comparison with useful dung rather than upgrading the idols into useful objects of worship.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ταύτῃ αὐτῇ τῇ μιᾷ καὶ ἀσυγκρίτῳ ἀμαρτίᾳ ψυχῆς ὄλεθρον ὀφείλοντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: For this one incomparable sin alone you truly owe the destruction of your soul
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the severe stated consequence, with the following if-you-persist condition retained in the main text.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκ οἶμαι, εἰ τοῦτο λέγων τις ἐρεῖ βασιλεῖ Τὴν ἴσην σοι ἀπονέμω τιμήν, οἵαν καὶ τοῖς νεκροῖς καὶ τῇ ἐρριμμένῃ κοπρίᾳ· οὐκ οἴομαι εἰ καλῶς ἀπαλλάξει.
lexical_decisions.chosen: I do not think so—if ... I do not think he will come off well.
lexical_decisions.rationale: The selected edition repeats the negative assertion οὐκ οἶμαι / οὐκ οἴομαι around a conditional and syntactic restart. Both assertions remain, rather than being compressed into one; the restart is a supplied feature, not alleged OCR corruption.

passages.text: Others say, “We shall be acting impiously if we abandon the objects of reverence handed down to us from our fathers, for it is like keeping something entrusted to us.” By this reasoning, then, even if someone is the child of a robber, or of a father, or of a man who lives shamefully, is the son, once he has become clear-minded, not to choose the better course, lest he act impiously and sin by not doing the same things as his parents? How senseless are those who say, “We worship these things so as not to trouble him himself,” as though God were troubled by being praised but not troubled by being blasphemed through ingratitude! Why, then, when rain is withheld, do you look to heaven for everything and offer prayers and entreaties? And when you succeed, why do you forget so quickly? For after reaping or gathering the vintage, you immediately assign the firstfruits to idols that are nothing, quickly forgetting the God who did you good. Then you go into sacred groves and temples and feast while performing sacrifices. For this reason some of you say, “These things have been well devised for comfort and feasting.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κἂν λῃστοῦ τις ἢ πατρὸς ἢ αἰσχροβίου
lexical_decisions.chosen: even if someone is the child of a robber, or of a father, or of a man who lives shamefully
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both printed ἢ disjunctions remain. The child relationship is inferred from the ensuing explicit son, not restored from missing text; the redundant father remains the supplied reading. Taking the first ἢ as conjectural ᾖ would create a smoother alternative, but that conjecture is not adopted.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκ ὀφείλει ὁ υἱὸς νήψας τὸ κρεῖττον ἑλέσθαι, ἵνα μὴ ἀσεβήσῃ καὶ μὴ τὰ ἴσα τοῖς γονεῦσιν ποιῶν ἀμαρτάνῃ;
lexical_decisions.chosen: is the son, once he has become clear-minded, not to choose the better course, lest he act impiously and sin by not doing the same things as his parents?
lexical_decisions.rationale: Once clear-minded keeps νήψας circumstantial. The main text reads the question as a reductio of the proposed obligation to preserve ancestral practices and attaches the second μή to ποιῶν: not repeating parental conduct would be treated as sin under that argument. The full material alternative reads οὐκ ὀφείλει as a rhetorical obligation question and the second μή as negating the clause ending in ἀμαρτάνῃ: Is the son, once clear-minded, not obliged to choose the better course, so that he does not act impiously and does not sin by doing the same things as his parents? That reading instead makes repeating the parents’ conduct the sin to avoid. Both scope decisions are disclosed; neither implies a source-corruption claim.

lexical_decisions.chosen: look to heaven for everything
lexical_decisions.rationale: The neuter accusative τὰ πάντα qualifies the scope of looking, not the nominative people looking. Looking wholly toward heaven is another viable adverbial rendering; for everything is selected in the petition-for-rain context.

passages.text: Senseless people, become just judges of what is being said. For even if one ought to give oneself over to bodily enjoyment here, which feast is better: one by rivers and woods and groves, where there are banquets and drinking parties and shaded places, or one where there is the frenzy of demons, cutting of hands, cutting off of genitals, fits of fury and madness, clipping of hair, boasts, possession, shrieks, and all those things done theatrically to astound the senseless, so that you offer their owed prayers and thanksgivings to things deader even than the dead?

lexical_decisions.chosen: cutting of hands, cutting off of genitals
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves both named ritual injuries soberly without euphemism or added detail.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to things deader even than the dead
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the pointed comparative and its rhetorical excess.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅπως τὰς αὐτῶν ὀφειλομένας εὐχὰς καὶ εὐχαριστίας καὶ νεκρῶν νεκροτέροις προσενέγκητε;
lexical_decisions.chosen: so that you offer their owed prayers and thanksgivings to things deader even than the dead?
lexical_decisions.rationale: Their preserves the printed third-person αὐτῶν alongside second-person you offer. It can refer to the previously mentioned senseless people, potentially including the audience. Your is a contextual identification alternative, but the main text does not silently harmonize the pronouns.

passages.text: And why do you do these things gladly? Since the serpent nesting within you, who sowed fruitless desire in you, does not want to tell you, I will remind you by explaining. It is like this: in the worship of God it is proclaimed that one must be clear-minded, exercise self-control, master anger, not appropriate what belongs to others, live justly, reasonably, steadily, and gently, and discipline oneself in deprivation rather than, when lacking something, take it unjustly from someone else and be filled. But among the so-called gods, the opposite happens. Some commands are also given to inspire awe at righteousness; yet even if you perform all the commands, ignorance of God alone is sufficient for your punishment. Nevertheless, you gather at the places you have assigned to them, gladly become drunk, and kindle altars. Their drifting sacrificial smoke, through the power, brings even the blind and deaf spirits to the place where they smell it. Thus, of those there, some are filled with possession, others with strange foods, while others turn to shameless conduct and others to thefts and murders. For the vapor of the blood there and the libation of wines set even the impure spirits themselves dancing. Lurking within you, they make you take pleasure in what goes on there, surround you through dreams with false visions, and punish you with countless afflictions. For under the pretext of the so-called sacrificial offerings you are filled with fierce demons, who also kill you while cunningly escaping your notice, so that you do not understand the plot against you. For under the pretext of some abuse, necessity, passion, anger, or grief, they remove you from life by hanging, by drowning you in water, by throwing you from a cliff, by your own hand, by a stroke, or by some other affliction.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ἔνια εἰς κατάπληξιν δικαιοσύνης παραγγέλλεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: Some commands are also given to inspire awe at righteousness
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase relates certain commands to an impressive effect associated with righteousness. An impressive display of righteousness is another viable rendering; the main text does not decide that all such commands are merely fraudulent.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ κνίσα ῥεμβομένη καὶ τὰ τυφλὰ καὶ κωφὰ πνεύματα διὰ τῆς ἐξουσίας ἄγει εἰς τὸν τῆς ὀσφρήσεως αὐτῶν τόπον.
lexical_decisions.chosen: Their drifting sacrificial smoke, through the power, brings even the blind and deaf spirits to the place where they smell it.
lexical_decisions.rationale: Smoke is the grammatical subject, but the possessor or source of ἐξουσία is not stated. The power leaves it unspecified. Its power, assigning power to the smoke, is a defensible contextual alternative, not an explicit Greek possessive. No divine or demonic source of the power is independently added.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ αὐτὰ χοροῖ τὰ ἀκάθαρτα πνεύματα
lexical_decisions.chosen: set even the impure spirits themselves dancing
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the dancing image, not merely attraction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by your own hand, by a stroke
lexical_decisions.rationale: By your own hand understands the demons as inducing the victims’ self-killing, supported by the listed pretexts and means of death. αὐτοχειρία can also be killing with one’s own hand, so direct killing by the demons themselves is a material alternative given the surrounding demonic subjects. Stroke preserves the separate ἀποπληξία without adding clinical detail.

passages.text: But none of us can suffer anything of this kind. Rather, they are themselves punished by us when, after entering someone, they beg us to let them come out slowly. But perhaps someone will say, “Some who revere God also fall into such afflictions.” I say that this is impossible. For the God-revering person is the one I mean, the one who truly reveres God, not someone merely called so. The one who truly is such carries out the commands of the law given him. If someone acts impiously, he is not reverent. In the same way, if a foreigner practices the law, he is a Jew; a Jew who does not practice it is a Greek. For the person who believes God practices the law, and through this faith also removes the other afflictions that resemble mountains and weigh him down. But the person who does not practice the law plainly deserts his post because he does not believe God. Thus, as a sinner who is not a Jew, because of sin he is overpowered by the afflictions appointed to punish sinners. By God’s will, determined from the beginning, punishment justly follows those who revere him on account of their transgressions. This happens so that, after exacting the sin like a debt through torment, it may present those who have turned back clean at the judgment of all. For just as luxury here becomes for the wicked a loss of eternal good things, so punishments are sent to Jews who transgress as an exaction, so that, after receiving the due for their transgression here, they may be released from the eternal punishment there.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they beg us to let them come out slowly
lexical_decisions.rationale: Takes us as the object of beg and demons as the implied subject of coming out. Permission is implicit. Beg us to withdraw slowly is another grammatical grouping, but the expulsion context favors the former.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a Jew who does not practice it is a Greek
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the author’s explicit Jew/Greek categories defined here through observance. Greek can function as Gentile in the religious argument; no literal change of ancestry is added.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those who have turned back
lexical_decisions.rationale: Keeps the turning verb distinct from μετανοέω/reorient.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as an exaction
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the debt-collection image of punishment.

passages.text: But you cannot say these things, for you do not believe that things there are as we say—I mean the place where everyone receives repayment. Therefore, ignorant of what benefits you, you are ambushed by temporary pleasures so as not to receive eternal things. We therefore try to demonstrate what benefits you, so that, fully assured about the promises of reverence toward God, through good actions you may be able to inherit with us the age without sorrow. Until you come to know us, then, do not be angry with us as though we were lying about the good things we want for you. For we have not begrudged bringing you what we consider true and good; on the contrary, we have been eager to make you fellow heirs of the good things we believe in. For this is how one must speak to unbelievers. But that we really speak truth about what we say you will not be able to know unless you first obey with a love of truth.

lexical_decisions.chosen: obey with a love of truth
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπακούω can be listen or obey; obey retains the demanded response while the adverb retains love of truth.

passages.text: For the present, therefore, even if the serpent lurking within you wishes to ambush you in countless ways, putting evil thoughts and distractions into you, you must contend against him all the more in this way: listen to us continually. For you who have been so greatly deceived must sit together and learn how to chant against him. Otherwise it is impossible. By chanting against him, I mean resisting his evil counsels with reason, remembering that from the beginning he brought death into the world through a promise of knowledge.

lexical_decisions.chosen: how to chant against him
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the incantation metaphor that the author immediately defines as rational resistance, not a newly supplied magical formula.

passages.text: Therefore the prophet of truth, knowing that the world was greatly deceived and seeing that it had agreed with evil, did not love peace with it, since that peace arose from error. Setting out that it ultimately brings death upon all who agree with evil, in place of error he cast into those who had become clear-minded an anger against the one who had ambushed them, like fire and resembling a sword. Holding out the word, he does away with ignorance through knowledge, as though cutting and separating the living from the dead. So, as evil was overcome by knowledge in accordance with the law, war gripped everything. For the sake of salvation a son who yielded separated from a disobedient father, or a father from a child, or a mother from a daughter, or a daughter from a mother—in short, relatives from relatives and friends from companions.

source_issues.source_quote: ὅτι εἰς τέλος ἐπιφέρει πᾶσιν τοῖς πρὸς κακίαν ὁμογνωμονοῦσιν παραθεὶς
source_issues.issue: The object of brings upon is implicit. Death in the main text is inferred from the immediately preceding death-language and ensuing living/dead contrast. The antecedent can be error-based peace or its sustaining error.

The selected, image-checked edition prints a period between the article τῶν and noun νεκρῶν. English reads them together as from the dead despite this intervening punctuation. This is a supplied print feature, not assumed OCR corruption; no replacement Greek has been introduced.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅτι εἰς τέλος ἐπιφέρει πᾶσιν τοῖς πρὸς κακίαν ὁμογνωμονοῦσιν παραθεὶς
lexical_decisions.chosen: Setting out that it ultimately brings death upon all who agree with evil
lexical_decisions.rationale: The object brought is implicit. Death is inferred from the end of 11.18 and the ensuing living/dead contrast. The it can be the peace founded on error or its sustaining error; no new punishment is specified.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a son who yielded
lexical_decisions.rationale: The recipient of yielding is not explicit. The saving instruction is contextual, but the English does not insert that recipient.

passages.text: And let no one say, “How is this just, for parents to be separated from children and children from parents?” It is entirely just. For if by staying with them they not only did them no good but also perished with them, how is it not just for the one who wants to be saved to be separated from the one who does not want to be saved but wants to perish together? Moreover, those who had understood what is better did not themselves want to be separated, but to remain with them and benefit them by teaching better things. Therefore the disobedient, unwilling to listen to them, themselves fought against them, separating them, persecuting them, and hating them. But those who suffered these things pitied them as people ambushed by ignorance and, taught to understand, prayed for those who mistreated them, having learned that ignorance is the cause of sin. For the teacher himself, when nailed up, prayed to the Father that the sin of those killing him might be forgiven, saying, “Father, forgive them their sins, for they do not know what they are doing.” Becoming imitators of the teacher themselves, in their sufferings they prayed for those who inflicted them, as they had been taught. Thus they did not separate because they hated their parents, since they even offered prayers for those who were not their parents but had become enemies, and try to love them as they were commanded.

lexical_decisions.chosen: taught to understand
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative connects instruction in understanding with the prayerful response, not with a newly supplied revelation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they ... separate
lexical_decisions.rationale: Bracketed letters are already supplied by the selected edition; no new restoration has been made.

lexical_decisions.chosen: who were not their parents
lexical_decisions.rationale: Follows the supplied bracketed reading and preserves the contrast with enemies.

lexical_decisions.chosen: when nailed up
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the physical nail-language.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀπὸ τοῦ μὴ θέλοντος, συναπολέσθαι δὲ βουλομένου;
lexical_decisions.chosen: from the one who does not want to be saved but wants to perish together?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The person described by βουλομένου remains the subject of co-perishing. To be saved repeats the contextual object of willing in the prior clause, not a new wish for other people’s destruction.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅθεν οἱ ἀπειθεῖς ἐπακούειν αὐτῶν μὴ θέλοντες αὐτοὶ αὐτοὺς ἐπολέμουν, χωρίζοντες, διώκοντες, μισοῦντες.
lexical_decisions.chosen: themselves fought against them, separating them, persecuting them, and hating them.
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expressed αὐτούς is taken as the shared object of the parallel participles, giving the disobedient people agency in imposing separation. Separating from them is an intransitive alternative, but it is less source-transparent after the statement that the instructed people did not want separation.

passages.text: But tell me: how do you love your parents? If you do so with a constant regard for what is just, I join in your prayer; but if merely as it happens, I do not, for even on a small pretext you can become their enemies. If you love with knowledge, tell us what “parents” means. You will say, “Founders of a family line.” Why, then, have you not loved the origin of all things, if you have undertaken to do this with a just mind? But even now you will say, “We have not seen him.” Why, then, do you flatter insensible things without having searched? And what of this? Even if it was difficult for you to know what God is, you could not fail to know what is not God, so that you might reason that God is not wood, not stone, not bronze, or anything else made of perishable matter.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the origin of all things
lexical_decisions.rationale: γένος links the argument to lineage and parentage. Origin or source here refers to God; progenitor of all is a viable more explicitly personal alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I join in your prayer
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the prayer compound; join in wishing this is also possible, rather than bare agreement.

lexical_decisions.chosen: And what of this?
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the separate rhetorical question introducing the final argument.

passages.text: Were they not shaped on a lathe by iron—and was not the iron that shaped them on a lathe softened by fire—and is not fire itself extinguished by water? Does not water get its motion from wind, and does not wind have the origin of its movement from the God who made all things? For this is what the prophet Moses said: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth. But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss, and God’s Spirit was borne over the water.” And when God speaks, this Spirit, like his hand, fashions everything, separating light from darkness and spreading out the visible heaven after the invisible one, so that the regions above may be inhabited by the angels of light, while those below may be administered by the human being together with all things made for his sake.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ δὲ ὕδωρ οὐχ ὑπὸ πνεύματος τὴν κίνησιν ἔχει
lexical_decisions.chosen: Does not water get its motion from wind
lexical_decisions.rationale: πνεῦμα can be wind or spirit. Wind fits the physical water-motion argument; the same word recurs as God’s Spirit in the quotation, preserving an important lexical link in these notes.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the origin of its movement
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here displacement or movement is intended, not religious ecstasy.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μετὰ τὸν ἀόρατον οὐρανὸν τὸν φαινόμενον ἐφαπλῶσαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: spreading out the visible heaven after the invisible one
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the visible/invisible distinction and after without supplying numbered heavens.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἢ γὰρ οὐχ ὑπὸ σιδήρου ἐτορνεύθησαν, — καὶ ὁ τορνεύσας σίδηρος ὑπὸ πυρὸς ἐμαλάχθη —
lexical_decisions.chosen: Were they not shaped on a lathe by iron—and was not the iron that shaped them on a lathe softened by fire—
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both forms of τορνεύω retain turning or lathe-working workmanship. Shaped alone is broader and would conceal the particular working image.

passages.text: For it was for you, the human being, that God commanded the water on the face of the earth to withdraw, so that the earth could offer you fruits. He made openings so that it might provide springs for you, streams of rivers might appear, and animals might be cast up. To put it briefly, so that everything could be at your service. Is it not for you that winds blow for the production of fruits, rains are brought, and seasonal turnings occur? Indeed, the sun and moon, together with the other stars, carry out their risings and settings for you, and rivers and lakes, together with all the springs, serve you. Therefore, just as greater honor was given to you, insensible though you are, so greater punishment through fire has been prepared for you in your ingratitude, because you were unwilling to know the one whom you ought to have known before all others.

lexical_decisions.chosen: He made openings
lexical_decisions.rationale: Bored holes or passages; no modern geological mechanism is specified.

lexical_decisions.chosen: and animals might be cast up
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the casting-up image, not generic creation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: and seasonal turnings occur
lexical_decisions.rationale: The turnings can concern the sun or seasons; the broader cyclical wording is retained.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ τρηδόνας ἐποίησεν, ἵνα σοι παράσχῃ πηγὰς
lexical_decisions.chosen: He made openings so that it might provide springs for you
lexical_decisions.rationale: It refers to the earth, the subject explicitly named in the preceding purpose clause and the bearer of the openings. The subject of παράσχῃ is unexpressed, so God, subject of made, remains a viable alternative: so that he might provide springs for you. The main text chooses earth without claiming the antecedent is uniquely settled.

passages.text: Even now, recognize from the lesser things the cause of all things, reasoning that water produces all things, that water receives the beginning of its motion from spirit, and that spirit has its origin from the God of all. This is how you ought to reason, so that through reason you may be able to reach God, in order that you may recognize your lineage, be born again through first-born water, and become an heir of the parents who begot you for incorruptibility.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ δὲ ὕδωρ ὑπὸ πνεύματος κινήσεως τὴν γένεσιν λαμβάνει
lexical_decisions.chosen: water receives the beginning of its motion from spirit
lexical_decisions.rationale: Takes ὑπὸ πνεύματος together as the source of motion, with κινήσεως dependent on γένεσιν, beginning of motion. This agrees with the explicit water-motion argument in 11.22. Alternatively πνεύματος can depend on κινήσεως, with γένεσις as water’s coming into being: through the movement of spirit. Spirit can also be wind; both lexical senses remain possible, but no creation-from-nothing claim is added.

lexical_decisions.chosen: be born again through first-born water
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the unusual birth-wording. Primordial water is a contextual alternative but would conceal the explicit birth epithet.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν πρὸς ἀφθαρσίαν γεννησάντων σε γονέων
lexical_decisions.chosen: the parents who begot you for incorruptibility
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source has plural parents and does not identify them in this clause; neither a singular parent nor specific identities are substituted.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἵνα ἐπὶ λόγῳ εἰς θεὸν καταντῆσαι δυνηθῇς, ὅπως ἐπιγνῶς σου τὸ γένος καὶ πρωτογόνῳ ἀναγεννηθῇς ὕδατι καὶ κληρονόμος καταστῇς τῶν πρὸς ἀφθαρσίαν γεννησάντων σε γονέων.
lexical_decisions.chosen: so that through reason you may be able to reach God, in order that you may recognize your lineage, be born again through first-born water, and become an heir of the parents who begot you for incorruptibility.
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains successive ἵνα and ὅπως purpose links: reasoning leads to reaching God, with recognition, rebirth, and inheritance introduced as the following purpose. The two links are not flattened into one list.

passages.text: Therefore come readily, like a son to a father, so that God may set down ignorance as the cause of your sins. But if, even after being called, you are unwilling or delay, you will perish by God’s just judgment, unwanted because you were unwilling. And do not imagine that if you become more reverent than all the reverent people who have ever existed, but remain unbaptized, you will ever be able to attain hope. For in this way you will rather undergo greater punishment, because you did not do good deeds in a good way. For doing good is good when it is done as God commanded. But if you are unwilling to be baptized as he determined, by serving your own will you are hostile to his purpose.

lexical_decisions.chosen: unwanted because you were unwilling
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the repeated will-wordplay and passive rejection; not being willed because you did not will is more formally literal.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you did not do good deeds in a good way
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the distinction between good deeds and doing them well.

passages.text: But perhaps someone will say, “What does being baptized in water contribute to reverence?” First, you do what God determined. Second, being born again out of water to God, out of fear you exchange the first birth that came to you through desire, and thus you can attain salvation; otherwise it is impossible. For the prophet swore to us in this way, saying, “Truly I tell you, unless you are born again in living water, into the name of Father, Son, Holy Spirit, you will certainly not enter the kingdom of the heavens.” Therefore come. For there is something merciful there, borne upon the water from the beginning, .... those baptized with the thrice-blessed naming, and rescues them from the punishment to come, offering to God, as gifts, the good deeds of the baptized themselves from their baptism onward. Therefore take refuge in the water, for this alone can quench the onrush of fire. The person not yet willing to come to it still bears the spirit of madness, because of which he is unwilling to come to “living water” for his own salvation.

source_issues.issue: Exactly four printed dots mark unavailable wording. The governing predicate before those baptized is left interrupted; no reconstruction is supplied.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αἰτίᾳ φόβου τὴν ἐξ ἐπιθυμίας πρώτην σοι γενομένην καταλλάσσεις γένεσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: out of fear you exchange the first birth that came to you through desire
lexical_decisions.rationale: Fear motivates the exchange; desire characterized the first birth. The replacement birth is the stated water-rebirth; physical birth is not explicitly labeled sinful.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐὰν μὴ ἀναγεννηθῆτε ὕδατι ζῶντι, εἰς ὄνομα πατρός, υἱοῦ, ἁγίου πνεύματος
lexical_decisions.chosen: unless you are born again in living water, into the name of Father, Son, Holy Spirit
lexical_decisions.rationale: Follows this quotation’s wording, not the wording of a familiar canonical verse; no unprinted conjunctions are inserted into the name sequence.

lexical_decisions.chosen: borne upon the water from the beginning, .... those baptized
lexical_decisions.rationale: Exactly four printed gap dots remain. The missing predicate governing those baptized is not restored, leaving the English visibly interrupted.
