lexical_decisions.chosen: with the thrice-blessed naming
lexical_decisions.rationale: Naming or invocation associated with baptism, described as thrice-blessed; no later doctrinal explanation is added.

lexical_decisions.chosen: bears the spirit of madness
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the historical author’s spirit-language; λύσσα is raging madness, also rabid frenzy, not a supplied modern clinical diagnosis.

passages.text: Come, then, whether you are righteous or unrighteous. For if you are righteous, all you lacked was to be baptized for salvation. But if unrighteous, in addition to being baptized for the forgiveness of things done in ignorance, doing good remains for you in addition to baptism, in proportion to your impiety. Therefore, whether you are righteous or unrighteous, hurry to be born to God, for delay brings danger because the time appointed for death is unknown. Through doing good, show your likeness to the Father who begets you out of water, honoring the true God as Father as one who loves truth. Honor to him is for you to live as he, being righteous, wills; the will of the righteous is not to act unjustly. Injustice is murdering, committing adultery, hating, coveting, and things like these; and there are many forms of these.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κατὰ ἀναλογίαν τῆς ἀσεβείας ἡ ἐπὶ τὸ βάπτισμα εὐποιΐα
lexical_decisions.chosen: doing good remains for you in addition to baptism, in proportion to your impiety
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains proportional doing-good in addition to baptism, neither rewriting baptism as merely symbolic nor deleting the required deeds.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ ἐξ ὕδατος γεννῶντί σε πατρί, διὰ τῆς εὐποιΐας τὴν ὁμοιότητα δείξας
lexical_decisions.chosen: Through doing good, show your likeness to the Father who begets you out of water
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves water-birth and likeness through conduct without supplying a further causal mechanism.

passages.text: Yet one must add to these something that does not concern dealings with human beings but belongs specifically to the worship of God. I mean keeping clean: not having intercourse with one’s own wife when she is menstruating, because God’s law commands this. What then? If keeping clean did not belong also to God’s worship, you would gladly roll about like beetles. Therefore, as human beings possessing something beyond the irrational animals—being rational—cleanse your heart of evils through heavenly reasoning, and wash your body with a bath. For keeping clean is truly good, not because bodily purity takes precedence over cleansing of the heart, but because cleanliness follows goodness. Our teacher even exposed some of the Pharisees and scribes among you as hypocrites, although they are set apart and, as scribes, know the laws better than others, because they purified only what is visible to people but neglected the pure things of the heart, visible to God alone.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ ἐν ἀφέδρῳ οὔσῃ τῇ ἰδίᾳ γαμετῇ μὴ κοινωνεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: not having intercourse with one’s own wife when she is menstruating
lexical_decisions.rationale: Makes the euphemistic monthly-separation term intelligible without embellishment; this is the ancient author’s restriction.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς οἱ κάνθαροι ἡδέως ἂν ἐκυλίεσθε
lexical_decisions.chosen: you would gladly roll about like beetles
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the comparison without supplying the substance in which the beetles roll.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐχ ὡς ὅτι προηγεῖται τῆς κατὰ τὴν καρδίαν κάθάρσεως ἡ τοῦ σώματος ἁγνεία
lexical_decisions.chosen: not because bodily purity takes precedence over cleansing of the heart
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the denial of bodily priority and the simultaneous affirmation of bodily cleanliness.

passages.text: So he truly used this express statement toward their hypocrites, not toward all of them. For he even said that some should be listened to, because they had been entrusted with Moses’ seat. But to the hypocrites he said, “Woe to you, hypocritical scribes and Pharisees, because you clean the outside of the cup and dish, but inside it is full of filth. Blind Pharisee, first clean the inside of the cup and dish, so that their outsides too may become clean.” And this is true. For when the mind has been enlightened by knowledge, the person who has learned can be good, and becoming clean follows this. Good care for the outward body comes from the inward understanding. Just as inattention to the body cannot produce care for the mind, so the person who is clean inside can also clean the outside. But the one who cleans the outside does this with regard to people, looking toward praise, and with the praise of the onlookers has nothing before God.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀπό γε τῆς κατὰ τὸ σῶμα ἀναισθησίας τῆς διανοίας πρόνοια γενέσθαι οὐ δύναται
lexical_decisions.chosen: inattention to the body cannot produce care for the mind
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀναισθησία can be lack of feeling, perception, or concern. Inattention is preferred in the care argument; bodily insensibility remains an alternative. The text is not changed to a word meaning washing or cleanliness.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ἐπαίνῳ τῶν ἱστορούντων παρὰ τῷ θεῷ οὐδὲν ἔχει.
lexical_decisions.chosen: and with the praise of the onlookers has nothing before God
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the contrast between human praise and standing before God without adding a specified reward.

passages.text: Who does not see that it is better not to come together with a woman during her monthly condition, but after she has become clean and been immersed? And after intercourse one must also immerse oneself. If you shrink from doing this, recall how you pursued the parts of purity when you worshiped insensible idols. Be ashamed that here, where you ought to undertake not, I say, the greater part, but simply the whole of purity, you become more reluctant. So consider the one who made you act there, and you will understand who it is that puts reluctance toward purity into you here.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after she has become clean and been immersed
lexical_decisions.rationale: In this repeated purity setting βαπτίζω denotes bodily immersion; the same verb is baptized in the initiation setting. The contextual gloss difference does not claim different Greek words.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after intercourse one must also immerse oneself
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains repeated immersion after sexual intercourse, not mere inward purity or a newly asserted doctrine of repeated initiation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ τὸ πλεῖον λέγω, ἀλλὰ μόνον καὶ ὅλον τὸ τῆς ἁγνείας ἀναδέξασθαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: not, I say, the greater part, but simply the whole of purity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The preceding parts (μέρη) and following whole (ὅλον) support a quantitative greater-part/whole contrast. More is another viable rendering of τὸ πλεῖον. Simply treats μόνον adverbially, while whole retains ὅλον; the phrase is not made into an unspecified greater thing.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: νοήσατε οὖν τὸν ἐκεῖ ὑμᾶς πεποιηκότα
lexical_decisions.chosen: So consider the one who made you act there
lexical_decisions.rationale: Act is an inferred complement from the preceding account of pursuing purity, not restored missing wording. The more literal the one who made you there, understood as making or forming them as they were, remains an alternative. The behavioral reading is preferred because the following clause concerns the one inducing current reluctance; neither unnamed agent is independently identified.

passages.text: But one of you will say, “Must we then do whatever we did among idols?” I tell you: not everything, but whatever you did well, and here to a greater degree. For whatever is done well in error derives from the truth, just as if something is done badly in the truth, it comes from error. Therefore reclaim what is yours from everywhere, not what belongs to others, and do not say, “If those who have been deceived do something good, we ought not to do it.” For by this reasoning, if someone who reveres idols does not murder, we ought to murder because the person in error does not murder.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀπολάβετε οὖν ὑμῶν πανταχόθεν τὰ ἴδια, μὴ τὰ ἀλλότρια
lexical_decisions.chosen: Therefore reclaim what is yours from everywhere, not what belongs to others
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the ownership/reclamation metaphor, not a blanket rejection of practices also found outside the community.

passages.text: No: rather, do more, so that if those in error do not murder, we do not even become angry; if the person in error does not commit adultery, we do not even think of it in the first place; if the person in error loves the one who loves him, we also love those who hate us; if the person in error lends to those who have, we also lend to those who do not have. In short, we who hope to inherit the boundless age ought to do better than the good things done by those who know only the present age. We know that if their deeds, examined alongside our deeds on the day of judgment, are found equal in good conduct, we too must be put to shame, while they, through error having done what is against them, must perish. I spoke of being put to shame in this respect: we did not do more than they did, although we also knew more than they did. But if we are to be put to shame for displaying good conduct equal to theirs and not more, how much more if we display less good conduct than theirs?

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἱ τὸν ἄπειρον αἰῶνα ἐλπίζοντες κληρονομεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: we who hope to inherit the boundless age
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἄπειρος means boundless or endless; αἰών remains age, contrasting the present age.

lexical_decisions.chosen: we also knew more than they did
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὧν is the comparative genitive supplying the comparison for πλεῖον ἐγνώκαμεν, not an object meaning knowledge about those people. Although in the main sentence makes the contextual contrast of greater knowledge but insufficient greater deeds readable; it is not a new independent fact.

lexical_decisions.chosen: good conduct
lexical_decisions.rationale: The three inflected occurrences of εὐποιία in this passage all use good conduct, preserving the repeated criterion in the equal/more/less comparison. Doing good and good deeds are legitimate general glosses, but unexplained variation here would conceal that repetition; good conduct is selected because each occurrence evaluates the parties’ comparative practice.

passages.text: That on the day of judgment the actions of those who have known the truth are indeed placed on an equal footing with the good deeds of those who have been deceived, the one who does not lie himself taught us ...., saying to those who neglected to come and listen to him, “The queen of the south will rise with this generation and condemn it, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom; and look, something greater than Solomon is here, and you do not believe.” To those among the people who were unwilling to reorient at his proclamation, he said, “Men of Nineveh will rise with this generation and condemn it, because on hearing they reoriented in response to Jonah’s proclamation; and look, something greater ... is here, and no one believes.” Thus, setting over against each of their acts of impiety those from the nations who had acted, to condemn those in reverence toward God who had not done even as much good as those who had been deceived, he admonished those with understanding not merely to do good things equally with the nations, but to do more. My discourse flowed on, taking its starting point from the need to observe menstrual separation and to immerse oneself after intercourse: not to reject such purity even if those who have been deceived practice it, since those in error who do good serve to condemn those in reverence toward God, although they themselves are not saved. For their honoring of purity is because of error, not because of worship of the true Father and God of all.

source_issues.issue: Exactly 4 printed gap dots remain in the English; no unavailable words are restored.
Exactly 3 printed gap dots remain in the English; no unavailable words are restored.

The selected edition supplies an isolated dot before τῆς. English reads the phrase with this generation across that punctuation. This single dot is distinguished from the section’s four-dot and three-dot printed gaps; it is not called an OCR error and no replacement Greek is proposed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who does not lie himself taught us ....
lexical_decisions.rationale: The selected edition has four gap dots; exactly four remain, without reconstruction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: and look, something greater ... is here
lexical_decisions.rationale: Exactly three gap dots remain. No familiar proper name from another witness is supplied.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they reoriented in response to Jonah’s proclamation
lexical_decisions.rationale: Uses POB reorientation terminology, traditionally repented, preserving the stated occasion of the response.

lexical_decisions.chosen: although they themselves are not saved
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the author’s explicit non-salvation claim about people in error who nonetheless do good.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to observe menstrual separation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The purity context concerns observance of menstrual separation, not merely monitoring a cycle. The menstrual period is a viable temporal rendering; if the noun is taken personally, the menstruating woman is another possible referent. The main text selects the separation observance.

lexical_decisions.chosen: their honoring of purity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The context of people practicing purity supports τιμή as their valuing or honoring the practice, with αὐτῶν related to that honoring. The esteem or value of their purity, attaching αὐτῶν to ἁγνείας, is a material alternative and is not excluded by the main rendering.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ταῖς τῶν πεπλανημένων εὐποιίαις αἱ τῶν ἀλήθειαν ἐγνωκότων ἰσάζονται πράξεις
lexical_decisions.chosen: the actions of those who have known the truth are indeed placed on an equal footing with the good deeds of those who have been deceived
lexical_decisions.rationale: Placed on an equal footing preserves the equality force of ἰσάζονται, central to the subsequent equal-good versus doing-more argument. It does not decide that every particular action necessarily receives an identical valuation; measured against alone would state comparison without the explicit equal-footing force.

passages.text: After saying this, he dismissed the crowds and, as usual, shared salt with his closest friends and rested. By acting and discoursing in this way, on each occasion he brought people securely to God’s law, exposing the supposed ones along with the supposed destiny, and showing that there is no spontaneity, but the world is governed according to providence.

lexical_decisions.chosen: shared salt with his closest friends
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains salt-sharing rather than merely an unspecified meal.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοὺς νομιζομένους μετὰ τῆς νομιζομένης γενέσεως
lexical_decisions.chosen: the supposed ones along with the supposed destiny
lexical_decisions.rationale: The masculine plural has no expressed noun, contextually the supposed gods. γένεσις can be birth or natal destiny; destiny fits the contrast with providence, with natal fate or horoscope as more specific alternatives.

lexical_decisions.chosen: there is no spontaneity
lexical_decisions.rationale: Spontaneous or chance occurrence; chance is a viable more idiomatic alternative.

passages.text: When three months had been completed, he instructed me to fast for days, led me to the nearby springs in the sea, and baptized me as into ever-flowing water. After our brothers had thus feasted at my God-given rebirth, not many days later he turned to the elders before the whole assembly and gave these instructions: “Our Lord and prophet, who sent us, explained to us how the evil one conversed with him for forty days and, having gained no power against him, promised to send apostles from among his own subjects to deceive. Therefore, above all, remember not to ... an apostle or teacher or prophet before he has compared his proclamation with James, who is called the brother of my Lord and has been entrusted in Jerusalem with administering the assembly of the Hebrews, and has come to you with witnesses. This is so that the evil that conversed with the Lord for forty days and gained no power, and afterward fell like lightning from heaven to earth, may not send out a herald against you, as it has now put Simon in our way, proclaiming in the name of your Lord under the pretext of truth, but sowing error. For this reason the one who sent us said, ‘Many will come to me in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves; recognize them by their fruits.’”

source_issues.issue: The three-dot gap leaves the governing action unavailable. Exactly three dots remain, with the negative, temporal relation, proclamation comparison and witnesses preserved rather than reconstruction from another witness.

The supplied edition has a question mark after days. It is recorded as a print/editorial feature without claiming its purpose is known; the surviving phrase is rendered for forty days, not made into an English question. This is distinct from the disclosed three-dot lacuna elsewhere in the section.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he instructed me to fast for days
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied wording gives days but no explicit number; none is restored.

lexical_decisions.chosen: baptized me as into ever-flowing water
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὡς qualifies the into-ever-flowing-water phrase and characterizes the baptism/water in this way. An alternative construal is that the springs provided water treated as continuously flowing. The wording does not assert that the water was only apparently flowing.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μὴ πρότερον . . . ἀντιβάλλοντα αὐτοῦ τὸ κήρυγμα Ἰακώβῳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: not to ... an apostle or teacher or prophet before he has compared his proclamation with James
lexical_decisions.rationale: Exactly three dots remain. The governing action is unavailable and is not supplied as receive or trust. The negative/before relation, comparison of proclamation, and subsequent witnesses remain.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the brother of my Lord
lexical_decisions.rationale: Keeps my here and your Lord later rather than harmonizing pronouns.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πολλοὶ ἐλεύσονται πρὸς μὲ ἐν ἐνδύματι προβάτων
lexical_decisions.chosen: Many will come to me in sheep’s clothing
lexical_decisions.rationale: Keeps the supplied to me, rather than importing a familiar to you from another witness.

passages.text: After saying these things, he sent the advance party to Antioch in Syria, telling them to wait there the following day. After they had gone, Peter drove away diseases, afflictions, and demons from large crowds who had been persuaded, baptized them in the nearby springs in the sea, and broke the Eucharist. He appointed Maron, who had received him and was by now mature, as overseer, designated twelve elders, appointed attendants, and organized arrangements for widows. He addressed the constituted body concerning the common or beneficial interest of the assembly and advised them to obey Maron the overseer. Since three months had now been completed, he took leave of those in Tripolis in Phoenicia and set out on the road to Antioch in Syria, with everyone accompanying us on our way with the appropriate honor.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to wait there the following day
lexical_decisions.rationale: The following is understood with the ordinary elliptical day; no exact date is supplied.

lexical_decisions.chosen: broke the Eucharist
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source combines breaking with Eucharist/thanksgiving, implicitly its bread. The breaking action is retained rather than merely offered thanks.

lexical_decisions.chosen: overseer
lexical_decisions.rationale: Translates the office’s sense; bishop is the conventional title alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ διακόνους δείξας καὶ χηρικὰ συστησάμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: appointed attendants, and organized arrangements for widows
lexical_decisions.rationale: διάκονοι can be attendants or deacons. χηρικά means matters/institutions for widows, not an invented beneficiary list.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπέρ τε τοῦ κοινοῦ ἢ συμφέροντος τῆς ἐκκλησίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: concerning the common or beneficial interest of the assembly
lexical_decisions.rationale: The interest phrase qualifies Peter’s speaking, not a property added to the order. Concerning is a topical rendering of ὑπέρ; for the benefit of gives its purposive alternative. The printed or (ἢ) remains rather than being silently changed to and.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπέρ τε τοῦ κοινοῦ ἢ συμφέροντος τῆς ἐκκλησίας τὴν τάξιν προσομιλήσας
lexical_decisions.chosen: He addressed the constituted body concerning the common or beneficial interest of the assembly
lexical_decisions.rationale: τάξις is understood as the constituted body or order being addressed, in context after institutional appointments. Speaking about organizational arrangements is a material alternative. The chosen interpretation gives the body as recipient while attaching the common/beneficial concern to the address, not inventing a that-served relative clause.

lexical_decisions.chosen: was by now mature
lexical_decisions.rationale: Mature is selected in the context of Maron’s appointment to leadership, allowing spiritual or moral readiness. Now complete or perfected is a material alternative, potentially fully initiated in the surrounding baptismal setting. Initiation is not an explicit or uniquely established technical meaning of τέλειον here, and the English does not add a specified ceremony.

passages.text: After leaving Tripolis in Phoenicia to make our way toward Antioch in Syria, we came to Orthosia and stayed there that same day. Because it was near the city we had left, and almost everyone there had already heard the proclamation, we stayed there one day and departed for Antaradus. Since many people were traveling with us, Peter spoke to Nicetas and Aquila, saying, “Because the large crowd of those traveling with us attracts no small amount of envy toward us as we enter each city, I have thought it necessary to consider how to ensure that neither these people are distressed by being prevented from staying with us nor we, by becoming conspicuous, fall prey to the envy born of malice. For this reason, I want you, Nicetas, and Aquila to go ahead of me separately, as two parties, each on his own, and to enter the Gentile cities.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἐκβάντες οὖν τὴν Τρίπολιν τῆς Φοινίκης ὡς ἐπὶ Ἀντιόχειαν τῆς Συρίας ἐλθεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: After leaving Tripolis in Phoenicia to make our way toward Antioch in Syria
lexical_decisions.rationale: The construction presents Antioch as the intended direction or destination of the journey, not as a place already reached.

lexical_decisions.chosen: had already heard the proclamation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The prefix προ- indicates prior hearing; κήρυγμα denotes the message proclaimed or the act of proclamation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the envy born of malice
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive links the envy with κακία, which may denote malice or wickedness; “the envy of wickedness” is a more formally literal alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: separately, as two parties, each on his own
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording depicts Nicetas and Aquila as divided into two units and isolated from the larger company. Alternatively, κατὰ συστήματα δύο could be understood as “in groups of two,” though the participle agrees with the two named men.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to enter the Gentile cities
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here τὰ ἔθνη designates non-Jewish peoples; “cities of the nations” is a more literal alternative.

passages.text: “I know that, now that you have heard this, you are disheartened about doing it, although you will be separated from me for an interval of not even two full days. I therefore want you to know that we who persuaded you love you who were persuaded many times more than you love us who persuaded you. Since we love one another, then, let us take thought for safety, as far as lies with us, by not irrationally doing whatever we want. Besides, you will not be away from me on any day when I am giving a discourse. For I have decided—as you yourselves know—to stay for days and discourse in the more prominent cities of the provinces. For now, go ahead to Laodicea, which is nearer to us, and after two or three days—as far as it depends on my own choice—I will catch up with you. Wait for me at the gates, you alone, because of the commotion, so that by entering together without noise we may be with you. From there, likewise, after we have stayed for days, others in your place should go ahead in daily rotation to the places beyond, preparing the lodgings.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: you are disheartened
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb expresses loss of heart or discouragement rather than simple sadness.

lexical_decisions.chosen: love ... many times more
lexical_decisions.rationale: πολλαπλάσιον gives a comparative idea of manifold or many-times-greater love.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ μὴ ἀλόγως ποιεῖν ἃ θέλομεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: by not irrationally doing whatever we want
lexical_decisions.rationale: The articular infinitive is instrumental, explaining how they are to attend to their safety.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you will not be away from me on any day when I am giving a discourse
lexical_decisions.rationale: The promise is that their brief advance journey will not cause them to miss a day on which Peter teaches.

lexical_decisions.chosen: because of the commotion
lexical_decisions.rationale: θρῦλος can denote noise, public stir, or widespread talk; the concern here is the attention created at the gates.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in daily rotation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase indicates service or assignments apportioned by the day; “by daily turns” is an alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: preparing the lodgings
lexical_decisions.rationale: ξενία can denote hospitality or guest accommodation; the practical task here is arranging places to stay.

passages.text: When Peter had said this, they were compelled to consent, saying, “It does not greatly distress us, lord, to do this, because we are commanded by you. First, being worthy, you were chosen by God’s providence to understand everything well and to give sound counsel. Besides, the necessity of going ahead separates us from you for at most two days. Even these are a long time when it comes to not seeing you, Peter our lord. Yet we reflect that those sent much farther ahead will be more distressed, since they have been commanded to wait longer for you in each city, grieving because they are deprived for a longer time of seeing your much-longed-for face. Although we are no less disheartened than they, we do not object to doing as you command, because it is beneficial.” After saying this together, they went ahead, having instructions to speak at the first inn to the crowd traveling with them, so that, after becoming dispersed from one another, they might enter the cities.

source_issues.issue: The image-checked selected edition prints ὁμῶς, not the normally adversative ὅμως. The translation follows the printed accentuation with “together.” Context could support “nevertheless” if the accentuation is an editorial or orthographic feature, but the supplied Greek has not been altered.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they were compelled to consent
lexical_decisions.rationale: συντίθεμαι here means agreeing to a proposal; the passive of ἀναγκάζω conveys their reluctant necessity.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for at most two days
lexical_decisions.rationale: In this context ἐπὶ τὸ πολύ is taken as marking an upper limit. “As a rule, for two days” is also grammatically possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πάντα καλῶς νοεῖν τε καὶ συμβουλεύειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: to understand everything well and to give sound counsel
lexical_decisions.rationale: πάντα is taken with the coordinated infinitives, while συμβουλεύειν denotes advising rather than merely deliberating privately.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those sent much farther ahead
lexical_decisions.rationale: προπέμπω here refers to dispatching people in advance, and πολὺ μακράν emphasizes the greater distance.

lexical_decisions.chosen: your much-longed-for face
lexical_decisions.rationale: περιπόθητος expresses intense longing or dearness, and πρόσωπον retains the concrete image of the face.

lexical_decisions.chosen: After saying this together, they went ahead
lexical_decisions.rationale: The selected edition prints ὁμῶς, whose accentuation supports “alike” or “together,” so the adverb is taken with the plural speakers. If the printed accentuation is an orthographic or editorial feature representing ὅμως, the contextual alternative is “Nevertheless, after saying this, they went ahead.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: after becoming dispersed from one another
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverb depicts the travelers becoming scattered rather than entering as an organized mass.

passages.text: So, after they had gone, I, Clement, was exceedingly glad that he had told me to remain with him. I answered, “I thank God that you did not send me away as you did my companions, since I would have died in anguish.” But he said, “What, then? If there should also be some need for you to be sent somewhere for the sake of instruction, will you die just because, for your benefit, you are separated from me for a short time? Would you not instead, after talking it over with yourself, cheerfully undertake to bear what has been commanded of you because necessity required it? Or do you not know that friends are always together in their memories, even if they are separated in body, while some who are together in body are, because of forgetfulness, far away in soul from their friends?”

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a raised point between πορευθέντων and οὖν, interrupting the expected genitive-absolute word sequence. The translation treats the surviving words as the continuous construction “So, after they had gone,” without changing any Greek letters.

lexical_decisions.chosen: since I would have died in anguish
lexical_decisions.rationale: In this context διαφωνέω carries the sense of failing, perishing, or dying, rather than making an outcry. Peter’s immediately following question, διὰ τοῦτο τεθνήξει, confirms the reference to death. The pluperfect with ἄν expresses the unreal result; “I would have perished in pain” is a close alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for the sake of instruction
lexical_decisions.rationale: μαθήματα can concern lessons, learning, or teaching; the Greek does not specify whether Clement would primarily receive or provide the instruction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for your benefit
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverb indicates that the temporary separation serves an advantageous or expedient purpose.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after talking it over with yourself
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase literally describes conversing with oneself and contextually implies inward reasoning or self-exhortation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: σύνεισιν αἰεὶ οἱ φίλοι ταῖς μνήμαις
lexical_decisions.chosen: friends are always together in their memories
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative presents memories as the sphere or means by which absent friends remain together.

lexical_decisions.chosen: are ... far away in soul from their friends
lexical_decisions.rationale: The accusative marks respect—“as to their souls”—while ἀποδημέω preserves the image of being away from home.

passages.text: And I answered, “Do not suppose, then, my lord, that my distress would have been irrational; rather, it would have rested on entirely sound reasoning. For since I have you, my lord, in place of everyone—father, mother, brothers, and relatives—you who, for God’s sake, became for me the cause of the truth that saves, I receive the greatest consolation by having you in place of everyone. Moreover, fearing the desire natural to my youthful prime, I was anxious whether, if separated from you, young man that I am, I would be weaker than desire. On this point I now have such resistance that it would be impossible for me to leave you even under some wrath from God. But since it is far better and safer for me to be with you, the one whom my mind has rightly determined beforehand to revere, I therefore pray to be with you always. Furthermore, I remember you saying in Caesarea, ‘If anyone wishes to accompany me, let him accompany me reverently.’ By ‘reverently,’ you said you meant causing no one grief in matters relating to God—for example, by leaving behind parents, a like-minded wife, or any companions devoted to reverence for God. Thus I am in every respect a suitable traveling companion for you. Even if you grant me the greatest favors, you still permit me to perform the duties of servants.”

source_issues.source_quote: ἠγωνίων μήπως ἀπολειφθείς σου, ἄνθρωπος ὢν νεώτερος, ὅπερ νῦν οὕτως ἐνστάσεως ἔχω, κἂν κατὰ τινὰ χόλον θεοῦ ἀποστῆναί σου ἀδύνατον εἰ ἥττων ἐπιθυμίας ἔσομαι
source_issues.issue: The verified wording is syntactically compressed, especially in the attachments of ὅπερ, ἐνστάσεως, κἄν, ἀδύνατον, and the final εἰ-clause. The translation takes ὅπερ resumptively as “on this point,” οὕτως ἐνστάσεως ἔχω as expressing strong resistance, ἀποστῆναί σου as the complement of ἀδύνατον, and εἰ ἥττων ἐπιθυμίας ἔσομαι as resuming ἠγωνίων μήπως. This avoids using the final clause twice. Alternatively, ὅπερ may refer specifically to the natural desire or to the entire feared circumstance, while οὕτως ... κἄν may be taken as a result construction under which being weaker than desire is declared impossible. That alternative leaves the immediately preceding ἀποστῆναί σου less naturally attached. No alteration of the selected Greek is proposed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: my distress would have been irrational
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally, Clement speaks of “suffering the things of sorrow”; the rendering expresses the claim in natural English without reducing λύπη to physical pain.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for God’s sake
lexical_decisions.rationale: διά with the accusative is causal here. “Because of God” is more literal; “through God” would normally require the genitive.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the truth that saves
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle directly characterizes the truth as saving and should not be reduced to merely helpful or correct teaching.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς ἀκμῆς τὴν ἐκ φύσεως ἐπιθυμίαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the desire natural to my youthful prime
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀκμή denotes one’s prime or youthful vigor, while ἐκ φύσεως presents the desire as natural to that stage of life.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἠγωνίων μήπως ἀπολειφθείς σου, ἄνθρωπος ὢν νεώτερος
lexical_decisions.chosen: I was anxious whether, if separated from you, young man that I am
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participles describe the circumstance feared by Clement. The final εἰ-clause is taken as resuming and completing this expression of anxiety.

lexical_decisions.chosen: it would be impossible for me to leave you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The infinitive immediately precedes ἀδύνατον and is taken as its complement. This keeps Clement’s inability to leave Peter distinct from his earlier fear about what might happen if Peter left him behind.

lexical_decisions.chosen: whether ... I would be weaker than desire
lexical_decisions.rationale: The clause is taken once, as completing ἠγωνίων μήπως, rather than both completing the earlier anxiety and supplying a second assertion that such weakness is impossible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ νοῦς μου αἰδεῖσθαι εὐλόγως προείληφεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: whom my mind has rightly determined beforehand to revere
lexical_decisions.rationale: προλαμβάνω here indicates a prior resolve or settled choice, and αἰδεῖσθαι conveys reverence or respectful regard.

lexical_decisions.chosen: causing no one grief in matters relating to God
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατὰ θεόν can mean “in relation to God,” “according to God,” or “in a godly matter.” The examples concern obligations to people connected with devotion to God.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a like-minded wife
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὁμόφρων describes one who shares the same outlook or purpose, here likely including religious commitment.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰς δούλων μοι ὑπηρεσίας συγχωρεῖς ποιεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: you ... permit me to perform the duties of servants
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase denotes subordinate personal service. “Slaves’ services” would make the bonded-status nuance more explicit, while “servants” follows the supplied wording policy.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Even if you grant me the greatest favors
lexical_decisions.rationale: εἰ καί is read concessively. Alternatively, the permission to serve may itself be presented as one of the greatest favors, though that relationship is not syntactically explicit.

passages.text:
When Peter heard this, he said jokingly, “What then do you think, Clement? Do you suppose that by sheer necessity you are to be assigned a place among my servants? For who will look after the many fine linen garments, together with the rings and footwear that accompany me? And who will prepare the pleasant and costly foods, which, being varied, require many skilled cooks—and all those things that, procured through every kind of greed, are prepared for the desire of effeminate people as though for a huge wild beast? But if a resolve has crept into you in this way, perhaps it is because you did not understand and did not know my way of life: I subsist on bread alone and olives, and only rarely on vegetables. The garment I have—a worn cloak—is this very one I am wearing, and I have no need of another or of anything else; indeed, in these things I have more than enough. For my mind, seeing all the eternal good things there, does not look around at any of the things here.

“Nevertheless, I welcome your good resolve, and with admiration I praise how readily you, a man accustomed to luxurious habits, have changed your way of life to one of mere necessities. For from childhood we—I and Andrew, who is my brother both by blood and according to God—were not only brought up as orphans but were also accustomed by poverty and hardship to a life of labor. We therefore now bear the hardships of the roads with ease. Consequently, if you listened to me, you would permit me, a working man, to perform a servant’s duties for you.”

source_issues.source_quote: πλὴν εἰ τοιαύτῃ σε προαίρεσις ὑπεισῆλθεν
source_issues.issue: The printed τοιαύτῃ is dative although προαίρεσις is nominative. The main translation provisionally understands τοιαύτῃ adverbially, “in this way.” A conjectural nominative τοιαύτη would instead give the more regular construction “if such a resolve has crept into you.” The image-checked printed reading has not been altered.
source_issues.proposed_reading: πλὴν εἰ τοιαύτη σε προαίρεσις ὑπεισῆλθεν

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μὴ ὑπ’ αὐτῆς ἀνάγκης σε εἰς δούλων μοι ταγῆναι τόπον;
lexical_decisions.chosen: Do you suppose that by sheer necessity you are to be assigned a place among my servants?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The μή-question is an incredulous, joking question. “Servants” follows the supplied wording policy for δοῦλος, while the underlying term can denote enslaved household members.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the many fine linen garments
lexical_decisions.rationale: σινδόνες can denote fine linen cloths or garments. The surrounding references to personal rings and footwear favor garments, though “fine linen cloths” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μετὰ τῶν ἐπομένων μοι δακτυλίων καὶ ὑποδήσεων
lexical_decisions.chosen: together with the rings and footwear that accompany me
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative μοι identifies Peter as the person whom the rings and footwear accompany or with whom they are associated; it does not make them accessories belonging to the linen garments.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅσα ἐκτεθηλυμμένων ἀνθρώπων ὡς θηρίῳ μεγάλῳ τῇ ἐπιθυμίᾳ ἐκ πάσης πλεονεξίας πορισθέντα ἑτοιμάζεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: all those things that, procured through every kind of greed, are prepared for the desire of effeminate people as though for a huge wild beast
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering retains the author’s disparaging description, the comparison of desire to a large wild beast, and the charge that these things are acquired through greed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἱμάτιόν μοι καὶ τριβώνιον ὑπάρχει τοῦτ’ αὐτὸ ὃ περιβέβλημαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: The garment I have—a worn cloak—is this very one I am wearing
lexical_decisions.rationale: τριβώνιον denotes a worn or rough cloak. The nouns are read appositionally, emphasizing that Peter possesses only the garment currently around him; alternatively, the wording could be represented more formally as “my garment and cloak are this very thing I am wearing.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: indeed, in these things I have more than enough
lexical_decisions.rationale: περισσεύομαι conveys abundance or surplus rather than mere adequacy.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἀνδρέας ὁ σύναιμος καὶ κατὰ θεὸν ἀδελφὸς ὢν ἐμός
lexical_decisions.chosen: Andrew, who is my brother both by blood and according to God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The literal expression “according to God” is retained rather than reduced to the interpretive label “spiritual brother.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: we bear the hardships of the roads
lexical_decisions.rationale: σκύλσεις can denote vexations, harassment, or hardships. “Hardships” suits the rigors of travel without restricting the expression to one kind of difficulty.

passages.text:
When I heard this, I began trembling and became tearful at such a statement from a man to whom all the people of the present generation are inferior in the matter of knowledge and piety. When he saw me in tears, he asked the reason for my tears. I said, “What wrong have I committed that you should say such a thing to me?”

Peter answered, “If it was wrong of me to speak of serving you, you were the first to do wrong, since you thought it proper to do this for me.”

I said, “It is not the same. It is entirely fitting for me to do this, but for you, the herald of God who saves our souls, it is a grievous thing to do this for me.”

Peter answered, “I would agree with you, except that our Lord, who came for the salvation of the whole world and who alone was noble above everyone, endured servitude so that he might persuade us not to be ashamed to perform servants’ services for our brothers, even if we happen to be exceedingly noble.”

I said, “If I think I can defeat you in argument, I am foolish. Nevertheless, I give thanks to God’s providence that I was deemed worthy to have you in the place of parents.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἷον λόγον εἶπεν ἀνήρ, οὗ πάντες οἱ τῆς νῦν γενεᾶς ἄνθρωποι τῷ τῆς γνώσεως καὶ εὐσεβείας λόγῳ ἥττους τυγχάνουσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: at such a statement from a man to whom all the people of the present generation are inferior in the matter of knowledge and piety
lexical_decisions.rationale: οἷον gives the statement an emphatic quality. The second λόγῳ is taken as indicating the respect or matter in which the present generation is inferior rather than as naming a separate discourse.

lexical_decisions.chosen: serving you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The infinitive denotes performing a subordinate or servile role for Clement. “Serving” is natural here, while the stronger status nuance of the cognate δουλεία is represented by “servitude” later in the passage.

lexical_decisions.chosen: since you thought it proper to do this for me
lexical_decisions.rationale: The infinitive is understood with Clement as its subject: he had considered it fitting to perform such service for Peter. A more formal rendering would be “having deemed it worthy to do this for me.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Συνεθέμην ἂν σοι, ἐπεὶ ὁ κύριος ἡμῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: I would agree with you, except that our Lord
lexical_decisions.rationale: The unreal “I would agree” is followed by the consideration that prevents agreement. Although ἐπεί commonly means “since,” its contextual force here can be expressed as “except that” or “were it not that.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: who alone was noble above everyone
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὐγενής can mean noble or well-born. The wording preserves the comparison with all others without specifying whether the author’s emphasis is social birth, inherent nobility, or both.

lexical_decisions.chosen: endured servitude
lexical_decisions.rationale: δουλεία denotes the condition or service of a servant or slave. “Servitude” preserves the stronger status nuance without specifying an episode not named by the source.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in the place of parents
lexical_decisions.rationale: The plural γονέων is retained: Clement regards Peter as occupying the place held collectively by his parents.

passages.text:
Peter asked, “Do you truly have no one related to you by birth?”

I answered, “There are indeed many prominent men of Caesar’s family. That is why Caesar himself, since my father had also been brought up with him, arranged for a female relative to be joined in marriage to my father. From her we were born, three sons: two before me, who were twins and were extremely like each other, as my father himself used to tell me. For I do not remember either them or the woman who bore me very well, but, as though through dreams, I call up a dim image of them.

“My mother, then, was called Mattidia, and my father Faustus. As for my brothers themselves, one was called Faustinus and the other Faustinianus. After I was born to them as their third child, my mother saw a dream—as my father used to recount—that unless she immediately took her twin sons and left the city of the Romans to live abroad for ten years, she was destined to die together with them by an utterly ruinous fate.”

source_issues.source_quote: ἐγὼ γὰρ οὔτε αὐτοὺς. οὔτε τὴν τεκοῦσαν πάνυ ἐπίσταμαι
source_issues.issue: The printed period interrupts the correlative construction οὔτε … οὔτε. The translation treats the clauses as grammatically continuous while preserving all the printed words. This appears to be an editorial punctuation oddity rather than missing content.
source_issues.proposed_reading: ἐγὼ γὰρ οὔτε αὐτοὺς οὔτε τὴν τεκοῦσαν πάνυ ἐπίσταμαι

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Οὐδεὶς δέ σου ἀληθῶς πρὸς γένος ὑπάρχει;
lexical_decisions.chosen: Do you truly have no one related to you by birth?
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρὸς γένος asks about kinship or family connection. “By birth” distinguishes this relationship from Peter’s preceding reference to brotherhood “according to God.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Εἰσὶν μὲν πολλοὶ καὶ μεγάλοι ἄνδρες, Καίσαρος πρὸς γένους ὄντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: There are indeed many prominent men of Caesar’s family
lexical_decisions.rationale: μεγάλοι describes the men as great or prominent, while Καίσαρος πρὸς γένους indicates family or kinship connection with Caesar.

lexical_decisions.chosen: since my father had also been brought up with him
lexical_decisions.rationale: σύντροφος can denote a childhood companion, foster-brother, or someone reared together with another. The rendering preserves shared upbringing without asserting formal fosterage.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐγὼ γὰρ οὔτε αὐτοὺς. οὔτε τὴν τεκοῦσαν πάνυ ἐπίσταμαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: For I do not remember either them or the woman who bore me very well
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπίσταμαι ordinarily means “know,” but the following reference to a dim mental image makes recollection the contextual sense. With the negation, πάνυ is represented as “very well.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὥσπερ δι᾿ ὀνείρων ἀμαυρὸν αὐτῶν τὸ εἶδος ἀναφέρω
lexical_decisions.chosen: as though through dreams, I call up a dim image of them
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀναφέρω here concerns bringing an image back to mind. The translation retains both the dreamlike comparison and the indistinctness of the remembered appearance.

lexical_decisions.chosen: unless she immediately took
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐξαυτῆς means “immediately” or “at once,” not “by herself.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πανολεθρίῳ μόρῳ ἅμα αὐτοῖς ἀποθανεῖν ἔχει
lexical_decisions.chosen: she was destined to die together with them by an utterly ruinous fate
lexical_decisions.rationale: πανολέθριος conveys complete ruin or destruction, μόρος can mean doom, fate, or death, and ἀποθανεῖν ἔχει expresses an impending or destined death. “By an utterly ruinous fate” preserves the source’s separate reference to doom without repeating “death” in English.

passages.text:
Our father, then, being devoted to his children, adequately supplied them for the journey with male and female servants, put them aboard a ship, and sent them away to Athens so that the boys would be educated together. But he kept only me, his son, with him as consolation. For this I give abundant thanks: that the dream had not commanded me too to leave the city of the Romans with my mother.

“When a year had passed, my father sent money to Athens for his own people and at the same time sent to learn how they were doing. But those who went did not return. In the third year my father, becoming despondent, likewise sent others with provisions. They came in the fourth year and reported that they had seen neither my mother nor my brothers, that the missing family had not even been in Athens itself, and that they had not found so much as a trace of anyone else who had gone away with them.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: being devoted to his children
lexical_decisions.rationale: φιλότεκνος describes strong affection for one’s children. “Devoted” suits both the father’s preparations and his subsequent search.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with male and female servants
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both the masculine and feminine forms are represented. In this household context they may denote enslaved attendants; “servants” follows the supplied wording policy while the possible bonded status remains disclosed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς τὰς Ἀθήνας ἅμα παιδευθησομένους ἐξέπεμψεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: sent them away to Athens so that the boys would be educated together
lexical_decisions.rationale: The masculine plural παιδευθησομένους most naturally refers to the twin sons rather than to their mother. ἅμα is taken as “together,” though “at the same time” is lexically possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐμὲ δὲ μόνον υἱὸν εἰς παραμυθίαν ἔσχεν μεθ᾿ ἑαυτοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: he kept only me, his son, with him as consolation
lexical_decisions.rationale: εἰς παραμυθίαν identifies Clement as a source of comfort or consolation after the others’ departure.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: χρήματα τοῖς αὐτοῦ ἅμα τε καὶ μαθεῖν τὸ πῶς διάγουσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: sent money to Athens for his own people and at the same time sent to learn how they were doing
lexical_decisions.rationale: τοῖς αὐτοῦ means “for his own people,” contextually the absent family. The agents sent to make inquiries are left implicit in this clause and become explicit in οἱ δὲ ἀπελθόντες, “those who went.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: that the missing family had not even been in Athens itself
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here the unexpressed subject is taken as Clement’s mother and brothers, because the searchers were sent to Athens and their report concerns the missing family. Alternatively, the continuing subject may be the searchers, reporting that they had not stayed or resided in Athens itself. The Greek does not explicitly mark a change of subject.

lexical_decisions.chosen: that they had not found so much as a trace
lexical_decisions.rationale: κἄν strengthens the negation: the searchers found not even a trace.

passages.text:
When my father heard these things, he became bewildered by his great grief. Not knowing where he should set out to search for them, he took me with him, went down to Portus, and repeatedly questioned many people about where each one had seen or heard of a shipwreck that had occurred four years earlier. One person named one place, another a different place. He in turn asked whether they had seen the body of a woman with young children washed ashore. . When those people said that they had seen many corpses in many places, my father groaned on hearing it. Yet, because his inward affections were in turmoil, he kept making irrational inquiries, since he was attempting to search so vast an expanse of sea. Still, he could be excused, because through his affection for those being sought he was being fed on empty hopes.

“And so, eventually, he placed me under guardians and left me in Rome when I was twelve years old. Then he himself went down to Portus in tears, boarded a ship, put out to sea, and departed on the search. From that time until this very day I have neither received any letters from him nor learned with certainty whether he is alive or dead. Rather, I suspect that he too has died somewhere, either overcome by grief or overtaken by shipwreck. The evidence for this is that it is now the twentieth year since then, and since that time I have heard no reliable news at all about him.”

source_issues.issue: The image-checked edition prints two dots separated by a space after ἐκβεβρασμένον. Their function remains uncertain: they may mark unavailable wording or may be an editorial punctuation oddity. The English retains exactly “. .” at this point and supplies no restoration. If the dots mark a lacuna, its content is unavailable.

The edition prints the unassimilated spelling ἐνβάς. It is intelligible as the participle ordinarily normalized as ἐμβάς, “having boarded.” The printed form is verified and no missing wording is involved.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to Portus
lexical_decisions.rationale: Πόρτος is treated as the proper name of Rome’s harbor rather than translated generically as “the port.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: a shipwreck that had occurred four years earlier
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase can designate a wreck from four years before the inquiry. A broader contextual alternative is “a shipwreck during the preceding four years.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: the body of a woman with young children washed ashore
lexical_decisions.rationale: βρέφη can denote infants or very young children. “Young children” avoids fixing their precise age, while ἐκβεβρασμένον depicts the woman’s body as cast or washed ashore.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν οὖν πολλὰ λεγόντων ἑωρακέναι πτώματα κατὰ πολλοὺς τόπους
lexical_decisions.chosen: When those people said that they had seen many corpses in many places
lexical_decisions.rationale: The neuter accusative plural πολλὰ is taken with the neuter accusative plural πτώματα, supported by their agreement and the parallel πολλοὺς τόπους. Alternatively, πολλὰ may attach adverbially to λεγόντων: “when those who spoke at length said that they had seen corpses in many places.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: because his inward affections were in turmoil
lexical_decisions.rationale: σπλάγχνα literally denotes inward organs and figuratively deep affections. “Inward affections” retains more of the source image than a purely abstract reference to emotion.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to search so vast an expanse of sea
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression emphasizes the immense extent of sea that he was irrationally attempting to investigate.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῇ πρὸς τοὺς ζητουμένους στοργῇ ἐλπίσιν ἐβουκολεῖτο κεναῖς
lexical_decisions.chosen: through his affection for those being sought he was being fed on empty hopes
lexical_decisions.rationale: βουκολέω literally evokes feeding or tending a herd and can figuratively mean sustaining or beguiling someone with expectations. The main rendering preserves the feeding image; “he was beguiled by empty hopes” is a less image-retentive alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he placed me under guardians
lexical_decisions.rationale: φροντισταί are people charged with oversight or care. “Guardians” suits the care of a twelve-year-old, though “caretakers” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἤδη λοιπὸν ἔκτοτε εἰκοστὸν ἔτος ἐστίν
lexical_decisions.chosen: it is now the twentieth year since then
lexical_decisions.rationale: The ordinal expression is retained rather than converted into an exact modern elapsed-year count.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀφ’ ἧς οὐδεμίαν τινὰ περὶ αὐτοῦ ἀλήθειαν ἤκουσα
lexical_decisions.chosen: since that time I have heard no reliable news at all about him
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀφ’ ἧς is understood elliptically as “since that time” or “since that day,” extending the absence of information from the father’s departure to the present. ἀλήθεια here denotes true or dependable information rather than abstract truth.

passages.text: But Peter, on hearing this, wept out of sympathy and immediately said to his genuine companions, “If anyone had suffered these things while living in reverence for God—the kinds of things this man’s father has suffered—he would immediately have attached the cause to the teaching of reverence for God, naming the evil one as responsible. So too it happens that the wretched nations suffer, and we who revere God are unaware of it. I have rightly called them wretched, because they wander here and do not obtain the hope there. For those who suffer distressing things while living in reverence for God suffer them as payment exacted for transgressions.”

source_issues.issue: The verified print places a full stop inside the prepositional phrase. The surviving words support reading ἐν with θεοσεβείᾳ continuously; treating the stop as intrusive editorial or printing punctuation is provisional but requires no missing text.

The verified printed form has rough breathing. It is interpreted as the contracted present of ἀλάομαι, “wander,” without altering the supplied spelling; the breathing is treated as a disclosed orthographic feature, not evidence for a capture-related verb.

lexical_decisions.chosen: wept out of sympathy
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves συμπάθεια as compassionate fellow-feeling rather than merely sadness.

lexical_decisions.chosen: his genuine companions
lexical_decisions.rationale: γνήσιοι characterizes those accompanying Peter as genuine or faithful; “genuine” retains the explicit adjective.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ τῆς θεοσεβείας λόγῳ τὴν αἰτίαν προσῆπτεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: attached the cause to the teaching of reverence for God
lexical_decisions.rationale: λόγος may mean teaching, account, or rationale; “teaching” fits the religious context, while the construction depicts attaching the cause to it.

lexical_decisions.chosen: naming the evil one as responsible
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιγράφω can mean inscribe, designate, or attribute; here it identifies the evil one as responsible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the wretched nations
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔθνη may mean nations, peoples, or, in a religious contrast, Gentiles. “Nations” preserves the broader wording without excluding the contextual sense “Gentiles.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: they wander here
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἁλῶνται is understood as the contracted present form of ἀλάομαι, “wander.” Contextually this may imply straying or wandering in error, but it does not denote being caught or convicted.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as payment exacted for transgressions
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔκπραξις denotes exaction or collection of what is due, here presenting suffering as payment associated with transgressions.

passages.text: After Peter had said this, one of our company dared to speak for everyone and urged him to sail earlier the next morning to Aradus, the island opposite, which I think was not even a full thirty stadia away, to view the two vinewood columns there, which were of enormous thickness. Peter, being accommodating, agreed and said, “When you disembark from the ship, do not go in all at once as a large group to see the things you desire. I do not want the citizens turning toward us.” So we sailed and, in a fraction of an hour, put in at the island. After getting out of the boat, we went in to where the vinewood columns stood; and at the same time, together with them, one person viewed one of Phidias’s works and another a different one.

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints ἀμπελίων. If the intended construction was an adjective directly modifying στύλων, the expected genitive plural of ἀμπέλινος would be ἀμπελίνων. The printed form might instead be construed as a genitive plural referring to vines or vineyards, but the later οἱ ἀμπέλινοι στύλοι supports the contextual sense “vinewood columns.” The selected reading remains unchanged, and the uncertainty does not prevent a defensible translation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἷς τις τῶν ἐν ἡμῖν τολμήσας ἀντὶ πάντων
lexical_decisions.chosen: one of our company dared to speak for everyone
lexical_decisions.rationale: The act supplied by τολμήσας is implicit; speaking is supported by the following request, while ἀντὶ πάντων means on behalf of all.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to view
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἱστορία here denotes inspection or sightseeing, not the writing of history.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the two vinewood columns there
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied print reads ἀμπελίων, not the genitive plural ἀμπελίνων expected if ἀμπέλινος directly modified στύλων. The later wording οἱ ἀμπέλινοι στύλοι identifies the same columns as vinewood or vine-related and therefore supports the contextual rendering “vinewood columns.” A possible normalization is disclosed in source_issues but is not substituted for the selected reading.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ γὰρ βούλομαι στρέμματα γίνεσθαι εἰς ἡμᾶς τῶν πολιτῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: I do not want the citizens turning toward us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source-transparent wording treats στρέμματα as turnings directed toward the visitors. In context this may mean attracting the citizens’ attention or causing them to turn and look; “the citizens turning against us,” implying hostility or disturbance, is also possible but is not required by the noun itself.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in a fraction of an hour
lexical_decisions.rationale: ῥοπή can denote a brief turn or moment; the phrase indicates a short portion of an hour, with “in a moment” also possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁμῶς ἅμα αὐτοῖς ἄλλος ἄλλο τι τῶν Φειδίου ἔργων ἐθεώρει
lexical_decisions.chosen: at the same time, together with them, one person viewed one of Phidias’s works and another a different one
lexical_decisions.rationale: The distributive ἄλλος ἄλλο τι is explicit. The referent of αὐτοῖς may be the columns or other members of the party, so the English pronoun preserves that ambiguity.

passages.text: Peter alone did not consider it necessary to go and view the sights there. But after watching closely for some time a woman who was sitting outside, in front of the doors, and begging for food, he said, “Woman, what limb are you missing, that you have submitted yourself to so great an indignity—I mean begging—instead of working with the hands God has given you to obtain your daily food?” She groaned and replied, “If only I had hands capable of working! But now they retain only the form of hands, since they are dead, tortured by my own bites.” Peter asked, “What is the cause of your having suffered this terrible thing?” She answered, “Weakness of soul, and nothing more. For if I had possessed a courageous resolve, a cliff was there, and so was the deep; from there I could have thrown myself and gained relief from the evils that cause me pain.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ τὴν τῶν ἐκεῖ ἱστορίαν γενέσθαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: to go and view the sights there
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἱστορία again denotes personal observation or sightseeing, and γενέσθαι with ἐπί conveys going for that purpose.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after watching closely for some time
lexical_decisions.rationale: πυκνά can indicate repeated or sustained attention, while κατανοέω denotes attentive observation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you have submitted yourself to so great an indignity
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὕβρις here denotes degrading treatment or humiliation rather than merely pride; ἀναδέχομαι presents her as taking it upon herself.

lexical_decisions.chosen: hands capable of working
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπουργεῖν literally means to serve or render assistance; in context it means functioning for useful work.

lexical_decisions.chosen: tortured by my own bites
lexical_decisions.rationale: The possessive ἐμῶν identifies the bites as hers, preserving the image of self-inflicted biting.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Weakness of soul
lexical_decisions.rationale: ψυχή may denote soul, life, or inner self; “soul” retains the author’s psychological and moral terminology.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a cliff was there, and so was the deep
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated imperfect ἦν presents the available means of death. A counterfactual English alternative would be “there would have been a cliff and the deep.”

passages.text: Peter said, “What then do you think, woman? That those who kill themselves are invariably released from punishment? Or are the souls of those who die in this way not punished in Hades with a worse punishment for their suicide?” She said, “If only I were convinced that souls really are found alive in Hades! Then I would gladly die, despising the punishment, so that I might see my dearly missed ones, even for a single hour.” Peter said, “I wanted to learn what it is that grieves you, woman. For if you tell me, in return for this favor I will fully assure you that souls live in Hades, and instead of a cliff or the deep I will give you a drug, so that, without torment, you may be able to exchange your way of life for living.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πάντως οἱ ἀναιροῦντες ἑαυτοὺς κολάσεως ἀπαλλάσσονται
lexical_decisions.chosen: those who kill themselves are invariably released from punishment
lexical_decisions.rationale: πάντως supplies the categorical force, while ἀναιροῦντες ἑαυτούς explicitly refers to taking one’s own life.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Or are ... not punished ... with a worse punishment
lexical_decisions.rationale: The negative μή is retained in the rhetorical alternative rather than being smoothed away, although the resulting English question is marked.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ἠγάπων τῆς κολάσεως καταφρονήσασα θανεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Then I would gladly die, despising the punishment
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀγαπάω with an infinitive can express being pleased or willing to do something; “gladly” conveys that idiomatic force.

lexical_decisions.chosen: my dearly missed ones
lexical_decisions.rationale: περιπόθητος describes people intensely longed for; “dearly missed” leaves their precise relationship unstated.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I will fully assure you
lexical_decisions.rationale: πληροφορέω here means to bring someone to full assurance or conviction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a drug
lexical_decisions.rationale: φάρμακον can mean a medicine, remedy, or poison. “Drug” preserves the ambiguity essential to the woman’s subsequent misunderstanding.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅπως ἀβασανίστως τοῦ ζῆν τὸν βίον μεταλλάξαι δυνηθῇς
lexical_decisions.chosen: so that, without torment, you may be able to exchange your way of life for living
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering takes τὸν βίον as the object of μεταλλάξαι and τοῦ ζῆν as the genitive counterpart in an exchange: her present way or course of life is exchanged for living. This fits Peter’s offer of a remedy while preserving the wording that the next section calls ambiguous. Alternatively, τὸν βίον may function within ζῆν τὸν βίον, “to live one’s life,” while τοῦ ζῆν marks what she departs from, yielding “depart from living your life.” Another possible attachment takes τοῦ ζῆν attributively or epexegetically with τὸν βίον, yielding “exchange the life you are living.” The construction therefore permits both continued-life and death-oriented understandings; the main rendering is contextual, not asserted as unique.

passages.text: The woman, not understanding what had been said ambiguously, was delighted by the promise and began to speak as follows: “As for my lineage and homeland, I do not think anyone could ever persuade me to disclose them. But what difference does it make to you whether you learn that or only the reason why, in my anguish, I deadened my own hands by biting them? Nevertheless, I will relate my own affairs as far as it is possible for you to hear them. I was of very noble birth, and at the command of a certain ruler I became the wife of a man related to him by blood. After having twin children, I had another son. But my husband’s brother went mad and fell no less deeply in love with me, unfortunate as I was and deeply devoted to chastity. Since I wanted neither to consent to my would-be lover nor to disclose to my husband his brother’s desire for me, I formed a plan so that I would neither defile myself by committing adultery, nor violate my husband’s bed, nor make brother an enemy to brother, nor subject the entire family, a prominent one, to everyone’s reproach. As I said, I resolved to leave the city with my twin children for a time, until the vile passion of the man who was flattering me in order to dishonor me should also cease. I did, however, leave my other son with his father as a consolation.”

source_issues.issue: The verified print places a raised dot between the negative μή and the participle it governs. Reading the words continuously yields a defensible construction; treating the dot as intrusive editorial or printing punctuation is provisional and does not imply missing text.

lexical_decisions.chosen: what had been said ambiguously
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀμφιβόλως explicitly identifies Peter’s preceding statement as having a double or uncertain sense.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Γένος μὲν καὶ πατρίδα εἰπεῖν οὐκ οἶμαι πεῖσαί ποτε δυνηθῆναί τινα
lexical_decisions.chosen: As for my lineage and homeland, I do not think anyone could ever persuade me to disclose them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering takes τινα as the subject of δυνηθῆναι and supplies the woman as the understood object of πεῖσαι, favoring reluctance to disclose in light of her following question. Alternatively, τινα may be the object of πεῖσαι and the woman the understood subject of δυνηθῆναι: “As for stating my lineage and homeland, I do not think I could ever convince anyone.” That reading emphasizes anticipated disbelief, possibly because her present condition contrasts with her claimed noble birth.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὀδυνωμένη δήγμασιν τὰς ἐμὰς ἐνέκρωσα χεῖρας
lexical_decisions.chosen: in my anguish, I deadened my own hands by biting them
lexical_decisions.rationale: δήγμασιν is taken instrumentally with ἐνέκρωσα, while ὀδυνωμένη describes her anguished condition.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as far as it is possible for you to hear them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording limits how much of her circumstances she will disclose; “as much as you are able to hear” is another possible rendering.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a man related to him by blood
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρὸς γένους indicates kinship, and αὐτῷ most naturally refers to the ruler.

lexical_decisions.chosen: fell no less deeply in love with me
lexical_decisions.rationale: The Greek retains a negative comparison without stating its standard. The English preserves “no less” rather than replacing the litotes entirely with a positive intensifier.

lexical_decisions.chosen: deeply devoted to chastity
lexical_decisions.rationale: σωφρονεῖν here concerns sexual restraint and honorable conduct, while ἀγαπάω expresses her strong commitment to it.

lexical_decisions.chosen: neither to consent to my would-be lover
lexical_decisions.rationale: συντίθεμαι means agree or consent; “would-be lover” makes clear that his desire had not been accepted.

lexical_decisions.chosen: nor to disclose to my husband
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀνατίθημι can mean refer, report, or entrust a matter to someone; “disclose” fits the concealed proposition.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦ ἐπὶ τῇ ἐμῇ ὕβρει κολακεύοντός με
lexical_decisions.chosen: of the man who was flattering me in order to dishonor me
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὕβρις may imply dishonor, outrage, or sexual violation. “Dishonor” is contextually defensible while leaving the more forceful alternatives disclosed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as a consolation
lexical_decisions.rationale: παραμυθία denotes comfort or consolation, explaining why one son remained with his father.

passages.text: However, so that these things might happen in this way, I devised the fabrication of a dream, as though someone had stood beside me at night and said, “Woman, leave the city immediately with your twin children for a time, until I tell you to return here, for you will suddenly die a terrible death together with your husband and all your children.” All the same, I did so. For as soon as I falsely told my husband about the dream, he himself became terrified and sent me by sea to Athens, together with my two sons, male and female servants, and a considerable amount of money, so that I might educate my sons, “until,” he said, “the one who gave the revelation decides that you should return to me.” Yet while I, wretched as I am, was sailing with my children, I was driven into these parts by unruly winds; when the ship broke apart in the night, I suffered shipwreck. After everyone else had died, I alone, unfortunate woman that I am, was swept along by a fierce wave and thrown onto a rock. Seated on it, wretched as I was, I did not cast myself into the deep, because I hoped to find my children alive—not even then, when my soul was intoxicated by the waves and I could easily have done it.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I devised the fabrication of a dream
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase means that she deliberately conceived a plan to fabricate a dream, not that she merely interpreted or experienced one.

lexical_decisions.chosen: All the same, I did so
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contextual rendering treats ὁμῶς concessively, like ὅμως, although the printed form can lexically suggest “likewise” or “in the same way.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: male and female servants
lexical_decisions.rationale: The reader-facing wording follows the supplied policy, but the Greek terms denote enslaved male and female household members—male slaves and female slaves or slave maids—not merely free hired workers.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who gave the revelation
lexical_decisions.rationale: χρηματίζω here concerns the supernatural communication in the alleged dream; alternatives include “the one who gave the warning” or “the one who delivered the oracle.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: by unruly winds
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally, the wording evokes being driven by the disorder or unruliness of winds.

lexical_decisions.chosen: thrown onto a rock. Seated on it
lexical_decisions.rationale: πέτρας is understood as genitive singular after ἐπί, agreeing with singular ἧς; taking it as accusative plural would produce a number mismatch.

lexical_decisions.chosen: my soul was intoxicated by the waves
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the metaphor of the soul made drunk or overwhelmed by the waves.

passages.text: However, when daybreak came, I kept looking around, crying loudly and wailing mournfully, searching for the dead bodies of my unfortunate babies. The local people took pity on me. Seeing that I was naked, they first clothed me and then searched the deep for my children. When they found none of what they were seeking, some of the hospitable women approached me for the sake of comfort, and each recounted her own troubles, so that through the shared experience of similar misfortune I might find comfort—which in fact grieved me even more. For I said that I was not so wicked as to find comfort in the misfortunes of others. Although many offered to take me in as a guest, one poor woman from this place pressed me so insistently that she compelled me to come to her own shelter. She said to me, “Take courage, woman. My husband too was a sailor and died at sea while still in the bloom of youth. Since then, although many have sought me in marriage, I have chosen to remain a widow because I long for my husband. Whatever both of us can procure by the work of our hands will be shared between us.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: my unfortunate babies
lexical_decisions.rationale: βρέφη denotes infants or very young children; “babies” retains that force rather than harmonizing it with the earlier designation “sons.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: searched the deep
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀνηραύνων is parsed here as a contracted third-person plural imperfect, not as a participle; with οἱ ἐπιχώριοι as its subject, it depicts the local people searching the sea’s depth. “Were searching the bottom” is another possible rendering.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ γὰρ ἔφην οὕτω κακὴ εἶναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: I was not so wicked
lexical_decisions.rationale: In context she rejects obtaining comfort from others’ suffering, so κακή has a moral sense. “So miserable” is lexically possible but less coherent with the following clause.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς ξενίαν πολλῶν με ἄγειν ἀξιουσῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: although many offered to take me in as a guest
lexical_decisions.rationale: ξενία refers to hospitality or lodging for a stranger; the wording may also be rendered “many asked to bring me into their homes.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: while still in the bloom of youth
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase describes the husband as being at a youthful age when he died.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἃ διὰ χειρῶν ἀμφότεραι πορίζειν δυνάμεθα
lexical_decisions.chosen: whatever both of us can procure by the work of our hands
lexical_decisions.rationale: διὰ χειρῶν points to what they can obtain through their own manual labor.

passages.text: And, so that I do not prolong for you words that are unnecessary, I lived with her because of her devotion to her husband. Before long, my hands—wretched woman that I am—were paralyzed by attacks of biting pain, and the woman who had taken me in, her whole body bound by some affliction, lies prostrate at home.
