Since, then, the compassion of the women from before has waned, and both I and the woman at home are incapacitated, for many years I have sat here, as you see, begging; and whatever I manage to obtain, I also carry home for my fellow sufferer’s sustenance. So much for my own affairs; let them have been told sufficiently. What remains is that you are preventing the fulfillment of your promise to give me the drug, so that I may give it to her as well, since she desires to die, and in this way I too may be able to depart from life, as you said.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: because of her devotion to her husband
lexical_decisions.rationale: φιλανδρία denotes love of or devotion to a husband. The immediate context favors the poor widow’s devotion, though the phrase could encompass the narrator’s corresponding marital devotion.

lexical_decisions.chosen: were paralyzed by attacks of biting pain
lexical_decisions.rationale: δήγματα literally denotes bites or stings and can describe sharp, biting pains; a more literal alternative is “were disabled by the bites.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: her whole body bound by some affliction
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὅλη indicates that the affliction affected her wholly, while συνδεθεῖσα retains the image of being bound.

lexical_decisions.chosen: lies prostrate at home
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect ἔρριπται presents the resulting prostrate condition as continuing at the time of the woman’s account; “has been laid prostrate at home” is another possible rendering.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐγὼ δὲ καὶ ἡ κατ’ οἶκον ἀμφότεραι ἐπισινεῖς τυγχάνομεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: both I and the woman at home are incapacitated
lexical_decisions.rationale: The present τυγχάνομεν describes both women as currently harmed, impaired, or afflicted, explaining their continuing need.

lexical_decisions.chosen: whatever I manage to obtain
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὐπορέω here concerns securing available resources rather than being generally wealthy.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ τῇ συνταλαιπώρῳ εἰς τροφὰς κομίζω
lexical_decisions.chosen: I also carry home for my fellow sufferer’s sustenance
lexical_decisions.rationale: εἰς τροφὰς expresses the purpose of what she brings—providing nourishment or sustenance—without requiring that everything obtained be edible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the drug
lexical_decisions.rationale: φάρμακον can mean medicine, drug, or poison. “Drug” preserves the lexical breadth, while the expressed desire for death supplies the lethal purpose in context.

lexical_decisions.chosen: depart from life
lexical_decisions.rationale: The construction is a euphemism for dying, literally involving a change or departure from living.

passages.text: When the woman had said this, Peter seemed, amid many thoughts, to stand suspended. I came up and said, “I have been going around looking for you for a long time. What are we to do now?” Peter instructed me to go on ahead and wait for him at the boat. Since there was no contradicting him when he gave an order, I did what had been commanded. But Peter, his heart throbbing with a faint suspicion—as he himself related everything to me later—questioned the woman, saying, “Tell me, woman, your origin and city and the names of your children, and I will give you the drug at once.” She was caught under pressure, unwilling to tell him but eager to receive the drug, so she contrived to say one thing in place of another. Even so, she said that she herself was an Ephesian and that her husband was a Sicilian; she likewise changed the names of all three children. Peter, thinking that she was telling the truth, said, “Alas, woman! I thought that today would be a day of great joy, because I suspected that you were a certain woman—the one I thought you were—whose circumstances I have heard and know exactly.” She adjured him, saying, “I beg you, tell me, so that I may know whether there is any woman more miserable than I am.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὸ λογισμῶν πολλῶν ὁ Πέτρος μετέωρος ἐδόκει ἵστασθαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: Peter seemed, amid many thoughts, to stand suspended
lexical_decisions.rationale: μετέωρος preserves an image of being suspended or unsettled; idiomatic alternatives include “stood perplexed” or “was lost in thought.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: your origin and city
lexical_decisions.rationale: γένος may refer to family, people, nationality, or origin. “Origin” leaves the scope open alongside the more specific request for her city.

lexical_decisions.chosen: caught under pressure
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase depicts her as constrained by conflicting pressures: reluctance to disclose the truth and desire to obtain the drug. More literally, it can mean “suffering compulsion.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: she contrived to say one thing in place of another
lexical_decisions.rationale: The idiom describes an ingenious evasion or lie while retaining the source’s wording pattern.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Even so, she said
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contextual rendering treats ὁμῶς concessively, like ὅμως. “Likewise” is possible for the printed form but fits the progression less well.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁμῶς καὶ τῶν τριῶν τέκνων ἤλλαξεν τὰ ὀνόματα
lexical_decisions.chosen: she likewise changed the names of all three children
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here the same printed adverb naturally coordinates the alteration of the children’s names with the false statements about her own and her husband’s origins.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑποπτεύσας σὲ τινὰ εἶναι, ἣν ἐνόμιζον
lexical_decisions.chosen: because I suspected that you were a certain woman—the one I thought you were
lexical_decisions.rationale: The deliberately repetitive rendering preserves Peter’s guarded identification. A smoother alternative is “suspecting you were someone I had in mind.”

passages.text: And Peter, who did not know how to lie, began out of compassion for her to tell the truth: “A certain person, by now a young man, accompanies me—a Roman citizen who desires teachings about reverence for God. He tells me how, though he has a father and two twin brothers, he sees none of them. ‘For my mother,’ he says, ‘as my father used to tell me, saw a dream and left the city of the Romans for a time with her twin children, so that she would not die by an evil fate; and after leaving with them, she has not been found.’ The husband of this woman—who is the young man’s father—himself also left to search for her and has not been found.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: who did not know how to lie
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase describes Peter as unpracticed or incapable in lying, not merely as unaware that a particular statement was false.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by now a young man
lexical_decisions.rationale: λοιπὸν ἤδη marks his present stage of life. Alternatives include “now already a young man” and “now at last a young man.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: who desires teachings about reverence for God
lexical_decisions.rationale: θεοσέβεια is piety or reverence directed toward God, while λόγοι here denotes words, discourses, or teachings.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἥ τε γὰρ μήτηρ (φησίν), ὡς ὁ πατὴρ διηγεῖτό μοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: ‘For my mother,’ he says, ‘as my father used to tell me’
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering treats μοι as retained first-person wording within the young man’s embedded report. A formally indirect alternative, “his mother ... as the father told me,” would make “me” refer to Peter, which is contextually difficult.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the city of the Romans
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the source’s descriptive expression rather than replacing it silently with the conventional name “Rome.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: die by an evil fate
lexical_decisions.rationale: μόρος denotes fate, doom, or the death allotted by fate; “meet a terrible death” is a smoother alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ δὲ ταύτης μὲν ἀνήρ, αὐτοῦ δὲ πατὴρ
lexical_decisions.chosen: The husband of this woman—who is the young man’s father
lexical_decisions.rationale: The paired description identifies the same person in relation first to the woman and then to the accompanying young man.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ αὐτὸς εἰς ἐπιζήτησιν αὐτῆς ἐκβὰς
lexical_decisions.chosen: himself also left to search for her
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording preserves both the emphatic αὐτός and the purpose expressed by εἰς ἐπιζήτησιν αὐτῆς.

passages.text: When Peter had said these things, the woman stopped and, as though from shock, fainted. Peter came over and paused, then urged her to recover a clear mind, trying to persuade her to say what exactly was happening to her. As though recovering from drunkenness, with the rest of her body gone limp, she regained control of herself so that she could bear the magnitude of the joy she was anticipating. Rubbing her face, she said, “Where is this young man?” Peter, who by now had discerned the whole situation, said, “You tell me first (for otherwise you have no way to see him)—.” In her eagerness she said, “I am the young man’s mother.” Peter said, “What is his name?” She replied, “Clement.” Peter said, “It is he. He was the one who spoke with me a short while ago, whom I instructed to wait for me in the ship.” Falling at Peter’s feet, she begged him to hurry to the ship. Peter said, “If you keep our agreement, I will do this too.” She said, “I will do everything; only show me my only child, for through him I will seem to see my two children who died here.” Peter said, “When you see him, remain quiet until we have left the island.” She said, “I will do so.”

source_issues.source_quote: Εἰπέ μοι σὺ πρῶτον (ἄλλως γὰρ τοῦτον ἰδεῖν οὐκ ἔχεις) —.
source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a terminal dash after Peter’s unfinished prompt and before the period. It may signal interrupted or deliberately incomplete speech, or it may be an editorial marker, but its function is uncertain. The marker is retained, and no unexpressed object or completion has been supplied.

lexical_decisions.chosen: stopped and, as though from shock, fainted
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιστήσασα marks her coming to a halt, while ἀπέψυξεν here describes a collapse or loss of consciousness rather than literal death.

lexical_decisions.chosen: paused, then urged her to recover a clear mind
lexical_decisions.rationale: The absolute ἐπισχών can mean that Peter paused or waited; alternatively, the context may suggest that he supported or steadied her. νήφειν denotes recovering mental clarity.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ δὲ ὥσπερ ἐκ μέθης τὸ λοιπὸν τοῦ σώματος παρεθεῖσα
lexical_decisions.chosen: As though recovering from drunkenness, with the rest of her body gone limp
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐκ preserves the image of emerging from drunkenness, while the participial phrase depicts the remaining bodily weakness accompanying her recovery.

lexical_decisions.chosen: she regained control of herself so that she could bear
lexical_decisions.rationale: The unusual sequence presents her as recovering sufficiently to withstand the anticipated joy; more formally, she “turned herself back” so as to be able to endure it.

lexical_decisions.chosen: You tell me first
lexical_decisions.rationale: No object of “tell” is expressed. The translation preserves the incomplete prompt rather than supplying what Peter requires her to tell him.

lexical_decisions.chosen: If you keep our agreement
lexical_decisions.rationale: συνθήκας denotes agreed terms or conditions, referring to Peter’s requirement that she remain composed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: my only child
lexical_decisions.rationale: μονογενές presents Clement as her unique or sole remaining child in this context; “only-born child” would misleadingly conflict with the immediately mentioned deceased children.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δόξω γὰρ δι’ αὐτοῦ τὰ δύο μου τὰ ἐνταῦθα τεθνηκότα ὁρᾶν τέκνα
lexical_decisions.chosen: for through him I will seem to see my two children who died here
lexical_decisions.rationale: δόξω with the infinitive is preserved as “I will seem to see,” expressing how seeing Clement will represent the two deceased children to her.

passages.text: Peter therefore took her by the hand and led her toward the ship. When I saw him leading a woman by the hand, I laughed; and I came over and, out of respect for him, tried to lead her in his place. The moment I touched her hand, she gave a great cry like a mother, wrapped herself around me, and fervently showered me, her own son, with kisses. Knowing nothing of the whole situation, I was trying to shake her off as though she were mad; yet, feeling deference toward Peter as well, I was becoming irritated.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς τιμὴν αὐτοῦ ἀντ’ αὐτοῦ χειραγωγεῖν αὐτὴν ἐπειρώμην
lexical_decisions.chosen: out of respect for him, tried to lead her in his place
lexical_decisions.rationale: Clement attempts to relieve Peter of the task as an expression of honor or respect.

lexical_decisions.chosen: she gave a great cry like a mother
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὀλολύζω denotes a loud, emotionally charged cry; the comparison explicitly characterizes it as maternal.

lexical_decisions.chosen: wrapped herself around me, and fervently showered me with kisses
lexical_decisions.rationale: περιπλέκομαι describes an enclosing embrace, while the intensive καταφιλέω conveys repeated or ardent kissing.

lexical_decisions.chosen: me, her own son
lexical_decisions.rationale: The accusative phrase stands in apposition to με and identifies Clement as her son from the mother’s perspective.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I was trying to shake her off as though she were mad
lexical_decisions.rationale: The imperfect depicts the ongoing or attempted action that Peter addresses with ἀποσειόμενος in the following section, rather than a completed dismissal.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αἰδούμενος δὲ καὶ τὸν Πέτρον ἐπικραινόμην
lexical_decisions.chosen: yet, feeling deference toward Peter as well, I was becoming irritated
lexical_decisions.rationale: αἰδέομαι with Peter as its object expresses regard or deference; the imperfect ἐπικραινόμην describes Clement’s developing vexation.

passages.text: Peter said, “Let her be! What are you doing, child Clement, shaking off the woman who truly gave birth to you?” When I heard this, I became covered in tears; and I threw myself upon the woman who had borne me, who had herself fallen down, and showered her with kisses. For as soon as this was said to me, I somehow began dimly to recall her appearance. Many crowds therefore came running to learn about the woman who had been begging, saying to one another, “Her son, a man of distinction, has recognized her.” When we wished to leave the island at once with my mother, she said, “My longed-for child, it is right to say farewell to the woman who took me in. She is poor and completely disabled and lies at home.” When Peter heard this, he marveled, as did all the surrounding crowds, at the woman’s noble disposition. Peter immediately ordered some people to go and carry the woman in on a cot. And likewise, when the cot had been brought in and set down, Peter said in the hearing of all the crowds, “If I am indeed a herald of truth, then, as grounds for faith among those standing by, so that they may know that there is one God, the one who made the world, let her rise immediately in health.” As soon as Peter said this, the woman rose, having been healed. She fell before Peter, and after showering her familiar friend with kisses, she asked what this might mean. Her friend briefly related to her the whole event of the recognition, and those who heard it were astounded. Then the mother, seeing that her hostess had been healed, asked that she too might receive healing. Peter laid his hand on her and healed her as well.

lexical_decisions.chosen: shaking off the woman who truly gave birth to you
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὄντως emphasizes that she is genuinely Clement’s birth mother, while the present participle recalls his ongoing attempt to push her away.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I became covered in tears
lexical_decisions.rationale: περίδακρυς depicts Clement as streaming with tears.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I threw myself upon the woman who had borne me, who had herself fallen down
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participles distinguish the mother’s prior collapse from Clement’s movement toward and onto her.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I somehow began dimly to recall her appearance
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀμαυρῶς marks the memory as indistinct, and the imperfect suggests an emerging recollection.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to learn about the woman who had been begging
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἱστορέω here can mean to investigate, inquire about, or learn the story of someone; “to see” is also possible but expresses the crowds’ curiosity less fully.

lexical_decisions.chosen: completely disabled
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive description indicates that her body has lost its strength or function; “completely paralyzed” is a possible narrower rendering.

lexical_decisions.chosen: some people to go
lexical_decisions.rationale: The indefinite pronoun refers to unspecified persons and does not identify their sex.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ὁμῶς ἐνεχθείσης καὶ τεθείσης τῆς κλίνης
lexical_decisions.chosen: And likewise, when the cot had been brought in and set down
lexical_decisions.rationale: The explicit genitive τῆς κλίνης is most naturally the shared subject of both coordinated participles. A split attachment—“when she had been brought in and the cot had been set down”—is contextually possible but less source-transparent. ὁμῶς is retained as “likewise” rather than being replaced with ὅμως.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as grounds for faith among those standing by
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase presents the healing as serving or producing the faith of those present.

lexical_decisions.chosen: her familiar friend
lexical_decisions.rationale: συνήθης identifies Clement’s mother as the healed woman’s accustomed or close associate.

lexical_decisions.chosen: seeing that her hostess had been healed
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here ἱστορέω is understood as observing or ascertaining the hostess’s healed condition; “having inquired about the healed hostess” remains possible.

passages.text: And then, in this way, Peter spoke about God and the worship that belongs to him, adding at the end: “If anyone wishes to learn these things accurately, let him come to Antioch, where I have decided to remain for several days, and learn the things that lead to his salvation. For surely it cannot be that you know how to leave your homelands for commerce or military service and travel to distant places, yet are unwilling to undertake even a three-day journey for eternal salvation.” After Peter’s address, in the presence of the entire crowd, I gave the woman who had been healed one thousand drachmas for provisions and entrusted her to a certain good man who was the foremost citizen of the city and was naturally disposed to do this with joy. After also distributing money to many others and thanking the women who had once comforted my mother, I sailed across to Antaradus together with my mother, Peter, and the remaining companions; and in this way we made our way to our lodging.

source_issues.source_quote: διὰ δὲ αἰώνιον σωτηρίαν μηδὲ τριῶν ἡμερῶν ὁδὸν πορευθῆναι θέλειν
source_issues.issue: The infinitive θέλειν is syntactically abrupt where a finite verb would make the contrast straightforward. The verified supplied reading remains intelligible as an anacoluthon within the preceding rhetorical construction and has been preserved in translation.
source_issues.proposed_reading: διὰ δὲ αἰώνιον σωτηρίαν μηδὲ τριῶν ἡμερῶν ὁδὸν πορευθῆναι θέλετε

lexical_decisions.chosen: the worship that belongs to him
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαφέρειν with the dative can denote what pertains or is proper to someone; θρησκεία here is religious worship or observance.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the things that lead to his salvation
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρός expresses relation or direction toward the hearer’s salvation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ γὰρ δὴ ἐμπορίας ἕνεκα ἢ στρατείας πατρίδας καταλιμπάνειν οἴδατε καὶ εἰς μακροὺς ἀπέρχεσθαι τόπους
lexical_decisions.chosen: For surely it cannot be that you know how to leave your homelands for commerce or military service and travel to distant places
lexical_decisions.rationale: The initial οὐ is retained as a rhetorical rejection of the inconsistent behavior Peter describes. Alternatively, the clause may be punctuated as a direct rhetorical question: “Do you not know how to leave ...?”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διὰ δὲ αἰώνιον σωτηρίαν μηδὲ τριῶν ἡμερῶν ὁδὸν πορευθῆναι θέλειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: yet are unwilling to undertake even a three-day journey for eternal salvation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the contrast and the negative force of μηδέ while expressing the syntactically abrupt infinitive θέλειν as part of the rhetorical rejection introduced by οὐ.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the foremost citizen of the city
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρῶτος describes the man’s leading civic standing, not merely his chronological position.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: φύσει μετὰ χαρᾶς τοῦτο ποιεῖν προῃρημένῳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: was naturally disposed to do this with joy
lexical_decisions.rationale: προαιρεῖσθαι here denotes settled willingness or inclination, qualified by φύσει.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to Antaradus
lexical_decisions.rationale: Antaradus is the conventional English form of the place-name Ἀντάραδος.

lexical_decisions.chosen: we made our way to our lodging
lexical_decisions.rationale: ξενία denotes guest lodging or quarters, and ὁρμάω here means to set out or proceed toward them.

passages.text: When we had arrived ... and had partaken of food and given thanks as usual, while there was still time, I said to Peter, “My lord Peter, my mother performed an act of love for humanity when she remembered the woman who had hosted her.” Peter answered, “Do you really think, Clement, that the woman who bore you has performed an act of love for humanity, in that she repaid the woman who received her after the shipwreck? Or did you make this statement as one bestowing a great favor on your mother? If, however, you spoke not as one showing favor but as one telling the truth, you seem to me not to understand what the greatness of love for humanity actually is. It is affection for anyone at all, insofar as that person is human, without anything that naturally prompts it. Nor do I dare call the hostess who received the woman who bore you after the shipwreck a lover of humanity on that account. For, cajoled by pity, she had been persuaded to become the benefactor of a woman who had suffered shipwreck, was mourning children, was a foreigner, was naked, was alone, and was bitterly lamenting her disasters. Since she was amid so many disasters, who, even among the impious, would not have pitied her on seeing her? Consequently, even the hostess does not appear to have performed in this way an act of love for humanity, but to have acted under pity that had been stirred toward benefaction by countless disasters. How much more, then, did the woman who bore you—after acquiring abundant means and repaying her hostess—perform an act not of love for humanity, but of friendship? There is a great difference between friendship and love for humanity: friendship arises from repayment, whereas love for humanity, without anything that naturally prompts it, loves and benefits every human being insofar as that one is human. If, then, the hostess who showed pity had also pitied and benefited enemies who had wronged her, she would have been a lover of humanity. But if the enemy is a friend for some reason and the friend is an enemy for some reason, such a person is a friend or enemy of some particular cause, not of the human being.”

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints exactly three dots after γενομένων δὲ ἡμῶν, marking unavailable content. The gap is retained exactly in the English, and no restoration has been supplied.
The printed period interrupts the phrase φιλανθρωπίας ἔργον. It has been treated provisionally as editorial punctuation rather than as a syntactic break; no Greek word has been altered.

The printed period separates the modal particle ἄν from the verb ἦν. The translation provisionally reads the words continuously as a normal contrary-to-fact construction while preserving every printed word.

lexical_decisions.chosen: When we had arrived ...
lexical_decisions.rationale: γενομένων ἡμῶν can describe the party’s arrival or presence, but the printed lacuna removes its following specification; the three dots are retained without restoration.

lexical_decisions.chosen: an act of love for humanity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expanded rendering preserves the etymological and argumentative connection among φιλανθρωπία, φιλάνθρωπος, and the later contrast with φιλία.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as one bestowing a great favor on your mother
lexical_decisions.rationale: Peter asks whether Clement’s judgment was an indulgent compliment to his mother rather than a true classification of her act.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ ἄνευ τοῦ φυσικῶς πείθοντος πρὸς οἱονδήποτε στοργὴ καθὸ ἄνθρωπός ἐστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: affection for anyone at all, insofar as that person is human, without anything that naturally prompts it
lexical_decisions.rationale: Peter defines love for humanity as affection grounded solely in the recipient’s humanity, without a natural or circumstantial inducement.

lexical_decisions.chosen: For, cajoled by pity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering retains the personifying force of κολακεύω: pity flatters, coaxes, or cajoles the hostess into action.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὸ ἐλέου τοῦ ἐπὶ μυρίαις συμφοραῖς πρὸς εὐεργεσίας κεκινημένου
lexical_decisions.chosen: under pity that had been stirred toward benefaction by countless disasters
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive participle most naturally modifies ἐλέου, personifying pity itself as moved toward doing good by the accumulation of misfortunes.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ μὲν φιλία ἐξ ἀμοιβῆς γίνεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: friendship arises from repayment
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀμοιβή can mean repayment, return, or reciprocity; “repayment” keeps the immediate connection with the mother’s recompense to her hostess.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ δὲ διὰ τί φίλη ἡ ἐχθρὰ καὶ διὰ τί ἐχθρὰ ἡ φίλη
lexical_decisions.chosen: But if the enemy is a friend for some reason and the friend is an enemy for some reason
lexical_decisions.rationale: διὰ τί may be interrogative, “why,” or causal, “for some reason.” The causal reading best continues the contrast between unconditional regard for a human being and attachment produced by a particular cause.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ τοιαύτη τοῦ τινὸς αἰτίου φίλη ἐστὶν ἢ ἐχθρά, οὐ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου
lexical_decisions.chosen: such a person is a friend or enemy of some particular cause, not of the human being
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the source’s compressed genitive contrast. Alternatively, it may mean that such a person is friend or enemy because of some particular cause, not because the other is human.

passages.text: And I answered, “Does it not seem to you, then, that even the innkeeper is humane, since she did good to a woman who was a stranger and whom she did not know?” Peter said, “I know that I can call her merciful, but I do not dare call her humane, since I would not even call a mother child-loving; for she has been persuaded by labor pains and upbringing to cherish her child. Just as the lover is flattered by familiarity and by the bed, and the friend by reciprocation, so also the person who shows mercy is flattered by misfortune. Nevertheless, the merciful person is close to the humane person, because he is persuaded to do good without hunting to receive anything. At least in this way he is humane.” And I said, “By what actions, then, can someone be humane?” Peter answered, “Since I see that you are eager to hear what an act of humaneness actually is, I will not hesitate to tell you. The humane person is one who does good even to enemies. Hear why this is so. Humaneness is male-and-female: its female part is called mercy, while its male part has been named love toward one’s neighbor. Every human being is a human being’s neighbor, not merely some particular human being; for the evil person and the good person, the enemy and the friend, are all human beings. Therefore, the person who practices humaneness must be an imitator of God, doing good to the righteous and the unrighteous, just as God himself provides everyone in the present world with both his sun and his rains. But if you wish to do good to good people, but no longer to evil people, or even to punish them, you are attempting to perform the work of a judge; you are not striving to possess the work of humaneness.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: humane
lexical_decisions.rationale: The term denotes active benevolence toward human beings. “Humane” maintains its connection with the recurring noun rendered “humaneness” without narrowing it to institutional philanthropy.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I would not even call a mother child-loving
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb “call” is carried forward from εἰπεῖν and λέγειν. More literally, τὴν τεκοῦσαν is “the woman who gave birth.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς καὶ ὁ ἐρῶν ὑπὸ τῆς συνηθείας κολακεύεται καὶ εὐνῆς καὶ ὁ φίλος ὑπὸ τῆς ἀμοιβῆς: οὕτω καὶ ὁ ἐλεῶν ὑπὸ τῆς συμφορᾶς.
lexical_decisions.chosen: Just as the lover is flattered by familiarity and by the bed, and the friend by reciprocation, so also the person who shows mercy is flattered by misfortune.
lexical_decisions.rationale: The predicate κολακεύεται is understood elliptically in all three members of the analogy. Its unusual image of being flattered or enticed is therefore retained throughout rather than weakened in the final member.

lexical_decisions.chosen: without hunting to receive anything
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the source’s hunting image and the idea of seeking some return.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Humaneness is male-and-female
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compound ἀρρενόθηλυς explicitly combines male and female. The striking image is preserved rather than reduced to “twofold”; “androgynous” would be another possible rendering.

lexical_decisions.chosen: its female part is called mercy
lexical_decisions.rationale: In this context ἐλεημοσύνη continues the discussion of showing mercy. “Almsgiving” is possible in other contexts but would be too narrow here.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πλησίον δὲ ἀνθρώπῳ ἐστὶν ὁ πᾶς ἄνθρωπος, οὐχ ὁ τὶς ἄνθρωπος
lexical_decisions.chosen: Every human being is a human being’s neighbor, not merely some particular human being
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the contrast between every human being and a neighbor restricted to some particular person.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κριτοῦ τὸ ἔργον ἐπιχειρεῖς πράττειν, οὐ τὸ τῆς φιλανθρωπίας σπουδάζεις ἔχειν.
lexical_decisions.chosen: you are attempting to perform the work of a judge; you are not striving to possess the work of humaneness
lexical_decisions.rationale: The second τὸ is taken elliptically with ἔργον carried forward, preserving the parallel between a judge’s work and the work of humaneness. It could more generally mean “what belongs to humaneness,” including the quality itself.

passages.text: And I said, “Surely God too, since he is going to judge then, as you teach us, is not humane?” Peter replied, “You are saying the opposite. For it is precisely because he will judge that he is humane. In loving and showing mercy to those who have been wronged, he punishes those who wronged them.” And I said, “Therefore, if I too do good to good people but punish those who commit injustice insofar as they have wronged human beings, am I humane?” Peter answered, “If, along with possessing foreknowledge, you also possessed authority to judge, you would rightly do this: on account of having received the authority, you would condemn those whom God created; and because of your foreknowledge, you would judge without error, acquitting some as righteous and condemning others as unrighteous.” And I said, “You have spoken correctly and truthfully, for it is impossible for someone who lacks foreknowledge to judge correctly. Sometimes some people appear good while secretly committing unlawful acts, while some good people are considered evil because of their enemies’ slander. But even if someone possesses authority to torture and interrogate and then judges, it would not even so be possible for him to judge justly in every case. For some who were murderers endured the tortures and were released as innocent, while others who were innocent did not endure the tortures, falsely testified against themselves as guilty, and were punished.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: You are saying the opposite
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression directly reverses Clement’s inference and does not require an expanded theological explanation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: insofar as they have wronged human beings
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀνθρώπους is read as the object of ἠδίκησαν, while καθό marks the respect or extent in which punishment is contemplated. Another possible rendering is “because they wronged human beings.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διὰ μὲν τὸ εἰληφέναι τὴν ἐξουσίαν καταδικάζων οὓς ὁ θεὸς ἐδημιούργησεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: on account of having received the authority, you would condemn those whom God created
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle καταδικάζων describes the exercise of the hypothetical authority. The striking reference to condemning people created by God is retained.

lexical_decisions.chosen: acquitting some as righteous
lexical_decisions.rationale: In this judicial context δικαιόω denotes declaring righteous or acquitting rather than making someone morally righteous.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐνίοτε γὰρ φαίνονταί τινες ἀγαθοί, ἀθέμιτα κρύφα διαπρασσόμενοι, ἔνιοι δὲ ἀγαθοὶ ὑπὸ διαβολῆς ἐχθρῶν κακοὶ ὑπολαμβανόμενοι.
lexical_decisions.chosen: Sometimes some people appear good while secretly committing unlawful acts, while some good people are considered evil because of their enemies’ slander.
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first ἐνίοτε is temporal, “sometimes,” but the second expression is ἔνιοι, “some people.” The translation therefore contrasts two groups rather than introducing an unsupported second temporal category.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐδὲ οὕτως τὸ πάντως δικαίως αὐτῷ δικάσαι ἐγίνετο
lexical_decisions.chosen: it would not even so be possible for him to judge justly in every case
lexical_decisions.rationale: πάντως is understood distributively in light of the contrasting examples that follow. “To judge altogether justly” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: falsely testified against themselves as guilty
lexical_decisions.rationale: The reflexive construction denotes making a false accusation or testimony against oneself, while αἴτιοι denotes culpability or guilt.

passages.text: And Peter said, “These points too are moderately sound, but hear the greater point. When some people sin or act well, among the things they now do some are their own and others belong to someone else; yet it is just for each person to be punished for his own sins or benefited for his own right actions. But it is impossible for anyone except a prophet alone, who possesses foreknowledge, to know which of the things done by someone are his own and which were not his own; for everything is seen to happen through him.” And I said, “I would like to learn how, among acts of injustice or right actions, some are one’s own and others belong to someone else.”

source_issues.source_quote: ποῖά, ἐστιν αὐτοῦ ἴδια, ποῖα δὲ οὐχ ἦν
source_issues.issue: The printed comma after ποῖά is editorially awkward, and the shift from present ἐστιν to past ἦν is abrupt. The supplied wording nevertheless permits a defensible translation without changing the Greek.

lexical_decisions.chosen: These points too are moderately sound
lexical_decisions.rationale: μετρίως gives qualified approval rather than complete endorsement. “These things too are reasonable to a degree” is another possible rendering.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἃ μὲν ἴδια αὐτῶν ἐστίν, ἃ δὲ ἀλλότρια
lexical_decisions.chosen: some are their own and others belong to someone else
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἴδια and ἀλλότρια contrast actions attributable to the person with actions whose agency or ownership belongs elsewhere.

lexical_decisions.chosen: benefited for his own right actions
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατόρθωμα denotes a right, successful, or virtuous action. “Achievement” is possible but could obscure the moral contrast with sins.

lexical_decisions.chosen: except a prophet alone, who possesses foreknowledge
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both the exception marked by πλήν and the exclusivity expressed by μόνῳ are retained.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ποῖά, ἐστιν αὐτοῦ ἴδια, ποῖα δὲ οὐχ ἦν
lexical_decisions.chosen: which ... are his own and which were not his own
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the supplied shift from present ἐστιν to past ἦν while supplying “his own” in the second member from the first. Regularizing ἦν to a present tense would require emendation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πάντα γὰρ δι’ αὐτοῦ γινόμενα βλέπεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: for everything is seen to happen through him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participial phrase is taken predicatively with βλέπεται: all the actions appear to occur through the person, even though only a prophet can discern which are truly the person’s own. It could also be construed as “everything that happens through him is seen.”

passages.text: And Peter answered, “The prophet of truth said, ‘The good things must come; but blessed (he says) is the one through whom they come. Likewise, the evil things must necessarily come; but woe to the one through whom they come.’ Now if evil things come through evil people and good things are borne through good people, what is each person’s own—being good or evil—must also belong to him on the basis of the things he did beforehand, through the coming of the subsequent good or evil things. These, being his own as matters of choice, have been arranged by God’s providence to pass through him. God’s judgment, then, is this: just as in a contest, the one who has passed through every hardship and been found blameless is to be deemed worthy of eternal life. For those who, by their own resolve, have come to the fore in good things are tested by those who, by their own resolve, have persisted in evil: they are persecuted, hated, reviled, plotted against, beaten, exploited, slandered, pressed into service, and abused, suffering all those things through which becoming angry and rushing toward retaliation seem reasonably to arise.”

source_issues.source_quote: οἱ γὰρ ἐν ἀγαθοῖς ἰδίᾳ βουλῇ προκύψαντες;
source_issues.issue: The printed Greek semicolon functions as a question mark, but the clause continues syntactically with ὑπὸ τῶν ... πειράζονται and is defensibly read as declarative. The punctuation is treated provisionally as an editorial oddity, not as evidence that wording is missing.
source_issues.proposed_reading: οἱ γὰρ ἐν ἀγαθοῖς ἰδίᾳ βουλῇ προκύψαντες,

source_issues.source_quote: ἐπεὶ οὖν κρίσις αὕτη θεῷ, ὥσπερ ἐπ᾽ ἀγῶνος τὸν διὰ πάσης κακουχίας διεληλυθότα καὶ ἄμεμπτον εὑρεθέντα, ἐκεῖνον ζωῆς αἰωνίου καταξιοῦσθαι —·
source_issues.issue: The construction is compressed, with a nominal statement followed by an accusative-and-infinitive formulation, and the closing dash and point are editorially unusual. The translation treats the infinitive as defining the stated judgment; this is provisional but defensible without restoring, deleting, or altering words.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ ἀγαθὰ ἐλθεῖν δεῖ, μακάριος δὲ (φησίν) δι’ οὗ ἔρχεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: The good things must come; but blessed (he says) is the one through whom they come
lexical_decisions.rationale: The positive form of the saying is translated as supplied rather than harmonized with a familiar parallel, and the separate parenthetical attribution φησίν is explicitly retained.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ κακὰ ἀνάγκη ἐλθεῖν, οὐαὶ δὲ δι’ οὗ ἔρχεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: the evil things must necessarily come; but woe to the one through whom they come
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀνάγκη expresses necessity. The singular Greek verb treats the neuter plural collectively, while idiomatic English uses a plural verb.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: προσεῖναι δεῖ ἑκάστῳ τὸ ἴδιον (τὸ ἀγαθὸν εἶναι ἢ κακόν) καὶ ἐξ ὧν προέπραξεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: what is each person’s own—being good or evil—must also belong to him on the basis of the things he did beforehand
lexical_decisions.rationale: The parenthesis identifies what is proper to the person as being good or evil. The compressed καὶ ἐξ ὧν προέπραξεν is taken as identifying the basis supplied by prior conduct; it could alternatively mean that the person’s character is known from what he previously did.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἅτινα ἴδια αὐτοῦ τῆς αἱρέσεως ὄντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: These, being his own as matters of choice
lexical_decisions.rationale: αἵρεσις is understood as personal choice or resolve. The compact genitive construction could also be represented as “belonging to his own choice.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὸ τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ προνοίας διελθεῖν ᾠκονόμηται
lexical_decisions.chosen: have been arranged by God’s providence to pass through him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The subject is the preceding good or evil things. “Through him” is contextually supplied from the repeated description of events coming through good or evil agents; a less agent-focused alternative is “have been arranged by God’s providence to run their course.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: God’s judgment, then, is this
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compressed nominal clause introduces the content expressed by the following accusative-and-infinitive construction. More formally, it could be rendered “For this, then, is judgment with God” or “Since this judgment belongs to God.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἱ γὰρ ἐν ἀγαθοῖς ἰδίᾳ βουλῇ προκύψαντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: For those who, by their own resolve, have come to the fore in good things
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering follows the supplied προκύψαντες from προκύπτω, conveying emergence or coming forward. It does not silently substitute προκόψαντες, which would more directly mean “advanced” or “made progress.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: pressed into service
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb denotes being compelled to perform service or labor, so the coercive force is retained.

lexical_decisions.chosen: rushing toward retaliation
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἄμυνα can denote defense or retaliatory action. “Retaliation” fits the following warning against responding to mistreatment in kind, though “self-defense” remains possible.

passages.text: “But the Teacher, knowing that those who do these things unjustly stand condemned because of earlier sins, and that through condemned people the spirit of evil carries out these things, counseled them, as people practicing humaneness, to have mercy on human beings insofar as they are human, even though through sin they become instruments of evil. He also counseled them, as far as it lay with them, while being wronged, to release the wrongdoers from condemnation, so that, just as sober people help drunk people, they might help them with prayers, fasts, and blessings, neither resisting nor retaliating, so that they would not force them to sin still more. For when suffering has in any event been decreed for someone, it is not reasonable for that person to be indignant with the one through whom the suffering comes, when he reflects that even if that person had not mistreated him, because he was in any event going to be mistreated, the suffering would have come through someone else. Why, then, am I indignant with the one who brought it about, when it has in any event been decreed that I suffer? But moreover, if on the pretext of retaliation we do the same things as evil people, then, apart from being second rather than first, we who are good do the same thing as evil people. And (as I said) one should not be indignant, knowing that by God’s providence evil people punish good people. Those, therefore, who are angry with those who punish them sin as people who insult God’s emissaries; but those who honor them and treat them with the opposite of what is considered injurious act reverently toward God, who has so resolved.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διὰ καταδίκων τὸ τῆς κακίας πνεῦμα ταῦτα ἐνεργεῖ
lexical_decisions.chosen: through condemned people the spirit of evil carries out these things
lexical_decisions.rationale: The condemned people are represented as intermediate agents through whom the spirit acts. The author’s claim is retained without theological harmonization.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοὺς μὲν ἀνθρώπους καθὰ ἄνθρωποί εἰσιν, καὶ δι᾽ ἁμαρτίας ὄργανα γινομένους κακίας ἐλεεῖν συνεβούλευσεν, ὡς φιλανθρωπίαν ἀσκοῦσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: counseled them, as people practicing humaneness, to have mercy on human beings insofar as they are human, even though through sin they become instruments of evil
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀσκοῦσιν is read as a dative plural participle referring to the implicitly counseled hearers. κακίας is taken with ὄργανα, while δι᾽ ἁμαρτίας identifies how people become such instruments. The concessive “even though” expresses the contrast between their humanity and their instrumental role.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as far as it lay with them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The idiom limits the action to what lies within their power. “As far as depended on them” is a more literal alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὥσπερ οἱ νήφοντες τοῖς μεθύουσιν βοηθῶσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: just as sober people help drunk people
lexical_decisions.rationale: Because νήφοντες is explicitly contrasted with μεθύουσιν, the literal sober-versus-drunk image is retained rather than generalized to “clear-minded.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: neither resisting nor retaliating
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀνθίστημι denotes resistance, while ἀμύνομαι can mean defending oneself or retaliating. The latter sense fits the repeated warning against returning harmful acts, though “nor defending themselves” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦ γὰρ παθεῖν πάντως κεκριμένου τινί
lexical_decisions.chosen: when suffering has in any event been decreed for someone
lexical_decisions.rationale: πάντως is understood as expressing inevitability in this argument. The genitive construction supplies the circumstance under which indignation is declared unreasonable.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Why, then, am I indignant with the one who brought it about
lexical_decisions.rationale: διατίθημι is elliptical here and refers to the person who occasioned the suffering. “The one who dealt with me this way” is another possible rendering.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ τὰ αὐτὰ τοῖς κακοῖς προφάσει ἀμύνης ποιῶμεν, παρὰ τὸ πρῶτοι δεύτεροι τὸ αὐτὸ τοῖς κακοῖς οἱ ἀγαθοὶ πράσσομεν.
lexical_decisions.chosen: if on the pretext of retaliation we do the same things as evil people, then, apart from being second rather than first, we who are good do the same thing as evil people
lexical_decisions.rationale: The datives τοῖς κακοῖς are comparative with τὰ αὐτά and τὸ αὐτό: the good do the same things as the evil, rather than doing those things to evil people. The compressed πρῶτοι δεύτεροι contrasts initiating the conduct with repeating it in response.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as people who insult God’s emissaries
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀπόστολοι is used generically for people functioning as sent agents, not necessarily for holders of the particular apostolic office. “Messengers” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τιμῶντες δὲ καὶ τὰ ἐναντία τοῖς ἀδικεῖν νομιζομένοις διατιθέμενοι αὐτοὺς
lexical_decisions.chosen: but those who honor them and treat them with the opposite of what is considered injurious
lexical_decisions.rationale: τοῖς ... νομιζομένοις is taken as neuter, referring to things considered injurious, which supplies a defensible comparison without adding a customary way in which wrongdoers are treated. A masculine construal is possible—“treating them in ways opposite to those regarded as doing wrong”—but leaves the exact relation of the comparison more compressed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς τὸν θεὸν τὸν οὕτω βουλευσάμενον εὐσεβοῦσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: act reverently toward God, who has so resolved
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὐσεβέω denotes reverent or pious conduct toward God. βουλεύομαι is understood as resolving or determining the providential arrangement; “who has planned it this way” is also possible.

passages.text: And in response I said, “Then those who do wrong are not responsible, since it is by God’s judgment that they wrong the righteous.” Peter said, “They most certainly do sin, for they have given themselves over to sinning. Therefore, with this knowledge, he chooses some from among them to punish justly those who have come to regret their former sins, so that, for the righteous, through punishment of this kind, the evil deeds done before their reorientation may be forgiven, while the ungodly punishers, who desire to maltreat others and are unwilling to reorient, have been permitted to maltreat the righteous in order to fill up the measure of their own penalty. For without God’s counsel not even a sparrow can fall into a trap; in the same way, even the hairs of the righteous are numbered by God.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅθεν εἰδὼς ἀπ᾽ αὐτῶν ἐκλέγεται τιμωρεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Therefore, with this knowledge, he chooses some from among them to punish
lexical_decisions.rationale: The subject is understood contextually as God, while the people chosen from among the wrongdoers are the understood subjects of the infinitive “to punish.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοὺς ἐπὶ τοῖς προτέροις ἁμαρτήμασιν μεταμεληθέντας δικαίως
lexical_decisions.chosen: those who have come to regret their former sins ... justly
lexical_decisions.rationale: μεταμέλομαι is distinguished from the subsequent μετάνοια language and rendered as regret. δικαίως is attached to the justice of the punishment; it could instead describe their regretting as rightly done.

lexical_decisions.chosen: before their reorientation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering follows the supplied terminology policy for μετάνοια while not adding an unstated destination such as “toward God.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: are unwilling to reorient
lexical_decisions.rationale: The moral redirection sense of μετανοεῖν is retained without an invented intensifier or destination.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in order to fill up the measure of their own penalty
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀναπλήρωσις denotes filling up or completing, while κόλασις here is the punishment accruing to the ungodly agents.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἄνευ γὰρ τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ βουλῆς οὐδὲ στρουθὸς ἐν παγίδι ἐνπεσεῖν ἔχει
lexical_decisions.chosen: without God’s counsel not even a sparrow can fall into a trap
lexical_decisions.rationale: βουλή is “counsel” or “purpose,” and the ἔχει plus infinitive construction is represented idiomatically by “can.” The explicitly named trap is retained.

passages.text: The righteous person is the one who, for the sake of what reason approves, fights against nature. For example, everyone has it by nature to love those who love them, but the righteous person tries also to love enemies, to bless those who revile him, and, moreover, to pray for enemies. He has mercy on those who wrong him; therefore he also refrains from wronging them in return. Likewise, he blesses those who curse him, gives way to those who strike him, withdraws before those who pursue him, greets those who do not greet him, shares what he has with those who have nothing, wins over the angry person, reconciles the enemy, exhorts the disobedient person, instructs the unbeliever, comforts the mourner, endures when abused, and does not become indignant when treated ungratefully. Having committed himself to loving his neighbor as himself, he has not feared poverty; rather, by distributing his own possessions to those who have nothing, he becomes poor. Nor, indeed, does he punish someone who sins. For the one who loves his neighbor as himself knows that, if he himself had sinned, he would not want to be punished; in the same way, he does not punish those who sin. And just as he wants to be flattered, blessed, and honored, and to have all his sins forgiven him, he himself does this same thing for his neighbor, because he loves that person as himself. In a word, what he wants for himself he also wants for his neighbor. For this is the law of God and of the prophets; this is the teaching of the truth. All this, then, is perfect love toward every human being and is the male part of humaneness, while showing mercy is its female part. This consists in feeding the hungry, providing drink to the thirsty, clothing the naked, visiting the sick, receiving a stranger, helping the person in prison to the extent possible while being sprinkled upon, and, in short, having mercy on anyone amid misfortunes.

source_issues.source_quote: τῷ ἐν εἱρκτῇ κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν ἐπιραινόμενον βοηθεῖν
source_issues.issue: The image-checked printed form ἐπιραινόμενον is an accusative singular middle/passive participle. It can belong to the understood accusative subject of βοηθεῖν, namely the person helping the prisoner, so the supplied wording admits the literal passive representation “while being sprinkled upon” without emendation. The middle alternative “while sprinkling oneself upon” is also formally possible. What the sprinkling signifies in this context remains uncertain, and no object or further explanation should be inferred from the wording alone.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ τοῦ εὐλόγου ἕνεκα τῇ φύσει μαχόμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who, for the sake of what reason approves, fights against nature
lexical_decisions.rationale: τὸ εὔλογον denotes what is reasonable or warranted by reason. The author’s image of conflict with nature is retained.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to love those who love them ... to love enemies
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first expression uses φιλέω reciprocally and the second uses ἀγαπάω. English “love” is used for both, while the distinct Greek roots and the contrast between natural reciprocity and enemy-love are disclosed here.

lexical_decisions.chosen: refrains from wronging them in return
lexical_decisions.rationale: The middle infinitive is understood contextually as retaliatory wrongdoing. A more formally passive reading, “refrains from being wronged further,” is grammatically possible but fits the surrounding acts of nonretaliation less readily.

lexical_decisions.chosen: gives way to those who strike him
lexical_decisions.rationale: συγχωρεῖ can mean either “gives way” or, in later usage, “forgives.” “Gives way” preserves the movement imagery reinforced by the following ὑποχωρεῖ, while “forgives those who strike him” remains a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς αὐτὸς ἁμαρτήσας οἶδεν τιμωρηθῆναι μὴ θέλειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: knows that, if he himself had sinned, he would not want to be punished
lexical_decisions.rationale: The aorist participle is read conditionally. It could instead refer to his actual past sin: “knows that, having himself sinned, he does not want to be punished.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: to be flattered
lexical_decisions.rationale: The potentially uncomfortable force of κολακεύω is preserved rather than softened to “treated kindly.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ ἄρρεν μέρος ... τὸ θῆλυ μέρος
lexical_decisions.chosen: the male part ... its female part
lexical_decisions.rationale: The author’s gendered division of perfect love and mercy is preserved without harmonization or explanation in the translation text.

lexical_decisions.chosen: humaneness
lexical_decisions.rationale: φιλανθρωπία denotes benevolence or love toward humanity; “humaneness” is used consistently here and in the following passage.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ ἐν εἱρκτῇ κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν ἐπιραινόμενον βοηθεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: helping the person in prison to the extent possible while being sprinkled upon
lexical_decisions.rationale: The accusative participle ἐπιραινόμενον is taken as agreeing with the understood accusative subject of βοηθεῖν—the helper—rather than with the dative prisoner. Its passive force is represented literally by “while being sprinkled upon.” A formally possible middle interpretation is “while sprinkling oneself upon,” but the contextual significance of either image remains uncertain.

passages.text: After hearing this, I said, “These things can be done, but I do not think that the ability to benefit enemies while enduring every outrage from them can belong to human nature.” Peter answered, “You have spoken correctly. For humaneness, since it is a cause of immortality, is given at great cost.” And I said, “How, then, can it be received into the mind?” Peter answered, “This, my friend Clement, can be acquired if someone becomes fully convinced that enemies who for a time maltreat those they hate become for those people the cause of release from eternal punishment; moreover, those people will love them intensely as benefactors. The path to acquiring this, my friend Clement, is one particular path: the fear of God. For at first the person who fears God cannot love his neighbor as himself, since such a thing does not enter the soul by command. Yet through fear directed toward God he can do what those who love do. Then, once he has thus performed the deeds of love, loving itself, like a bride, is presented to fear as to a bridegroom. And so, as she gives birth to humane thoughts, she makes the one who has acquired her immortal, as an image resembling God, his nature being incapable of violation by decay.” Likewise, after he had set out for us the discourse on humaneness, evening overtook us, and we turned to sleep.

source_issues.source_quote: ὁμῶς τὸν τῆς φιλανθρωπίας ἐκθεμένου ἡμῖν λόγον
source_issues.issue: The genitive singular aorist middle participle ἐκθεμένου, here meaning “having set out,” has no explicitly stated genitive subject; Peter is readily supplied from the preceding speech, and λόγον functions as its accusative object. The printed adverb ὁμῶς may mean “likewise,” “equally,” or “together,” whereas the concessive sense “all the same” would normally be written ὅμως. The supplied reading remains defensibly translatable without emendation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκ οἴομαι δυνατὸν ἀνθρωπείᾳ προσεῖναι φύσει
lexical_decisions.chosen: I do not think that the ability ... can belong to human nature
lexical_decisions.rationale: προσεῖναι expresses being present in or belonging to something; δυνατός supplies the ability whose presence in human nature Clement doubts.

lexical_decisions.chosen: humaneness ... is given at great cost
lexical_decisions.rationale: πολλοῦ δίδοται presents humaneness as something obtained for much or at a high price, not as something easily granted.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Πῶς οὖν σύνεστιν ἐν νῷ λαβεῖν;
lexical_decisions.chosen: How, then, can it be received into the mind?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves both acquisition language in λαβεῖν and the explicitly mental location ἐν νῷ. The question may more idiomatically mean, “How, then, can one acquire it?”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αἰωνίου κολάσεως ἀπαλλαγῆς αὐτοῖς αἴτιοι γίνονται· προσέτι δὲ αὐτοὺς ὡς εὐεργέτας σφόδρα ἀγαπήσουσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: become for those people the cause of release from eternal punishment; moreover, those people will love them intensely as benefactors
lexical_decisions.rationale: The sufferers are taken as the referents of αὐτοῖς and as the understood subject of ἀγαπήσουσιν, while αὐτούς refers back to the enemies. Repeating “those people” makes the selected referents clear without changing the claim.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπεὶ τὸ τοιοῦτο κελεύσει οὐ προσέρχεται τῇ ψυχῇ
lexical_decisions.chosen: since such a thing does not enter the soul by command
lexical_decisions.rationale: κελεύσει is taken instrumentally: love does not arise in the soul merely through being commanded.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ ἀγαπᾶν ὡς νύμφη οὖσα προσφέρεται ὡς νυμφίῳ τῷ φόβῳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: loving itself, like a bride, is presented to fear as to a bridegroom
lexical_decisions.rationale: The personification and bridal image are preserved. τὸ ἀγαπᾶν is formally an infinitive, so “loving itself” retains the emphasis on the act or condition of loving.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as she gives birth to humane thoughts
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine pronoun follows the immediately preceding bride imagery, and τίκτουσα retains the explicit image of giving birth.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς εἰκόνα θεοῦ ὁμοίαν, ὑπὸ φθορᾶς ὑβρισθῆναι μὴ δυναμένην τὴν αὐτοῦ φύσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: as an image resembling God, his nature being incapable of violation by decay
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὁμοίαν is taken with the image as resembling God. ὑβρίζω is rendered “violation” to preserve its stronger force than simple damage, while φθορά is “decay” or “corruption.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁμῶς τὸν τῆς φιλανθρωπίας ἐκθεμένου ἡμῖν λόγον
lexical_decisions.chosen: Likewise, after he had set out for us the discourse on humaneness
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐκθεμένου is a genitive singular aorist middle participle of ἐκτίθημι, here carrying the transitive sense “having set out.” Peter is supplied contextually as its understood subject, and λόγον is its accusative object. The printed ὁμῶς is rendered “likewise”; “together” or “equally” remains possible.

passages.text: At dawn Peter came in and said, “Let Clement, his mother Mattidia, and my wife sit together in the carriage.” And so it was done. As we set out on the road toward Balaneae, my mother asked me how my father was doing. I said, “He went away in search of you and my twin brothers, Faustinus and Faustinianus, and cannot be found. I think he has died, given how long it has been, either suffering shipwreck, meeting disaster on the road, or wasting away with grief.” When she heard this, she became tearful and sighed in sorrow. Yet her joy at finding me somewhat softened the grief the recollection brought. We arrived at Balaneae. On the following day we came to Paltus, and from there to Gabala; on the next we arrived at Laodicea. There, before the gates, Nicetas and Aquila met us, kissed us warmly and led us to our lodging. Seeing that it was a fine, large city, Peter said, “It is worthwhile to stay here for some days, for generally a large population is better able to produce the people being sought.” Nicetas and Aquila asked me who this unfamiliar woman was. I said, “My mother, whom God granted me to recognize through my master Peter.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: given how long it has been
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase is read temporally, with a long interval understood from the father’s unresolved absence: that elapsed time grounds Clement’s inference of death. “Most likely” is a possible probability-oriented rendering, but it does not directly preserve the contextual basis in elapsed time; the revised main text therefore prefers the temporal interpretation. Death remains an inference expressed by “I think,” not verified knowledge.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the people being sought
lexical_decisions.rationale: Peter’s generalization about a crowd can refer to missing persons in this recognition narrative; it can also mean the people sought for his mission. The main text does not specify which group.

lexical_decisions.chosen: my master Peter
lexical_decisions.rationale: κύριος here is a respectful human title for Peter, not an identification with the divine Lord. “My lord Peter” is the more formal alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ καταφιλήσαντες ἦγον ἐπὶ τὴν ξενίαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: kissed us warmly and led us to our lodging
lexical_decisions.rationale: καταφιλήσαντες expresses affectionate kissing; no separate embrace is added. The source elsewhere distinctly names embraces when it intends them.

passages.text: After I said this, Peter gave them a summary of everything: how, as soon as they had gone ahead, I, Clement, had told him about my family; about my mother’s departure with her twin children on the fabricated pretext of the dream; and also about my father’s departure to search for her. Then he told how he himself, Peter, after hearing these things, went onto the island, encountered the woman, saw her begging, and asked the reason for her begging. He learned her family background, her way of life, the fabricated dream, and the children’s names—mine, the one left with my father, and those of the twin children who traveled with her—and how they were supposed to have died in the depths.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ὡς ἐν βυθῷ ὑπενοεῖτο τεθνηκέναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: and how they were supposed to have died in the depths
lexical_decisions.rationale: The subject of the infinitive is unexpressed and the finite verb singular can be impersonal. The main text links the supposed death to the twin children just named; a reference to the mother as one presumed dead is also possible. The supposition is not presented as an actual death.

passages.text: After Peter had related these things in summary, Nicetas and Aquila were astounded and said, “Master and Lord of all, is this true, or is it a dream?” Peter said, “If we are not asleep, it is true.” After a short pause for thought, they said, “We are Faustinus and Faustinianus. From the beginning of your account, we looked at one another and made many conjectures about ourselves, wondering whether what was being said might not concern us, while reflecting that many similar things happen in life. That is why we kept silent, our hearts pounding. But when we looked to the end of the account and saw that what was being said concerned us, then we disclosed who we were.” Saying this, they went in to their mother in tears, found her sleeping, and wanted to embrace her at once. But Peter stopped them, saying, “Let me bring you in and present you to your mother, so that the great sudden joy does not drive her out of her senses, since she is asleep and her spirit is occupied by sleep.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἆρά γε, δέσποτα καὶ κύριε τῶν ἁπάντων
lexical_decisions.chosen: Master and Lord of all
lexical_decisions.rationale: The address is retained without adding an explicit “God”; the wording can be an exclamation addressed to the universal divine ruler within the dialogue. It is not silently made an assertion that Peter rules everything.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μὴ ἄρα οὐχ ἡμῖν διαφέρει τὰ λεγόμενα
lexical_decisions.chosen: wondering whether what was being said might not concern us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The nested interrogative/negative particles convey their hesitant recognition. The English “might not” keeps the negated question without imposing a uniquely certain expected answer.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ πνεῦμα ὑπὸ τοῦ ὕπνου ἀπησχολημένον
lexical_decisions.chosen: her spirit is occupied by sleep
lexical_decisions.rationale: πνεῦμα may be spirit or the animating breath; no modern theory of unconsciousness is added.

passages.text: When she had had enough sleep and awakened, Peter began speaking with my mother about reverence for God, saying first, “Woman, I want you to know the way of life of our religion. We worship one God, who made the world you see, and we keep his law. Its first requirements include worshiping him alone, treating his name as holy, honoring parents, being chaste, and living pleasantly. In addition, since we do not live without distinctions, we do not partake of the nations’ table; indeed, we cannot even dine with them, because they live impurely. But whenever we persuade them to think and do what belongs to the truth, and baptize them with a certain thrice-blessed invocation, then we gather at table with them. Even if someone happens to be a father, mother, wife, child, brother, or anyone else who feels natural affection, we cannot dare to dine with that person: we do this as a distinctive religious practice. So do not regard your son’s not dining with you as an insult, until you think and do the same things as he does.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: living pleasantly
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied adjective’s adverbial form refers to pleasant living; it is not changed to a conjectural “uprightly” or made a command to indulgence.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with a certain thrice-blessed invocation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The singular description of a naming or invocation is retained; no specific baptismal formula or persons are supplied.

lexical_decisions.chosen: we do this as a distinctive religious practice
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression can also be understood as “we do this especially on religious grounds.” The main wording keeps the religious distinction and does not present the rule as a universal modern obligation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἢ ἄλλος τις ἐκ φύσεως στοργὴν ἔχων
lexical_decisions.chosen: or anyone else who feels natural affection
lexical_decisions.rationale: The active participle ἔχων makes that other person the holder of affection. Its object is unexpressed and is not replaced by a different, unnamed person who feels affection toward this one.

passages.text: When she heard this, she said, “What, then, prevents me from being baptized today? Before I saw you, I turned away from the so-called gods with this reasoning: though I made many sacrifices to them almost every day, they did not stand beside me in my needs. And what need is there even to speak about adultery? Not even when I was rich did luxury deceive me into it, nor has the poverty that followed been able to force me into it. I have held fast to chastity as the greatest beauty, and because of it I came into such distress. Nor do I think you are unaware, my master Peter, that greater desire comes from good spirits. Therefore, having remained chaste in good spirits, I do not sell myself to pleasures in dejection. But do not suppose that even now my soul is free of suffering, though it has received some consolation through recognizing Clement. For the grief over my two children comes back in and dims even that limited joy. What grieves us is not so much that these children were lost at sea as that, without divine reverence toward God, their bodies were destroyed along with their souls as well. Their father, my husband, as I learned from Clement, went away to search for both me and our sons and has been missing for so many years; he has certainly died. For the poor man loved me because of chastity and loved his children. Thus, deprived of all of us, whom he loved above everything, the old man perished through the greatest despondency.”

source_issues.source_quote: λυπεῖ γὰρ ἡμᾶς οὐ τοσοῦτον τὸ ἐν τῇ θαλάσσῃ τούτους παραπολέσθαι, ὅσον τὸ χωρὶς τῆς θείας εἰς θεὸν εὐσεβείας διαφθαρῆναι μετά γε τῶν ψυχῶν αὐτοῖς καὶ τὰ σώματα. παραινέσω μὲν γὰρ περὶ αὐτῶν ὅτι ἐν θαλάσσῃ διεφώνησαν, ἀλλ’ οὐχ ὅτι πρὸς τούτοις ἐκτὸς τειχῶν θρησκείας θεοῦ φθαρέντες τὰ σώματα καὶ τὰς ψυχὰς ἀπώλοντο.
source_issues.issue: Verified layout correction: Lagarde 1865 printed page 135, PDF page 177, prints these as TWO parallel alternative readings, not two successive statements. Main English uses the complete left reading. Complete alternative RIGHT reading, replacing that sentence only: “For I will offer counsel concerning them, that they perished in the sea, but not that, in addition to this, being destroyed in their bodies outside the walls of worship of God, they also lost their souls.” After either alternative, the common speech resumes with the children’s father and husband. No manuscript-siglum attribution is invented from the transcription. The former interleaved source sequence is preserved here exactly as a provenance record, NOT as a coherent ancient sentence: λυπεῖ γὰρ ἡμᾶς οὐ τοσοῦτον τὸ ἐν παραινέσω μὲν γὰρ περὶ αὐτῶν ὅτι ἐν τῇ θαλάσσῃ τούτους παραπολέσθαι, θαλάσσῃ διεφώνησαν, ἀλλ’ οὐχ ὅτι ὅσον τὸ χωρὶς τῆς θείας εἰς θεὸν εὐσε- πρὸς τούτοις ἐκτὸς τειχῶν θρησκείας βείας διαφθαρῆναι μετά γε τῶν ψυχῶν θεοῦ φθαρέντες τὰ σώματα καὶ τὰς αὐτοῖς καὶ τὰ σώματα. ψυχὰς ἀπώλοντο. The corrected order comes from independent image evidence and changes the reading order, not any surviving Greek word. The earlier syntactic blocker concerned this wrongly interleaved sequence; it is reassessed because the verified layout now distinguishes the two complete alternatives, not merely to obtain acceptance.

source_issues.source_quote: παραινέσω μὲν γὰρ περὶ αὐτῶν ὅτι ἐν θαλάσσῃ διεφώνησαν, ἀλλ’ οὐχ ὅτι πρὸς τούτοις ἐκτὸς τειχῶν θρησκείας θεοῦ φθαρέντες τὰ σώματα καὶ τὰς ψυχὰς ἀπώλοντο.
source_issues.issue: In the separately labelled right alternative, παραινέσω is future, “I will offer counsel,” not a rewritten “I am consoled” or “I accept.” The following ὅτι clauses are construed as the content about which counsel is offered: sea-death, contrasted with losing souls as well outside God’s worship. A causal attachment of ὅτι could instead present those matters as reasons for the counselling; that remains possible. φθαρέντες τὰ σώματα is taken with the accusative of respect, “being destroyed in their bodies,” followed by “they also lost their souls.” The expression “outside the walls of worship of God” retains the source’s unusual walls metaphor. The wording is not replaced with the left reading’s cleaner comparison, and no theological reconciliation is supplied.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πολλὰ σχεδὸν καθ’ ἡμέραν θυούσης αὐτοῖς
lexical_decisions.chosen: though I made many sacrifices to them almost every day
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverb σχεδόν modifies the regularity, while πολλὰ preserves the many offerings. The concessive relationship comes from the contrast with the gods’ failure to help, not from an added claim about what was sacrificed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: from good spirits
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὐθυμία denotes cheerfulness or confident spirits; “prosperity” is a contextual alternative given the contrast of wealth and poverty. The main text retains the paired contrast with δυσθυμία, dejection, rather than uniquely identifying the cause as wealth.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I do not sell myself
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb can denote selling or giving oneself over. The poverty and sexual context supports “sell myself,” while “give myself over” remains possible. No sexual details are added.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: λυπεῖ γὰρ ἡμᾶς οὐ τοσοῦτον τὸ ἐν τῇ θαλάσσῃ τούτους παραπολέσθαι, ὅσον τὸ χωρὶς τῆς θείας εἰς θεὸν εὐσεβείας διαφθαρῆναι μετά γε τῶν ψυχῶν αὐτοῖς καὶ τὰ σώματα.
lexical_decisions.chosen: What grieves us is not so much that these children were lost at sea as that, without divine reverence toward God, their bodies were destroyed along with their souls as well
lexical_decisions.rationale: This is the complete left parallel reading, selected for the main English rather than combined with the right column as consecutive speech. The negative comparison, sea-loss, lack of divine reverence toward God, bodies, and souls are all retained. The dative αὐτοῖς is reflected in “their bodies,” with the bodies as the subject of destruction. παραπολέσθαι conveys their being lost or perishing; the compound may suggest perishing together or being additionally lost, but no separate unnamed casualty is supplied. The woman’s belief that the children died is not changed into a claim that they actually died.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὸ σωφροσύνης με ἀγαπῶν φιλότεκνος ἦν
lexical_decisions.chosen: loved me because of chastity and loved his children
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first causal description is retained rather than weakened to a merely chaste manner of loving. φιλότεκνος describes affection for children; the main text expresses it directly without adding a legal or familial status.

passages.text: While my mother was saying this, the boys, who were listening as Peter had advised, could no longer contain themselves. They stood up and embraced her, weeping abundantly and covering her with kisses. She said, “What does this mean?” Peter answered, “Woman, steady your mind courageously, so that you may enjoy your children. These are your sons Faustinus and Faustinianus, whom you said had died in the depths. How they are alive, after dying in your presence on that extremely dreadful night, and how one of them is now called Nicetas and the other Aquila, they themselves will be able to tell you. We too have to learn it along with you.” When Peter said this, my mother was so overjoyed that she nearly died from faintness. When we revived her, she sat down, came to herself, and said, “My longed-for children, please tell us what happened to you after that terrible night.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: after dying in your presence
lexical_decisions.rationale: Peter echoes her belief about the shipwreck rather than independently asserting an actual death and resurrection. “Having died as far as you were concerned” is a contextual alternative; the main text keeps the sharper surviving wording.

lexical_decisions.chosen: on that extremely dreadful night
lexical_decisions.rationale: χαλεπωτάτῃ is superlative and may have elative force, “extremely dreadful.” This preserves its intensification while not requiring a uniquely worst night. “Most dreadful” is the formal superlative alternative; the later positive χαλεπή remains “terrible.”

passages.text: Nicetas, henceforth Faustinus, began to speak: “That very night, when the ship was breaking apart, as you know, some men who were not afraid to plunder in the depths picked us up and put us in a boat. Rowing, they took us sometimes along the shore and sometimes sent for provisions, bringing us to Strato’s Caesarea. There, with us weeping from hunger, fear, and blows—all to keep us from rashly saying anything they did not want said—and after also changing our names, they managed to sell us. A very distinguished woman named Justa, a convert to the Jews, bought us, kept us in the place of children, and diligently educated us in every branch of Greek learning. As we grew up and became sensible, we loved the religion and applied ourselves to learning, so that in discussions with the other nations we could expose their error. We also mastered the philosophers’ teachings, especially the most godless—I mean those of Epicurus and Pyrrho—so that we could refute them more effectively.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: kept us in the place of children
