lexical_decisions.rationale: Their purchase and subsequent treatment are both retained. The text does not explicitly describe a legal adoption or manumission.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the most godless
lexical_decisions.rationale: The superlative belongs to the narrator’s evaluation of the philosophers, not an added evaluation by the translator.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κἀκεῖ δακρύοντας ἡμᾶς λιμῷ φόβῳ τε καὶ πληγαῖς, ὅπως μή τι προπετὲς λαλήσωμεν τῶν αὐτοῖς μὴ δοκούντων, ἔτι δὲ καὶ τὰ ὀνόματα ἡμῶν ἀλλάξαντες, πωλῆσαι ἠδυνήθησαν.
lexical_decisions.chosen: with us weeping from hunger, fear, and blows—all to keep us from rashly saying anything they did not want said—and after also changing our names, they managed to sell us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative hunger, fear, and blows accounts for the children’s weeping and coercive treatment, rather than directly describing the means of a sale. The ὅπως-clause gives the purpose of that coercion; the subsequent renaming is introduced as an additional act. The revision keeps those attachments instead of assigning the speech-prevention purpose exclusively to renaming.

passages.text: “Having become almost companions from childhood with a certain magician, Simon, we came close to being deceived through friendship. There is an account about a certain man: when he appears in kingship, the [ὁ ... ων] of those who have revered God will be able to live immortally and without pain. But these things, mother, will be explained to you more precisely at the proper time. Just when we were about to be deceived by Simon, a companion of our master Peter, called Zacchaeus, took us in and warned us not to be deceived by the magician. When Peter arrived, he brought us to him, so that, by giving us full assurance, he might persuade us about the matters pertaining to reverence for God. Therefore, mother, we also pray that you may share in the good things we have been granted, so that we may partake of salt and table together. This, then, mother, is why you thought we had died: on that extremely dreadful night pirates carried us off on the open sea, while you supposed we had perished.”

source_issues.issue: The edition prints a three-dot gap with surviving ὁ and ων around it. These are retained literally as [ὁ ... ων], without restoring a person, group, or participle. The surrounding phrase is therefore visibly incomplete; the missing content has not been recovered.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in kingship
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase may indicate appearing in royal rule or within a kingdom; the main text chooses the former without supplying a realm or identifying the man.

lexical_decisions.chosen: salt and table
lexical_decisions.rationale: The concrete shared-meal language is retained rather than reduced to social friendship.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὗ φανέντος ἐν βασιλείᾳ τῶν θεοσεβησάντων ὁ ... ων ἀθανάτως καὶ ἀλύπως βιῶσαι ἔχει
lexical_decisions.chosen: when he appears in kingship, the [ὁ ... ων] of those who have revered God will be able to live immortally and without pain
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text attaches τῶν θεοσεβησάντων, “of those who have revered God,” to the incomplete subject marked by ὁ ... ων. This is supported by the contrast between the appearing man and the group benefiting from immortal, painless life, but it does not restore that subject’s missing letters. A material alternative attaches the genitive to βασιλείᾳ: “when he appears in the kingdom/kingship of those who have revered God, the [ὁ ... ων] will be able to live immortally and without pain.” Neither attachment is uniquely established; the three-dot gap remains unchanged and no lost wording is supplied.

lexical_decisions.chosen: on that extremely dreadful night
lexical_decisions.rationale: The superlative χαλεπωτάτῃ can be elative, “extremely dreadful,” as in 13.6. This preserves its intensity without requiring that this was the uniquely worst night. “Most dreadful” is the formal superlative alternative.

passages.text: After Faustinus said this, our mother fell at Peter’s feet, begging and requesting that he send for her hostess and baptize both her and the hostess immediately. “Let there be no day,” she said, “from the time I have recovered my own children, on which I am deprived of dining with them.” When we too joined our mother in pleading for this, Peter said, “What do you think? Am I alone unfeeling, because I do not want you to dine with your mother after I have baptized her today? But she must fast at least one day before being baptized. Even this is because she simply uttered a statement on her own behalf that I recognized as a sufficient expression of her faith; otherwise she needs many days to be weaned from Greek religion.”

source_issues.source_quote: ἀφ’ ἧς τὰ ἐμαυτῆς. ἀπέλαβον τέκνα
source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a full stop after ἐμαυτῆς, interrupting the continuous grammatical connection with ἀπέλαβον τέκνα. The English reads the surviving words continuously as “from the time I have recovered my own children.” The supplied Greek and its printed punctuation are not changed; no missing wording is restored. This is a disclosed editorial punctuation feature, not an assertion of OCR error or publication-blocking source corruption.

lexical_decisions.chosen: she needs many days to be weaned from Greek religion
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb denotes being de-Hellenized, here in a discussion of religious preparation, not renouncing Greek language or ethnicity. “To be freed from pagan practice” is an alternative but less transparent about the Greek category.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after I have baptized her today
lexical_decisions.rationale: The nominative singular participle agrees with Peter, the speaker. The English explicitly makes him the baptizer, not the children. Its event is within the rhetorical question’s contemplated action, not a statement that baptism has already occurred.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅπως αὐτήν τε καὶ τὴν ξενοδόχον αὐτῆς μεταπεμψάμενος ἐξαυτῆς βαπτίσῃ
lexical_decisions.chosen: that he send for her hostess and baptize both her and the hostess immediately
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text construes the summoning participle as directed to the hostess and the finite baptism verb as directed to both women, because the mother is already before Peter pleading. The coordinated accusatives can more broadly be objects of both verbs: “that he summon her and her hostess and baptize them immediately.” This material alternative is preserved; the narrower participial attachment is contextual rather than uniquely expressed by the Greek, and the source is not changed.

passages.text: I said, “Tell us what statement she uttered that revealed her faith.” Peter said, “Her request that the hostess who had been her benefactor be baptized with her. She would not have asked for this to be given to the woman she loved unless she herself had first come to regard the gift of baptism as something great. Therefore I condemn many people when, after being baptized and saying that they believe, they do nothing worthy of faith and do not urge even those they love—I mean their wives, sons, or friends—to this. For if they have believed that God grants eternal life at baptism together with good deeds, they would without delay have urged those they loved to be baptized. But one of you will say, ‘They love them and care for them.’ This is foolish. Why, then, when they see them ill, being led away to death, or suffering other terrible things, do they lament and pity them? In the same way, if they had believed that eternal fire awaits those who do not worship God, they would not have stopped admonishing them, or, when they saw them disobedient, grieving over them as unbelievers, being fully assured of the punishment against them. Now, then, I will send for the hostess and question her whether she chooses to love the law conveyed through us, and then we will do what is required accordingly.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ζωὴν αἰώνιον σὺν ἔργοις καλοῖς δωρεῖσθαι τὸν θεὸν ἐπὶ τῷ βαπτίσματι
lexical_decisions.chosen: God grants eternal life at baptism together with good deeds
lexical_decisions.rationale: σὺν ἔργοις καλοῖς is preserved alongside baptism; it can qualify the granting as connected with good works or characterize the life/gift together with them. The text’s combination is not recast as baptism only symbolizing or independently causing salvation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: This is foolish
lexical_decisions.rationale: εὔηθες can mean simple or naive as well as foolish; here it challenges the adequacy of an objection, not their loved ones’ intelligence.

passages.text: “Since your mother approaches baptism with faith, let her fast at least one day before baptism.” But she swore, “For two of the days that have passed, while telling the woman about the recognition, I was unable to partake of food because of my great joy, except for a little water yesterday alone.” Peter’s wife testified to her oath, saying, “She has indeed tasted nothing.” Aquila—or rather, henceforth Faustinianus—said, “Then nothing prevents her from being baptized.” Peter laughed and answered, “But this is not a baptismal fast, since it did not take place for that purpose.” Faustinus answered, “Perhaps, then, God, wishing our mother not to be separated from the table for even one day after recognizing us, arranged the fast beforehand. For just as she remained chaste in ignorance, doing what accords with the truth, so perhaps God has now arranged for her to fast a day beforehand, in ignorance, for the sake of the true baptism, so that from the very first day of recognizing us she may partake of salt with us.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: since it did not take place for that purpose
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied ἤ literally introduces “or.” The main English “since it did not take place for that purpose” treats this as an explanatory reformulation: the earlier abstention is not a baptismal fast precisely because it was not undertaken for baptism. A more source-transparent explanatory disjunction is “But this is not a baptismal fast—or, rather, it did not take place for that purpose.” This preserves the printed disjunctive form while making the reformulation readable. “Unless it took place for that purpose” is only a contextual paraphrase of the criterion, not a direct alternative rendering of the printed ἢ μὴ clause and not a different Greek reading. No source correction is asserted.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a day beforehand
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine day is understood from the surrounding fasting discussion; no longer duration is added.

passages.text: Peter said, “Let not evil overcome us by taking care and a mother’s affection as a pretext. Rather, let us—you, and I with you—hold out for today, and tomorrow she will be baptized. Indeed, the hour of today is not suitable for baptism.” And we all agreed together that it should be done this way.

lexical_decisions.chosen: evil
lexical_decisions.rationale: This can be abstract badness or personified evil. The main text leaves the personification without explicitly naming a devil.

lexical_decisions.chosen: let us—you, and I with you—hold out for today
lexical_decisions.rationale: The shared exhortation and repeated reference to “you” are both retained in grammatical English. The text calls for holding out through the day; no new independent baptismal requirement is supplied.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρόφασιν εὑροῦσα τὴν πρόνοιαν καὶ τεκούσης στοργήν
lexical_decisions.chosen: by taking care and a mother’s affection as a pretext
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόνοια can mean care, concern, or forethought, as well as providence. Its pairing here with a mother’s affection supports ordinary care as the excuse Peter warns against; the source does not name whose care it is. “By finding a pretext in providence and a mother’s affection” remains a lexical alternative, particularly in light of Faustinus’s preceding proposal of divine arrangement. The main text does not uniquely impose divine governance as the meaning.

passages.text: That very evening we all enjoyed Peter’s teaching. From the occasion provided by our mother, he showed us why the outcomes of chastity are good, whereas those of adultery, being grievous, naturally bring destruction upon an entire family, if not quickly, then at least eventually. “Chastity,” he said, “is so pleasing to God that even to those who are in error he assigns some small favor for it in the present life. For salvation there is given only to those who have been baptized because of their hope in him and who act righteously with chastity. You have seen this happen in your mother’s case—I mean the good outcomes. Perhaps, had she committed adultery, she would have been killed. Therefore, because she remained chaste, God had mercy on her, averted the murder directed against her, and restored the children who had been taken away.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: an entire family
lexical_decisions.rationale: γένος may also mean lineage or kind; the family-recognition narrative supports the family sense here.

lexical_decisions.chosen: salvation there
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contrast with the present life points beyond this life; the English retains the deictic “there” instead of adding a named place.

passages.text: “But perhaps someone will say, ‘How many have perished because of chastity?’ I say it was because of insensibility. For a woman who becomes aware, or who finds that someone has become a suitor, must immediately flee association with him as she would a blazing fire or a rabid dog. This is what your mother did, truly loving the beauty of chastity. Therefore she was preserved and received with us the knowledge of the eternal kingdom. A woman who wants to remain chaste must know that, envied by evil, she has many who plot against her under the pretext of love. Yet by the single resolve to remain chaste, continuing honorable and gaining victory over them all, she will be able to be saved. For the prophet said that, even if someone does every good thing, for the single sin of committing adultery one must be punished.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν αἰσθανομένην ἢ γενομένου τινὸς ἐραστοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: a woman who becomes aware, or who finds that someone has become a suitor
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text carries the perception expressed by αἰσθανομένην into the second alternative by ellipsis: “who finds” is not a second printed perception verb. γενομένου τινὸς ἐραστοῦ is a genitive absolute stating someone’s becoming a suitor. A viable alternative retains it as a circumstance of the required flight: “For the woman who becomes aware—or when someone has become a suitor—must immediately flee association with him.” The main text instead treats both alternatives as ways the danger becomes apparent, supported by the initial perception language and immediate call to flee. The printed ἤ is retained in both analyses. A smoother “who notices that someone has become a lover” suppresses that disjunction and is therefore only a paraphrase, not a direct rendering of this edition. ἐραστής can mean pursuing lover or suitor, not necessarily someone whose advances have been accepted.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by evil
lexical_decisions.rationale: The agent can be personified evil or human wickedness; no particular demon or person is supplied.

passages.text: “The chaste woman, doing God’s will, becomes a good reminder of his first creation: God, being one, created one woman for one man. She remains still more chaste if she does not forget the creation, foresees the punishment, and is not unaware of the loss of eternal good things. The chaste woman, delighting in those who wish to be saved, is a reverent example to those who revere God, for she is a rule of good living. The woman who wishes to remain chaste cuts off occasions for abuse. But if she is abused without giving an occasion, as by an enemy, God blesses and vindicates her. The chaste woman longs for God, loves God, delights God, glorifies God; she gives people no occasion for abuse. The chaste woman perfumes the assembly with good honor and glorifies it by her dignity. She is also the teachers’ praise and works alongside them as they exercise chastity.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: a rule
lexical_decisions.rationale: The woman embodies a norm or rule of good living; she is not made a new written statute.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the assembly
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun denotes the gathered community, not specifically its building or an institution of a later era.

lexical_decisions.chosen: works alongside them as they exercise chastity
lexical_decisions.rationale: σωφρονοῦσι agrees with the teachers as a dative participle. It can also imply her collaboration with them in fostering chastity; the main reading keeps their own chastity explicit.

passages.text: “The chaste woman adorns herself for the Son of God as for a bridegroom, clothed in the honorable light. Her beauty is the good order within her soul. She breathes a perfume: her good reputation. She is clothed in beautiful head-coverings, modesty, and wears precious pearls, the words that teach chastity. She is white when her understanding has been made radiant. She looks in a beautiful mirror, gazing upon God. She uses beautiful adornment, instructing her soul through fear toward God. Beautiful is the woman who is not shackled with gold but freed from desires for temporary things. The chaste woman is greatly desired by a great king; she is betrothed to him, kept for him, loved by him. The chaste woman gives no occasion for being desired except by her own husband. The chaste woman is distressed when desired by another. The chaste woman loves her husband inwardly, kisses him affectionately, flatters him, pleases him, serves him, and obeys him in everything except disobeying God. For the woman who obeys God is chaste in soul and pure in body even without guards.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: λευκὴ δὲ τυγχάνει, ὅταν τὰς φρένας ᾖ λελαμπτρυμμένη
lexical_decisions.chosen: She is white when her understanding has been made radiant
lexical_decisions.rationale: The whiteness is part of the preceding apparel/adornment imagery and is explicitly connected to the mind. It is not rendered as a claim about skin color.

lexical_decisions.chosen: loves her husband inwardly
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐνδιαθέτως marks inward disposition or sincere affection. “From the heart” is an idiomatic alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: serves him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb is stronger than occasional assistance and can denote servile service. The hierarchical marital claim remains the ancient speaker’s; it is not softened into equal partnership or supplemented with a claim of legal ownership.

passages.text: “Foolish, then, is every man who separates his own wife from fear of God. For the woman who does not fear God does not fear her husband either. If she does not fear God, who sees invisible things, how will she keep her invisible choice chaste? And how will she remain chaste if she does not come to hear the words that teach chastity? How could she receive admonition? How will she remain chaste without guards if she is not taught about God’s coming judgment and is not fully assured of the eternal loss that follows a little pleasure? Therefore, on the contrary, compel her, even unwilling, always to attend the discourse that teaches chastity; coax her.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: her invisible choice
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase concerns an inward decision or intention not visible to people. “Her inward will” is another rendering.

lexical_decisions.chosen: even unwilling
lexical_decisions.rationale: The coercive force of ἀνάγκασον, compel, and the wife’s unwillingness are both retained as the speaker’s instruction, not softened to a consensual invitation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: coax her
lexical_decisions.rationale: The imperative can mean flatter or cajole; the persuasion does not erase the preceding command to compel.

passages.text: “Much better still, if you lead her by the hand and come, so that you too may become chaste. For you will wish to become chaste so that you may know the outcome of honorable marriage—and you will not shrink back if you love, I mean, becoming a father, loving your own children, and being loved by your own children. A man who wants a chaste wife is himself chaste. He renders the goodwill he owes, eats with her, is with her, comes with her to the discourse that teaches chastity, does not grieve her, does not quarrel without cause, does not make himself hateful, and provides whatever good things he can. What he does not have, he makes up for with affectionate persuasion. The chaste woman does not wait to be coaxed; she recognizes her husband as master, bears his poverty when he is poor, goes hungry with him when he is hungry, travels away with him when he travels away, comforts him when he is distressed, and, even if she has a larger dowry, submits as though she had nothing. The husband, even if his wife is poor, should consider her chastity a great dowry. The chaste woman uses a sufficient amount of food and drink, so that, when her body has grown fat, she is not dragged down in her soul by its weight toward unlawful desires. Moreover, she does not spend time alone with young men and is suspicious of old men. She rejects disorderly laughter; assigning herself to God alone, she does not stumble. She delights in hearing honorable words and rejects those not spoken for chastity.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: the goodwill he owes
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase denotes owed goodwill or benevolence; a specifically sexual marital duty can be contextually heard but is not named.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with affectionate persuasion
lexical_decisions.rationale: The same root as “coax” can mean flattery or cajoling. Here it makes up for absent material goods; the main text does not change it into financial compensation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: she is not dragged down in her soul
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive is preserved with τὴν ψυχήν as accusative of respect. The isolated dot before τὴν is printed punctuation, not a multi-dot lacuna; it is not represented as missing wording.

passages.text: “God is witness: one adultery is many murders. And the dreadful thing is that the terrifying and impious nature of its murders is not seen. For when blood has been shed, a dead body lies there, and the horror of the calamity shocks everyone. But adultery’s murders of the soul, though more fearful, because people do not see them, give those who dare an unhesitating impulse. Know, human being, whose breath you have for life, and you will certainly not want it to be defiled. God’s breath is defiled by adultery alone, and for this reason it brings the one who defiled it into fire: it hastens to hand the offender over to eternal punishment.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: one adultery is many murders
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compressed equation and its force are preserved as the speaker’s metaphorical claim about souls, not reduced to merely causing unhappiness.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by adultery alone
lexical_decisions.rationale: The exclusivity is explicit and retained, without harmonizing it with broader accounts of sin.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτὴ τὸν μιάναντα εἰς πῦρ καταστᾷ
lexical_decisions.chosen: it brings the one who defiled it into fire
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine pronoun refers grammatically to God’s breath. It is not silently replaced by a different subject such as God or the sinner.

passages.text: As Peter was saying this, he saw the good and chaste Mattidia weeping for joy. Thinking that she had become sorrowful at the recollection of what had happened, he said, “Take courage, woman. While many have suffered many evils because of adultery, you have not suffered because of chastity, and for this reason you did not die. And even if you had died, you would have had your soul saved. Did you leave your homeland, Rome, because of chastity? Yet through that occasion you found truth, the diadem of the everlasting kingdom. Have you been in danger in the depths? Yet you did not die, and if you had died, the depths themselves would have become baptism for you, dying for chastity, toward your soul’s salvation. Were you separated from your children? For a little while: coming from legitimate seed, they have been found in better circumstances. Did you beg for food while starving? Yet you did not defile your body through prostitution. Did you torment your body? Yet you saved your soul. Did you flee an adulterer so as not to defile your husband’s bed? Yet, because of chastity, God, who knows of your flight, will fill the husband’s place. Were you grieved and left alone, separated for a little while from husband and children? Yet you were bound to leave them all at death’s appointed time. Better that you were separated willingly because of chastity than that, later, unwillingly, you should perish because of those very sins.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: you have not suffered because of chastity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The negative is retained, though the surrounding account relates her hardships to protecting chastity. It can contrast the true cause of suffering with its occasion, but the translation does not rewrite it as “you suffered because of chastity.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτός σοι ὁ βυθὸς διὰ σωφροσύνην θνησκούσῃ βάπτισμα ἐγίνετο
lexical_decisions.chosen: the depths themselves would have become baptism for you, dying for chastity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The conditional claim of baptism through death for chastity is explicitly the speaker’s; no sacramental qualification is inserted to reconcile it with the following teaching.

lexical_decisions.chosen: coming from legitimate seed
lexical_decisions.rationale: The language concerns the children’s origin from a legitimate union. The main text retains seed imagery and does not add a biological or doctrinal theory.

lexical_decisions.chosen: will fill the husband’s place
lexical_decisions.rationale: The promised replacement or fulfillment of the husband’s place is retained; its precise nature is not defined as sexual or institutional.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἅτινα γνησίας ἰόντα σπορᾶς ἐν τοῖς κρείττοσιν εὕρηται.
lexical_decisions.chosen: coming from legitimate seed, they have been found in better circumstances
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes τοῖς κρείττοσιν as neuter, referring to better circumstances, supported by the recovery of the children after danger and separation. “Among better things” is a more literal neuter rendering but can obscure the situational sense. The same form permits a masculine interpretation, “among better people,” which would locate them with a better group, for example their present associates, rather than characterize their circumstances. Neither interpretation is uniquely established; the legitimate-origin wording is retained separately and no particular group is named.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἤπερ ἄκουσα μετὰ χρόνον ἐφ’ ἁμαρτίαις αὐταῖς ἀπωλλύου
lexical_decisions.chosen: than that, later, unwillingly, you should perish because of those very sins
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes ἐπί with the dative causally: the sins cause the perishing. The surrounding contrast among chastity, sin, death, and salvation supports that reading. A circumstantial attachment is also possible, “than that, later, unwillingly, you should perish in those very sins,” describing the condition in which she perishes rather than explicitly naming its cause. Neither attachment is uniquely required by the preposition alone.

passages.text: “So it is much better for the first things to be distressing. Even when they are present, the hope that they will pass keeps them from causing too much sorrow, and expectation of something better even gives joy. Above all, I want you to know how greatly chastity pleases God. The chaste woman is God’s choice, God’s delight, God’s glory, God’s child. Chastity is so great a good. If it were not the law that not even a righteous person may enter God’s kingdom unbaptized, perhaps those among the nations who are in error could have been saved through chastity alone. That is why I am greatly disheartened about those who remain chaste in error: having chosen chastity without good hope, they are hesitant about being baptized. Therefore they are not saved, because God’s decree is established that an unbaptized person must not enter his kingdom.” After he had said these things and still more, we turned to sleep.

lexical_decisions.chosen: not even a righteous person ... unbaptized
lexical_decisions.rationale: The emphatic exclusion of even a righteous unbaptized person is retained, rather than interpreting δίκαιον impersonally as “it is not right.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: without good hope
lexical_decisions.rationale: This describes the chaste people still in error; it is not turned into an assertion that they have already received the speaker’s hope of salvation.

passages.text: Peter woke much earlier than his daily custom, came in to us, woke us, and said, “Let Faustinus and Faustinianus, together with Clement and the members of the household, follow me, so that we may go to a sheltered place by the sea and baptize her where no one can watch.” We went to the shore, found a calm, clean place among some rocks, and he baptized her. We brothers withdrew for the women’s sake, together with a brother and some others, bathed, and then came back and took the women with us. Going in this way to a hidden place, we prayed. Then, because of the crowd, Peter sent the women ahead, directing them to go by another road to the lodging, and permitted only us among the men to accompany our mother and those same women. We went to the lodging and spoke with one another while waiting for him to come. After a considerable number of hours Peter arrived, broke the bread with thanksgiving, put salt on it, and gave it first to our mother and then to us, her sons. Thus we dined with her and blessed God.

lexical_decisions.chosen: together with a brother
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source has singular ἀδελφῷ after the plural brothers. An additional fellow member of the community may be intended; he is left unnamed rather than silently omitted or identified as Peter.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν ἄρτον ἐπ’ εὐχαριστίᾳ κλάσας καὶ ἐπιθεὶς ἅλας
lexical_decisions.chosen: broke the bread with thanksgiving, put salt on it
lexical_decisions.rationale: The thanksgiving and salt are both explicit. The text is not supplemented with wine or made an explicit identification of a later eucharistic rite.

passages.text: Then, seeing that the crowd had come in, Peter sat down, told us to sit beside him, and began his instruction, first persuading us of the reason why he had sent us ahead from the baptism and had himself arrived late. He gave the following reason: “As soon as you withdrew,” he said, “an old laborer came in with us, inquisitively concealing himself. Having watched us beforehand, as he later admitted, to see what we would do when we entered the sheltered place, he came out secretly and followed. At a suitable place he approached, greeted me, and said, ‘I have followed you for a long time, wanting to speak with you, but I was ashamed, lest you be angry at me for being inquisitive. Now, if you wish, I will tell you what seems true to me.’ I answered, ‘Tell us what you think is good, and we will welcome you, even if what is said is not actually good, since with a good intention you have wanted to say what seems good to you.’”

lexical_decisions.chosen: inquisitively concealing himself
lexical_decisions.rationale: The reflexive use of “steal” means hiding or stealing along rather than theft of property. The note preserves the figurative wording’s furtiveness.

lexical_decisions.chosen: and we will welcome you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The object is the man, not necessarily an endorsement of the truth of his statement, as the following concession makes clear.

lexical_decisions.chosen: began his instruction, first persuading us
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both the guiding explanation of ὑφηγεῖται and the persuasive force of πείθων are represented. The latter can mean satisfying or convincing the listeners concerning the reason; it is not reduced to merely providing information.

passages.text: “The old man began speaking in this way: ‘When I saw that you had bathed in the sea and withdrawn to the hidden place, I secretly approached and watched to see what you would do on entering a concealed place. When I saw you praying, I withdrew. Pitying you, however, I waited so that I might speak to you as you came out and persuade you not to be deceived. For there is neither God nor providence; everything is subject to destiny assigned at birth. I am fully convinced of this from what I have suffered, having studied the discipline carefully for a long time. So do not be deceived, child. Whether you pray or not, you are bound to suffer what comes from natal destiny. For if prayers or doing good had any power, I myself would be in better circumstances. Now, if this poor clothing of mine does not mislead you, you will not disbelieve what I say. Once, when I had great material abundance, I sacrificed much to the gods and provided much for the needy; yet, though I prayed and acted reverently, I could not escape what was fated.’ I said, ‘What have you suffered?’ He answered, ‘There is no need to speak of it now. Perhaps at the end you will hear who I am, whose family I belong to, and in what circumstances of life I have come to be. For now I want you to be fully convinced that everything is subject to natal destiny.’”

lexical_decisions.chosen: destiny assigned at birth / natal destiny
lexical_decisions.rationale: γένεσις literally refers to birth or origin; in this discussion it denotes fate inferred from a nativity or astrological birth configuration. The later explicit reference to astrology supports this contextual rendering, not a blanket substitution for every use of the word.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὔτε γὰρ θεός ἐστιν οὔτε πρόνοια
lexical_decisions.chosen: For there is neither God nor providence
lexical_decisions.rationale: The denial is the old man’s stated position, not an assertion added by the narrator or translator.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τίς τε ὢν ἐγὼ καὶ τίνων
lexical_decisions.chosen: who I am, whose family I belong to
lexical_decisions.rationale: The elliptical plural genitive can concern ancestry or kin. It is not supplied as a particular named family.

passages.text: “I said, ‘If everything is subject to natal destiny and you are fully convinced that this is so, your advice reflects thoughts contrary to your own. For if even thinking cannot occur contrary to natal destiny, why do you labor in vain, advising that something happen which cannot happen? Moreover, even if natal destiny has existence, do not hurry to persuade me not to worship the master of the stars as well, at whose will even what is not to happen can happen. For what is subordinate must always obey its ruler. Worshiping the supposed gods, however, is superfluous if natal destiny prevails. For nothing happens contrary to what seems good to fate, nor can they themselves do anything, being subject to their universal natal destiny. If natal destiny exists, it is incompatible with not ruling first. It cannot be subordinate, since, being ungenerated, it has nothing older than itself.’”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὗ θέλοντος καὶ μὴ γενέσθαι τι, γενέσθαι δυνατόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: at whose will even what is not to happen can happen
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes the negated infinitive as characterizing an event not otherwise destined to happen; the final γενέσθαι then states that it can happen at the ruler’s will. This supplies the contextual relation to destiny in English, not a Greek emendation. Another possible linkage places μὴ γενέσθαι directly within what the ruler wills: “when he wills even that something not happen, its happening is possible.” That is more difficult in the argument, but the negation’s attachment is not uniquely established here. The main text does not omit either occurrence of “happen” or the negative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ γένεσις ἐστιν, ἀντίκειται τὸ μὴ πρῶτον ἄρχειν. ὑποκεῖσθαι οὐ δύναται ὡς ἀγένητον ἑαυτοῦ πρεσβύτερον μηδὲν ἔχον
lexical_decisions.chosen: If natal destiny exists, it is incompatible with not ruling first. It cannot be subordinate, since, being ungenerated, it has nothing older than itself
lexical_decisions.rationale: The conditional is retained. The nearest named referent is natal destiny, read as the ungenerated principle hypothesized by fatalism. The neuter ἀγένητον can refer to an understood principle rather than agree directly with feminine γένεσις. A reference back to God or an ungenerated divine principle is also possible and would change which ruler is said to be unsubordinated. The pronoun “it” deliberately does not add a noun identifying the unexpressed subject uniquely.

passages.text: “As we were saying such things to one another, a large crowd gathered. Then, looking at the crowd, I said, ‘I and my people have inherited from our ancestors the worship of God and have a command not to attend to natal destiny—I mean the discipline of astrology. For this reason I have paid it no attention. Thus I am not experienced in astrology; I will explain the things in which I am experienced. Since I cannot refute natal destiny from the very science concerning natal destiny, I wish to demonstrate in another way that affairs are governed by providence, and that everyone will receive honor or punishment according to what he does. Whether now or later makes no difference to me, provided that everyone will certainly receive the consequences of what he has done. Here is the proof that natal destiny does not exist. If someone standing here lacks eyes, has a crippled hand, a lame foot, or some other bodily condition that has no possibility of returning to health and lies beyond every profession of healing—someone whom even astrologers do not profess to heal, because nothing of this sort has happened throughout the long span of time—and I, by petitioning God, provide the healing, when such a condition could never obtain correction through natal destiny: if this happens in this way, are not those who blaspheme the God who made everything doing wrong?’ The old man answered, ‘Is saying that everything is subject to natal destiny blasphemy?’ I answered, ‘Very much so. For if all people’s sins, acts of impiety, and licentious deeds come from stars, and the stars were appointed by God to do these things, so that they bring about every grievous thing, everyone’s sins are referred back to him who placed natal destiny in the stars.’”

lexical_decisions.chosen: my people
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source denotes a people or tribe; its proper name is not supplied in the English.

lexical_decisions.chosen: every profession of healing
lexical_decisions.rationale: This can refer to every promise or claim of healing as well as a healing occupation. The main text keeps the claim that the condition lies beyond professed healing ability.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁπότε ἐκ γενέσεως κατόρθωσιν τὸ τοιοῦτο οὐδέποτε λαβεῖν ἠδυνήθη
lexical_decisions.chosen: when such a condition could never obtain correction through natal destiny
lexical_decisions.rationale: The hypothetical demonstration’s premise is retained as Peter’s argument. No actual present healing or empirical validation is asserted by the translation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὃν οὐδὲ ἀστρολόγοι ἰᾶσθαι ἐπαγγέλλονται, ὅτι μὴ ἀπὸ τοῦ μακροῦ αἰῶνος τοιοῦτόν τι γέγονεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: someone whom even astrologers do not profess to heal, because nothing of this sort has happened throughout the long span of time
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text reads ὅτι causally and μὴ as negating γέγονεν: the lack of precedent explains the absence of astrologers’ healing claims. The following statement that such correction never occurred through natal destiny supports that linkage. A material alternative takes ὅτι μὴ as an exception marker: “someone whom even astrologers do not profess to heal, except insofar as something of this sort has occurred since long ago.” That reading qualifies their claims by admitting an exception tied to historical precedent, rather than supplying the categorical causal denial in the main text. The supplied μὴ is retained, not silently corrected to οὐ; this is a disclosed attachment choice, not a transcription defect.

passages.text: “The old man answered, ‘You have truly spoken greatly, but my own awareness stands in the way of all your incomparable proof. For I am an astrologer, and formerly lived in Rome. Becoming friends with someone related to Caesar, I knew precisely his natal configuration and that of his wife, and I observed their deeds actually fulfilled in accordance with their natal destiny. I cannot be persuaded by your argument. For the arrangement of her nativity was one that produces adulteresses who fall in love with their own servants and die in water abroad. And this is just what happened: falling in love with her own servant and unable to bear the reproach, she fled with him, lodged in a foreign land, shared his bed, and perished at sea.’”

lexical_decisions.chosen: my own awareness stands in the way
lexical_decisions.rationale: συνείδησις can mean conscience or personal knowledge/awareness. His ensuing firsthand account supports awareness, not a modern clinical diagnosis.

lexical_decisions.chosen: their own servants
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source’s servants have bonded status and belong to the women’s households. “Slaves” would make the legal ownership more explicit; “servants” follows the supplied POB policy while this note preserves ownership and dependency.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the arrangement
lexical_decisions.rationale: The word describes the configuration of the nativity, not a clinical disposition. “Horoscopic configuration” is the more technical alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: φυγοῦσα σὺν αὐτῷ, ἐν ἀλλοδαπῇ ὁρμήσασα
lexical_decisions.chosen: she fled with him, lodged in a foreign land
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text reads ὁρμήσασα in the lodging or anchoring sense of ὁρμέω: she stopped or stayed in the foreign land. ἐν ἀλλοδαπῇ is the location of that action, not its destination. The form can alternatively be read from ὁρμάω as setting out or moving, giving “having set out in a foreign land.” The narration of flight followed by sharing a bed supports lodging as the main contextual choice, without asserting it uniquely or changing the Greek.

passages.text: “I answered, ‘How do you know that the woman who fled, after going abroad, married the servant and, having married him, died?’ The old man said, ‘I know the truth securely—not that she married him, since I did not even know that she was in love. But after her departure her husband’s brother told me everything about her love, and how, being honorable—being the brother, after all—he did not wish to defile the bed; and how the poor woman, desiring him but ashamed before him and of the reproach—for she cannot be blamed, since natal destiny compelled her to do and suffer these things—fashioned a dream, whether true or false I cannot say. For he said that she had said, “Someone appeared to me in a vision and ordered me to leave the city of the Romans immediately with my children.” Her husband, anxious that she and his sons should be safe, immediately sent them to Athens to be educated, together with their mother and servants, but kept with him a third, younger son, since the one giving the message in the dream had permitted that son to remain with him. After a long time passed without his receiving letters from her, and after he himself had sent to Athens repeatedly, he took me with him as more devoted to him than anyone else and went to search for her. So I willingly shared many hardships with him during the journey, remembering that in his former prosperity he had made me a partner in everything, loving me above all his friends. We sailed away from Rome itself, came to these parts of Syria, and put in at Seleucia. Not many days after we disembarked, he died in despondency. I came here, sold myself, and from then until now have provided my food through the work of my hands.’”

lexical_decisions.chosen: married the servant
lexical_decisions.rationale: The question uses marriage explicitly and is not reduced to the earlier description of sharing a bed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ ἀδελφὸς ὁ τοῦ ἀνδρὸς αὐτῆς
lexical_decisions.chosen: her husband’s brother
lexical_decisions.rationale: The relative narration then uses ambiguous pronouns concerning the honorable brother and the woman’s desire. The main text retains that person and those pronouns without harmonizing this with the prior assertion about a servant or identifying the two men as one.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὄνειρον εἴτε ἀληθῆ εἴτε ψευδῆ ἐπλάσατο οὐκ ἔχω λέγειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: fashioned a dream, whether true or false I cannot say
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb can mean fabricated or fashioned. The following uncertainty about truth is retained, rather than replaced by a categorical claim that the dream was false.

lexical_decisions.chosen: sold myself
lexical_decisions.rationale: The reflexive sale is explicit and is not softened to merely hiring himself out. The narrative does not identify a purchaser or legal arrangement.

passages.text: “After the old man said this, I understood from his account that the old man he said had died was your father. I did not wish to bring up your circumstances with him until I had consulted you. But after learning where he was staying and telling him where I was staying, for accuracy’s sake I asked only this: ‘What was the old man’s name?’ He said, ‘Faustus.’ ‘And his twin sons’ names?’ He answered, ‘Faustinus and Faustinianus.’ ‘And the third son’s?’ He said, ‘Clement.’ ‘And what was the name of their mother?’ He said, ‘Mattidia.’ So, joining in the weeping out of sympathy, I dismissed the crowds and came to you, so that after sharing the salt I might consult you about these things. I did not want to tell you before we partook of salt, lest, overcome by grief, you spend the day of baptism in mourning, when even angels rejoice.” While Peter was saying this, all of us were weeping with our mother. Seeing us weep, he said, “Now let each of you bear what has been said courageously through fear toward God. Your father did not die today, but long ago, as you yourselves said in conjecture.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὃν ἔλεγεν τεθνάναι γέροντα, αὐτὸς ἦν (ἐξ ὧν ἔλεγεν) ὁ ὑμέτερος πατήρ
lexical_decisions.chosen: the old man he said had died was your father
lexical_decisions.rationale: Peter here identifies the reportedly deceased subject of the story, not yet explicitly the living speaker himself. The old man’s later identity is not read backward into Peter’s present assertion.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after sharing the salt
lexical_decisions.rationale: The concrete salt-sharing expression is retained in this meal context rather than made an unspecified conversation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκ ἐβουλήθην τὸ καθ’ ὑμᾶς αὐτῷ συναντιβαλεῖν, μέχρις ἂν ὑμῖν προσανάθωμαι.
lexical_decisions.chosen: I did not wish to bring up your circumstances with him until I had consulted you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The personal dative αὐτῷ identifies the old man as the participant in the contemplated conversation. συναντιβαλεῖν suggests bringing accounts together for comparison or exchanging information; “compare your circumstances in discussion with him” is a more explicit alternative. Peter withholds that exchange with the man, not merely an internal comparison with an account.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὸ συμπαθείας οὖν ἐγὼ σύνδακρυς γενόμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: So, joining in the weeping out of sympathy
lexical_decisions.rationale: σύνδακρυς expresses shared weeping, not merely one person’s tears. The main wording retains Peter’s sympathy and joining in tears without specifying an otherwise unexpressed other participant.

passages.text: When Peter said this, my mother could not bear it and cried aloud, “Alas, husband! Loving us, you yourself died without judgment, while we live, see the light, and partake of food.” When this single lament had thus ended, there was the old man, coming in too. Just as he was about to ask the cause of the cry, he looked at the woman and said, “Alas! What does this mean? Whom do I see?” He approached, looked more closely, was seen in turn, and embraced her. Both were fainting from sudden joy; though they wanted to speak to one another, they were seized with speechlessness from their insatiable joy and could not keep control. But after a little while my mother said, “I have you, Faustus, sweetest to me in every way! How are you alive, when just a little earlier we heard you were dead? But these are our sons: Faustinus, Faustinianus, and Clement.” When she said this, we three fell upon him and covered him with kisses, faintly recalling his appearance.

source_issues.issue: The supplied edition prints a period after the elided μετ’. The English construes μετ’ with οὐ πολὺ as “after a little while” despite that intervening punctuation. This is a disclosed printed/editorial feature; the Greek period is not deleted or claimed as an OCR error, and no lacuna or missing word is restored.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡμᾶς ἀγαπῶν ἀκριτὶ αὐτὸς μὲν ἐτελεύτησας
lexical_decisions.chosen: Loving us, you yourself died without judgment
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text attaches ἀκριτί to ἐτελεύτησας, dying, reading the lament as contrasting his death with their continuing life. The adverb may mean without discrimination, decision, or deliberation; “without judgment” does not assert that a tribunal, hearing, or legal proceeding was involved. A material alternative attaches it to ἡμᾶς ἀγαπῶν: “loving us without discrimination/deliberation, you yourself died.” That reading characterizes the manner of his love rather than his dying. The immediate focus on death in the lament motivates the main attachment, but the proximity to the preceding participle leaves the alternative viable and not uniquely settled.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Both were fainting
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb can denote dying or perishing. Their subsequent speech and embrace support deathlike faintness or loss of consciousness here, not actual death followed by resurrection.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀμαυρῶς πως τὴν μορφὴν αὐτοῦ ἀνεφέρομεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: faintly recalling his appearance
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb can mean bringing back or reproducing. Their childhood separation supports recollection of his appearance rather than verbally describing it for an unstated audience.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὕτω δὲ τῆς μιᾶς ταύτης ὀλολυγῆς παυσαμένης, ἰδοὺ καὶ ὁ γέρων εἰσῄει
lexical_decisions.chosen: When this single lament had thus ended, there was the old man, coming in too
lexical_decisions.rationale: “Thus” represents οὕτω, and “there was” preserves ἰδού’s attention-directing, presentational force rather than flattening the entrance to a plain temporal report. The following καί is retained as “too.” This introduces the sudden appearance without adding a new person or gesture.

passages.text: Seeing this, Peter said, “Are you Faustus, this woman’s husband and the father of her children?” He said, “I am.” Peter said, “Why, then, did you tell me your own story as though it concerned someone else, speaking of hardships, grief, and a tomb?” My father answered, “Being related to Caesar and not wishing to become widely known, I recast the account in the person of someone else, so that my own identity would not be understood. For I knew that, if I became known, the local rulers would hear, summon me, and, doing what would please Caesar, invest me with worldly prosperity, which I had renounced. For, having judged those I loved most to be dead, I could not give myself over to life’s luxury.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: widely known
lexical_decisions.rationale: The term concerns being made conspicuous or talked about. His intention is avoiding recognition, not a claim that he has escaped lawful punishment.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς ἄλλου τινὸς τὴν ἐξήγησιν ἀνετυπωσάμην
lexical_decisions.chosen: I recast the account in the person of someone else
lexical_decisions.rationale: The old man explains deliberate third-person presentation. No earlier part of his narrative is silently rewritten to anticipate this admission.

passages.text: Peter said, “You did these things as you had planned. But as for natal destiny, were you then insisting on it falsely, or were you affirming it as true?” My father said, “I will not lie to you: I was genuinely affirming natal destiny as something that exists. For I am not uninitiated in the theory. Besides, there was also with me an Egyptian man named Annubion, best among astrologers. He became my friend at the beginning of my travels and declared the death of my wife along with our children.” Peter said, “Then are you now convinced by what has happened that the claims concerning natal destiny do not hold together?” My father answered, “I must set before you everything that comes into my mind, so that, hearing answers to these things, I can learn by these [points] of this refutation. I know that astrologers are wrong about many things but also tell the truth about many. So I suspect that, in what they determine accurately, they tell the truth, whereas, in what they get wrong, they do so through ignorance. Thus I suppose the discipline itself holds together, but they say false things through ignorance because not everyone can determine everything accurately.” Peter answered, “Hold back: perhaps in the things about which they tell the truth, they happen to hit upon it rather than speaking from precise knowledge. For some of the many things said are bound to come about.” The old man said, “How, then, can one become fully convinced about this: whether what concerns natal destiny holds together or not?”

source_issues.source_quote: ἵνα πρὸς αὐτὰ ἀκούων μανθάνειν ἔχω τοῖσδὲ τούτου ἐλέγχου
source_issues.issue: The sequence τοῖσδὲ τούτου ἐλέγχου is syntactically compressed: τοῖσδε is dative plural while “of this refutation” is genitive singular. The main text supplies only a bracketed generic head, “[points],” taking the dative instrumentally and the genitive as qualifying those implied points: learning by these points of this refutation while hearing replies to the doubts. Another contextual reading would refer to means or stages of refutation rather than particular points. The wording is not emended into a dative plural noun or described as an OCR error. The referential details remain uncertain and require independent review.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: περὶ δὲ γενέσεως ἄρα ψευδόμενος διισχυρίζου· ἢ ὡς ἀληθεύων ἐβεβαίους;
lexical_decisions.chosen: as for natal destiny, were you then insisting on it falsely, or were you affirming it as true?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The two alternatives are both retained. ὡς ἀληθεύων can concern the speaker’s sincere claim to truth as well as actual truth; the father’s answer distinguishes sincerity from the theory’s validity.

lexical_decisions.chosen: So I suspect that
lexical_decisions.rationale: The particle marks a tentative possibility or concern; the ensuing contrast is framed as a suspicion, not asserted as established astrological science.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Hold back: perhaps
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἄπεχε can be a caution to pause or refrain. “Consider whether perhaps” is a contextual alternative, but the main text retains the imperative’s restraint rather than treating the matter as proved.

lexical_decisions.chosen: best among astrologers
lexical_decisions.rationale: The relative superlative ranks Annubion as best among astrologers without adding “the only” or requiring that no one shares that rank. Merely placing him among a group of the best would weaken the source’s wording. An elative “an exceptionally good astrologer” is possible for this adjective, but the explicit plural genitive supports the relative main reading.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀνάγκη γὰρ πᾶσα ἐκ πολλῶν τῶν λεγομένων ἀποβαίνειν τινά.
lexical_decisions.chosen: For some of the many things said are bound to come about
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀποβαίνειν here denotes predictions coming about or proving fulfilled. “Come about” makes that result clear without adding a separate causal mechanism or claiming that all predictions succeed.

passages.text: While both were silent, I said, “Since I know the discipline precisely, but my master and my father do not know it in the same way, I would like, if Annubion himself were present, to hold a discussion in my father’s presence. For then the matter could become clear, with an expert holding the inquiry with another expert in the same field.” My father answered, “Where, then, can Annubion be encountered?” Peter said, “In Antioch. For I learn that Simon the magician is there, and Annubion, who follows him, is inseparable from him. So, when we get there, if we actually find them, the inquiry can take place.” And after we had talked together at length, filled with joy at the recognition and giving thanks to God, we turned to sleep when evening overtook us.

lexical_decisions.chosen: my master
lexical_decisions.rationale: This refers to Peter in the ongoing discussion, not a newly introduced speech of the divine Lord.

lexical_decisions.chosen: an expert ... with another expert in the same field
lexical_decisions.rationale: The same-field relation is explicit; the translation does not certify the underlying astrological discipline as true.

lexical_decisions.chosen: if we actually find them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The conditional prevents the planned inquiry from being reported as already conducted.

lexical_decisions.chosen: And after we had talked together at length
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied ὁμῶς gives the collective sense, together or in common; πολλὰ supplies the extent of their discussion. Both are preserved. The unfamiliar adverb is neither silently replaced by ὅμως nor characterized as an OCR error.

passages.text: When dawn came, our father went in with our mother and the three sons to where Peter was. He greeted him and sat down; then we too sat down at Peter's bidding. Looking directly at our father, Peter said, ‘I am eager for you to become of one mind with your wife and children, so that you may share their way of life here and, there too, after the soul's separation from the body, be with them free from sorrow. Or does not your being apart from one another cause the greatest distress to both you and them?’ Our father answered, ‘Very much indeed.’ Peter said, ‘If being separated from one another distresses you even here, since after death you are certainly bound not to be together, will it not distress you much more—you, a wise man, being separated from your family because of your opinion, and them suffering still more in knowing that eternal punishment awaits you for thinking otherwise, by the pronouncement of an explicit decree?’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁμόφρονά σε γενέσθαι γυναικὶ καὶ τέκνοις
lexical_decisions.chosen: you to become of one mind with your wife and children
lexical_decisions.rationale: The desired agreement concerns their beliefs in the ensuing discussion; it is not reduced to living at the same address or expanded into agreement on every possible matter.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μετὰ θάνατον πάντως ὀφειλόμενον ὑμῖν μετ’ ἀλλήλων μὴ εἶναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: since after death you are certainly bound not to be together
lexical_decisions.rationale: The clause states the anticipated separation emphatically within Peter's warning. Its connection to the father's different beliefs is supplied by the surrounding explicit clauses, not by removing the source's certainty.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by the pronouncement of an explicit decree
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive adjective can mean expressly stated or definite. Decree or ordinance preserves the authoritative ruling; the source does not identify a particular quoted verse or name its speaker here.

passages.text: Our father said, ‘But, dearest friend, souls are not punished in Hades, since the soul dissolves into air as soon as it leaves the body.’ Peter said, ‘Until we persuade you about this, then, answer me: does it not seem to you that, while you do not suffer distress because you disbelieve in punishment, they, being convinced of it, must be troubled about you?’ Our father said, ‘Your argument follows.’ Peter said, ‘Why, then, will you not relieve them of their very great sorrow about you by agreeing with our worship? I do not mean from embarrassment, but from good judgment, listening to what I tell you and judging whether it is so or not. If things are as we say, you will share enjoyment with your dearest ones here and share their rest there. But if, in examining your arguments, you show that what we say is a false myth, you will do well even so: having brought them to your own way of thinking, you will stop them from relying on empty hopes and free them from false fears.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῇ θρησκείᾳ συνθέμενος, οὐ δυσωπίᾳ λέγω, ἀλλ’ εὐγνωμοσύνῃ
lexical_decisions.chosen: by agreeing with our worship? I do not mean from embarrassment, but from good judgment
lexical_decisions.rationale: Θρησκεία concerns religious observance or worship; our is inferred from Peter's invitation. Δυσωπία can denote shamefaced compliance or reluctance to disappoint, contrasted with sound judgment rather than mere social acquiescence.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐν τῇ τῶν λόγων σου σκέψει
lexical_decisions.chosen: in examining your arguments
lexical_decisions.rationale: The possessive your is retained rather than silently changed to our. The father's own examination or examination of his arguments can both be heard in the genitive construction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: share their rest
lexical_decisions.rationale: The future middle addresses the father and continues the togetherness expressed by the preceding compound. Rest is retained without adding a location or detailed doctrine of the afterlife not given here.

passages.text: Our father said, ‘You seem to me to be saying many reasonable things.’ Peter said, ‘Tell me, then, what is holding you back from coming to our faith, so that we may begin to speak directly to it. There are many things that hold people back. For those already convinced, there are the demands of purchases, business, farming, anxieties, and things of that sort. For unbelievers, among whom you too belong, there are assumptions: thinking that gods who do not exist do exist, or that everything is subject to birth-fate or to chance, or that souls are mortal, or that our message is false because there is no providence.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: everything is subject to birth-fate
lexical_decisions.rationale: Genesis here can denote the determining configuration or fate associated with birth, as distinguished from chance in the next alternative. Birth-fate keeps the birth wording visible; fate determined by the stars at birth is a fuller contextual alternative, but stars are not expressly named in this clause.

lexical_decisions.chosen: chance
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun refers to spontaneous occurrence without directing providence. It is not rendered automation, a misleading modern technical association.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the demands of purchases, business, farming, anxieties
lexical_decisions.rationale: The plural occupations or lack of leisure is the governing idea, and all four listed sources of preoccupation are retained.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἢ θεοὺς τοὺς οὐκ ὄντας εἶναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: thinking that gods who do not exist do exist
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering takes the substantivized not-being expression existentially, so that the error concerns treating nonexistent gods as existent. This follows the explicit being/not-being contrast in the phrase. A material predicative alternative is thinking that those who are not gods are gods, which denies their divinity rather than their existence. The main text does not claim that the existential attachment is unique.

passages.text: ‘But I say that everything is governed by God's providence, judging from what has happened to you: your separation from your family for so many years. Since, if they had remained with you, perhaps they would not have listened to the teachings of reverence for God, their journey abroad with their mother was arranged, along with shipwreck, presumed death, and loss of contact. So too was their education in Greek and godless doctrines, so that, knowing them, they might be better able to refute them. After this came their love for the teaching of reverence for God and their ability to join me in helping my proclamation; then their brother Clement's coming together with us, and thus their mother's being recognized and becoming fully convinced of the divinity through healing. Shortly afterward came the twins' being recognized and recognizing in turn, and, on the following day, meeting you and your recovering your family. I do not think that so great and swift a harmony, converging from every direction upon one intended aim, is without providence.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ναυφραγίῳ καὶ θανάτου ὑπονοίᾳ καὶ ἀπαρτίᾳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: along with shipwreck, presumed death, and loss of contact
lexical_decisions.rationale: The list describes the circumstances of the family separation. Ἀπαρτία is read as absence of news or contact in this context; the translation does not supply a particular duration beyond the previously stated years.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ οὕτως τὴν μητέρα ἐπιγνωσθῆναι καὶ ὑπὸ θεραπείας τὴν θεότητα πληροφορηθῆναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: and thus their mother's being recognized and becoming fully convinced of the divinity through healing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text continues the mother as the inferred subject of the second passive infinitive and takes the accusative divinity as the content of her conviction. That connects her recognition with her resulting assurance. A material alternative takes divinity as the expressed accusative subject of that infinitive, parallel to mother as subject of the first: and the divinity was fully confirmed through healing. Neither reading establishes whose divinity is meant, and the English does not identify Peter or the mother as divine.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ δίδυμα τέκνα ἐπιγνωσθέντα καὶ ἐπιγνόντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: the twins' being recognized and recognizing in turn
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both passive and active recognition are retained. The unexpressed object of their recognition is not replaced by an invented named person in this clause.

lexical_decisions.chosen: upon one intended aim
lexical_decisions.rationale: The convergence is toward one aim of intention or purpose. Agreement of belief is a possible contextual emphasis for γνώμη, but the preceding arrangement of events favors an intended aim without naming a separate planner in this phrase.

lexical_decisions.chosen: so great and swift a harmony
lexical_decisions.rationale: The degree of magnitude expressed by τοσαύτην is distinguished from the speed expressed by ταχεῖαν, rather than collapsing both into so swift.

passages.text: Our father began to say to Peter, ‘Do not suppose, my dearest Peter, that I have not been thinking about the message you proclaim. Indeed, at the end of this past night, when Clement urged me at length to agree with the truth you proclaim, I answered, “What newer instruction can anyone give beyond what the ancients advised?” He smiled gently and said, “There is a great difference, father, between the teachings of reverence for God and those of philosophy. For the message of truth has its proof from prophecy, whereas the teaching of philosophy offers fine language and seems to present its proofs from conjectures.” Having said this, however, he set out for me, as an example, the teaching about love for humanity that you had explained to him. It seemed to me, rather, utterly unjust. I will tell you how. He said that it was just for someone to offer the other cheek as well to the person striking his cheek; to give his head-covering too to the person taking his cloak; to go two miles with the person compelling him to go one; and other things of this sort.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ δὲ τῆς φιλοσοφίας καλλιλογίας παρέχων ἐκ στοχασμῶν δοκεῖ παριστᾶν τὰς ἀποδείξεις
lexical_decisions.chosen: the teaching of philosophy offers fine language and seems to present its proofs from conjectures
lexical_decisions.rationale: The favorable-sounding language and the qualification seems are retained alongside the criticism of conjectural proofs. The translation does not replace conjecture by observation or prophecy.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν περὶ φιλανθρωπίας μοι ἐξέθετο λόγον
lexical_decisions.chosen: he set out for me ... the teaching about love for humanity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The term is a broad humane love or kindness toward human beings. Love for humanity keeps its human object explicit and connects it with the ensuing discussion of humane treatment.

lexical_decisions.chosen: his head-covering
lexical_decisions.rationale: The garment can be a scarf, kerchief, or head-covering. It is distinguished from the cloak named immediately before it, rather than replaced by the tunic familiar from another form of the saying.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Having said this, however
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verified selected print reads ὁμῶς, not the usual adversative accentuation ὅμως. The main text interprets the continuation adversatively: after contrasting the two teachings he nevertheless gives the example. Non-adversative alike or together is a lexical alternative for the printed form. This interpretation is not a change to the source or a claim that the Greek has been normalized to ὅμως.

passages.text: Peter answered, ‘But you judged unjust what is most just. If you wish, listen.’ The father said, ‘I very much wish to.’ Peter said, ‘Suppose there are two hostile kings, each with a separate territory. If one king's subject is discovered in the other's country and thereby owes death, but is released from punishment with a slap rather than death, does not the one who released him appear humane?’ The father said, ‘Very much so.’ Peter said, ‘What, then, if this same man takes from someone something of that person's own, or even something belonging to someone else, and is caught for it? If he gives double, although he owes fourfold and death because he was caught within the enemy's borders, does it not seem to you that the one who took double and released him from death is humane?’ The father said, ‘It appears so.’ Peter said, ‘What then? Should not someone in another's kingdom, and that of a wicked enemy at that, for the sake of staying alive, flatter everyone, yield beyond what is demanded by those who compel service, greet those who do not greet him, reconcile enemies, avoid quarreling with angry people, freely provide his possessions to everyone who asks, and do other things of this sort?’ The father said, ‘I would all the more reasonably endure everything, if indeed he puts staying alive before these things.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἴδιόν τι τινὸς αὐτὸς οὗτος ἀφέληται ἢ καὶ ἀλλότριον
lexical_decisions.chosen: this same man takes from someone something of that person's own, or even something belonging to someone else
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contrast is read as the victim's own property versus another person's property in the victim's possession. An alternative takes own in relation to the person doing the taking. The main rendering makes the contextual property relations intelligible without changing the two expressed categories into a single generic theft.

lexical_decisions.chosen: yield beyond what is demanded by those who compel service
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb refers to impressed or compulsory service, with yielding to a greater extent. The rendering retains the excess compliance without introducing a specific journey or distance into this general instruction.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ ἑαυτοῦ ἀδεῶς παντὶ αἰτοῦντι παρέχειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: freely provide his possessions to everyone who asks
lexical_decisions.rationale: Ἀδεῶς can mean without fear or hesitation. Freely is read as unhesitating willingness, not a claim that the hostile country is safe or that the possessions carry no monetary value.

lexical_decisions.chosen: if indeed he puts staying alive before these things
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source moves from the father's first-person willingness to an expressed third-person verb. He retains the hypothetical person as its subject rather than silently replacing it with I; the comparison is preference for life over the burdens just listed.

passages.text: Peter said, ‘Is it not, then, the case that those whom you said were being wronged are themselves trespassers, since they are in another's kingdom, and are taking more than their due to the extent that they possess anything? Those thought to be doing wrong grant each person on the opposing side as much as they allow that person to have. For these things belong to those who have chosen the present. They are so humane as even to permit them to live. That is how the illustration stands; now hear the actual matter. When the prophet of truth was present, he taught us that the creator and God of all assigned two kingdoms to two beings, a good one and an evil one. He gave the evil one the kingdom of this present world, together with a law, so that he might have authority to punish wrongdoers; to the good one, the coming eternal age. He made each human being free, with authority to assign himself to whichever he wishes: either the present evil or the future good. Those who have chosen the present have authority to be rich, live luxuriously, enjoy themselves, and do whatever they can, for they will have none of the good things to come. But those who have decided to receive the things of the future kingdom may not consider any of the things here their own, since they belong to another king, except only water and bread—and these obtained with sweat to sustain life, since voluntary death is not permitted—and also a single covering. For one is not allowed to stand naked because of heaven, which sees everything.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτοὶ παρορισταὶ τυγχάνουσιν, καθὰ ἐν ἑτέρου εἰσὶν βασιλείᾳ, καὶ τοσοῦτον πλεονέκται εἰσίν
lexical_decisions.chosen: trespassers ... taking more than their due
lexical_decisions.rationale: These words occur in the clause about being in another's kingdom. The first denotes crossing a boundary, the second grasping or claiming an excessive share. The rendering does not replace their property-based accusation by a general description of sinful attitudes.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δυσίν τισιν ἀπένειμεν· βασιλείας δύο, ἀγαθῷ τε καὶ πονηρῷ
lexical_decisions.chosen: assigned two kingdoms to two beings, a good one and an evil one
lexical_decisions.rationale: The two recipients are distinct from the creator assigning their realms. The English supplies beings for the substantivized adjectives without naming either as a second creator or as a particular named angel.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἢ τῷ παρόντι κακῷ ἢ τῷ μέλλοντι ἀγαθῷ
lexical_decisions.chosen: either the present evil or the future good
lexical_decisions.rationale: These substantivized adjective forms permit reference to the present evil and future good as conditions or realms, alongside the preceding recipients of the kingdoms. The translation retains the broad evil/good antithesis instead of forcing every occurrence to name an individual being; the inflected forms themselves do not settle masculine versus neuter reference.

lexical_decisions.chosen: because of heaven, which sees everything
lexical_decisions.rationale: Heaven is the expressed all-seeing subject. It may function as a reverential reference to heavenly observation, but the main text does not silently replace it with God or infer a particular observer.

passages.text: ‘If, then, you wish to hear the precise account of the matter, those whom you said a little earlier were being wronged are, rather, themselves doing wrong. For they, having chosen what is to come, live in the present among the wicked, sharing many of the same things with them: life itself, light, bread, water, clothing, and some other things of that kind. But those whom you thought were doing wrong share nothing with the good men in the things to come.’ The father answered, ‘Now that you have persuaded me that those doing wrong are themselves being wronged, while those being wronged are instead taking more than their due, the whole matter seems to me even more utterly unjust. Those who seem to be doing wrong permit many things to those who chose the future; those who seem to be wronged themselves do wrong, because there they do not provide equivalent things to those who permitted them here what they themselves permitted them.’ Peter said, ‘This is not unjust either, because each person has authority to choose the present or the future, whether small or great. A person who has chosen by his own judgment and will is not wronged—not even, I say, if he chooses the small things, since the great things lay before him; for the small things too lay before him.’ The father said, ‘You have spoken rightly. For one of the Greek sages has also said, “Responsibility belongs to those who choose; God is not responsible.”’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἱ δὲ ἀδικεῖν ὑπὸ σοῦ νομισθέντες ἐν τοῖς ἐσομένοις ἀγαθοῖς ἀνδράσιν οὐδὲν συνυπάρχουσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: those whom you thought were doing wrong share nothing with the good men in the things to come
lexical_decisions.rationale: Good men is read together as the persons with whom no future sharing occurs. A possible alternative takes good with future good things; the supplied masculine ἀγαθοῖς ἀνδράσιν supports the main attachment.

lexical_decisions.chosen: what they themselves permitted them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated pronouns return to the present-world benefactors and the recipients. The English retains the repetition of granting rather than adding a new category of compensation absent from the clause.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπεὶ προέκειτο τὰ μεγάλα· προέκειτο γὰρ αὐτῷ καὶ τὰ μικρά
lexical_decisions.chosen: since the great things lay before him; for the small things too lay before him
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both statements about available choices, in their printed order, are retained. The repetition is not silently rewritten into a different conditional argument.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Responsibility belongs to those who choose; God is not responsible
