lexical_decisions.rationale: The contrast concerns accountability or blame for choice. The Greek sage remains unnamed because this passage does not identify him.

passages.text: ‘But explain this argument to me as well. I remember Clement telling me that we suffer wrongs and sufferings for the forgiveness of sins.’ Peter said, ‘That too is right. For we who have chosen the future, when we possess things in excess—whether clothes, food, drink, or anything else—possess sins, because we ought to have nothing, as I explained a little earlier. For all, possessions are sins. Their deprivation, however it happens, is a removal of sins.’ The father said, ‘It follows, as you have distinguished two territories of the two kings, leaving each of those under their authority to choose what he wishes. But what about sufferings? Do we suffer these justly too?’ Peter said, ‘Most justly. Since the rule for those being saved is, as I said, that no one should possess anything, yet many possess many things—which are, in other words, sins—for this reason, out of God's surpassing love for humanity, sufferings are brought upon those who do not live with complete sincerity. This is so that, because of their measure of love for God, they may be saved from eternal punishments through temporary penalties.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: For all, possessions are sins
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative all and the wordplay between possessions and sins are retained as Peter's claim within this argument. The categorical wording is not softened into merely a warning against excessive attachment.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the rule for those being saved
lexical_decisions.rationale: Ὅρος can mean a boundary, definition, or determining rule. Here the following infinitive gives a rule of possession; territorial boundary remains a live echo of the preceding kingdoms illustration.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those who do not live with complete sincerity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverb concerns purity or sincerity of conduct. Completely is not an invented moral intensifier but expresses the adverb's undiluted quality; live purely is a concise alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διὰ τὸ ποσῶς φιλόθεον προσκαίροις τιμωρίαις αἰωνίων σωθῶσιν κολάσεων
lexical_decisions.chosen: because of their measure of love for God, they may be saved from eternal punishments through temporary penalties
lexical_decisions.rationale: The limited degree of God-love is retained, as is the contrast between temporary and eternal punishment. The translation does not add a named intermediate place or impose a later doctrinal account of the mechanism.

passages.text: The father said, ‘What then? Do we not see many impious people who are poor? Are these too among those being saved just because of that?’ Peter said, ‘Not necessarily. Poverty is not acceptable if someone desires what he ought not. Thus some are rich in their intention while poor in money, and are punished as people desiring to grasp more than their due. Nor is someone necessarily righteous simply because he is poor. He may be destitute in money yet desire or even do what he ought above all not to do. He may worship idols, blaspheme, engage in sexual immorality, or live indifferently, whether swearing falsely, lying, or living unfaithfully. Nevertheless, our teacher pronounced the faithful poor blessed—not because they had provided anything, for they had nothing, but because, committing no sin, they cannot be condemned solely for not giving alms because they have nothing.’ The father said, ‘Truly, the facts seem entirely consistent with the premise. That is why I have decided to hear the whole account in order.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: are rich in their intention while poor in money
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contrast is between chosen desire and actual means, not a claim that the poor secretly possess wealth. Intention preserves the volitional force of προαίρεσις.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἢ γὰρ εἴδωλα σέβει ἢ βλασφημεῖ ἢ πορνεύει ἢ ἀδιαφόρως ζῇ, ἢ ἐπιορκῶν ἢ ψευδόμενος ἢ ἀπίστως βιούς.
lexical_decisions.chosen: live indifferently, whether swearing falsely, lying, or living unfaithfully
lexical_decisions.rationale: Indifference concerns disregard for moral distinctions, not merely lack of strong emotion. The main wording groups the final participles as explanations of living indifferently; the transition from finite verbs to participles supports that attachment. A material alternative takes the repeated ἢ phrases as continued coordinate alternatives in the wrongdoing list: or swearing falsely, or lying, or living unfaithfully. The repeated or supports that reading, so the main grouping is not presented as uniquely established.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μηδὲν ἁμαρτάνοντες, ἐπὶ μόνῳ τῷ τὴν ἐλεημοσύνην μὴ ποιεῖν διὰ τὸ μὴ ἔχειν καταδικασθῆναι οὐκ ἔχουσι
lexical_decisions.chosen: committing no sin, they cannot be condemned solely for not giving alms because they have nothing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participial qualification is retained; the argument concerns the faithful poor who do not otherwise sin, not a declaration that every poor person is sinless. The two negatives concern not giving and inability to condemn on that sole ground, and are both represented.

passages.text: Peter said, ‘Since, then, you are now eager to learn about our worship, I owe you an orderly account, beginning with God himself and showing that he alone must be called God, and that no others should be called or considered gods. Whoever acts otherwise must be punished eternally, as one who has committed the greatest impiety against the very Master of all.’ After saying this, he laid his hands on those troubled by afflictions, the sick, and those possessed by demons, prayed, healed them, and dismissed the crowds. Then he went inside, partook of his customary salt, and slept.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτὸν μόνον δεῖ λέγειν θεόν, ἑτέρους δὲ μήτε λέγειν μήτε νομίζειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: he alone must be called God, and ... no others should be called or considered gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both naming and regarding others as gods are prohibited. The rendering does not narrow the claim merely to verbal forms of address.

lexical_decisions.chosen: partook of his customary salt
lexical_decisions.rationale: The plural salt expression may function as a reference to simple customary fare or a shared table. The main text keeps the expressed salt rather than supplying bread or a detailed meal not named here; customary fare is a smoother metonymic alternative.

passages.text: At dawn Peter went out and stood at his usual place for discussion, where he saw a large crowd assembled. Just as he was about to speak, one of his attendants came in and said, ‘Simon has arrived from Antioch. Having learned as early as last evening that you had promised to give a discourse on sole sovereignty, he is ready, together with Athenodorus the Epicurean, to come upon you while you speak and publicly oppose everything you say in any way in support of sole sovereignty.’ While the attendant was saying this, look—Simon himself was coming in with Athenodorus and some other companions. Before Peter could say anything, Simon spoke first:

lexical_decisions.chosen: on sole sovereignty
lexical_decisions.rationale: The discussion concerns the rule of the one God, not a particular human monarchy. Sole sovereignty retains the political-rule image without replacing it everywhere by the broader modern term monotheism.

lexical_decisions.chosen: of his attendants
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun denotes one who serves Peter. An ecclesiastical deacon is possible, but a formal office is not established by this occurrence alone.

passages.text: ‘I learned that yesterday you promised Faustus to demonstrate today, presenting your discourse in order and beginning with the Master of all himself, that he alone must be called God, that no others should be called or considered gods, and that whoever acts otherwise must be punished eternally. Above all, I am truly astounded at your recklessness in hoping to persuade a wise man, an old man at that, to your own wishes. But you will not achieve your designs, especially with me present here to expose your false arguments. Perhaps, had I not been present, the wise old man would have been deceived, since he is unfamiliar with the books publicly credited among the Jews. For now I will pass over lengthy arguments so as to expose your promise more quickly. Therefore begin to say what you promised in our own presence, for we know the scriptures. If, however, ashamed of exposure, you wish to pass over your promise in our presence, that too is sufficient proof that you are lying, because you did not dare to speak before those who know the scriptures. And why am I now waiting for you to speak, when I have the greatest witness to your promise in the old man standing here?’ Having said this, he looked directly at our father and said, ‘Tell me, most honored of all men, did not this man promise to demonstrate to you today that there is one God, that one should not call or consider anyone else a god, and that whoever acts otherwise, as someone sinning most grievously, must be punished eternally? Or will you not answer me?’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτὸν μόνον δεῖ λέγειν, ἄλλους δὲ μήτε λέγειν μήτε νομίζειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: he alone must be called God, that no others should be called or considered gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: God is the understood predicate supplied by the discourse and explicitly repeated later in the same passage. Both calling and regarding are retained.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν παρὰ Ἰουδαίοις δημοσίᾳ πεπιστωμένων βίβλων
lexical_decisions.chosen: the books publicly credited among the Jews
lexical_decisions.rationale: The books' accepted authority is attributed to the Jewish community in Simon's speech. Credited or held trustworthy is the sense, not a claim that their contents have already been proved in this debate.

passages.text: Our father said, ‘You would rightly demand testimony from me, Simon, if Peter had first denied it. As things stand, I will not be ashamed to say what needs saying. I think you want to debate while cut through by anger, which is unfitting for you to do and for us to listen to. It means witnessing a quarrel, not being helped toward truth. Knowing from Greek education how inquirers should proceed, I will now remind you. Let each of you set out his own doctrine, and let your arguments be directed against the other. If Peter alone sets out his view while you keep yours silent, an argument you put forward might press against both his view and yours. Although both of you were defeated by the argument, you would not both appear defeated: the one who set out his view would, but the equal defeat of the one who did not set out his view would not be evident. He might even be thought to have won.’ Simon answered, ‘I will do as you say, but I fear that, having already been won over by his words, you will not be a truth-loving judge.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: cut through by anger
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle preserves the image of being cut or sawn through. The main text does not substitute a fire image; sawn through by anger is a more specific lexical alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ εἰς ἕτερον οἱ λόγοι γενέσθωσαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: and let your arguments be directed against the other
lexical_decisions.rationale: The reciprocal contrast of two speakers supports each directing argument toward the other. It does not require appointing an unnamed third interlocutor.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ἀμφοτέρους ὑμᾶς ὑπὸ τοῦ λόγου ἡττηθέντας μὴ φαίνεσθαι ἡττημένους
lexical_decisions.chosen: Although both of you were defeated by the argument, you would not both appear defeated
lexical_decisions.rationale: The next clauses specify that only the openly stated position would visibly lose. Both actual defeat and asymmetric appearance are retained, without changing the hidden position into a victorious one.

passages.text: Our father answered, ‘Do not force me to agree with you without judgment so that I may seem a truth-loving judge. If you wish to hear the truth, I am more predisposed toward your view.’ Simon said, ‘How are you predisposed when you do not know what I think?’ Our father said, ‘That is easy to know; listen to how. You promised to expose Peter as lying when he says there is one God. It is entirely clear that someone promising to convict the speaker of one God of falsehood does not, if he speaks truly, say the same thing. For if he says the same thing as the one speaking falsely, he too is lying. But if he says the opposite and proves it, then he speaks truly. You cannot, then, call the man who says there is one God a liar unless you believe there are many gods. I too say there are many gods. Since I say the same thing as you before the inquiry, I am more predisposed toward you. In this respect you have no need to be anxious about me; Peter does, since I still think the opposite of him. After your inquiry, I hope, as a truth-loving judge who has stripped off preconception, to agree with the prevailing argument.’ When our father had said this, a subdued cry of praise arose from the crowds because he had argued in this way.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the one speaking falsely
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes the participle in a middle sense concerning false speech, since the conditional argument compares two speakers making the same supposedly false assertion. A material passive alternative is the one being falsely accused or lied about. That passive sense does not itself establish the accused person as actually false; neither reading is presented as uncontested, and the conditional remains hypothetical.

lexical_decisions.chosen: who has stripped off preconception
lexical_decisions.rationale: The clothing-removal image and the need to set aside a prior opinion are both retained, rather than changing the father's initial shared belief into an already completed conversion.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ δὲ τὸν ἕνα λέγοντα ψεύσματος ἐλέξαι ἐπαγγελλόμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: someone promising to convict the speaker of one God of falsehood
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied print has ἐλέξαι. Convict follows the context, especially the preceding explicit ἐλέγξειν and the charge of falsehood, rather than treating the form as choosing a speaker. Normalization to ἐλέγξαι would be a proposed Greek change, not the supplied reading. No OCR error or independently verified corrected print is claimed.

passages.text: And Peter likewise said, ‘I am ready to do as the mediator of our discussion has said, and now, without any further delay, I will set out my view about God. I too say that there is one God, who made heaven, earth, and everything in them. It is not permitted to call or consider anyone else a god.’ Simon said, ‘But I say that the scriptures trusted among the Jews speak of many gods, and that God is not angry at this, because he himself has spoken of many gods through his scriptures.’

source_issues.source_quote: ἄλλον. δὲ οὔτε λέγειν οὔτε νομίζειν ἔξεστιν.
source_issues.issue: The selected print places a full stop after ἄλλον before δὲ. The English treats the surviving words as one intelligible construction. This is disclosed punctuation treatment, not a lacuna, a supply of missing words, or an allegation that a corrected Greek print has been verified.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the mediator of our discussion
lexical_decisions.rationale: The role concerns moderation of the exchange, not a theological mediator between God and humanity.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ αὐτὸν διὰ τῶν γραφῶν αὐτοῦ πολλοὺς θεοὺς εἰρηκέναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: because he himself has spoken of many gods through his scriptures
lexical_decisions.rationale: The divine subject and possessive scriptures are retained as Simon's stated reason. They do not represent an independent translator's conclusion about scriptural authorship or polytheism.

lexical_decisions.chosen: And Peter likewise said
lexical_decisions.rationale: The selected print reads ὁμῶς, ordinarily alike or likewise, and that sense is preserved. It does not itself mean the adversative nevertheless normally spelled ὅμως; no accentual normalization has been supplied. Likewise concerns Peter's joining the exchange and does not assert that his doctrine agrees with the father's preceding many-gods view.

passages.text: ‘Indeed, in the law's first utterance he even appears to speak of them as like himself. For it is written that the first human had received God's command to eat from every tree in the garden, but not to eat from the tree of knowing good and evil. The serpent, through the woman, persuaded them to eat on the promise that they would become gods, and caused them to see. Then, when they had come to see, God said to them, “Look, Adam has become like one of us.” Thus the serpent, saying, “You will be like gods,” appears to have spoken as though gods exist, all the more so since God too testified, saying, “Look, Adam has become like one of us.” So the serpent, who said that there are many gods, did not lie. Again, the writing, “You shall not speak evil of gods, and you shall not speak badly of the rulers of your people,” indicates many gods, of whom he does not even wish evil to be spoken. Elsewhere too it is written, “Has another god dared to go in and take for himself a nation from the midst of a nation, as I, the Lord God, have?” In saying, “Has another god dared,” he spoke as though others exist. And elsewhere, “Gods who did not make heaven and earth, let them perish,” as those who did not make them are going to perish. Somewhere else it says, “Watch yourself, lest you go and worship other gods whom your fathers did not know,” as though other gods exist, whom he also tells them not to follow. And again, “The names of other gods shall not rise upon your lips.” Here too he speaks of many gods, whose names he does not wish to be named. Again it is written, “The Lord your God, he is God of gods.” And again, “Who is like you, Lord, among gods?” And again, “God of gods, the Lord.” And again, “God stood in an assembly of gods, and in their midst he judges gods.” So I wonder how, when so many utterances testify in writing that there are many gods, you do not firmly assert that one must neither call them gods nor believe that they exist. For the rest, if you have anything to say in response to these clear statements, speak before everyone.’

source_issues.issue: This wording is supplied within editorial square brackets in the selected edition. The English translates that supplied wording, including the negative and the destruction clause; it is not an independent recovery or proof that the bracketed words survive unbroken in the underlying witness. There is no printed dotted gap here to invent or fill.

lexical_decisions.chosen: caused them to see
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb can mean look up or regain sight. The ensuing Adam quotation and the related form ἀναβλέψασιν support their coming to sight or awareness here; opened their eyes is an idiomatic alternative but supplies an unexpressed anatomical object.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ταύτῃ μᾶλλον ἢ καὶ θεὸς ἐπεμαρτύρησεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: all the more so since God too testified
lexical_decisions.rationale: The awkward comparative sequence is read as reinforcing the serpent's statement with God's corroboration. More literally, all the more in this respect—or even God testified. The main text makes the evidentiary link intelligible without changing who speaks or testifies.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ διαβεβαιοῦσαι μὴ δεῖν μήτε λέγειν μήτε εἶναι νομίζειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: you do not firmly assert that one must neither call them gods nor believe that they exist
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both the printed οὐ and the subsequent prohibition's negatives are retained. The resulting question is rhetorically awkward in Simon's argument; the initial negative is not silently deleted or changed into a different Greek word to resolve the difficulty.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the Lord God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The quoted Greek title is translated Lord, not replaced by Yahweh, since this is the wording quoted by the ancient author rather than a fresh translation from a Hebrew divine-name occurrence.

passages.text: Peter said, ‘Hear a briefer reply to what you have said. The law itself, which has often spoken of gods, itself says to the Jewish multitude, “Look, to the Lord your God belong the heaven of heaven and everything in them.” This includes the point that, even if gods exist, they are under him, that is, under the God of the Jews. Again, “For the Lord your God, he is God in heaven above and on earth below, and there is no other besides him.” Somewhere else scripture says to the Jewish multitude, “The Lord your God, he is God of gods,” as though to say that even if gods exist, they are under the God of the Jews. Elsewhere scripture says of him, “The great and true God, who shows no partiality and will accept no gift, rendering justice to orphan and widow.” In calling the God of the Jews great, true, and one who renders justice, scripture indicated that the others are small and not true. Elsewhere too scripture says, “As I live, says the Lord, there is no other god besides me. I am first; I am after these things; besides me there is no god.” Again, “You shall fear the Lord your God and worship him alone.” And again, “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one Lord.” Indeed, many utterances seal with an oath that God is one and that there is no god besides him. So I wonder how, when so many utterances testify that there is one God, you say there are many.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ οὐρανὸς τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, καὶ πάντα ὅσα ἐστὶν ἐν αὐτοῖς
lexical_decisions.chosen: the heaven of heaven and everything in them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The singular heaven of heaven and the ensuing plural pronoun are preserved as quoted, rather than harmonized with a different scriptural form.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ λαμβάνει πρόσωπον οὐδὲ μὴ λάβῃ δῶρον
lexical_decisions.chosen: shows no partiality and will accept no gift
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first idiom concerns favoritism rather than literally taking a face. The second names a gift in a judicial context, where bribe is a plausible explanatory alternative; the main wording keeps the source's expressed noun.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I am first; I am after these things
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied expression after these things is translated rather than replaced with the familiar but unprinted title last.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κύριος ὁ θεὸς ὑμῶν κύριος εἷς ἐστίν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the Lord your God is one Lord
lexical_decisions.rationale: The quoted word order permits the traditional one-Lord rendering or the Lord is one. The main rendering keeps the repeated Lord and the explicit numerical one, without importing a different creed or Hebrew wording.

passages.text: Simon said, ‘My argument with you from the beginning was to expose you from the scriptures as lying when you say one must not speak of many gods. That is why I showed many written utterances: the divine scriptures themselves speak of many gods.’ Peter said, ‘The very scriptures that speak of many gods themselves also brought this before us, saying, “The names of other gods shall not rise upon your lips.” So I did not speak against what is written, Simon.’ Simon said, ‘Listen to a reply to that too, Peter. You seem to me to sin in speaking against them, since scripture says, “You shall not speak evil, and you shall not speak badly of a ruler of your people.”’ Peter said, ‘I do not sin, Simon, in foretelling their destruction in agreement with the scriptures. For it is written, “Gods who did not make heaven and earth, let them perish.” This does not mean, as you interpreted it, that some did make them and will not perish. For the maker is shown to be one by what is written from the beginning: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” It did not say “the gods.” Somewhere else it says, “The firmament announces the work of his hands.” And in another place it is written, “The heavens themselves will perish, but you will remain forever.”’

lexical_decisions.chosen: themselves also brought this before us, saying
lexical_decisions.rationale: The printed form is treated as a form of παράγω, bringing forward or passing by. The main text preserves its presentation sense, with this pointing to the following quotation. A material intransitive alternative is passed before us, saying. The quoted prohibition functions as instruction, but that function is not substituted for the movement or presentation verb; no Greek correction is supplied.

lexical_decisions.chosen: firmament
lexical_decisions.rationale: The term denotes the established heavenly expanse in the quoted cosmological language. It is not modernized into a scientifically specified atmosphere or an otherwise unexpressed material dome.

passages.text: Simon said, ‘To show that there are many gods, I presented clear utterances from the scriptures. You have brought as many, or even more, utterances from those same scriptures to show that there is one God, the God of the Jews. In answer to my saying that one must not speak evil of gods, you added, to show that there is one maker, that those who did not make must perish. In answer to my saying that one must speak of gods, since the scriptures also speak of them, you showed that one must not utter their names, because the same scripture says not to utter the names of other gods. Since, then, the scriptures themselves say that there are many gods and at other times that there is only one, and sometimes say not to speak evil of them and at other times to speak evil of them, what must we conclude from this except that the scriptures themselves mislead us?’

lexical_decisions.chosen: what must we conclude
lexical_decisions.rationale: The question is about the inference required by the stated premises, retaining the necessity expressed by δεῖ rather than substituting mere ability.

lexical_decisions.chosen: mislead
lexical_decisions.rationale: The term means leading astray or deceiving, not merely presenting a neutral diversity of views. Its accusation is retained as Simon's argument.

passages.text: Peter said, ‘They do not mislead; they expose, bringing into the open the evil intention against God that lurks like a serpent within each person. For they lie before us resembling many different impressions. Each person, having his own intention like wax, looks over them and finds everything in them. Whatever kind of god he wants to exist, he presses upon them his intention, which, as I said, resembles wax, and takes its impression. Since, then, anyone finds in them whatever he wishes to think about God, one person takes impressions of many gods from them. We, however, have taken the image of the one who truly exists, recognizing the true impression from our own form. Moreover, the soul within us is clothed in his image for immortality. If I abandon the begetter of this image, it too must abandon me by a just judgment, recognizing me as unjust from that very act of audacity. Coming from a just one, it will justly abandon me, and thus I shall perish in soul after punishment, when the help from it has departed. If there is another god, let him first clothe me in another appearance, another form, so that through the body's new form I may recognize the new god. But even if he changes the form, will he also change the soul's substance? If he changes that too, I am no longer myself, having become another in both form and substance. Let him therefore fashion others, if there is another. But there is not. If there were, he would have fashioned them. Since he has not fashioned them, being nonexistent, let him leave the one who truly exists alone. For there is no such one except in Simon's opinion alone. I accept no other God besides the one who created me.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: impressions
lexical_decisions.rationale: The scriptures' differing patterns are likened to forms that stamp wax. Impressions keeps the molding image that develops in the verbs of pressing and taking an imprint; types or models are lexical alternatives.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ταύτης τὸν γεννήτορα ἐὰν καταλίπω, δικαίᾳ κρίσει καὶ αὐτή με καταλιπεῖν ἔχει
lexical_decisions.chosen: If I abandon the begetter of this image, it too must abandon me by a just judgment
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine pronouns are read as referring to the immediately preceding image in which the soul is clothed. The soul itself is a grammatically possible alternative, but the ensuing loss of assistance and destruction as to the soul favors the protecting image as what departs.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ὡς ἀπὸ δικαίου δικαίως καταλείψει με
lexical_decisions.chosen: Coming from a just one, it will justly abandon me
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase from a just one is read as the image's provenance from the righteous creator. A more literal alternative is and, as from a just one, it will justly abandon me; the main text does not make the unjust person just in order to remove the tension.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν ψυχὴν μετὰ κόλασιν, τῆς ἀπ’ αὐτῆς ἀπολειφθείσης βοηθείας, φθαρήσομαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: I shall perish in soul after punishment, when the help from it has departed
lexical_decisions.rationale: The accusative soul is taken as the respect in which destruction occurs, and it continues the image as the help's source. This conditional destruction is not softened into bodily death alone or harmonized with the later description of souls as immortal.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐδεὶς γὰρ ἔστιν ἢ μόνῃ γνώμῃ. Σίμωνος
lexical_decisions.chosen: For there is no such one except in Simon's opinion alone
lexical_decisions.rationale: The negative concerns the proposed other god. The genitive Simon's completes opinion across the printed punctuation; no second speaker or missing sentence is invented.

passages.text: Simon said, ‘Since I see you speaking more frequently on behalf of the God who fashioned you, learn from me how you are impious even toward him. Those who fashioned you appear to be two, as scripture says, “And God said, Let us make a human in our image and according to likeness.” “Let us make” indicates two or more, but certainly not one.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον κατ’ εἰκόνα ἡμετέραν καὶ καθ’ ὁμοίωσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Let us make a human in our image and according to likeness
lexical_decisions.rationale: The plural deliberative form and our are central to Simon's inference and retained. The second phrase does not repeat an expressed possessive, so the English does not add a second our.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Those who fashioned you appear to be two
lexical_decisions.rationale: Fashioned repeats the preceding πλάσαντός, preserving Simon's shared wording and its distinction from make in the quotation. You is understood from the preceding God who fashioned you, rather than identifying an additional created object not in the context.

passages.text: Peter answered, ‘There is one who said to his own wisdom, “Let us make a human.” Wisdom, with which he himself always rejoiced as with his own spirit, is united with God like a soul, but extends from him like a hand, creating the whole. For this reason one human also came into being, and from him the female came forth. Though one in kind, it is a pair. For through extension and contraction the one is considered two. Thus I act rightly in rendering all honor to one God as to parents.’ Simon said, ‘What then? Even if the scriptures speak of other gods, will you not accept them?’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἥνωται μὲν ὡς ψυχὴ τῷ θεῷ, ἐκτείνεται δὲ ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ ὡς χείρ
lexical_decisions.chosen: is united with God like a soul, but extends from him like a hand
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both soul and hand comparisons are retained as the author's own account of wisdom. The rendering does not convert these comparisons into a later creedal definition or a separate independent creator.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ μία οὖσα τῷ γένει δυάς ἐστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Though one in kind, it is a pair
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine one and the noun pair can concern the human kind represented by male and female, with a possible continuing analogy to wisdom. The English leaves the collective referent broad instead of introducing a second named divine person.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κατὰ γὰρ ἔκτασιν καὶ συστολὴν ἡ μονὰς δυὰς εἶναι νομίζεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: For through extension and contraction the one is considered two
lexical_decisions.rationale: The numerical unity and duality are translated into accessible English while preserving both spatial-process terms. A unit is considered a pair is a more technical alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to one God as to parents
lexical_decisions.rationale: The singular one God and plural parents are both retained. The comparison is not silently normalized to one parent or expanded into two gods.

passages.text: Peter answered, ‘Whether scriptures or prophets speak of gods, they speak to test their hearers. For it is written: “If a prophet arises among you, giving you signs and wonders, and that sign and wonder comes to pass, but he says to you, ‘Let us go and worship other gods whom your fathers did not know,’ you shall not listen to that prophet. Your hands shall be the first to stone him, for he tempted you to turn away from the Lord your God. If you say in your heart, ‘How did he perform that sign or wonder?’ you shall surely know that the tempter was testing you to see whether you fear the Lord your God.” It was said that the tempter was testing, but it appears differently after the removal to Babylon. For God, who knows everything (as can be shown from many passages), would not test in order to learn for himself, since he knows everything beforehand. If you wish, we will discuss this, and I will show that God has foreknowledge. The claim that he is ignorant has been shown to be false and itself written as a test. Thus, Simon, we cannot be made to stumble either by scriptures or by anyone else; neither are we deceived into accepting many gods, nor do we agree with any statement spoken against God.’

source_issues.issue: The selected image-checked print places a middle dot immediately before γραφῶν. The English translates the surviving wording without assigning the point lexical content. No letters are corrected, no wording restored, and no OCR error or established lacuna is inferred from this apparent print feature.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you shall surely know
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle plus finite verb repeats the knowing root for emphasis. The main rendering expresses that assurance without adding a new source of knowledge.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the tempter was testing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The agent is a substantivized participle, the one who tests or tempts, not a separately supplied Greek noun. The main English varies the lexical roots as tempter and testing; it does not reproduce the Greek's repeated root. A neutral, root-transparent alternative is the one who tests was testing, or the tester was testing. Tempter is chosen because the preceding act tempts toward apostasy and Peter argues against identifying the agent with an omniscient God who needs to learn. The neutral testing interpretation remains a viable lexical alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἑτέρως δὲ μετὰ τὴν εἰς Βαβυλῶνα μετοικεσίαν φαίνεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: but it appears differently after the removal to Babylon
lexical_decisions.rationale: The clause asserts a difference in presentation after the Babylonian displacement. It does not specify a scribe, manuscript, or exact replacement wording, so none is supplied.

passages.text: ‘For we ourselves know from the scriptures that angels have been called gods: I mean the one who spoke at the bush and wrestled with Jacob, as well as the one born as Emmanuel and the one called Mighty God. Moreover, Moses became a god to Pharaoh, though in reality he was a human. So too the idols of the nations. But for us there is one God, one: the one who made created things and ordered everything, whose son the Messiah also is. In obedience to him, we recognize the false things in the scriptures. Moreover, supplied by the fathers with the true things of the scriptures, we know only one who made the heavens and the earth, the God of the Jews and of all who choose to worship him. The fathers, declaring this to be true by reasoning that loves God, handed him down to us, so that we might know that anything said against God is false. But I will say something even beyond this: if things are not as I have said, may it be my lot, and that of those who love the truth, to run the risk for speaking well of the God who made us.’

source_issues.issue: The selected print has a point immediately before δὲ. The English translates the surviving words as a continuous construction, without assigning the point lexical content. No letters are corrected or missing wording restored; the apparent print feature is not labeled an OCR error or an established lacuna.

lexical_decisions.chosen: angels have been called gods
lexical_decisions.rationale: The following examples remain within Peter's statement about appellations. Their inclusion is retained without imposing or repairing the author's classification to fit a later theological system.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὗ καὶ ὁ χριστὸς υἱός, ᾧ πειθόμενοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: whose son the Messiah also is. In obedience to him
lexical_decisions.rationale: Christos functions independently as a title, so Messiah follows the supplied policy. Also preserves the additive καὶ but does not by itself establish other sons. The relative him is grammatically compatible with the Messiah or God; the main text leaves that pronoun unexpanded rather than resolving its antecedent silently.

lexical_decisions.chosen: declaring this to be true by reasoning that loves God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective can mean God-loving or beloved by God. The argument's insistence on reverent thinking supports the active sense; reasoning dear to God is a material alternative. The truth qualification is retained without adding a new creed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: περὶ εὐφημίας τοῦ πεποιηκότος ἡμᾶς θεοῦ κινδυνεύειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: to run the risk for speaking well of the God who made us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The willingness to risk being wrong is explicitly tied to reverent speech about the creator. The translation does not turn it into a denial that any risk exists.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ ἐπὶ τῆς βάτου λαλήσας καὶ τῷ Ἰακὼβ παλαίσας
lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who spoke at the bush and wrestled with Jacob
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first two participles share the single article ὁ, which motivates a shared-subject rendering. This differs from the repeated articles before the subsequent Emmanuel and Mighty God designations. The English preserves that grammatical pattern without independently assigning the subject a later theological identity.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ᾧ πειθόμενοι ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν τὰ ψευδῆ ἐπιγινώσκομεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: In obedience to him, we recognize the false things in the scriptures
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes from the scriptures as identifying the source material in which false things are recognized. The following contrast with the scriptures' true things supports this material-source reading. A material alternative attaches the phrase to recognition as its evidentiary basis: In obedience to him, we recognize what is false from the scriptures, meaning by scriptural evidence. Neither attachment is claimed to be uniquely established.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦτον καὶ θεοφιλεῖ λογισμῷ ἀληθὲς ὂν δογματίσαντες οἱ πατέρες παρέδοσαν ἡμῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: The fathers, declaring this to be true by reasoning that loves God, handed him down to us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering understands the neuter phrase ἀληθὲς ὂν as characterizing the preceding assertion about the one creator, while masculine τοῦτον identifies the God handed on. A material alternative takes ὂν substantivally as being: having affirmed this one as a true being through God-loving reasoning, the fathers handed him on to us. The supplied gender distinction is retained and disclosed, not corrected or diagnosed as OCR corruption.

passages.text: When Simon heard this, he said, ‘Since you say that one must not believe even a prophet who gives signs and wonders but speaks of another god, knowing that he also deserves death, then your teacher too, who gave signs and wonders, was reasonably put to death.’ Peter answered, ‘Our Lord neither declared that gods exist besides the one who created everything nor proclaimed himself to be God. But he reasonably pronounced blessed the person who said that he was the son of the God who ordered everything.’ Simon answered, ‘Does it not seem to you, then, that one who comes from God is God?’ Peter said, ‘Tell us how this can be. We cannot tell you this, because we did not hear it from him.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: nor proclaimed himself to be God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The denial is retained as the author's Peter states it. It is not corrected or softened to conform to a denominational account of Christ's identity.

lexical_decisions.chosen: one who comes from God is God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The origin phrase is rendered openly. God versus a god is a material English article alternative; the Greek argument concerns application of the divine designation rather than a newly specified rank in a pantheon.

passages.text: ‘Besides, it belongs to the Father not to have been begotten, but to the Son to have been begotten. What is begotten is not comparable with what is unbegotten or even self-begotten.’ Simon said, ‘Even if it is not the same in respect of generation?’ Peter said, ‘One who is not in every respect the same as another cannot have all the same designations as that one.’ Simon said, ‘That is assertion, not demonstration.’ Peter said, ‘Why do you not understand that the one is self-begotten or even unbegotten, whereas the other, being begotten, cannot be called the same, not even if the begotten one is of the same substance as the begetter .... But learn this too: human bodies have immortal souls clothed in God's breath. Having come forth from God, they are of the same substance, but are not gods. If they are gods, then by that reasoning the souls of all humans—those who have died, those living, and those yet to be born—are gods. But if, persisting in your argument with me, you say that they too are gods, what great distinction remains even for the Messiah in being called God? For he has what everyone also has.’

source_issues.issue: The edition prints four dots after the begetter clause. The English preserves exactly four dots, without supplying a missing verb or continuation. Its rendering of is in the preceding conditional clause provides ordinary English copular syntax and does not claim to restore the unavailable wording after the clause.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: γεννητὸν δὲ ἀγεννήτῳ ἢ καὶ αὐτογεννήτῳ οὐ συγκρίνεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: What is begotten is not comparable with what is unbegotten or even self-begotten
lexical_decisions.rationale: The three generation terms and their distinctions are retained. Self-begotten is not silently collapsed into unbegotten, and the comparison is not rewritten to assert a later creedal formula.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Εἰ καὶ τῇ γενέσει οὐ ταὐτόν ἐστιν;
lexical_decisions.chosen: Even if it is not the same in respect of generation?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes εἰ καί concessively in response to the preceding distinction and preserves οὐ as actual nonidentity. A material alternative interprets the utterance as a negative question seeking assent: Is it not the same even in respect of generation? That alternative remains a negative question, not an affirmative conditional. Generation can mean coming-to-be or birth and is not silently replaced by substance.

lexical_decisions.chosen: of the same substance
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase is retained both in the conditional argument about the begotten one and the subsequent account of souls. The passage's own distinction between shared substance and the title God is not harmonized with another theological position.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in being called God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied dative form occurs in the title-ascription expression. The English preserves the intended naming construction without supplying a further predicate or claiming to correct the printed Greek.

passages.text: ‘We call God the one whose distinctive property cannot belong to another. For just as he is called boundless because he is infinite in every direction, and it is altogether necessary, since another cannot likewise be infinite, that being called boundless not be a property of another—if anyone says this is possible, he lies, for two things infinite in every direction cannot coexist, since each is bounded by the other—so it is natural for the unbegotten to be one. Even if he has a shape, in this way too the incomparable is one. For this reason he is also called Most High, because, being above all, he has everything subject to himself.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μὴ εἶναι ἴδιον τὸ καλεῖσθαι ἀπέραντος
lexical_decisions.chosen: that being called boundless not be a property of another
lexical_decisions.rationale: The negative is retained, and of another is inferred from the immediately preceding statement that another cannot likewise be infinite. If distinctive property is instead attached to God without that contextual complement, the clause appears to deny the distinctiveness it argues for. The main reading preserves the negation and supplies the contextually available referent, not a conjectural alteration of the Greek.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Even if he has a shape
lexical_decisions.rationale: The conditional concession is retained. The phrase does not deny shape in order to impose a different doctrine of divine incorporeality.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Most High
lexical_decisions.rationale: The superlative title is translated and immediately explained by the source's claim of superiority over all.

passages.text: Simon said, ‘Surely “God,” which everyone says, is not his unutterable name, that you insist so strongly even about the name, so that it may not be given to another?’ Peter said, ‘I know that this is not his unutterable name, but the one spoken by human convention. If you give this to another, you will attach the unspoken one to another too. In terms of intention, the spoken name is an advance toward the unspoken one. On this account the insult is reckoned also against what has not yet been spoken, just as honor directed toward what is known is referred to what is not yet known.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: unutterable name
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective can denote a name not to be divulged or spoken. Secret name is another possible emphasis; the subsequent spoken/unspoken contrast supports unutterable without specifying the hidden name's letters.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ λεγόμενον ὄνομα τοῦ μὴ λεγομένου πρόοδός ἐστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the spoken name is an advance toward the unspoken one
lexical_decisions.rationale: Advance toward reads the movement from the public designation to the unspoken name, because the preceding conditional traces giving the spoken name to another into consequently attaching the unspoken name to another. A materially different genitive reading is the spoken name is a going-forth of the unspoken one, or its outward expression, in which the movement originates in the unspoken name. Both directions are disclosed; the main text is contextual rather than a claim that the genitive uniquely means toward. No hidden name or magical utterance is supplied.

passages.text: Simon said, ‘I wished to know, Peter, whether you truly believe that the human form has been patterned after his form.’ Peter said, ‘Truly, Simon, I am fully convinced that this is so.’ Simon said, ‘How can death dissolve the body when it is patterned by the greatest seal?’ Peter said, ‘It is the form of a righteous God. When it begins to do wrong, the image within it flees, and so the body dissolves, in order that the form may disappear and an unrighteous body may not possess the form of a righteous God. The dissolution, however, concerns not the seal but the body that was sealed. The sealed thing is not dissolved without the one who sealed it. Thus it is not permitted even to die without judgment.’ Simon said, ‘What need was there, then, to give the form of such a one to the human raised from the earth?’ Peter said, ‘This happened because of the creating God's love for humanity. For in respect of substance everything is superior to human flesh—I mean the ether, the sun, the moon, the stars, air, water, fire, in a word, everything else too. These things, having come into being for human service and being superior in substance, gladly endure serving what is inferior in substance because of the form of the superior one. For just as those honoring a clay statue of a king have their honor referred to the one whose form the clay bears, so all creation gladly serves the human made from earth, looking toward that one's honor.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὰν οὖν ἀδικεῖν ἄρξηται, ἡ ἐν αὐτῷ ἰδέα φεύγει
lexical_decisions.chosen: When it begins to do wrong, the image within it flees
lexical_decisions.rationale: It refers to the body or embodied person under discussion. The distinction between the departing image and the dissolving sealed body is maintained, rather than replacing image with a named material organ.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἄνευ δὲ τοῦ σφραγίσαντος τὸ σφραγισθὲν οὐ λύεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: The sealed thing is not dissolved without the one who sealed it
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase does not explicitly name permission, presence, or action as the sense of without. The English leaves that relation broad; without the sealer's permission is a contextual explanatory alternative but adds an unexpressed noun.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in respect of substance
lexical_decisions.rationale: The comparison concerns what things consist of, not their moral worth. Its repetition distinguishes superior substance from the honor attached to the inferior human body's divine form.

lexical_decisions.chosen: looking toward that one's honor
lexical_decisions.rationale: The king-statue comparison points to the superior original whose form the human bears. That one preserves the pronoun while the note identifies its contextual direction; it does not claim that earth itself is the king.

passages.text: ‘See, Simon, what kind of God you wish to persuade us to be ungrateful toward! The earth still carries you, perhaps wishing to see who would dare to think as you do. For you were the first to dare what no one had dared, the first to utter what we heard for the first time. We were the first and only ones to witness God's boundless patience in the face of such impiety from you—not that of some other god, but of the one who created the world, against whom you dared to be impious. No chasms opened in the earth, no fire was sent down from heaven or advanced to burn people, no rain was withheld, no multitude of wild beasts was sent from the thickets, and God's destructive wrath did not begin even against us because of one sinner, as in the case of spiritual adultery, which is worse than adultery according to the flesh. For is not the one who then punished sins the God who created heaven and earth? For even now, most grievously blasphemed, he would have inflicted the greatest punishment. But, on the contrary, he is patient and calls us to reorientation toward God. He has destructive arrows stored in his treasuries for the destruction of the impious, which he will release like living creatures when he takes his seat to repay his enemies with judgment. Therefore let us fear the righteous God whose form the human body bears as an honor.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἴσως δὲ ἰδεῖν βουλομένῃ τίς σοι τὰ ὅμοια φρονεῖν τολμήσοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: perhaps wishing to see who would dare to think as you do
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine participle is read as continuing the personified earth, despite its oblique inflection beside the nominative earth. Perhaps qualifies the conjecture; the English does not replace the earth with an unexpressed masculine observer.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ γὰρ ἔστιν ὁ τότε ἐπεξελθὼν τὰ ἁμαρτήματα οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς κτίστης θεός;
lexical_decisions.chosen: For is not the one who then punished sins the God who created heaven and earth?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The printed negative question is retained rather than turned into a categorical identification or categorical denial. Its relation to the following counterfactual punishment and contrasting patience is rhetorically difficult. A reading that challenges the attribution of the earlier punishments to the creator is materially possible; the main text preserves the question rather than deleting the negative or resolving the theology by emendation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: calls us to reorientation toward God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied English policy uses reorientation for moral-spiritual redirection, with toward God where the context supports the destination. Here the creator's invitation contrasts with the preceding impiety against him; us is the contextually inferred addressee, not a claim that God himself must reorient.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: συντελοῦντα βέλη πρὸς συντέλειαν τῶν ἀσεβῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: destructive arrows ... for the destruction of the impious
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated completion or ending root describes final, destructive force. The English retains the destructive aim and the arrows image without supplying a specific weapon technology.

lexical_decisions.chosen: like living creatures
lexical_decisions.rationale: The life-bearing comparison is explicit; it does not say that the arrows are literally a named species of animal or angel.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς ἐπὶ μοιχείας πνευματικῆς τῆς κατὰ σάρκα χείρονος ὑπαρχούσης
lexical_decisions.chosen: as in the case of spiritual adultery, which is worse than adultery according to the flesh
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main reading takes adultery according to the flesh as the genitive of comparison and attaches worse being to spiritual adultery. It is favored by the surrounding rebuke, which presents Simon's impiety as especially serious. A material alternative takes adultery according to the flesh as subject of a genitive absolute: adultery according to the flesh being worse. That reverses the comparison and is not excluded by morphology alone. This is a disclosed attachment ambiguity, not an unverified printing defect.

passages.text: After Peter had said this, Simon answered, ‘Since I see you cleverly hinting that the things written against the creator in the books are not true, tomorrow I will show from your teacher's words that he says the creator is not the highest God.’ Having said this, Simon went out. Peter said to the crowds standing there, ‘Even if Simon can harm us in no other way concerning God, at least he prevents you from hearing the words that can purify the soul.’ At these words from Peter, much murmuring arose among the crowds, who said, ‘What necessity is there to let him come in here and speak his blasphemies against God?’ Peter heard and said, ‘May speech against God for the testing of human beings find its sufficient limit in Simon. For, as the Lord said, “There will be false apostles, false prophets, sects, and ambitions for rule.” These, as I conjecture, will take their beginning from Simon, who blasphemes God, and cooperate in saying the same things against God as Simon does.’ Having said this with tears, he beckoned the crowds with his hand. As they came forward, he laid his hands on them, prayed, and dismissed them, telling them to assemble earlier in the morning. Having said this, and groaning, he went inside and slept without even taking food.

source_issues.issue: The selected edition supplies this conjunction in editorial brackets. Its sense is translated as that, without claiming independent recovery of an unbroken witness.

The selected edition supplies the beginning of in the books within brackets, including part of the noun. The English translates the supplied complete expression; it does not invent additional lost wording or a dotted gap.

The selected edition brackets the completion of tomorrow and the following from. These supplied words are translated as printed; the translation is not a new reconstruction of their underlying witness.

The supplied print accents this as ἐὰν. The English follows the permissive infinitive sense allow, supported by accusative αὐτόν and infinitive λέγειν, rather than treating it as a conditional conjunction. The usual infinitive accent ἐᾶν would be a proposed accentual normalization, not the supplied reading. No OCR error or independently verified corrected accent is claimed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὔ[ριον ἀπὸ] τῶν τοῦ διδασκάλου σου λόγων δείξω τὸν δημιουργὸν μὴ ἀνώτατον λέγοντα εἶναι θεόν.
lexical_decisions.chosen: tomorrow I will show from your teacher's words that he says the creator is not the highest God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text infers the teacher as the unexpressed object of show and subject of saying from the explicit reference to the teacher's words; the creator is the subject of the being infinitive. A materially different direct attachment makes λέγοντα agree with τὸν δημιουργόν: I will show from your teacher's words the creator saying that he is not the highest God. The reference to the teacher's words motivates the main inference but does not make it explicit or uncontested.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Γένοιτο μέχρι Σίμωνος ἀρκετὸν γενέσθαι τὸν κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ πρὸς πειρασμὸν ἀνθρώπων λόγον
lexical_decisions.chosen: May speech against God for the testing of human beings find its sufficient limit in Simon
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wish concerns the sufficiency and limit of the testing discourse in Simon. May it suffice as far as Simon is a more literal alternative; the English does not change the wish into a prediction that no later blasphemy will occur.

lexical_decisions.chosen: sects, and ambitions for rule
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first noun can mean factions or schools and the second loves of ruling or power-seeking. Sects and ambitions for rule preserve both social division and desire for control, without assigning later denominational names.

passages.text: On the next day, then, Peter, who was about to debate with Simon, woke rather early and prayed. Just as he finished, Zacchaeus came in and said, “Simon is sitting outside, speaking with some of his own people, about thirty of them.” Peter said, “Let him speak until a crowd gathers, and then let us begin the debate. In this way we can hear what he says, prepare ourselves to address it, and go out and speak.” And that is what happened. Zacchaeus went out and, not long afterward, came back in and reported to Peter the statements Simon had made against Peter.

lexical_decisions.chosen: reported to Peter
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb can denote comparison or putting statements before someone; reported fits the messenger’s relay of Simon’s speech, not a second debate with Peter.

passages.text: He said, “He accuses you, Peter, of being a servant of evil, of having great power in magic, and of filling people’s souls with images in a way worse than idolatry. He seemed to offer this as proof that you are a magician, saying: ‘I know about myself that I think things through when I am alone, but when I come to debate with him, I do not remember a single argument. For while he is speaking, my mind is occupied with recalling the things I had thought of saying to him when I came, and I do not hear anything at all that he says. Since I do not experience anything like this with anyone else, but only with him, how am I not being bewitched by him? That whatever he teaches is worse than idolatry will be clear to anyone with understanding once I explain it. For there is no other benefit than for the soul to become free of idols of every kind. When it imagines a form, it is bound by fear; it withers with anxiety about suffering something, and, being altered, becomes possessed. Yet in its possession it seems to most people to be sound-minded.

lexical_decisions.chosen: being a servant of evil
lexical_decisions.rationale: This is Simon’s reported accusation, not the narrator’s verdict. ὑπηρέτης is an assistant or subordinate.

lexical_decisions.chosen: filling ... with images
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the mental-image vocabulary that structures Simon’s criticism, not generic deception alone.

lexical_decisions.chosen: idols of every kind
lexical_decisions.rationale: The bracketed letters already belong to the supplied edition’s reading. No new restoration is made.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in its possession
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the demon/possession language; raves or acts like one possessed is a possible phenomenological rendering.

passages.text: This is what Peter gives you under a promise of making you sound-minded. For under the pretext of one God he seems to free you from many lifeless idols. These do not do their worshipers much harm, because with their very eyes they can see that they are stone, bronze, gold, or some other lifeless material. Therefore, knowing that what is seen is nothing, the soul cannot be haunted by fear in the same way through the visible thing. But when, through deceptive teaching, it looks toward a fearsome God, it is uprooted from its natural condition. I say these things not because I advise you to revere idols, but because Peter, while seeming to free your souls from fearsome images, makes each of your minds possessed by a more fearsome image, introducing a God with a form—and, moreover, supremely just. With this comes terror, and shuddering for the soul that thinks of it, capable even of loosening the tension of sound reasoning. For the mind, placed in such a storm, has its brightness muddied like deep water by a violent wind. Therefore, if he comes for your benefit, let him not, while seeming to dissolve your relatively mild fears arising from lifeless forms, introduce in their place a fearsome form of God. But does God have a form? If he does, he has a shape. If he has a shape, how is he not bounded? If bounded, he is in a place. If in a place, he is less than the place containing him. If less than something, how is he greater, stronger, or higher than all? So much for these matters.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς φοβερὸν θεὸν ἀποβλέπουσα τῶν κατὰ φύσιν ἐκβαθρεύεται.
lexical_decisions.chosen: when ... it looks toward a fearsome God, it is uprooted from its natural condition
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the upheaval/derangement image and the author’s contrast with nature; this remains Simon’s reported position.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν ὀρθῶν λογισμῶν ἐκλῦσαι τοὺς τόνους
lexical_decisions.chosen: loosening the tension of sound reasoning
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the tension image rather than merely saying it makes thinking difficult.

lexical_decisions.chosen: form ... shape ... bounded
lexical_decisions.rationale: Keeps distinct vocabulary in the chain of argument. Bounded denotes spatial delimitation, not simply weakness.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: φοβερῶν ἰδεῶν δοκῶν ἀπαλλάσσειν ὑμῶν τὰς ψυχάς, φοβερωτέρᾳ ἰδέᾳ τὸν ἑκάστου ὑμῶν ἐνθουσιᾶν ποιεῖ νοῦν
lexical_decisions.chosen: while seeming to free your souls from fearsome images, makes each of your minds possessed by a more fearsome image
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἰδέα can denote form, appearance, or a mental representation. Images preserves the visual thread through idols, imagined forms, and God in a form without asserting that every image is a physical statue. Ideas or conceptions is a material cognitive alternative but would conceal the unqualified visual sense in modern English.

passages.text: It is also obvious that he does not truly believe even the things said by his own teacher, for he proclaims the opposite of them. For, as I learn, his teacher said to someone, “Do not call me good, for the good one is one.” But when he says “good,” he no longer means that just one whom the scriptures proclaim, who kills and gives life—kills those who sin and gives life to those who live according to his judgment. That he really did not call the maker good is clear to anyone able to think it through. For the maker was known to Adam, whom he formed; to Enoch, who pleased him; to Noah, whom he saw to be righteous; likewise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; and also to Moses, the people, and the whole world. Yet Peter’s teacher Jesus came and said, “No one knew the Father except the Son, just as no one knows the Son except the Father, and those to whom the Son wishes to reveal him.” Therefore, if the one present was himself the Son, from his coming he revealed to those he wished the one unknown to all. Thus the Father was unknown to everyone before him, not being this one who was known to all.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μή με λέγε ἀγαθόν, ὁ γὰρ ἀγαθὸς εἷς ἐστίν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Do not call me good, for the good one is one
lexical_decisions.rationale: Keeps the wording actually quoted here, not a familiar expanded Gospel form. Simon’s distinction between good and just is retained as his argument.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the maker
lexical_decisions.rationale: δημιουργός denotes creator or maker, not automatically an evil demiurge; the speaker’s proposed distinction is not editorially endorsed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ δικαίῳ ὁραθέντι Νῶε
lexical_decisions.chosen: to Noah, whom he saw to be righteous
lexical_decisions.rationale: δικαίῳ is taken predicatively, righteous being what God perceived in Noah, fitting the list of people pleasing or accepted by the maker. To righteous Noah, whom he saw is the material attributive alternative: righteousness is then Noah’s epithet rather than the content of the seeing. Both retain Noah as the person seen by God; neither reverses the action into Noah seeing God.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐδεὶς ἔγνω τὸν πατέρα, εἰ μὴ ὁ υἱός, ὡς οὐδὲ τὸν υἱόν τις οἶδεν εἰ μὴ ὁ πατήρ
lexical_decisions.chosen: No one knew the Father except the Son, just as no one knows the Son except the Father
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the distinct Greek knew/knows forms instead of homogenizing the quoted tenses.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀγαθὸν δὲ εἰπὼν οὐκέτι ἐκεῖνον λέγει τὸν δίκαιον
lexical_decisions.chosen: But when he says “good,” he no longer means that just one
lexical_decisions.rationale: No longer retains the additional οὐκέτι force. It can express the logical consequence under the good designation—no longer under that description—rather than necessarily a chronological change of belief. The clause remains Simon’s argument, not a narrator’s endorsement.

passages.text: And in saying this, Jesus does not even agree with himself. For sometimes, in other statements drawn from the scriptures, he establishes a fearsome and just God, saying, “Do not fear the one who kills the body but can do nothing to the soul. Fear the one who can cast both body and soul into the Gehenna of fire. Yes, I tell you, fear this one.” That he really said to fear this one as a just God, to whom he also says the wronged should cry out, is shown when he gives a parable on this and adds its explanation, saying, “If, then, the unjust judge acted in this way because he was petitioned repeatedly, how much more will the Father bring vindication for those who cry to him day and night? Or do you think that because he is patient with them, he will not do it? Yes, I tell you, he will do it, and quickly.” But whoever says that God vindicates and repays establishes him as just by nature, and not good. Further, he also gives thanks to the Lord of heaven and earth. If he is Lord of heaven and earth, he is acknowledged as maker; and being maker, he is just. Calling him good at one time and just at another, he does not agree even in this way. Thirdly, his wise disciple insisted yesterday that direct perception is more adequate than an apparition, not knowing that direct perception can be human, whereas an apparition is acknowledged to belong to divinity.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: the Gehenna of fire
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the named place and fire qualification, not the distinct Hades term.

lexical_decisions.chosen: vindication
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐκδίκησις can be vengeance or the securing of justice. Vindication fits the wronged petitioners while retaining the punitive repayment explained afterward.

lexical_decisions.chosen: direct perception is more adequate than an apparition
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐνάργεια here is direct evident encounter, contrasted with ὀπτασία, an apparition. The polemical wise disciple is not softened into neutral description.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐνίοτε γὰρ ἄλλαις φωναῖς τῶν ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν φοβερὸν καὶ δίκαιον συνίστησι θεὸν
lexical_decisions.chosen: For sometimes, in other statements drawn from the scriptures, he establishes a fearsome and just God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text takes τῶν ἀπὸ τῶν γραφῶν partitively, other statements among those derived from scripture. The subsequent fear, judgment, and Lord-of-heaven-and-earth material continues Simon’s contrast with the scriptural just maker, favoring this reading. The comparative-genitive alternative is with statements different from those from the scriptures; that would distinguish rather than include the statements’ scriptural derivation. The supplied wording permits both and is not emended.

passages.text: “By these and similar statements, Peter, Simon, standing outside and speaking to the crowds, seems to me to be disturbing most of them. So go out immediately and dissolve his false arguments by the power of truth.” After Zacchaeus said this, Peter prayed as usual and went out. He stood in the place of the previous day, greeted the crowds in the customary manner of reverence toward God, and began to speak as follows: “Our Lord Jesus, being a true prophet—as I will also give assurance about this at the proper time—made concise declarations about matters important to the truth, for these two reasons. First, he addressed people who revered God and knew to believe what he uttered as a declaration, for what was said was not foreign to their customary practice. Second, because he had a limited time to proclaim, he did not employ demonstrative argument, so that he might not spend all his allotted time on arguments. Otherwise he would have been occupied with explaining a few statements that could be understood through effort of soul, and would thus not have presented the arguments important to truth more extensively. For he declared what he wished as to a people able to understand, among whom we too belong. Whenever, on a rare occasion, we did not understand something he said, we asked him privately, so that none of what he said would remain unintelligible to us.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in the place of the previous day
lexical_decisions.rationale: The elliptical before one refers to one day before; no new location is invented.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ τῆς ἀποδείξεως οὐκ ἐχρῆτο λόγῳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: he did not employ demonstrative argument
lexical_decisions.rationale: Distinguishes concise pronouncement from developed proof, not truthful from untruthful speech.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν ὑπὸ πόνου ψυχῆς νοεῖσθαι δυναμένων
lexical_decisions.chosen: that could be understood through effort of soul
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the intellectual effort supplied by the source rather than rendering the matters permanently incomprehensible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοὺς ἀληθείᾳ διαφέροντας μὴ ἐπὶ πλεῖον εἰσφέρειν λόγους
lexical_decisions.chosen: would thus not have presented the arguments important to truth more extensively
lexical_decisions.rationale: λόγους expressly denotes arguments or discourses presented, distinguished from the earlier matters about which declarations were made. Presented retains introducing them into discussion, not simply naming their topics.

passages.text: Knowing, then, that we knew everything he had said and could supply the proofs, when he sent us to the uninstructed nations to baptize them for forgiveness of sins, he commanded us to teach them first. Of these commands, this is the first and great one: to fear the Lord God and serve him alone. The God he said to fear is the one whose angels belonging to the least of the believers among us stand in heaven continually beholding the Father’s face. For he has a form for the sake of primary and sole beauty, and all his members, not for use. He does not have eyes in order to see from there, for he sees from every side, being in body incomparably brighter than the seeing spirit within us and more radiant than every light, so that compared with him the sun’s light is reckoned darkness. Nor does he have ears in order to hear, for from every side he hears, understands, moves, acts, and makes. He has the most beautiful form for the human being’s sake, so that the pure in heart may be able to see him and rejoice in that for which they endured these things. For with his form, as with a most magnificent seal, he stamped out the human being, so that the human being might rule and have dominion over all and everything might serve him. Therefore, judging him to be the whole and the human being his image—he himself invisible, but his image, the human being, visible—the one who wishes to revere him honors his visible image, namely the human being. Whatever someone does to a human being, whether good or evil, is referred to him. Therefore judgment from him will go forth to all, assigning to each what is deserved, for it vindicates his form.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μορφὴν γὰρ ἔχει διὰ πρῶτον καὶ μόνον κάλλος
lexical_decisions.chosen: he has a form for the sake of primary and sole beauty
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the unusual first/only qualification of beauty. For beauty first and alone is another possible grouping, treating first adverbially; neither reading makes the form a merely metaphorical appearance.

lexical_decisions.chosen: being in body ... brighter
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the author’s explicit bodily attribution to God without conforming it to a later account of divine incorporeality.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῇ γὰρ αὐτοῦ μορφῇ ὡς ἐν μεγίστῃ σφραγῖδι τὸν ἄνθρωπον διετυπώσατο
lexical_decisions.chosen: with his form, as with a most magnificent seal, he stamped out the human being
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the form/seal/imprint sequence and its relation to human dominion.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κρίνας εἶναι τὸ πᾶν αὐτὸν καὶ τὴν αὐτοῦ εἰκόνα τὸν ἄνθρωπον
lexical_decisions.chosen: judging him to be the whole and the human being his image
lexical_decisions.rationale: Attaches κρίνας to the following worshipper, whoever wishes to revere him. The worshipper judges God, not himself, to be the whole. Continuing God as subject of a determination from the preceding sentence is a possible contextual alternative: God determined himself to be the whole and the human being his image. The main text chooses the more direct attachment to the following grammatical subject, avoiding a dangling divine determination. The precise God/whole relation is left at the source’s abstract wording, without a later metaphysical explanation.

passages.text: But someone will say, “If he has a form, he also has a shape and is in a place. And if he is in a place and contained by it as something lesser, how is he great above all? And how can he also be everywhere while having a shape?” To the person saying this, one can first say: those around Simon persuade people to believe such thoughts about him; but we know to be true the things attested by our Lord Jesus Christ. Proofs that this is so must be supplied to you, not on the basis of a command. But first I will speak about place and God. Place is what does not exist, whereas God is what exists; and what does not exist cannot be compared with what exists. For how can place have existence, unless it is a second region, such as heaven, earth, water, air, and any other body, if there is one, which would also fill the void there? It is called void for this reason: because it is nothing. For ‘nothing’ is a more suitable name for it. For what is the so-called void—some sort of vessel that contains nothing? Yet the vessel itself, being empty, is not itself place; rather, place is that in which the void itself is, if indeed it is a vessel. For what exists must necessarily be in what is nothing. But this is what I mean by what does not exist, which some call place: it is nothing. But how can what is nothing be compared with what exists, except as opposites, so that what exists is not [place], but what does not exist is called place? But even if it is something, although many examples press to come forth from me as proof, I wish to use just one, to show that what contains is not invariably stronger than what is contained. The sun is a circular shape and is wholly contained by air, but it illuminates the air, heats it, and cuts through it. And if the sun is absent from it, the air is enveloped in darkness, and wherever a part of it becomes bright, it grows cold as though dying. But by the sun’s rising it is illuminated again, and wherever it is warmed by the sun it is also adorned with greater beauty. And the sun does these things by its presence, although its substance is bounded. What, then, still prevents God, as the maker and master of this and all things, while he himself has shape, form, and beauty, from having the presence proceeding from him extended infinitely?

source_issues.source_quote: καὶ οὗ ἂν αὐτοῦ μέρους λαμπρὸν γένηται, ὡς νεκρούμενον ψύχεται
source_issues.issue: The wording associates becoming bright with cooling, which is puzzling in this analogy. Bright is nevertheless what the supplied text says; no emendation to dark has been made.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡμεῖς δὲ ἀληθεῖς γινώσκομεν τὰς μαρτυρουμένας
lexical_decisions.chosen: we know to be true the things attested
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine plural has no expressed noun; things or statements attested expresses the ellipsis without adding an extra source claim.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ μὲν ὂν μὴ ᾖ, τὸ δὲ μὴ ὂν τόπος λέγηται
lexical_decisions.chosen: what exists is not [place], but what does not exist is called place
