The discrepancy has been referred to the parent for a separate direct print-word check; this candidate follows the supplied selected Greek rather than certifying the incidental reading.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I give thanks to you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb can express acknowledging, praising, or confessing; thanksgiving fits the address to the Lord for revelation, without adding a distinct confession of sins.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Even if our Lord had said
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the hypothetical concession and its relation to the following denial of a different God, rather than presenting the proposed wording as Peter’s admission of the actual quotation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: since Isaiah also said
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the source’s attribution to Isaiah, not an imported correction from another biblical witness.

lexical_decisions.chosen: refers to things once known to them
lexical_decisions.rationale: Interprets the physical ἔγνω / σμένων fragments together as a perfect passive participial expression, known, with the hidden things as its contextual antecedent and the wise as the recipients of prior knowledge. The verified fragment supplies the ν previously omitted in transcription; no further Greek letters are added. Joining the printed letter sequence for interpretation gives the participial sense associated with ἐγνωσμένων, while the initial accent and physical word division remain anomalous and are disclosed, not silently normalized. As of things once known to them is a more formally elliptical English alternative to refers to things once known to them.

lexical_decisions.chosen: that is, knowledge of the secrets
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the author’s explicit equation of key with knowledge of secrets, without adding an independently named esoteric system.

passages.text: And do not say, “He acted impiously toward the wise by hiding these things from them.” Far be it from us to suppose this. For he did not act impiously. Rather, because they hid the knowledge of the kingdom and neither entered themselves nor allowed those who wished to enter, for this reason, in accordance with justice, just as they themselves hid the ways from those who wished, so the secrets were also hidden from them. This was so that what they had done might happen likewise to them, and with the measure they measured, it might be measured to them equally. For the worthy person is owed knowledge of what he does not know; but from the unworthy person it is taken away, even if he seems to possess it and is wise in other matters, and given to the worthy, even if in the duration of their discipleship they are infants.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κἂν ἐν τοῖς χρόνοις τῆς μαθητείας ὦσιν νήπιοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: even if in the duration of their discipleship they are infants
lexical_decisions.rationale: Infants here is explicitly qualified by time in discipleship, not necessarily literal nursing children. The metaphor is retained rather than silently harmonizing all infant-language.

passages.text: If someone says, “Nothing was hidden from the sons of Israel, because it is written, ‘Nothing escaped you, Israel; for do not say, Jacob, “The way was hidden from me,”’” one must understand that the matters important to the kingdom were hidden from them, but the way leading into the kingdom, which is a manner of life, was not hidden. This is why he also says, “For do not say that the way was hidden from me.” The way is the manner of life, since Moses too says, “Look, I have set before your face the way of life and the way of death.” In agreement the teacher said, “Enter through the narrow and constricted way, through which you will enter life.” Elsewhere, when someone asked, “What must I do to inherit eternal life?” he pointed out the law’s commandments.

lexical_decisions.chosen: which is a manner of life
lexical_decisions.rationale: πολιτεία here is conduct or way of living, not a political constitution.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διὰ τῆς στενῆς καὶ τεθλιμμένης ὁδοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: through the narrow and constricted way
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains way as quoted here, not an imported gate from another witness.

passages.text: From Isaiah’s saying in God’s person, “But Israel did not know me, and the people did not understand me,” it does not follow that Isaiah too was hinting at a God other than the known maker. Rather, through a different riddle he called the known one unknown, because the people, ignorant of the known God’s just disposition, sinned and did not suppose that they would be judged by the good God. Therefore, after saying, “But Israel did not know me, and the people did not understand me,” he added, “Woe, sinful nation, people full of sins.” For, as I said, through ignorance of his justice they were without fear and became full of sins, supposing him only good, in the sense that he would not pursue their sins.

lexical_decisions.chosen: just disposition
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the disposition/character sense; the argument concerns ignorance of justice, not ignorance that any deity exists.

lexical_decisions.chosen: only good
lexical_decisions.rationale: Keeps the restrictive only, which is central to the polemic against separating goodness from judgment.

passages.text: Some sinned in this way from the supposition that, because of his goodness, he does not judge; others from the opposite view. For, supposing the statements of the scriptures against God to be true, although they are unjust and false, they did not know his true divinity and power. Therefore, supposing that he is ignorant, delights in murders, lets the wicked off through gifts of sacrifices, and also deceives, lies, and does everything unjust, they themselves, thinking they had acted like God, insisted while sinning that they were acting reverently. Therefore they were immovable toward what is better, and when admonished did not turn back. For they had no fear, considering themselves made like God through such actions.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰς γὰρ κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ τῶν γραφῶν φωνάς, ἀδίκους οὔσας καὶ ψευδεῖς
lexical_decisions.chosen: the statements of the scriptures against God ... although they are unjust and false
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the historical speaker’s explicit criticism of certain scriptural statements. It is neither softened nor presented as the translator’s own verdict about scripture.

lexical_decisions.chosen: did not turn back
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the turning verb distinct from μετανοέω/reorient.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐκ τῆς διὰ τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἀκρίτου ὑπολήψεως
lexical_decisions.chosen: from the supposition that, because of his goodness, he does not judge
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text understands a supposition of God’s non-judging character, because 18.18 explicitly links presumed goodness with absence of pursuit of sins and judgment. Alternatively ἀκρίτου qualifies ὑπολήψεως: from the uncritical or unexamined supposition prompted by his goodness. On that attachment the adjective characterizes the supposition, not God’s judging activity. Neither reading is treated as a source defect.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτοὶ ὡς ὅμοια θεοῦ ποιήσαντες, ἁμαρτάνοντες ἰσχυρίζοντο εὐσεβεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: they themselves, thinking they had acted like God, insisted while sinning that they were acting reverently
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὡς presents the alleged imitation from their viewpoint, not a fact affirmed by the narrator, who just called the accusations about God false. Had acted retains the retrospective aorist participle, while thinking makes their rationale explicit.

passages.text: One might reasonably say that the words, “No one knew the Father except the Son, just as no one knows the Son except the Father,” were addressed to those who supposed him to be like this. And rightly so. For had they known, they would not have sinned by believing books really written against God for testing. Elsewhere too, wishing to show them more clearly the cause of their error, he says, “This is why you are deceived: you do not know the true things in the scriptures, and for this reason you are also ignorant of God’s power.” Therefore every person who wants to be saved must become, as the teacher said, a judge of the books written for testing. For he said this: “Become approved money changers.” Money changers are needed because the counterfeit is also mixed in with the genuine.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the true things in the scriptures
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the distinction within the scriptures asserted by the author; it is not replaced by simply the scriptures.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for testing
lexical_decisions.rationale: πειρασμός can mean testing or temptation. The argument treats problematic books as a test of discernment; the temptation alternative remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Become approved money changers
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the money-changing analogy and the approved/genuine versus counterfeit contrast.

passages.text: After Peter said these things, Simon pretended to be shocked at what had been said about the scriptures and, as though alarmed, said, “Far be it from me and those who love me to listen to your statements. Until I knew that you held these views about the scriptures, I put up with you and conversed; but now I withdraw. I ought, however, to have withdrawn at the beginning, because I heard you say, ‘I believe no one who says anything against the one who created the world: neither angels nor prophets, neither scriptures nor priests, neither teachers nor anyone else, even if someone performs signs and wonders, even if he visibly flashes in the air or reveals through visions or dreams.’ Who, then, can persuade you, whether rightly or wrongly, to think anything other than what you have decided, when you remain so firmly and immovably in your own knowledge?”

lexical_decisions.chosen: pretended to be shocked
lexical_decisions.rationale: The narrator explicitly presents the shock as pretense, rather than leaving its sincerity open.

lexical_decisions.chosen: visibly flashes in the air
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the vivid flashing and airborne manifestation, not a generic vision.

passages.text: As Simon said this and was about to go out, Peter said, “Hear this further thing from me, then go wherever you wish.” Simon turned and remained, and Peter said, “I know how you were astounded then when you heard me say, ‘Whoever says anything against the God who created the world, I do not believe him.’ Now hear something greater than this. If the God who created the world really were in character such as the scriptures describe him, and even if in some other way he were incomparably evil, beyond what either the scriptures could say or anyone else could even conceive, I would nevertheless not stop revering him alone and doing his will. For I want you to know and be persuaded that the person who has no affection for his own maker can never have it for another either. If he does have it for another, he has it contrary to nature and does not know that he has from evil the love of the unjust, since he cannot even keep that love firm. And if there really is someone else above the maker, being good he will receive me all the more because I love my own Father; but he will not receive you, knowing that you abandoned your maker by nature—I do not say father—for a greater hope, without concern for what is reasonable. Thus, if you find someone superior even to him, he knows that you will abandon him too someday, especially since he has not become your father, when you have abandoned even your true father.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐὰν τῷ ὄντι ὁ τὸν κόσμον κτίσας θεὸς τὴν γνώμην τοιοῦτος ὢν τυγχάνῃ
lexical_decisions.chosen: If the God who created the world really were in character such as ...
lexical_decisions.rationale: The description is explicitly hypothetical. The severe conditional is preserved, not rewritten as an assertion that the maker is evil.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐκ πονηροῦ τὸν τῶν ἀδίκων ἔρωτα ἔχων
lexical_decisions.chosen: he has from evil the love of the unjust
lexical_decisions.rationale: From evil adopts the impersonal reading of πονηροῦ, since the immediate context does not identify a personal evil agent. From an evil one or the evil one is grammatically possible but is not asserted through imported theology. Love of the unjust may be love characteristic of unjust people or love directed toward them; the main phrase retains that ambiguity.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν φύσει σου ποιητὴν (οὐ γὰρ λέγω πατέρα)
lexical_decisions.chosen: your maker by nature—I do not say father
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves Peter’s pointed change from father to maker in addressing Simon rather than harmonizing all parent-language.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὕτως εἰ καὶ αὐτοῦ κρείττονα εὑρήσεις
lexical_decisions.chosen: Thus, if you find someone superior even to him
lexical_decisions.rationale: Superior retains broader comparative κρείττονα without specifying the basis of superiority. Better or stronger are material alternatives, but the argument about changing allegiances does not require strength alone.

passages.text: But you will say, “He knows that no one else is above him, and for this reason he cannot be abandoned.” Then thanks are due to there being no other! Yet he knows the disposition of your mind to be ready for ingratitude. If, knowing you to be ungrateful, he receives you, but knowing me to be grateful does not admit me, according to your account he is irrational, not acting reasonably. Thus, Simon, you are a subordinate of evil without knowing it.” Simon replied, “Then tell us: from where has evil grown?” Peter said, “Since today you already moved to go out and said that from now on you would not listen to me as a blasphemer, if you wish to learn, come tomorrow and I will explain. I will also allow you to examine me as you wish, without contentiousness.” Simon said, “I will do as seems good to me.” After saying this, he went away. None of those who had entered with him went out with him; instead, falling at Peter’s feet, they asked to obtain forgiveness for having been attached to Simon and to be received as they reoriented. Peter welcomed both those feeling regret and the other crowds, laid his hands on them, praying and healing the afflicted among them. Thus, as he dismissed them, he instructed them to hurry at dawn. After saying this, he went inside with his companions and did the customary things in preparation for the rest that pressed upon them, since evening had arrived.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Then thanks are due to there being no other
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the ironic thanks and the existential absence, not a moral endorsement of Simon’s fidelity.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to be received as they reoriented
lexical_decisions.rationale: Uses POB reorientation terminology for the moral-spiritual response, traditionally repenting.

lexical_decisions.chosen: those feeling regret
lexical_decisions.rationale: Keeps μεταμέλομαι’s regret/remorse sense distinct from the preceding μετανοέω, rather than homogenizing both as reorienting.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰ εἰωθότα πρὸς τὴν ἐπείγουσαν ἡσυχίαν ἐποίησεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: did the customary things in preparation for the rest that pressed upon them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The customary practices are not enumerated here; neither a meal nor a particular prayer is invented.

passages.text: On the next day Peter came forward rather early in the morning. Seeing Simon waiting for him with many others, he greeted the crowd and began to speak with them. But the moment he began, Simon interrupted and said, “Set aside these long preliminaries of yours and answer me as I question you concerning the matter at hand. For I perceive—as I know from what I have heard from the beginning...—that your sole aim is to use every device to demonstrate that the Creator himself alone is a blameless God, and that, in your resolve, you have so great a longing to insist on this that you even dare to call false certain passages of the writings that plainly accuse him. For this reason, I have resolved today to prove that it is impossible for him, being the creator of everything, to be blameless. I can begin the proof now, provided you answer what I ask you.”

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints exactly three dots between ἐπακηκοὼς and ἐπίσταμαι, apparently marking unavailable wording or a printed break in the construction. The translation retains exactly three dots and supplies no restoration.

source_issues.source_quote: καὶ τοσοῦτον προαίρεσιν πόθον ἔχοντα διισχυρίζεσθαι, ὡς καὶ ἐνίας τῶν γραφῶν περικοπὰς σαφῶς καταλεγούσας αὐτοῦ τολμᾶν ψευδεῖς λέγειν
source_issues.issue: The attachment of ἔχοντα is uncertain. The main text takes it as referring back to Peter in συννοῶ σε, so that Peter has the longing to insist and consequently dares to call passages false. It could formally modify τὸν δημιουργόν, yielding a sense such as ‘to show the Creator ... as having such a longing to insist,’ although that makes the following shift to Peter as the understood subject of τολμᾶν less direct. A looser construal making the Creator’s longing the content of Peter’s insistence would require διισχυρίζεσθαι to function separately rather than directly completing πόθον. No change to the supplied Greek is proposed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: rather early in the morning
lexical_decisions.rationale: The comparative adverb indicates an earlier-than-usual or notably early time.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰς τὸ προκείμενον πυνθανομένῳ μοι ἀπόκριναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: answer me as I question you concerning the matter at hand
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves both the subject under discussion and Simon’s demand that Peter answer his question.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to use every device
lexical_decisions.rationale: μηχανή here denotes a contrivance, method, or strategic means, with Simon’s accusatory force retained.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν δημιουργὸν αὐτὸν δεῖξαι μόνον ἄμεμπτον εἶναι θεὸν
lexical_decisions.chosen: to demonstrate that the Creator himself alone is a blameless God
lexical_decisions.rationale: μόνον is taken as singling out the Creator as the one who is a blameless God; it could alternatively be attached more closely to the predicate.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ τοσοῦτον προαίρεσιν πόθον ἔχοντα διισχυρίζεσθαι, ὡς καὶ ἐνίας τῶν γραφῶν περικοπὰς σαφῶς καταλεγούσας αὐτοῦ τολμᾶν ψευδεῖς λέγειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: and that, in your resolve, you have so great a longing to insist on this that you even dare to call false certain passages of the writings that plainly accuse him
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔχοντα is taken as resuming σε and therefore referring to Peter, while διισχυρίζεσθαι completes πόθον: Peter longs to insist on his claim. προαίρεσιν is understood as an accusative of respect, ‘in respect of resolve.’ This keeps Peter as the subject of the linked longing, insistence, and daring.

lexical_decisions.chosen: passages of the writings that plainly accuse him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The personal genitive αὐτοῦ and Simon’s polemical context support the hostile sense ‘speak against’ or ‘accuse,’ though a more neutral rendering such as ‘give an account concerning him’ is lexically possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: provided
lexical_decisions.rationale: The particle γε strengthens the stated condition for beginning the proof.

passages.text: “Do you say that there is a ruler of wickedness, or not? For if you say there is not, I can prove from many things, including statements of your teacher, that there is. But if you reasonably acknowledge that the evil one exists, I will carry the argument forward in due sequence.” Peter replied, “It is impossible for me to deny the voice of my teacher. I therefore acknowledge that the evil one exists, because the teacher who spoke truth in everything often said that he exists. For example, he acknowledges that the one who conversed with him for forty days had tested him. Somewhere else, too, I know that he said, ‘If Satan drives Satan out, he has become divided against himself. How, then, can his kingdom stand?’ He also made it clear that he had seen the evil one fall like lightning from heaven. Elsewhere he said, ‘The one who sowed the evil seed is the devil.’ And again, ‘Do not give the evil one an opportunity.’ In giving counsel he also said, ‘Let your yes be yes and your no, no; anything beyond these comes from the evil one.’ And in the prayer he handed down we have the words, ‘Rescue us from the evil one.’ Somewhere else, too, he promised to say to those who act impiously, ‘Go away into the outer darkness, which the Father prepared for the devil and his angels.’ So that I do not prolong the argument excessively, I know that my teacher often said that the evil one exists. Therefore I too agree that he exists. Now, if you have something to say as the next step, as you promised, say it.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: a ruler of wickedness
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἡγεμών denotes a leader or ruler; the phrase presents a personal power presiding over wickedness.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐκ πολλῶν καὶ τῶν τοῦ διδασκάλου σου
lexical_decisions.chosen: from many things, including statements of your teacher
lexical_decisions.rationale: The nouns governed by τῶν are implicit; ‘statements’ supplies the contextual sense without treating the teacher himself as evidence.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I will carry the argument forward in due sequence
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπομένως indicates a logically consequent or orderly next stage.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπὶ τεσσαράκοντα ἡμέρας διαλεχθέντα πεπειρακέναι αὐτόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who conversed with him for forty days had tested him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The accusative participle supplies the unexpressed subject of πεπειρακέναι, while αὐτόν is its object. Context favors the evil one as the tester and the teacher as the one tested, although neither referent is named within the clause.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Do not give the evil one an opportunity
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόφασις can mean a pretext, occasion, or opportunity; ‘opportunity’ suits something granted to the evil one.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he promised to say
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπέσχετο ordinarily means ‘promised.’ The rendering is not harmonized to a familiar Gospel saying or softened to ‘threatened.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: λοιπὸν εἴ τι ἔχεις ἐπομένως λέγειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Now, if you have something to say as the next step
lexical_decisions.rationale: λοιπόν and ἐπομένως together mark the next consequence in Simon’s proposed argument.

passages.text: Simon said, “Since, then, you have reasonably acknowledged that the evil one exists, tell us from the writings how he came to be—if indeed he came to be—and by whom and why.” Peter replied, “Pardon me, Simon, for not daring to say what has not been written. If you say that it has been written, show it. But if, since it has not been written, you too are unable to show it, why do we put ourselves in danger by making declarations about things not recorded? Or have we not believed that we will be judged, not only for what we do but also for what we say in belief, and is that why we speak more boldly about God?” Simon, understanding that this had been aimed at his recklessness, said, “Leave me to take the risk, but do not use what you call blasphemy as a pretext for retreat. For I perceive that you want to draw back so that you may escape being refuted before the crowds: at one time on the ground that you fear hearing blasphemies, and at another on the ground that, since it has not been written how, by whom, and why the evil one came to be, one must not dare to say more than Scripture. Therefore, as a reverent man, you confirm this alone: that he exists. But in devising these tactics you deceive yourself, not knowing that if it is blasphemy to investigate the evil one precisely, the responsibility lies with me, the accuser, not with you, the one defending God. And if the matter under investigation is unwritten and for that reason you do not wish to investigate it, there are certain adequate paths capable of demonstrating the matters under investigation no less than writings can. For example, is it not necessary that the evil one—whom you too say exists—be either originated or unoriginated?”

source_issues.source_quote: Ἐπεὶ οὖν εὐγνωμονήσας ὡμολόγησ[ας] εἶναι τὸν πονηρόν, ἀπὸ γραφῶν ἡ[μῖν] λέγε τὸ πῶς γέγονεν (εἴπερ γέγο[νε]) καὶ ὑπὸ τίνος καὶ διὰ τί. καὶ ὁ Πέτρος Σ[ύγ]γνωθί μοι, Σίμων, μὴ τολμῶντι εἰπεῖν [ἃ] μὴ γέγραπται.
source_issues.issue: The selected, image-checked text contains square-bracketed sequences within several words and around ἃ. The translation follows the complete forms explicitly supplied by the selected text and adds no further restoration.

source_issues.source_quote: ὁτὲ μὲν ὡς δεδιὼς βλασ[φημί]ας ἀκοῦσαι, ὁτὲ δὲ (ἐπεὶ μὴ γέ[γρα]πται πῶς καὶ ὑπὸ τίνος καὶ διὰ τί [γέ]γονεν ὁ πονηρός)
source_issues.issue: The selected text again marks parts of words with square brackets. The translation follows the supplied completed forms βλασφημίας, γέγραπται, and γέγονεν without inventing additional wording.

source_issues.source_quote: ὅτι μὴ, χρὴ πλεῖον τῆς γραφῆς τολμᾶν λέγειν
source_issues.issue: The printed comma after μὴ disrupts the contextually expected construction. The translation provisionally attaches μὴ to χρὴ, yielding ‘one must not dare,’ while preserving every supplied word.
source_issues.proposed_reading: ὅτι μὴ χρὴ πλεῖον τῆς γραφῆς τολμᾶν λέγειν

lexical_decisions.chosen: reasonably
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle commends Peter as having acted with good sense or fairness in making the admission.

lexical_decisions.chosen: how he came to be—if indeed he came to be
lexical_decisions.rationale: The parenthetical qualification leaves open the possibility that the evil one did not originate.

lexical_decisions.chosen: for what we say in belief
lexical_decisions.rationale: πιστεύοντες may mean ‘while believing’ or ‘as matters of belief’; the chosen wording preserves the connection between belief and speech.

lexical_decisions.chosen: aimed at his recklessness
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀπόνοια can denote folly, desperation, or reckless audacity. Simon understands Peter’s warning as directed at his own conduct.

lexical_decisions.chosen: being refuted before the crowds
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔλεγχος can denote refutation, exposure, or censure; the public debate favors ‘refuted.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: to investigate the evil one precisely
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀκριβόω here means to ascertain exact details. ‘Give a precise account of the evil one’ is also possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ αἰτία περὶ ἐμὲ τὸν κατήγορον τυγχάνει, οὐ περὶ σὲ τὸν συνηγοροῦντα τῷ θεῷ
lexical_decisions.chosen: the responsibility lies with me, the accuser, not with you, the one defending God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The legal contrast between an accuser and an advocate is preserved.

lexical_decisions.chosen: be either originated or unoriginated
lexical_decisions.rationale: The pair concerns whether the evil one came into being. ‘Created or uncreated’ is possible but could narrow γενητός prematurely to deliberate creation.

passages.text: Peter said, “It is necessary.” Simon replied, “Therefore, if he is originated, he came into being through God himself, who made everything: either begotten like a living creature, or projected as substance and coming about outside through mixture. For if the matter from which he came to be was outside him, whether animate or inanimate, he came to be either through God himself or from himself, or even arose from things that do not exist; he belongs to the class of things that are relative to something, or he always existed. Since, then, all the paths toward discovering him have, as I think, been distinguished here, it is necessary that he be discoverable by traveling one of them. One seeking an origin must therefore travel each path and, upon finding the responsible party, understand that he is subject to blame. Is that not so? What do you think?”

source_issues.source_quote: [εἰ γὰρ] ἐκτὸς ἦν αὐτοῦ ἡ ὕλη ἔμψυχος [οὖσα] ἢ ἄψυχος, ὅθεν γέγονεν, ἢ δι’ αὐτοῦ [τοῦ] θεοῦ ἢ ἀφ’ ἑαυτοῦ ἢ καὶ ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων [συμ]βέβηκεν
source_issues.issue: The selected text explicitly marks εἰ γάρ, οὖσα, τοῦ, and part of συμβέβηκεν with square brackets. The translation follows these supplied readings without adding an independent restoration.

source_issues.source_quote: ἢ δι’ αὐτοῦ [τοῦ] θεοῦ ἢ ἀφ’ ἑαυτοῦ ἢ καὶ ἐξ οὐκ ὄντων [συμ]βέβηκεν, τῶν πρὸς τὶ ἐστὶν ἢ αἰεὶ ἦν
source_issues.issue: The sequence is syntactically compressed. The main text carries the evil one forward as the implied subject of γέγονεν, συμβέβηκεν, ἐστίν, and ἦν because ὅθεν γέγονεν resumes the surrounding inquiry into how the evil one originated. Alternatively, ἡ ὕλη may remain the subject or controlling topic: the clauses would then concern the origin and status of the matter from which the evil one arose—whether that matter came through God, from itself, or from nonbeing, whether it belongs among relative or dependent things, or whether it always existed. No alteration of the supplied Greek is proposed.
The referent of αὐτοῦ may be God, as the sequence most naturally suggests, or the evil one. The translation retains the pronoun ‘him’ rather than resolving it explicitly.
The selected text prints the alpha of πάσης within square brackets. The translation follows the supplied completed word and supplies no additional restoration.

lexical_decisions.chosen: begotten like a living creature
lexical_decisions.rationale: The comparison presents ordinary animal generation as one possible mode of origin.

lexical_decisions.chosen: projected as substance
lexical_decisions.rationale: The philosophical language describes a projection or emanation in respect of substance; ‘emanated substantially’ is a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: coming about outside through mixture
lexical_decisions.rationale: κρᾶσις denotes mixing or blending, while συμβαίνω can describe coming together or coming about. The precise cosmological mechanism remains compressed in the Greek.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the matter ... whether animate or inanimate
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔμψυχος and ἄψυχος distinguish matter possessing life or soul from lifeless matter.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he belongs to the class of things that are relative to something
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase uses the philosophical category of relatives, things whose identity is stated in relation to something else. Under the alternative syntactic grouping, it describes the matter rather than the evil one.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: π[ά]σης οὖν ὁδοῦ (ὡς οἶμαι) ἐνταῦθα διῃρημένης
lexical_decisions.chosen: all the paths ... have, as I think, been distinguished here
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαιρέω suggests an exhaustive division or differentiation of possible avenues of inquiry.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εὑρόντα τὸν αἴτιον ὑπὸ μέμψιν αὐτὸν εἶναι νοεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: upon finding the responsible party, understand that he is subject to blame
lexical_decisions.rationale: αὐτόν is taken as referring to the responsible cause or agent just found. It could grammatically be heard as referring back to the evil one, but the argument seeks whom to blame for his origin.

passages.text: Peter said, “It seems to me that if he is shown to have come into being through God, the one who made him should not yet be subject to blame, for perhaps his usefulness might prove more necessary than everything else. But if he should even be shown not to have come into being, but to have existed always, neither in this case is the Creator blameworthy, since he is superior to all things: even if he has been unable to put an end to a beginning that has no beginning because he lacks the nature required to do so; or if, though able, he does not abolish him, having judged it unjust to impose an end on one who received no beginning, and making allowance for one who is evil by nature because he cannot become anything else, even if he should have the desire to become something else. But if, while wanting to make him good, he were unable, even so he is good, because he wants to but cannot. And in the very respect in which he is powerless, he is the most powerful of all, because the possibility is left to no one else. But if there is someone else who is able and yet does not put matters right, then, in the respect in which he is able but does not put matters right, he stands acknowledged as evil, since he does not stop him, as though taking pleasure in the things done by him. But if that other cannot do so either, better is the one who, besides being unable, ‘does not hesitate’ to benefit us as far as possible.”

source_issues.source_quote: Ἐμοὶ δοκεῖ, ἐὰν· ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ φανῇ γεγονὼς
source_issues.issue: The printed punctuation after ἐὰν interrupts the conditional phrase. The translation provisionally reads the condition continuously with ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ while altering no Greek wording.
source_issues.proposed_reading: Ἐμοὶ δοκεῖ, ἐὰν ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ φανῇ γεγονὼς

source_issues.source_quote: εἰ καὶ ἀνάρχῳ ἀρχῇ τέλος [ἐπιθ]εῖναι διὰ τὸ μὴ φύσιν ἔχειν οὐ δεδύ[νητ]αι, ἢ δυνατὸς ὢν οὐκ ἀναιρεῖ αὐ[τόν], ἄδικον κρίνας ἀρχὴν μὴ εἰλη[φ]ότι τέλος ἐπιθεῖναι
source_issues.issue: The selected text marks portions of ἐπιθεῖναι, δεδύνηται, αὐτόν, and εἰληφότι with square brackets. The translation follows the completed forms explicitly supplied by the selected text and makes no additional restoration.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μήπως τὸ χρήσιμον αὐτοῦ πάντων ἀναγκαιότερον εὑρεθείη
lexical_decisions.chosen: for perhaps his usefulness might prove more necessary than everything else
lexical_decisions.rationale: μήπως introduces a cautious possibility here. It can also have the preventive force ‘lest his usefulness prove,’ but Peter’s argument depends on withholding blame because such usefulness may be discovered.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to have existed always
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase explains what it would mean for the evil one not to have come into being.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a beginning that has no beginning
lexical_decisions.rationale: The deliberately paradoxical repetition of ἀρχή is preserved. ‘Beginningless principle’ is a more technical alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: because he lacks the nature required to do so
lexical_decisions.rationale: The implicit subject is taken as the Creator, explaining his inability to end the beginningless being. It is also possible to take the subject as the beginningless being or principle: ‘because it has no such nature.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: making allowance for one who is evil by nature
lexical_decisions.rationale: πεφυκότι presents evil as the being’s natural condition, while συγγνῶναι denotes pardon or allowance. The infinitive is construed with the decision not to destroy him; alternatively, it may remain under ἄδικον κρίνας, producing ‘judging it unjust ... to pardon one who is evil by nature.’

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ εἰ τοῦ γενέσθαι τὸ ἐπιθυμεῖν ἔχοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: even if he should have the desire to become something else
lexical_decisions.rationale: The complement ‘something else’ is carried forward from the immediately preceding clause; the Greek literally speaks of possessing the desire to become.

lexical_decisions.chosen: while wanting to make him good
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀγαθόν is taken predicatively of the evil one. An alternative is ‘wanting to do something good,’ but the preceding question of whether the evil one can become otherwise favors the chosen rendering.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐν ᾧ ἀδυνατεῖ πάντων ἐστὶ δυνατώτατος
lexical_decisions.chosen: in the very respect in which he is powerless, he is the most powerful of all
lexical_decisions.rationale: The paradoxical juxtaposition of inability and supreme power is preserved rather than explained away.

lexical_decisions.chosen: does not put matters right
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατορθόω can mean to succeed, act rightly, or set something right. The argument concerns an able agent who fails to correct the evil situation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κρείττων ὁ πρὸς τῷ ἀδυνατεῖν κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν ἡμᾶς εὐεργετεῖν ‚οὐκ ὀκνῶν.‘
lexical_decisions.chosen: better is the one who, besides being unable, ‘does not hesitate’ to benefit us as far as possible
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρὸς τῷ with the infinitive means ‘in addition to,’ and κατὰ τὸ δυνατόν limits the beneficence to what is possible. The selected text’s quotation marks around οὐκ ὀκνῶν are represented by inner quotation marks.

passages.text:
And Simon said, “When I have discussed with you each of the points I proposed and shown you who is responsible for evil, then I will also answer what you have said and demonstrate that the God whom you call blameless is liable to blame.”

And Peter said, “Since, from what you have been saying from the beginning, I perceive that you are intent on nothing other than subjecting God to blame as the leader of evil, I have resolved to accompany you along every path you wish and show that God is beyond all blame.”

And Simon said, “You say these things as one who loves the one you have taken to be God, but you are not speaking the truth.”

And Peter said, “But you, as an evil man who hates the God you have failed to know, let loose blasphemous words.”

And Simon said, “Remember that you compared me to a leader of evil.”

And Peter said, “I confess that I lied when I compared you to the evil one, for I was compelled to do so because I could not find anyone equal to you or even worse than you. That is why I compared you to the evil one, for you prove to be much more wicked than even the leader of evil. No one can show that the evil one has spoken against God, but all of us who are present can attest that you boldly denounce him.”

And Simon said, “One who seeks the truth owes it to no one to concede anything contrary to what is. Otherwise, why does he seek at all? What then? Could I not likewise, setting aside an exact investigation of the facts, spend all my time praising a God whom I do not know?”

lexical_decisions.chosen: who is responsible for evil
lexical_decisions.rationale: The masculine substantive αἴτιος can identify the responsible agent or cause. The personal wording suits the ensuing inquiry into the leader of evil.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς κακίας ἡγεμόνα τὸν θεὸν ὑποβάλλειν μέμψει
lexical_decisions.chosen: subjecting God to blame as the leader of evil
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑποβάλλειν μέμψει depicts placing or exposing someone under censure, while ὡς κακίας ἡγεμόνα states the alleged basis for that censure.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the one you have taken to be God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect of νομίζω presents Peter as having regarded or supposed this one to be God. “The God in whom you have believed” is possible but less directly reflects the verb’s evaluative sense.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν γὰρ [πο]νηρὸν οὐδεὶς κατειπόντα θεοῦ δεῖξαι δύναται
lexical_decisions.chosen: No one can show that the evil one has spoken against God
lexical_decisions.rationale: καταλέγω here means speak against, denounce, or malign. The rendering does not import the broader claim that the evil one never otherwise opposes God.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐδὲν οὐδενὶ ὀφείλει παρὰ τὸ ὂν χαρίζεσθαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: owes it to no one to concede anything contrary to what is
lexical_decisions.rationale: χαρίζεσθαι can mean grant a favor or make a concession, and παρὰ τὸ ὄν contrasts such favor with reality as it is.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ἐγὼ οὐ δύναμαι, παρεὶς ἀκριβοῦν τὰ πράγματα, εἰς ἐγκώμιον οὗ μὴ ἐπίσταμαι θεοῦ τὸν πάντα μου δαπανᾶν χρόνον;
lexical_decisions.chosen: Could I not likewise, setting aside an exact investigation of the facts, spend all my time praising a God whom I do not know?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The printed question is taken as a sarcastic question about what Simon could do instead of investigating. οὗ μὴ ἐπίσταμαι θεοῦ is understood as an attracted relative construction referring to the unknown God.

passages.text:
And Peter said, “You are not blessed enough to praise him, nor indeed are you able to do this good thing, for then you would be full of him. For this is what our teacher, who does not lie, said: ‘A mouth speaks from the heart’s abundance.’ Therefore you, overflowing with an evil purpose because of ignorance, speak against the only good God, without yet suffering what your daring words deserve. If you suppose there will be no judgment, perhaps you actually think there is no God. Therefore, because you fail to recognize such great patience on his part, you drive him still further toward desperate action.”

And Simon said, “Do not hope to cow me with fear so that I refrain from seeking from you what is true in the examples. I long so greatly for truth that, for its sake, I would not hesitate to undertake even the risk. But concerning the points I proposed to you at the beginning—if indeed you have anything to say—speak now.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Οὔτε τοσοῦτον εἶ μακάριος αὐτὸν ὑμνεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: You are not blessed enough to praise him
lexical_decisions.rationale: τοσοῦτον with the infinitive expresses the degree required for praising God, not merely the quantity of praise.

lexical_decisions.chosen: A mouth speaks from the heart’s abundance
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering follows the wording supplied here rather than harmonizing it with a familiar canonical form; the Greek has neither a definite article before “mouth” nor an added possessive.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅθεν σὺ περισσευόμενος προαιρέσει κακῇ ἀγνοίας αἰτίᾳ καταλέγεις τοῦ μόνου ἀγαθοῦ θεοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: Therefore you, overflowing with an evil purpose because of ignorance, speak against the only good God
lexical_decisions.rationale: προαίρεσις denotes a chosen disposition, purpose, or moral intention. The causal expression ἀγνοίας αἰτίᾳ is attached to that evil purpose; it could instead qualify the act of speaking against God.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅθεν τῆς τοσαύτ[ης] αὐτοῦ μακροθυμίας οὐκ ἀντιλαμβανόμενος ἐπὶ πλεῖον πρὸς ἀπόνοιαν αὐτὸν ἐκτείνεις
lexical_decisions.chosen: Therefore, because you fail to recognize such great patience on his part, you drive him still further toward desperate action
lexical_decisions.rationale: The masculine αὐτόν most directly refers to God, making him the object of ἐκτείνεις. ἀπόνοια can denote desperation, recklessness, or drastic resolve. An alternative contextual interpretation is “you extend yourself still further into recklessness,” but that requires taking αὐτόν reflexively or loosely.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: φόβῳ δυσωπήσειν με μὴ ζητεῖν σοι τῶν παραδειγμάτων τὰ ἀληθῆ
lexical_decisions.chosen: cow me with fear so that I refrain from seeking from you what is true in the examples
lexical_decisions.rationale: δυσωπέω can mean shame, overawe, or intimidate. The infinitive with μή states the result Simon rejects, while σοι marks Peter as the person from whom the truth is sought.

lexical_decisions.chosen: if indeed you have anything to say
lexical_decisions.rationale: The idiom concerns having something available to say, not merely possessing the physical ability to speak.

passages.text: And Peter said, “Since you force us to dare to speak as people who have accurately discovered God’s methods—and this though we are humans unable to ascertain precisely even the methods of those like ourselves—then, at least for the sake of those standing by, I will discuss what you wish instead of maintaining the most reverent silence. I agree with you that there is a certain leader of evil, about whose origin Scripture did not dare to say either something true or something false. Nevertheless, let us explore together, from many angles, how he came to be—if indeed he came to be—and let us choose from among the apparent possibilities the one that speaks more reverently. For this is securely inferred from what is probable: first, that one should accord God the more reverent account, especially in this way, when all suspicions have been cleared away and another adequate and safer supposition is available. Nevertheless, even before the investigation I promise you that every path of inquiry can show him alone—God—to be beyond blame.”

source_issues.source_quote: ἐπεὶ ἐκ τῶν εἰκότων λαμβάνεται τοῦτο βεβαίως, ὃ μὲν ὅτι θεῷ τὸ εὐφημότερον δοῦναι πρέπει, ταύτῃ μᾶλλον πασῶν ὑπονοιῶν καθαρθεισῶν καὶ ἄλλης ἱκανῆς καὶ ἀκινδυνοτέρας παρακειμένης ὑποψίας
source_issues.issue: The supplied, image-checked wording is syntactically compressed, especially at ὃ μὲν ὅτι, and no balancing δέ follows μὲν. The translation takes the clause as introducing a first or principal consideration: that the more reverent account should be accorded to God when a sufficient and safer supposition is available. Alternatively, ὃ μὲν may begin an unfinished first reason. No alteration to the selected reading is assumed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὰς τοῦ θεοῦ τέχνας ἀκριβῶς ἐφευρόντας λέγειν
lexical_decisions.chosen: to speak as people who have accurately discovered God’s methods
lexical_decisions.rationale: τέχναι can denote arts, devices, designs, or methods. The participle is represented as describing the capacity in which they would presume to speak; a more strictly temporal rendering would be “to speak after accurately discovering God’s methods.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: [οὗ] τὴν γένεσιν ἡ γραφὴ οὔτε ἀληθὲς [οὔ]τε ψευδὲς εἰπεῖν ἐτόλμησεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: about whose origin Scripture did not dare to say either something true or something false
lexical_decisions.rationale: The paired negatives portray Scripture as making neither kind of pronouncement about the origin. The wording is preserved rather than simplified to “Scripture says nothing.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: let us choose from among the apparent possibilities the one that speaks more reverently
lexical_decisions.rationale: τὰ δοκοῦντα may mean apparent possibilities or proposed opinions. εὐφημότερον is comparative and favors the account that speaks more auspiciously or reverently of God.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐκ τῶν εἰκότων λαμβάνεται τοῦτο βεβαίως
lexical_decisions.chosen: this is securely inferred from what is probable
lexical_decisions.rationale: εἰκότα are probable considerations rather than certainties. The source’s juxtaposition of probability with secure inference is retained.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἄμεμπτον αὐτὸν μόνον δύναται δεῖξαι τὸν θεόν
lexical_decisions.chosen: can show him alone—God—to be beyond blame
lexical_decisions.rationale: μόνον is taken with αὐτόν, identifying God alone as blameless. It could instead be attached adverbially to δύναται, yielding “can only show God to be blameless.”

passages.text:
Nevertheless, as you said, if the evil one is something that came into being, then either he came to be as a living creature, or was put forth in substance by God, or was compounded externally; or his choice resulted from the compounding, or it happened to arise without compounding and without God’s counsel. Or he came to be from things that did not exist, or by God from what exists nowhere in any way; or else outside God there was either lifeless or animate matter from which he came to be; or he fashioned himself; or he came into being by God; or he is one of the things that exist in relation to something else; or he always existed. For we cannot say that he does not exist, since we agreed together that he exists.

And Simon said, “You have divided all the paths concerning him well—the main question about him. It is now my part, after scrutinizing the division, to show you that the Creator is liable to blame; but your task is to prove, as you promised, that he is beyond all blame. I wonder whether you will be able to do so. First, if the evil one came into being from God as a living creature, he consequently possesses the same evil as the one who put him forth.”

And Peter said, “Not necessarily. For we see many among human beings who are good yet have fathered bad children, others who are bad yet have had good children, still others who are bad yet produce good offspring, and others who are good yet have become parents of both bad and good children. Thus the first man who was created fathered the unrighteous Cain and the righteous Abel.”

In response Simon said, “You act foolishly by discussing God while using human examples.”

And Peter said, “Then tell us about God without using human examples, while still making it possible for what you say to be understood. But you will not be able to do so.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: if the evil one is something that came into being
lexical_decisions.rationale: γενητός can mean generated, originated, or created. The broader wording avoids deciding in advance which mode of origination the ensuing alternatives support.

lexical_decisions.chosen: was put forth in substance by God
lexical_decisions.rationale: προβάλλω can describe putting forth or emanation, and οὐσιωδῶς indicates that this occurs with respect to substance. The antecedent of αὐτοῦ is understood contextually as God.

lexical_decisions.chosen: was compounded externally
lexical_decisions.rationale: κεράννυμι denotes mixing or compounding. ἔξω may mean externally or outside God; the Greek does not explicitly state the reference point here.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἢ ἐκτ[ὸς] ἦν θεοῦ ἢ ὕλη ἄψυχος οὖσα ἢ ἔμψυχος ὅθεν γέγονεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: or else outside God there was either lifeless or animate matter from which he came to be
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering takes ἐκτὸς θεοῦ with the existence of matter and treats ἄψυχος and ἔμψυχος as alternatives describing that matter. It is also possible to divide the sequence as “or he was outside God; or there was lifeless or animate matter from which he came to be.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: or he is one of the things that exist in relation to something else
lexical_decisions.rationale: τὰ πρός τι is philosophical language for relative or relational entities—things defined through a relation to something else.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Καλῶς πάσας αὐτοῦ τὰς ὁδοὺς διεῖλες, τὸ κεφάλαιον αὐτοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: You have divided all the paths concerning him well—the main question about him
lexical_decisions.rationale: τὸ κεφάλαιον may denote a heading, summary, chief point, or principal question. The punctuation leaves its exact attachment compressed, so the translation treats it as an appositional summary of the division.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς αὐτῆς τοῦ προβάλλοντος κακίας τυγχάνει
lexical_decisions.chosen: he consequently possesses the same evil as the one who put him forth
lexical_decisions.rationale: The subject remains the evil one, while τοῦ προβάλλοντος identifies the producer whose evil Simon infers from the offspring’s nature.

passages.text: For instance, what were you saying at the outset? That if the evil one came into being from God, being of the same substance as God, then God too is evil. But when I showed from the very example you yourself supplied that bad people come from good people and good people from bad people, you did not accept it, saying that the example was human. Therefore I in turn do not now accept that God has been begotten, because begetting belongs to human beings, not to God. But neither can God be good or evil, just or unjust, nor indeed prudent, a living creature, or anything else that can belong to human beings, for such qualities belong to human beings. And if, when investigating God, we must not ascribe to him the good qualities belonging to human beings, there is nothing left to conceive, say, or investigate except this alone: his purpose, which he himself permitted us to understand, so that, when judged, we may be without excuse concerning the things that, although we knew them, we did not keep.

source_issues.issue: The supplied reading interrupts a single expected adjective with a hyphen, whitespace, and a period. The context and the surviving letters indicate ἀνθρώπινον, “human.” This is treated as an apparent typographical interruption in the selected print, not as a lacuna or missing content.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ ἐκ θεοῦ ὁ πονηρὸς γεγένηται, τῆς αὐτῆς αὐτῷ ὢν οὐσίας, καὶ πονηρός ἐστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: if the evil one came into being from God, being of the same substance as God, then God too is evil
lexical_decisions.rationale: The subject of the final ἐστιν is implicit. Taking it as God avoids the tautology that the evil one is evil and matches Peter’s summary of Simon’s attempt to blame the Creator. A formally possible but contextually weaker rendering is “then he too is evil.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: from the very example you yourself supplied
lexical_decisions.rationale: The emphatic οὗπερ and αὐτός attribute the example to Simon, even though Peter developed its comparison in the preceding exchange.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I in turn do not now accept that God has been begotten
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect passive infinitive presents God as having undergone generation. The surprising assertion is retained as part of Peter’s reductio rather than changed into “God begets.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: nor indeed prudent, a living creature
lexical_decisions.rationale: φρόνιμος means prudent, sensible, or practically wise. ζῷον is rendered broadly as “a living creature,” preserving Peter’s analogy with human predicates.

lexical_decisions.chosen: his purpose
lexical_decisions.rationale: προαίρεσις can mean choice, intention, purpose, or moral disposition. Here it refers to the divine purpose made knowable for human accountability.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅπως κρινόμενοι ἀναπολόγητοι ὦμεν περὶ ὧν γνόντες οὐκ ἐφυλάξαμεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: so that, when judged, we may be without excuse concerning the things that, although we knew them, we did not keep
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀναπολόγητοι means without a defense or excuse, and φυλάσσω here concerns observing or keeping what was known.

passages.text:
When Simon heard this, he said, “You will not pressure me into keeping silent about his essence and investigating only his purpose. For it is possible both to think and to speak about his essence—I mean, starting from the good qualities belonging to human beings. For example, being alive and being dead belong to a human being, but to God belongs not being dead, but being alive—and being alive eternally. Again, human beings can be evil or good, but to God belongs being incomparably good. And, so that I may not prolong the argument at length, the better of the qualities belonging to human beings belong eternally to God.”

Peter said, “Tell me, Simon: does it belong to human beings to beget evil and good people and to do evil and good things?”

Simon said, “It does.”

Peter said, “Since you have spoken this way, the better of the qualities belonging to human beings must be assigned to God. Since human beings beget evil and good people, God can beget only good people; and since human beings do evil and good things, he himself delights in doing only good things. Thus, concerning God, either it is possible not to speak of the qualities belonging to human beings and to remain silent, or it is reasonable to assign to him the better of the good qualities belonging to human beings. In this way, he alone is the cause of all good things.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Οὐ δυσωπήσεις με περὶ τῆς οὐσίας αὐτοῦ σιωπή[σαν]τα περὶ τῆς προαιρέσεως αὐτοῦ [ζη]τεῖν μόνης.
lexical_decisions.chosen: You will not pressure me into keeping silent about his essence and investigating only his purpose.
lexical_decisions.rationale: The future with οὐ is taken as Simon’s negative declaration of refusal, fitting his ensuing claim that God’s essence can be discussed. The aorist participle σιωπήσαντα is rendered as attendant action coordinated in English with ζητεῖν. A temporally stricter alternative is “You will not pressure me, after I have kept silent about his essence, to investigate only his purpose,” while interrogative punctuation is grammatically possible but less suitable to the argumentative context.

lexical_decisions.chosen: about his essence
lexical_decisions.rationale: οὐσία denotes God’s being or essence here, whereas the plural οὐσίαι in the next section denotes elemental substances.

lexical_decisions.chosen: being alive and being dead
lexical_decisions.rationale: The perfect infinitive τεθνάναι denotes the state of having died or being dead, not merely the process of dying.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the better of the qualities belonging to human beings
lexical_decisions.rationale: προσόντα denotes attributes or qualities that belong to someone, and κρείττονα selects those regarded as superior.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ δὲ θεῷ τὸ ἀσυγκρίτῳ ἀγαθῷ εἶναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: to God belongs being incomparably good
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀσυγκρίτῳ may describe the good as incomparable or convey the adverbial sense “incomparably”; the latter produces natural English without changing the claim.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὕτως π[ερὶ θεοῦ] ἢ οὐ τὰ ἀνθρώποις προσόντα λέγειν καὶ σιωπᾶν ἔστιν ἢ τῶν ἀνθρώποις προσόντων κα[λῶν] εὖλογόν ἐστιν ἀπονέμειν αὐτῷ τὰ κ[ρείτ]τονα
lexical_decisions.chosen: Thus, concerning God, either it is possible not to speak of the qualities belonging to human beings and to remain silent, or it is reasonable to assign to him the better of the good qualities belonging to human beings
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering lets ἔστιν govern the coordinated infinitives and takes οὐ directly with λέγειν. If οὐ is instead given wider scope, the first member could be read “it is not possible to speak of the qualities belonging to human beings and remain silent,” but that produces a less fitting contrast with the second alternative.

passages.text: Simon said, “Then, if God is responsible only for good things, what remains to be understood except that some other principle produced evil, or perhaps it is ungenerated?” Peter said, “Neither did some other power produce the evil one, nor is evil ungenerated, as I will show at the end. For now my task is to demonstrate, as I promised at the beginning, that God is blameless in every way. We have granted, then, that God possesses the better things that belong to human beings incomparably. Therefore it is also possible for him to be the one who sends forth the four substances—I mean the hot and the cold, the moist and the dry. These, being primary, simple, and unmixed, have an appetite for neither side. But, sent forth by God and mixed outside, they can become a living being with a choice to destroy evil people. Thus, though everything has been produced from him, the evil one neither comes from elsewhere nor has received his wickedness from God himself, who made everything. Wickedness cannot exist with him, because the substances, being neutral, were separated out and sent forth from him. When, outside, they were mixed by his skill at his will, the desire for the destruction of evil people occurred. But the wickedness that occurred cannot destroy good people, even if it should wish to, for by law it has authority against those who sin. So, not knowing each person’s character, he gains experience against them, and, having exposed them, punishes them.” Simon said, “Since God is capable of mixing the elements and making mixtures for what he wishes, for whatever choices he wishes to arise, why did he not make each person’s constitution inclined to choose good things?”

source_issues.issue: The supplied selected-edition text has an unmatched opening bracket after κ and a nested bracketed ί. “Simon said” and the conjunction are translated from the supplied letters, but this note preserves the unusual bracket form. It is not silently normalized, claimed as an OCR error, or used to invent any missing words. The other square brackets in this passage supply portions of words as printed, rather than dot-count gaps.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the one who sends forth
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun describes an emitter or producer by projection; “emanator” is a technical alternative. The main text retains sending-forth language, not a claim that the passage explicitly teaches creation from nothing.

lexical_decisions.chosen: possesses the better things ... incomparably
lexical_decisions.rationale: The statement concerns superior qualities among those attributed to humans. “Possesses incomparably superior qualities” is a more idiomatic alternative, but the main text preserves the comparative and the separate adverb.

lexical_decisions.chosen: have an appetite for neither side
lexical_decisions.rationale: The two sides can be understood as good and evil in the argument; neither is inserted as a newly printed noun.

lexical_decisions.chosen: were separated out
lexical_decisions.rationale: The unusual perfect participle conveys distinction or separation of the substances in this argument. “Carefully distinguished” is possible, but a claim of affectionate separation is not imposed merely from the compound’s form.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν κατ’ αὐτῶν λαμβάνει [ἐμ]πειρίαν καὶ διελέγξας τιμωρεῖ
lexical_decisions.chosen: he gains experience against them, and, having exposed them, punishes them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The hostile κατ’ αὐτῶν is retained. Contextually this can be rendered “he tests them and, after proving their wrongdoing, punishes them”; the main text does not add a specific trial method or identify the implicit object of exposure more narrowly than the people concerned.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς ἃ βούλεται πρὸς ἃς βούλεται γενέσθαι προαι[ρέ]σεις
lexical_decisions.chosen: for what he wishes, for whatever choices he wishes to arise
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both overlapping purpose/relative phrases are represented, not reduced to a single clause. The second feminine relative anticipates the plural choices.

passages.text: Peter said, “Our present task is to show how the evil one came to be—if indeed he has come to be—and by whom. As for whether this happened without blame, when I have completed the argument now before us, I will then show how and why he came to be, and I will establish that the one who made him is blameless. Nevertheless, we said that the four substances were put forth by God, and thus, by the intention of the one who combined them, the choice of evil things arose just as he wished. For if it had arisen contrary to his purpose, or from some other substance or even some other cause, God’s plan would not have been secure, since rulers of evil might continually arise against his will and wage war against his designs. But it is impossible for matters to be this way. For no living being—and especially one fit to rule—can come into being by accident, since everything that comes into being must come into being through someone.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: As for whether this happened without blame
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression is elliptical, with the preceding coming-to-be understood. “Whether he came to be blamelessly” is formally possible, but the continuation shows that the issue is whether blame attaches to the maker.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ οὕτως βουλῇ τοῦ συγκρίναντος συμβέβηκεν ὡς ἠθέλησεν ἡ τῶν κακῶν προαίρεσις
lexical_decisions.chosen: and thus, by the intention of the one who combined them, the choice of evil things arose just as he wished
lexical_decisions.rationale: The neuter sense of κακῶν gives the source-transparent “evil things,” with the genitive dependent on προαίρεσις. Alternatively, κακῶν may be masculine and refer to evil people; in light of the preceding purpose of destroying them, the phrase may evoke a purpose concerning evil people, but an explicitly oppositional relationship such as “against” is not expressed by the genitive itself.

lexical_decisions.chosen: God’s plan would not have been secure
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally, the phrase is “the firmness of the plan.” The rendering expresses the plan’s settled reliability; God is supplied as the contextual possessor.

lexical_decisions.chosen: or even some other cause
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόφασις can denote a cause, occasion, alleged reason, or pretext. “Cause” fits the argument about an independent basis for the evil one’s emergence.

lexical_decisions.chosen: rulers of evil might continually arise
lexical_decisions.rationale: κακίας may identify what these rulers govern or embody. “Leaders in wickedness” is another possible rendering.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐδὲν γὰρ ζῷον καὶ ταῦτα ἡ[γε]μονικὸν
lexical_decisions.chosen: no living being—and especially one fit to rule—
lexical_decisions.rationale: καὶ ταῦτα emphasizes an additional noteworthy circumstance: the being is not merely alive but ruling or fitted to command.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by accident
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase denotes coming about incidentally or as a mere chance occurrence, in contrast with production by an agent.

passages.text:
Simon said, “What then? Does matter, being coeternal and equal in power with him, put forth rulers against him as an enemy, rulers who hinder his designs?”

Peter said, “If matter is eternal, it is not anyone’s enemy. For what exists forever is also incapable of suffering; and being incapable of suffering, it is blessed; and being blessed, it cannot become receptive to enmity, since, by its eternal constitution, it has no fear of being deprived of anything. Why, rather, does matter not love the Creator, since it is seen bringing forth fruits as food for all those generated by him? And why has it not feared him as the stronger, as it acknowledges by trembling through earthquakes and as, while surging in great waves, it very quickly obeyed the Teacher, who was sailing and commanded calm, and became quiet? What then? Did the demons not come out while both fearing and honoring him? And did not others, first pleading to enter pigs, make their request, since they did not have authority even to enter pigs without his consent?”

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints an apostrophe after the infinitive. It is retained in the source quotation as a confirmed editorial or typographic feature but contributes no separately recoverable lexical content to the English and is not treated as evidence for restored letters.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ ὕλη αὐτῷ σύγχρονος οὖσα καὶ ἰσοδύναμος
lexical_decisions.chosen: matter, being coeternal and equal in power with him
lexical_decisions.rationale: σύγχρονος here describes simultaneous eternal existence with God, while ἰσοδύναμος asserts equality of power.

lexical_decisions.chosen: incapable of suffering
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀπαθής can mean unaffected, impassible, or incapable of suffering. The argument connects it with freedom from deprivation and fear, so the fuller reader-facing expression is used.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀιδίῳ κτίσει στερηθῆναί τινος μὴ πεφοβημένη
lexical_decisions.chosen: since, by its eternal constitution, it has no fear of being deprived of anything
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative ἀιδίῳ κτίσει has uncertain force. The main rendering understands it causally or instrumentally as matter’s eternal constitution; “in eternal creation” or “as an eternal created thing” are formally conceivable but contextually difficult.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πῶς δ’ οὐχ ὡς κρείττονα πεφόβηται, ὡς καὶ διὰ τῶν σεισμῶν τρέμουσα ὁμολογεῖ καὶ ὡς μεγάλα κυματουμένη τῷ διδασκάλῳ πλέοντι καὶ γαλήνην ἐπιτάξαντι τάχιστα πεισθεῖσα ἡσύχασε;
lexical_decisions.chosen: And why has it not feared him as the stronger, as it acknowledges by trembling through earthquakes and as, while surging in great waves, it very quickly obeyed the Teacher, who was sailing and commanded calm, and became quiet?
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both evidentiary clauses remain attached to the rhetorical question about matter’s fear of the stronger. The dative participles πλέοντι and ἐπιτάξαντι describe the Teacher whom matter obeyed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: while both fearing and honoring him
lexical_decisions.rationale: προτιμάω can mean prefer, esteem highly, or honor. The Teacher is the implied object of both infinitives.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἄλλοι δὲ εἰς χοίρους εἰσελθεῖν πρότερον παρακαλοῦντες ἠξίουν
lexical_decisions.chosen: And did not others, first pleading to enter pigs, make their request
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle παρακαλοῦντες and finite verb ἠξίουν express distinct but closely related acts. The translation retains both the prior pleading and the ensuing request rather than collapsing them into one verb.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς μηδὲ τοῦ εἰς χοίρους εἰσελθεῖν’ ἄνευ τῆς αὐτοῦ συγχωρήσεως ἐξουσίαν ἔχοντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: since they did not have authority even to enter pigs without his consent
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὡς introduces the basis implied by their request, and συγχώρησις here denotes permission or consent.

passages.text: Simon said, “What then? Does that which is lifeless have the natural capacity to produce bad and good things?” Peter said, “On this account it is neither good nor bad, because it does not act by choice, being lifeless and insensible. Therefore here too one can discern how, though lifeless, it brings forth living things, and though insensible, it appears to fashion skillfully formed shapes of both animals and plants.” Simon said, “What then? If God himself animated it, is he not himself the cause of the bad things it brings forth?” Peter said, “If God animated it according to his own will, his spirit works on it, and there is no longer anything hostile to God, equal in power to him, or impossible for him, because everything he brings about comes about as he wills. But you will say, ‘He himself is the cause of evil, if he himself works bad things through it.’ What, then, will you call the bad things? Venomous creeping creatures and deadly herbs, or demons, or also some other things capable of troubling human beings? These—the ..... fine things—would not have existed if the human being had not sinned, on account of which death entered. For while the human being was ......, the venom of creeping creatures was not at work, nor the effects of bad herbs; disturbances by demons did not occur, nor did any other affliction have the natural capacity to attach itself to him. But through sin he fell away from being immortal and has, as I said, become susceptible to every affliction. But if you say, ‘Why, then, did human nature originally come into being susceptible to death?’ I tell you: because of freedom of choice. For if we were not susceptible to death, as immortals we could not be punished for a sin committed with freedom of choice. Thus, because of a somewhat greater immunity to suffering, even if we were bad by choice, justice too would be weakened, since those with bad choices could not be punished because of immunity to suffering.”

source_issues.issue: The former selected transcription read ὢν, being, but the independently blind-checked print crop now reads ὧν with rough breathing and circumflex. This is a documented print-transcription correction, not a grammatical conjecture. The blind receipt notes that the breathing/circumflex strokes are crowded and partly merged, with the breathing contour less distinct; that ink uncertainty remains disclosed. The main text uses the selected relative reading and does not certify each crowded stroke as perfectly clear.

The selected edition prints exactly five dots before λεπτά. Exactly five remain in English, without filling the lost qualification or substituting a complete reconstructed phrase. Fine is a rendering of the surviving adjective, with subtle, thin, or small as lexical alternatives.

source_issues.source_quote: θάνατος παρεισῆλθε...... γὰρ ὄντος τοῦ ἀνθρώπου
source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints exactly six dots between death entered and for ... the human being being. Exactly six remain in English, moved to the open complement position after was to keep the surviving being-clause readable without identifying its missing qualification. No immortal or other adjective is restored from the later explicit immortality statement. An alternative retaining the physical interruption order is death entered ...... For while the human being existed, but that bare existential English risks obscuring the missing state. The main reading makes the unresolved state visible, not recovered.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ ἄψυχος οὖσα φύσιν ἔχει ἐμφύειν τὰ κακὰ καὶ τὰ ἀγαθά;
lexical_decisions.chosen: Does that which is lifeless have the natural capacity to produce bad and good things?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine subject is not independently named in this supplied section, so that which is lifeless preserves it without introducing an unprinted matter noun. φύσιν ἔχει expresses a natural capacity or constitution, distinct from moral choice. Produce renders engender or cause to grow.

lexical_decisions.chosen: though lifeless, it brings forth living things
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the repeated lifeless/living contrast; literally without soul versus things possessing soul or animate things. The main text does not turn absence of sensory life into absence of every productive capacity.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκ αὐτὸς αἴτιός ἐστιν ὧν αὕτη τίκτει κακῶν;
lexical_decisions.chosen: is he not himself the cause of the bad things it brings forth?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The corrected ὧν is a genitive plural relative linking the bad things to what it produces, with its genitive attracted to κακῶν governed by cause of. It is not the participle being. Cause preserves the causal claim, rather than replacing it with a conclusion about guilt.

lexical_decisions.chosen: his spirit works on it
lexical_decisions.rationale: God’s spirit is the expressed agent working on the previously lifeless subject. The clause is conditional on God having animated it according to his will; it is not an independently asserted account of how every bad thing arises.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκέτι τῷ θεῷ ἐχθρόν τι ἐστιν ἢ ἰσοδύναμον ἢ ἀδύνατον
lexical_decisions.chosen: there is no longer anything hostile to God, equal in power to him, or impossible for him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative God is understood with the coordinated predicates: hostile to him, equal in power to him, or impossible for him. Impossible represents a limit on capability, not moral opposition; the subsequent everything as he wills supports this reading. Powerless is another lexical sense of ἀδύνατον if read as an intrinsic predicate of the thing, but would not give the same shared-dative argument.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἅπερ τὰ ..... λεπτὰ οὐκ ἂν ἦν
lexical_decisions.chosen: These—the ..... fine things—would not have existed
lexical_decisions.rationale: Exactly five printed dots remain before fine. λεπτά can mean fine, subtle, thin, or small; fine here is not a commendation of moral goodness. The gap prevents identifying any missing qualification or more precise category; none is restored.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὗ εἵνεκεν θάνατος παρεισῆλθε...... γὰρ ὄντος τοῦ ἀνθρώπου
lexical_decisions.chosen: on account of which death entered. For while the human being was ......
lexical_decisions.rationale: On account of which takes the preceding sin event as the causal antecedent, supported by through sin later in the section. On whose account, referring to the human being, is another possible relative attachment. The six-dot gap is retained as the unspecified state associated with the ensuing being-clause; English places the visible gap after was rather than restoring an adjective or any lost words before the Greek γάρ.

lexical_decisions.chosen: have the natural capacity
lexical_decisions.rationale: As in the opening question, φύσιν ἔχει concerns natural capacity, not choice or intention. The main text keeps the claim that afflictions did not have capacity to attach to him, rather than saying only that they happened not to do so.

lexical_decisions.chosen: because of freedom of choice
lexical_decisions.rationale: αὐτεξούσιον is being in one’s own power or self-determination, here the reason susceptibility to death permits accountability. The distinction between freely chosen sin and mere natural production remains.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ οὕτως διὰ τὸ ἀπαθὲς πλεῖόν τι, κἂν τῇ προαιρέσει ἦμεν κακοί, ἡ καὶ δικαιοσύνη ἐξησθένει
lexical_decisions.chosen: Thus, because of a somewhat greater immunity to suffering, even if we were bad by choice, justice too would be weakened
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main text attaches πλεῖόν τι to immunity to suffering, preferring its immediate placement after τὸ ἀπαθές within the cause phrase, before the intervening even-if clause. The preceding contrast between hypothesized immortals and death-susceptible beings supports reading a greater degree of immunity. The indefinite τι is represented by somewhat. A materially different attachment takes πλεῖόν τι adverbially with ἐξησθένει across the intervening clause: Thus, because of immunity to suffering, even if we were bad by choice, justice too would be weakened somewhat more. That reading places the degree on weakening justice rather than on immunity. The printed comma does not uniquely settle the attachment. Something more in the immunity to suffering is a more literal version of the main attachment, not a substitute for disclosing this adverbial alternative; no additional agency, privilege, or restored Greek is asserted.

passages.text:
In response, Simon said, “What else do I still have to say about the evil one except that God made him out of what did not exist? On this account the maker is evil: he made what did not exist come to exist, even though he could have made him good, since the being brought into existence possessed no nature of his own for choosing evil.”

Peter said, “Making him out of what did not exist, with a power of choice, is like the argument we stated earlier: by making his constitution such that he delights in evils, the maker himself appears responsible for what came into being. Since, then, both have a single solution, we will later discuss why he made him delight in the destruction of evil people.”

Simon said, “If he also made the angels with freedom of action, but the evil one departed from being righteous, why has he also been honored with rule? Through the honor he has given him, the one who honored him appears to delight in evils.”

Peter said, “If God appointed him, after he had rebelled, to rule over those like himself, ordering him to inflict punishment on sinners according to law, he is not unjust.
