lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb denotes careful discrimination or separation. “Carefully selected” is possible, but the surrounding mixture terminology favors differentiation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἔξω δὲ αὐτῆς κατὰ τὴν τοῦ προβαλόντος βουλὴν κραθείσης πρὸς τὴν κρᾶσιν ἡ κακοῖς χαίρουσα προαίρεσις
lexical_decisions.chosen: but when that substance had been mixed externally according to the will of the one who brought it forth, the disposition that delights in evils arose in connection with the mixture
lexical_decisions.rationale: αὐτῆς is taken as the subject of the genitive absolute and as referring to the already mentioned fourfold substance; ἔξω describes its external mixing. Alternatively, ἔξω αὐτῆς may mean “outside it,” with an unexpressed subject of κραθείσης, but that reading would imply an additional constituent not explicitly named here.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ συμβεβηκυῖα κακοῖς χαίρουσα προαίρεσις ἐπεγένετο
lexical_decisions.chosen: the disposition that delights in evils arose afterward as an accidental feature
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording distinguishes the contingent disposition from the underlying substance and states that it arose subsequently.

lexical_decisions.chosen: made credible by conjectures
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase refers to reasoned conjectures or inferences rather than certain demonstrations.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as one who does not know
lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase literally describes the speaker as not possessing something, with knowledge or secure understanding supplied from context. “As one who does not possess it” is a more formal alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: things honored by silence
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression presents silence as the honor properly accorded to secret matters.

passages.text:
When Peter had said these things, a certain Lazarus, himself one of the followers, said, “Tell us how the reconciliation is possible: how can it be reasonable for the evil one, who was appointed by a righteous God to be the punisher of those who acted impiously, later to be sent with his angels and the sinners into the lower darkness? For I remember that the Teacher himself said this too.”

Peter said, “I too acknowledge that the evil one does nothing evil in this respect, insofar as he carries out the law given to him. Although he has an evil disposition, nevertheless, because of his fear of God, he does nothing unjustly. But because he slanders teachers of truth as a snare for the undiscerning, this same being is also called the Slanderer.

“As for our truthful Teacher’s saying that he and his angels would depart with the deceived sinners into the lower darkness, it has an explanation like this. The evil one, having been allotted a constitution that delights in darkness, descends with his fellow-servant angels into the darkness of Tartarus and takes pleasure in it, for darkness is congenial to fire. But human souls, being drops of pure light, are drunk in together by a substance of alien fire; and since they do not have a nature capable of dying, they are punished according to their deserts.

“But if the ruler of wickedness, being a human being, is not sent into the darkness because he does not delight in it, then this constitution of his that delights in evils can be recombined into the good one’s disposition, and thus, as good, he will be judged to coexist. This is all the more so because, although he had been allotted a constitution that delights in evils, on account of his fear of God he did nothing contrary to what seemed right to God’s law. And surely, when the high priest Aaron’s staff became a snake and was transformed back again into a staff, Scripture mystically foreshadowed this with reference to the recombination of the evil one’s transformation, which will take place later and which is yet to be.”

source_issues.source_quote: γενησομένην τῆς τροπῆς μετασύγκρισιν μυστηριωδῶς ἡ γραφὴ ἐσομένην
source_issues.issue: Both γενησομένην and ἐσομένην appear to describe the feminine μετασύγκρισιν, producing a redundant and syntactically awkward pair of future expressions. The confirmed printed wording is represented by “which will take place later and which is yet to be” rather than emended.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Tell us how the reconciliation is possible
lexical_decisions.rationale: συμφωνία denotes agreement or consistency; Lazarus asks how the apparently conflicting claims can be reconciled. “Tell us the consistency” is a more formal alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: διαβάλλων δὲ διδασκάλους ἀληθείας εἰς ἐνέδραν τῶν ἀκρίτων
lexical_decisions.chosen: But because he slanders teachers of truth as a snare for the undiscerning
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive τῶν ἀκρίτων is read objectively: the slandering of the teachers serves to ensnare the undiscerning. It can instead be read subjectively, yielding “into an ambush laid by the undiscerning against the teachers,” which would make the undiscerning responsible for the ambush rather than its targets.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Slanderer
lexical_decisions.rationale: This preserves the explicit association with the preceding act of slandering. The conventional title “Devil” is an alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: constitution
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun literally denotes a mixture but here refers to the being’s composite constitution.

lexical_decisions.chosen: are drunk in together
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive participle preserves the drinking image applied to drops of pure light being taken into alien fire.

lexical_decisions.chosen: be recombined into the good one’s disposition
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive ἀγαθοῦ is taken substantivally as “of the good one.” A qualitative reading, “into a disposition toward good,” is contextually possible but less directly reflects the genitive construction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as good, he will be judged to coexist
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀγαθός is taken predicatively of the ruler of wickedness. Alternatively, it may be substantival—“the good one will be judged to coexist”—though the companion with whom he coexists would remain implicit.

lexical_decisions.chosen: And surely
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering takes the particle as an emphatic transition introducing the scriptural confirmation that follows. Its force is not certain: a tentative “And perhaps” and the scalar “Not to mention that” are also defensible, and the confirmed printed punctuation does not decide among them.

passages.text:
After Lazarus, Joseph—himself also one of the followers—said, “Correctly, everything sa.....; and grant me this too, since I wish to learn: why, for everyone, from the same words ......... some are persuaded, while others refuse to believe?”

Peter said, “The words are not incantations, so that anyone who hears must necessarily believe. Rather, the fact that some are persuaded and others are not intelligently demonstrates freedom of choice.”

We all blessed him who had said these things.

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a five-dot lacuna after the surviving beginning εἴρ. That beginning is recognizable as part of a saying-verb, but the unavailable ending could determine person, voice, and other grammatical information. The fragmentary English “sa.....” preserves the five dots without supplying those unavailable features.

source_issues.source_quote: διὰ τί πᾶσι τῶν αὐτῶν λόγων ......... οἱ μὲν πείθονται
source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a nine-dot lacuna between λόγων and οἱ. The surviving syntax remains incomplete; all nine dots are retained, and no missing verb or participle is restored.

lexical_decisions.chosen: incantations
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun denotes charms or magical spells intended to compel an effect, contrasting with freely given belief.

lexical_decisions.chosen: necessarily
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverb expresses the inevitability that would characterize an incantation’s effect.

lexical_decisions.chosen: freedom of choice
lexical_decisions.rationale: The term denotes self-determination or freedom of agency.

lexical_decisions.chosen: refuse to believe
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb can express disbelief, resistance, or disobedience; the immediate contrast with being persuaded favors “refuse to believe.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: We all blessed him who had said these things
lexical_decisions.rationale: The accusative participle εἰπόντα describes the object of εὐλογήσαμεν. Peter is its contextual referent; the construction is not an unexpressed object followed by a temporal participle.

passages.text: Just as a meal was about to be served to us, someone slipped in and said, “Appion the Many-Victor has just arrived from Antioch with Annoubion and is staying as Simon’s guest.” When our father heard this, he rejoiced and said to Peter, “If you permit me, I will go greet Appion and Annoubion, who have been my friends from earliest youth. Perhaps I may persuade Annoubion to debate Clement about nativity.” Peter said, “I permit it, and I commend you for fulfilling the duties of friendship. But consider how, by God’s providence, everything conducive to your full assurance is converging from every direction and producing the fitting harmony. I say this because Annoubion’s arrival has proved advantageous to you.” Our father replied, “I truly see that this is so.” After saying this, he went to Simon.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Appion the Many-Victor
lexical_decisions.rationale: πλειστονίκης is treated as an epithet denoting numerous victories rather than silently transliterated as another personal name.

lexical_decisions.chosen: about nativity
lexical_decisions.rationale: In this debate setting γένεσις concerns birth or nativity, particularly as a subject of astrological determinism; “birth” or “genesis” remains possible more generally.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπαινῶ τὰ φίλων σε πληροῦντα μέρη
lexical_decisions.chosen: I commend you for fulfilling the duties of friendship
lexical_decisions.rationale: The idiom describes performing the part or duties belonging to friends; the English avoids reproducing the awkward literal image of “parts.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πανταχόθεν συντρέχει τὰ πρὸς τὴν σὴν πληροφορίαν οἰκείαν ἀποτελοῦντα τὴν ἁρμονίαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: everything conducive to your full assurance is converging from every direction and producing the fitting harmony
lexical_decisions.rationale: οἰκείαν is taken with τὴν ἁρμονίαν as “fitting”; attachment to πληροφορίαν, yielding something like “your own assurance,” is also grammatically possible.

passages.text: As for us who were with Peter, we spent the whole night asking questions one after another, remaining awake because of the pleasure and joy produced by what was being said. When the night was already beginning somehow to brighten, Peter looked at me and my brothers and said, “I am perplexed about what your father decided.” While he was saying this, our father arrived there and found Peter discussing him with us. Seeing Peter disheartened, he greeted him and explained why he had slept outside. We stared at him in astonishment, seeing Simon’s appearance but hearing the voice of our father Faustus. As we recoiled from him and regarded him with loathing, our father was astounded at being treated so harshly and hostilely by us. Only Peter, who saw his natural form, said to us, “Why do you push your father away in disgust?” We and our mother replied, “To us this man looks like Simon, though he has our father’s voice.” Peter said, “For you, only his unbewitched voice is recognizable; but to my unbewitched eyes his appearance too is visible as it really is: he is not Simon but Faustus, your father.” Then, looking directly at our father too, he said, “......... appearance of yours is not visible to them, but Simon’s—the most impious man’s—is; and to us .........”

source_issues.source_quote: ......... όν σου εἶδος αὐτοῖς οὐ φαίνεται, ἀλλὰ Σίμωνος τοῦ ἀσεβεστάτου καὶ ἡμῖν .........
source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints two lacunae of nine dots each. After the first gap, only όν survives, either as an isolated form or as the ending of a lost word, and it cannot receive a secure independent English rendering. Both nine-dot gaps remain explicit, and no restoration of either gap or of the broken construction is supplied.

lexical_decisions.chosen: we spent the whole night ... remaining awake
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here νήφω concerns wakeful alertness during the night rather than literal abstinence from intoxication; “remaining clear-minded” is possible but less closely fitted to the overnight setting.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Seeing Peter disheartened, he greeted him and explained
lexical_decisions.rationale: The unexpressed person seen as disheartened is taken to be Peter, whom the arriving father has just found discussing him. Reference to another participant is formally possible but less natural in context.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μόνος δὲ Πέτρος τὴν κατὰ φύσιν αὐτοῦ ὁρῶν μορφὴν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Only Peter, who saw his natural form
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατὰ φύσιν identifies the form belonging to Faustus’s real nature, in contrast to the magically imposed appearance.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ὑμῖν μὲν ἡ ἀμάγευτος αὐτοῦ φωνὴ μόνη γνώριμός ἐστιν, ἐμοῦ δὲ τοῖς ἀμαγεύτοις ὀφθαλμοῖς
lexical_decisions.chosen: For you, only his unbewitched voice is recognizable; but to my unbewitched eyes
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀμάγευτος is rendered as freedom from magical alteration or deception, preserving the repetition applied first to the voice and then to Peter’s eyes.

passages.text: While Peter was discussing these things, one of the advance party came in from Antioch ..........., saying to Peter, “My master, I want you to know that Simon, publicly performing many wonders in Antioch and calling you a magician and a sorcerer, prepared them for such hatred that everyone longed, upon your coming into the city there, to take a taste of your very flesh. Therefore we, the advance party, together with our brothers whom you had placed with Simon, seeing the city roaring loudly against you, secretly gathered in the same place and considered what we should do. While we were at a loss, Cornelius the centurion arrived, sent by Caesar to the governor of the province—the one whom the Lord healed in Caesarea when he was possessed by a demon. We secretly sent for Cornelius, and he learned from us the reason for our despondency. When asked to help, he most eagerly promised to frighten Simon and drive him away, provided we assisted him in his undertaking. When we readily promised to do everything, he said, ‘While I, through many friends, secretly spread word around that I have come to arrest him, and claim that I am searching for him—since Caesar, having killed many magicians and learned what concerns him, sent me to search for him, so that he may punish him as he did the magicians before him—let your people who are with him also report back, as though they have heard secretly from somewhere that I was sent to arrest him. Perhaps, hearing this, he will be frightened and flee.’ Since, then, we had thought of doing something else, it nevertheless happened this way. For, having heard many of the outsiders telling him privately, doing him great favors, and also our insiders who had been planted there, and as though he had received advice from his own people, he decided to withdraw. So he fled Antioch with Athenodorus and has come here, as we have heard. Therefore we advise you not yet to set foot in that city, until we see whether, in his absence, they will be able to forget the slander against you.”

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints an eleven-dot gap between Antioch and the participle “saying.” Exactly eleven dots remain in the main English. No missing participle, arrival formula, or other lost word is restored from another edition.

source_issues.source_quote: πάντα ἄνθρωπον εἰς τὴν ἐκεῖ ἐπιδημήσαντος τῶν σαρκῶν
source_issues.issue: This passage uses the human-authorized, independently image-checked Greek prefix proposed by F. Wieseler, Adnotationes criticae, 1859, printed page 326 / PDF page 347. The former selected Lagarde prefix is preserved exactly here: πάντα ἄνθρωπον τῶν ἐκεῖ ἐπιδημησάντων σαρκῶν. The selected prefix is: πάντα ἄνθρωπον εἰς τὴν ἐκεῖ ἐπιδημήσαντος τῶν σαρκῶν. Wieseler’s printed proposal is followed by cett.; ONLY the explicitly verified Greek prefix was adopted, not an invented expansion of that abbreviation. The remaining αὐτῶν ἀπογεύσασθαί σου is unchanged from Lagarde. Wieseler also proposes τῇ ἐκεῖ as an alternative to the destination construction; it is noted as another editorial proposal, not silently selected. These are scholarly conjectures, not new manuscript collations or recovery of a uniquely established original. The prior candidate could not securely link the uncurated plural-participle/flesh sequence; the present interpretation is reassessed on the documented changed prefix and the articular flesh phrase, with the remaining attachments disclosed rather than invented. Fresh independent review must judge the entire construction.

source_issues.source_quote: φυγαδεύειν αὐτόν. ἐάν γε αὐτοῦ τῷ ἐγχειρήματι ὑπουργήσωμεν.
source_issues.issue: The English attaches the condition “provided we assisted him” to Cornelius’s promise despite the selected edition’s full stop before ἐάν. The Greek punctuation is not changed or labelled an OCR error; no missing words are restored.

source_issues.source_quote: κολάσῃ. καὶ οἱ ὑμέτεροι οἱ συνόντες αὐτῷ
source_issues.issue: The English continues the initial genitive-absolute circumstance of spreading an announcement into the later imperative asking their people to report back, despite the printed stop after κολάσῃ. This makes the relation explicit without supplying a new main verb to the initial clause or deleting the source period. An alternative presentation can leave the earlier circumstance as a marked sentence fragment before the command; the continuous English is preferred because the later imperative supplies the action coordinated with Cornelius’s proposed announcement.

The verified Lagarde print has the eight-letter sigma-form ὑπολῆσαι, with circumflex, and it is retained unchanged. Independently checked primary lexical evidence is E.A. Sophocles, Greek Lexicon of the Roman and Byzantine Periods, 1900, printed page 1121 / PDF page 1147: under ὑπο-λανθάνω = λανθάνω it explicitly cites “Clementin. 461 A ὑπολῆσαι, to forget.” The accent in the lexicon’s quoted form remains uncertain in the independent image reading, possibly circumflex or acute (ὑπολήσαι); that uncertainty does not alter the independently verified Lagarde accent or the sigma. The lexicon attests an interpretation of this unusual form but does not establish ordinary classical morphology. The expected cessation-form comparison ὑπολῆξαι would be hypothetical and is NOT adopted; no Greek emendation or identification with ὑπολήγω is made. The supplied evidence request, response, and receipt hashes bind the supporting dictionary check in the generation packet. Fresh independent translation review is still required.

The selected word is Wieseler’s independently image-verified critical proposal, printed page 327 / PDF page 348: περικομποῦντος. The former selected Lagarde word is retained exactly here as provenance: περισκοποῦντος. The change is editorial and conjectural, not a newly verified manuscript reading. It replaces the looking-around/examining sense with announcing-around, permitting the perfect infinitive to express the announced arrival. No other wording or printed punctuation is silently altered, and independent source-and-translation review remains required.

lexical_decisions.chosen: one of the advance party
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun identifies those who go ahead. “One of those who had gone ahead” is a less collective alternative. A military role or formal title is not added.

lexical_decisions.chosen: calling you a magician and a sorcerer
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both accusations are retained. γόης can mean a conjurer, sorcerer, or deceiving charlatan; the magical context supports “sorcerer,” without independently confirming either accusation as true.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς γλίχεσθαι πάντα ἄνθρωπον εἰς τὴν ἐκεῖ ἐπιδημήσαντος τῶν σαρκῶν αὐτῶν ἀπογεύσασθαί σου.
lexical_decisions.chosen: everyone longed, upon your coming into the city there, to take a taste of your very flesh
lexical_decisions.rationale: The current selected prefix has singular genitive ἐπιδημήσαντος, understood circumstantially with the addressee Peter as the visitor identified by the later σου. The nominal “your coming” preserves the aorist participle’s completed-arrival perspective without asserting that the future arrival has already happened. The feminine τὴν has an implicit location, naturally the city discussed here and explicitly named later; the English supplies “city,” but no Greek noun is restored or inserted. The now articular τῶν σαρκῶν αὐτῶν permits postposed αὐτῶν to agree with σαρκῶν intensively, “the flesh itself,” not as the possessive “their flesh.” The unchanged σου supplies Peter as possessor; English “your very flesh” represents that reading. The English repeats “your” to identify both the visitor and flesh-owner as the same addressed man; it does not claim that two Greek pronouns are printed or that both syntactic links are uniquely settled. A possessive reading of αὐτῶν, “their flesh,” remains formally possible but leaves its relation to σου difficult in this context. This is a candidate analysis of the curated whole construction, not acceptance inferred merely from the existence of a critical proposal.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν ὑπὸ σοῦ τῷ Σίμωνι ὑποβεβλημένων ἀδελφῶν ἡμῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: our brothers whom you had placed with Simon
lexical_decisions.rationale: The placement is done by Peter, expressed through ὑπὸ σοῦ, and involves the community’s brothers with Simon. ὑποβάλλω here can imply covertly planting or introducing them, as the later insiders description suggests. No additional act of conversion or betrayal is supplied.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὃν ἐν Καισαρείᾳ δαιμονῶντα ἰάσατο ὁ κύριος
lexical_decisions.chosen: the one whom the Lord healed in Caesarea when he was possessed by a demon
lexical_decisions.rationale: The masculine relative can refer to the immediately preceding provincial governor, or reach back to Cornelius. The English “the one” leaves that personal referent unassigned rather than uniquely choosing either man. δαιμονῶντα is rendered in the author’s demonic category, not converted into a modern diagnosis.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἐμοῦ διὰ πολλῶν φίλων κρύφα εἰς σύλληψιν αὐτοῦ ἐληλυθέναι περικομποῦντος καὶ ζητεῖν αὐτὸν φάσκοντος
lexical_decisions.chosen: While I, through many friends, secretly spread word around that I have come to arrest him, and claim that I am searching for him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The selected περικομποῦντος is Wieseler’s explicitly printed editorial proposal, meaning proclaiming or spreading a claim around; it is not the former περισκοποῦντος, looking around or examining. The perfect infinitive ἐληλυθέναι now supplies the content of that announcement, “that I have come,” with εἰς σύλληψιν expressing its stated purpose. The accompanying φάσκοντος gives the claim that Cornelius is searching for Simon. The main text connects the genitive-absolute circumstance with the later imperative asking their people to report back; the printed intervening stop is separately disclosed. The words are Cornelius’s proposed announcement in the reported plan, not independent confirmation of an actual arrest order.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπεὶ τοίνυν ἕτερόν τι ποιεῖν ἐπενοήσαμεν, ὅμως οὕτως ἐγένετο
lexical_decisions.chosen: Since, then, we had thought of doing something else, it nevertheless happened this way
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both the opening ἐπεί and the contrasting ὅμως are preserved, without changing the printed conjunction to a different Greek word. A more idiomatic contextual interpretation is “Although we had thought of doing something else, it nevertheless happened this way”; that shifts ἐπεί toward a concessive English link rather than its causal “since,” and is not uniquely established.

lexical_decisions.chosen: doing him great favors
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source’s great-favor language is retained as describing the outside informants’ service to Simon. Unlike a different reading with ὡς, the selected εἰς phrase is not automatically translated “as though” doing favors.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς κατὰ σοῦ διαβολῆς ἐκείνου ἀπόντος ὑπολῆσαι δυνήσονται
lexical_decisions.chosen: whether, in his absence, they will be able to forget the slander against you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The plural subject of δυνήσονται is the people of the city under discussion; the slander is the genitive object of forgetting, not a nominative subject that itself subsides. The unchanged sigma-form ὑπολῆσαι is interpreted through Sophocles’s directly cited lexical evidence under ὑπολανθάνω, “forget,” rather than the cessation lemma ὑπολήγω. This is a fresh rendering of the supplied Greek using a dictionary gloss, not an adaptation of an older English passage translation.

passages.text: When the advance messenger had reported these things, Peter looked directly at our father and said, “Do you hear, Faustus? Your transformation was brought about by Simon the magician, as is now evident. Thinking that Caesar was seeking him for harm, he fled in fear, placing his own form upon you so that, when you died, grief would come upon your children.” Hearing this, our father wept and lamented, saying, “You have judged correctly, Peter. Annoubion ...... of mine, because he loved me, cryptically disclosed the plot, and I did not believe.........., since I deserved to suffer.”

source_issues.source_quote: Καίσαρος γὰρ νομίσας ἐπὶ κακῷ αὐτὸν ζητεῖν
source_issues.issue: The edition prints the genitive Καίσαρος, although the contextual reading takes Caesar as the subject of ζητεῖν, for which the accusative Καίσαρα would ordinarily be expected in this infinitival construction after νομίσας. Καίσαρα is only a proposed grammatical regularization; the translation retains the contextually defensible interpretation without claiming that the regularization is printed.

The selected edition prints a six-dot lacuna before μού. The surviving “of mine” indicates a lost description or relationship, but its wording cannot be recovered. All six dots remain explicit, and no description is restored.

source_issues.source_quote: καὶ οὐκ ἐπίστευ.........., ἐπειδὴ τοῦ παθεῖν ἤμην ἄξιος
source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints ten dots immediately after the surviving verbal stem ἐπίστευ-. The precise verbal ending and any following words are unavailable; the ten-dot gap is retained without supplying an object or other lost content.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὸ Σίμωνος τοῦ μάγου ἡ μεταμόρφωσίς σου γέγονεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Your transformation was brought about by Simon the magician
lexical_decisions.rationale: The construction presents Simon as the agent responsible for Faustus’s altered appearance.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Καίσαρος γὰρ νομίσας ἐπὶ κακῷ αὐτὸν ζητεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Thinking that Caesar was seeking him for harm
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπὶ κακῷ indicates harmful or punitive intent without specifying the precise punishment. The contextual interpretation of Caesar as the seeker is retained despite the printed case irregularity disclosed in source_issues.

lexical_decisions.chosen: placing his own form upon you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The concrete image of putting Simon’s appearance around or upon Faustus is retained rather than reduced to simple resemblance.

lexical_decisions.chosen: cryptically disclosed the plot
lexical_decisions.rationale: μυστηριωδῶς indicates an indirect, mysterious, or cryptic disclosure; ἐπιβουλή is a hostile plot or design.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ οὐκ ἐπίστευ.........., ἐπειδὴ τοῦ παθεῖν ἤμην ἄξιος
lexical_decisions.chosen: and I did not believe.........., since I deserved to suffer
lexical_decisions.rationale: The first-person speaker and the following first-person ἤμην support “I,” but the precise ending of ἐπίστευ- and any further lost wording remain unavailable. The English does not supply an object of belief.

lexical_decisions.chosen: because he loved me
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering takes φιλέω as affection and the present participle causally: his affection motivates the confidential warning. This is supported by 20.11, where Faustus calls Annoubion and Appion friends from his earliest age, and by Annoubion’s disclosure of the hostile plot here. The materially different while kissing me is also viable: φιλέω can denote kissing, and the participle may describe an accompanying action rather than its cause. The main text does not claim that affection is the only lexical sense or that a concomitant kiss is excluded.

passages.text: After our father said this, not long afterward ....... to us, reporting Simon’s flight to us and that he had set out for Judea that very night. He found our father beating himself and saying with lamentation, “Alas, wretch that I am! Though I heard that he was a magician, miserable man that I am, I refused to believe it. After being recognized by my wife and children for a single day, I quickly returned to my former calamity of being unknown.” Our mother, lamenting, kept tearing out her hair, while we groaned in distress over our father’s alteration, unable to understand what on earth it was. When Annoubion heard and saw these things, he stood open-mouthed. Before everyone, Peter said to us children, “Believe me: this is Faustus, your father. I therefore command you to pay him the regard due to a father, for God will provide some occasion through which, after stripping off Simon’s form, he will plainly reveal your father’s form again.” After saying this to us, he looked at our father and said, “I permitted you to greet Appion and Annoubion because you acknowledge that they have been your friends since childhood, not to associate with Simon the magician.”

source_issues.source_quote: μετ᾽ οὐ πολὺ ....... πρὸς ἡμᾶς τὴν Σίμωνος ἡμῖν δηλῶν φυγὴν
source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a seven-dot lacuna after “not long afterward.” The missing subject and finite expression governing “to us” are unavailable. All seven dots remain explicit, and the arriving reporter is not identified.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εὗρε δὲ τὸν πατέρα ἡμῶν κοπτόμενον
lexical_decisions.chosen: He found our father beating himself
lexical_decisions.rationale: κόπτομαι can describe striking oneself as an embodied act of mourning; the accompanying lament supports retaining that concrete action.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς μίαν ἡμέραν ἐπιγνωσθεὶς συμβίῳ καὶ τέκνοις
lexical_decisions.chosen: After being recognized by my wife and children for a single day
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιγινώσκω here concerns recognition of identity, while σύμβιος denotes one’s spouse or life-partner; the context identifies Faustus’s wife.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν προτέραν τῆς ἀγνοίας ἦλθον συμφοράν
lexical_decisions.chosen: I returned to my former calamity of being unknown
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀγνοία is understood contextually as his family’s failure to recognize him, not merely as intellectual ignorance.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἀννουβίων δὲ ταῦτα ἀκούων καὶ ὁρῶν ἀχανὴς ἔστη
lexical_decisions.chosen: When Annoubion heard and saw these things, he stood open-mouthed
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀχανής preserves the visible image of standing open-mouthed in stunned astonishment; “stood aghast” or “stood dumbfounded” conveys the reaction but not the image as directly.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to pay him the regard due to a father
lexical_decisions.rationale: προσέχειν calls for attention, adherence, or care toward Faustus in his paternal identity; “attend to him as a father” is more literal but less idiomatic.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δι᾽ ἧς τὴν Σίμωνος ἀποδυσάμενος μορφὴν τὴν τοῦ πατρὸς ὑμῶν προδήλως ἀναδείξει πάλιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: through which, after stripping off Simon’s form, he will plainly reveal your father’s form again
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering takes Faustus as the understood subject of “stripping off” and “revealing,” since the middle image naturally depicts him shedding Simon’s form. The nearest explicit subject is God, so taking God as the agent of the removal and revelation is grammatically possible, though less natural with the stripping image.

passages.text: And the father said, “I sinned; I confess it.” Annoubion said, “I too, together with him, ask you to pardon a noble and good old man who was deceived, for the unfortunate man has become the plaything of the notorious fellow. Still, I will tell you how it happened. This good old man came to greet us. At that very hour, all of us who were present there happened to be listening together to Simon, who wanted to flee that night because he had heard that certain men were coming from somewhere, here to Laodicea, under a royal order to search for him. When Faustus entered, Simon, revealing what was in his own mind, spoke to us as follows: ‘When he arrives, have him share salt with you. I will prepare an ointment so that, after dining, taking it, and anointing his own face, he may appear to everyone to have my form. But you, having first been anointed by me with the juices of a certain plant, will not be deceived by his strange form; to everyone else, however, Faustus will appear to be Simon.’”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: παίγνιον γὰρ γέγονεν ὁ δυστυχὴς τοῦ περιβοήτου
lexical_decisions.chosen: the unfortunate man has become the plaything of the notorious fellow
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the image of Faustus as another person’s plaything and the substantival force of περιβοήτου without inserting Simon’s name.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀκηκοὼς ἐπιδημήσειν ποθέν τινας ἐνταῦθα τῇ Λαοδικείᾳ
lexical_decisions.chosen: because he had heard that certain men were coming from somewhere, here to Laodicea
lexical_decisions.rationale: ποθέν means “from somewhere,” while ἐνταῦθα and τῇ Λαοδικείᾳ locate their expected arrival.

lexical_decisions.chosen: revealing what was in his own mind
lexical_decisions.rationale: θυμός can refer to an inward impulse, disposition, intention, or anger. The ensuing disclosure favors the broader contextual rendering without excluding its forceful emotional nuance.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἁλῶν αὐτὸν ἐλθόντα συμμετασχεῖν ὑμῖν ποιήσατε
lexical_decisions.chosen: When he arrives, have him share salt with you
lexical_decisions.rationale: Ἁλῶν is defensibly the genitive plural of ἅλς, “salt,” as the object of συμμετασχεῖν. Sharing salt depicts participation in the meal; no correction to the printed reading is required.

lexical_decisions.chosen: an ointment
lexical_decisions.rationale: μύρον denotes perfumed oil or ointment, and the subsequent anointing supports “ointment.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δειπνήσας καὶ ἀναλαβὼν τὸ ἴδιον χρίσας πρόσωπον
lexical_decisions.chosen: after dining, taking it, and anointing his own face
lexical_decisions.rationale: The ointment is understood as the object taken, while τὸ ἴδιον ... πρόσωπον is read together despite the intervening participle.

lexical_decisions.chosen: his strange form
lexical_decisions.rationale: ξένης describes the transformed appearance as strange, foreign, or unfamiliar to the observers.

passages.text:
While he was setting these things forth, I said, “What benefit do you now gain from such a scheme?” Simon said, “First, those who are searching for me will seize him and then cease their search against me. And even if he should be killed by the royal hand, his children—who abandoned me, prosphygont........., and are working together—will experience the greatest grief.”

“For now, Peter, I confess the truth to you: I was afraid of the .........stō—to disclose this. But Simon did not even give us time to speak privately ..........mōn to him; as for Simon’s evil counsel—it appeared. At any rate, in the middle of the night Simon got up and fled toward Judea, escorted by both Appion and Athenodorus. I then pretended that my body was unwell so that, by remaining behind after they had left, I might make him return at once to his own home, in case he might be able to escape notice while hiding among you, lest he be seized as Simon by those searching for Simon and die under the royal wrath. I therefore sent him away to you at an unseasonable hour, and out of concern for him I came by night both to see him and to leave very quickly, before those who sent....................., having returned.”

Then, looking at us, he said, “I, Annoubion, see your father’s true form, being one who has been anointed by Simon himself—I gave this account beforehand—so that the true form of Faustus might appear to my eyes. Being utterly astounded, therefore, I marvel at Simon’s magic: though you are standing here, you do not recognize your own father.” As the father, the mother, and we ourselves wept over the misfortune common to us all, Annoubion also sympathized with us and shed tears.

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints nine dots after the surviving incomplete form προσφυγόντ. Its lexical stem suggests seeking or taking refuge, but its completion and the missing intervening wording are unavailable. The translation retains the transliterated fragment and exactly nine dots without restoration.

The selected edition prints nine dots between the accusative article τὸν and the incomplete surviving fragment στω. The gap prevents determination of their relationship to one another and to μηνύειν. The translation therefore preserves the article, gap, and fragment without identifying the missing person or changing τὸν.

source_issues.source_quote: ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ καιρὸν ἡμῖν ὁ Σίμων ἐδίδου πρὸς τὸ ἰδιάζειν .......... μῶν αὐτῷ τὴν ἐκ τοῦ Σίμωνος κακὴν ἐφάνη βουλήν
source_issues.issue: Ten printed dots interrupt the sentence and are followed by the incomplete fragment μῶν. The surviving accusative phrase τὴν ... κακὴν ... βουλήν does not straightforwardly function as the subject of ἐφάνη. The English presents the wording as an anacoluthic, detached fragment rather than silently changing the accusative to a nominative; the missing connection remains unavailable.

The selected edition prints twenty-one dots. The lost material prevents determination of how τοὺς πέμψαντας and the nominative participle ἐπανελθών were connected. The exact gap and surviving syntactic fragments are retained without restoration.

lexical_decisions.chosen: should be killed by the royal hand
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the source’s personifying image of the royal hand rather than reducing it to an abstract governmental authority.

lexical_decisions.chosen: fled toward Judea
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπί with the accusative marks the direction of Simon’s flight.

lexical_decisions.chosen: return at once to his own home
lexical_decisions.rationale: The idiom can refer to one’s home, possessions, affairs, or people. Faustus’s return to his family makes “home” contextually suitable, though the expression itself is broader.

lexical_decisions.chosen: at an unseasonable hour
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverbial genitive denotes action at an unusually late, early, or otherwise inconvenient hour.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐναλειψάμενος ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ τοῦ Σίμωνος ὢν προδιηγησάμην
lexical_decisions.chosen: being one who has been anointed by Simon himself—I gave this account beforehand
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὢν is translated as a nominative participle agreeing with the speaker. προδιηγησάμην is treated parenthetically; alternatively, the participles may be attached differently within the interrupted sentence.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅτι ἑστῶτες τὸν ὑμέτερον οὐ γνωρίζετε πατέρα
lexical_decisions.chosen: though you are standing here, you do not recognize your own father
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle ἑστῶτες is retained and understood concessively; a more mechanically circumstantial rendering would be “standing here, you do not recognize.”

passages.text:
Then Peter promised us that our father’s form would be restored. He said to him, “You have heard, Faustus, about our circumstances. Therefore, when the deceptive form laid upon you becomes useful to us and you assist us in the matters we command, then I too will restore your true form to you, after you have first done what I tell you.”

The father said, “Anything that is possible for me I will do with the greatest eagerness; only restore my form to my own people.” Peter answered, “You yourself heard with your own ears from my advance messengers, who came from Antioch and said that Simon had been there and had vehemently incited the crowds against me, calling me a magician, a murderer, a deceiver, and a sorcerer—to such an extent that everyone there longs to taste my flesh. You will therefore do as I say: leave Clement with me and go ahead of us to Antioch with your wife and also with your sons Faustinus and Faustinianus. Certain others will accompany you as well, whom I judge capable of serving my purpose.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῆς τοῦ πατρὸς μορφῆς τὴν ἀποκατάστασιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: that our father’s form would be restored
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀποκατάστασις denotes restoration to a former condition, here explicitly the father’s appearance.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the deceptive form laid upon you
lexical_decisions.rationale: περίκειμαι presents the form as something placed around or upon Faustus, while πλάνος characterizes it as deceptive.

lexical_decisions.chosen: my advance messengers
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantival plural refers to people sent ahead of Peter; “forerunners” is another possible rendering.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to taste my flesh
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the violent bodily image rather than generalizing it as a desire merely to kill Peter; the Greek uses the plural σαρκῶν.

lexical_decisions.chosen: go ahead of us to Antioch
lexical_decisions.rationale: The following narrative has Faustus reach Antioch before Peter and later notify him. Formally, προάγω with an object can also mean “lead us onward.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: serving my purpose
lexical_decisions.rationale: θέλημα denotes Peter’s will or intended purpose here, and ὑπουργέω denotes rendering practical assistance.

passages.text: “With these people, in Antioch ....... while you appear as Simon, publicly proclaim your own meta........: ‘I, Simon, proclaim these things to you. I confess: unjustly I katapseu........ is a deceiver, not a murderer, not a sorcerer, nor is he any of the vile things I previously went so far as to say about him while driven by anger. I beg you—I myself, who brought upon him the hatred among you—stop hating him. For he is a true apostle of the true prophet sent by God for the salvation of the world. Therefore I myself also advise you to obey him concerning what he proclaims, since your entire city will be utterly destroyed. I want you to know the reason why I have confessed these things to you. This very night, angels of God were severely scourging me, the impious man, as an enemy of the herald of truth. Therefore I appeal to you: even if I myself should come on another occasion and speak while making an attempt against Peter, do not accept me. For I confess openly to you: I am a magician, I am a deceiver, I am a sorcerer. For perhaps it is possible through reorientation to put away the sins previously committed by me.’”

source_issues.source_quote: μετὰ τούτων ἐν τῇ Ἀντιοχείᾳ ....... ἐν ὅσῳ
source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints seven dots after Ἀντιοχείᾳ. The unavailable predicate or connective has not been restored, and the translation retains exactly seven dots.

Only the incomplete fragment μετα survives before the eight printed dots. The identity, completion, and meaning of the noun are unavailable. The translation therefore retains the fragment as “meta” followed by exactly eight dots rather than supplying “change,” “reorientation,” or another completed noun.

source_issues.source_quote: ὁμολογῶ ἀδίκως καταψεύ ........ ἔστι πλάνος, οὐ μιαιφόνος, οὐ γόης
source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints eight dots after the incomplete verbal form καταψεύ. Its completion, object, and any further words are unavailable, so the fragment is transliterated and the gap remains explicit. The surviving clause is ἔστι πλάνος, without a printed negation; the translation therefore preserves “is a deceiver.” Any qualification or negation that might once have stood in the gap has not been restored.

lexical_decisions.chosen: while you appear as Simon
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐν ὅσῳ gives the period during which Faustus visibly bears Simon’s form.

lexical_decisions.chosen: not a murderer
lexical_decisions.rationale: μιαιφόνος evokes bloodshed and blood-pollution and functions here as an accusation of murderous violence.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὅσα ποτὲ φαῦλα περὶ αὐτοῦ λέγων ἔφθανον
lexical_decisions.chosen: any of the vile things I previously went so far as to say about him
lexical_decisions.rationale: φθάνω with the participle can convey previously or anticipatorily doing something, or going so far as to do it. “Previously hastened to say” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτὸς ἐγὼ ὁ τοῦ πρὸς ὑμᾶς μίσους αἴτιος αὐτῷ γεγονώς
lexical_decisions.chosen: I myself, who brought upon him the hatred among you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The context favors taking πρὸς ὑμᾶς as locating the hatred among or in relation to the listeners and αὐτῷ as marking Peter as the affected person. A more directional reading, “the hatred toward you,” is grammatically possible, but its relationship to αὐτῷ would remain uncertain.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἄγγελοί με τοῦ θεοῦ τὸν ἀσεβῆ ... δεινῶς ἐμαστίγουν
lexical_decisions.chosen: angels of God were severely scourging me, the impious man
lexical_decisions.rationale: Retains the appositional accusation τὸν ἀσεβῆ and the continuing force of the imperfect verb.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through reorientation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The term denotes moral redirection in this context and does not itself specify an added destination.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to put away the sins previously committed by me
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀπολύω can mean release, dismiss, or put away. The construction permits a nuance of either removing the sins or obtaining release from them.

passages.text:
As Peter was giving these instructions, the father said, “I know what you want, so do not weary yourself. For when I get there, I will take no less care to say what ought to be said about you.” Peter again instructed him, “When you perceive that the city has turned from its hatred and now desires to see us, send word and inform me, and we will catch up with you there. When I arrive there, on that very day I will drive away your alien form and make your own form appear unmistakably to your people and to everyone else.”

After saying this, he arranged for the sons, my brothers, to accompany him, and he commanded our mother Mattidia and some of the more loyal people to go with him. But the mother regarded going with him reluctantly. “For I appear to be an adulteress while consorting with Simon’s form. If I am indeed compelled to go with him, it is impossible to recline on the same couch with him. And I do not know whether I will be persuaded even to go with him.”

When she hesitated to leave, Annoubion encouraged her and said, “Believe me and Peter, and also the very voice, that .... is your husband, whom I love no less than you do. And I myself, for him, sym.........” When Annoubion had said this, the mother promised to go with him.

source_issues.source_quote: αὐτῇ δὲ τῇ φωνῇ ὅτι .... ἐστὶν ὁ σὸς σύμβιος
source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints four dots where wording identifying the husband would be expected. The context may suggest a demonstrative, but no restoration has been supplied; the translation retains exactly four dots.

The edition preserves καὶ αὐτός, the dative αὐτῷ, and only the incomplete prefix συμ- before nine printed dots. The missing verb, its tense, and the resulting claim are unavailable; the prefix could belong to a compound expressing accompaniment, assistance, sympathy, agreement, or another relationship. The translation retains “I myself,” represents αὐτῷ provisionally as “for him,” and leaves “sym” followed by exactly nine dots without inventing a predicate.

lexical_decisions.chosen: so do not weary yourself
lexical_decisions.rationale: κάμνω can mean grow weary or exert oneself laboriously; the father indicates that Peter need not labor over further explanation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the city has turned from its hatred
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive τοῦ μίσους is taken as the state from which the city changes. “Changed with respect to its hatred” is also grammatically possible but less directly contrasts with its new desire to see Peter.

lexical_decisions.chosen: we will catch up with you there
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπικαταλαμβάνω here denotes overtaking or joining Faustus after he has gone ahead.

lexical_decisions.chosen: appear unmistakably
lexical_decisions.rationale: The adverb means without deception or mistake, reversing the deceptive appearance imposed by Simon.

lexical_decisions.chosen: some of the more loyal people
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantival comparative can describe more genuine, trustworthy, or devoted associates. “More genuine ones” is a more formally transparent alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Μοιχὰς γὰρ εἶναι δοκῶ τῇ Σίμωνος συνοῦσα μορφῇ
lexical_decisions.chosen: For I appear to be an adulteress while consorting with Simon’s form
lexical_decisions.rationale: δοκῶ may mean “I appear” or “I consider myself.” The context emphasizes the adulterous appearance created by accompanying someone who visibly bears Simon’s form.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to recline on the same couch with him
lexical_decisions.rationale: κλίνη may denote a couch or bed; the literal posture is retained while the marital implication remains contextual.

lexical_decisions.chosen: whom I love no less than you do
lexical_decisions.rationale: The reassurance favors comparing Annoubion’s love for the husband with Mattidia’s love for him. The elliptical comparison can alternatively mean “whom I love no less than I love you.”

passages.text: But Peter ......... diōtata, God orders our affairs. For we have Annoubion with us .......... ogon. For when we are staying in Antioch, this man will thereafter discuss nativity with us more sincerely, as a friend. And so, when the father set out by night for nearby Antioch with those whom Peter had instructed, together with Annoubion, at dawn the next day, before Peter went out for the discussion, Appion and Athenodorus returned to Laodicea, having sent Simon ahead, seeking the father. When Peter learned this, he ordered them to enter. After they had entered and sat down, they asked, “Where is Faustus?” Peter answered, “We do not know. For after coming to you that very evening, he was no longer seen by his own people. Yesterday at dawn Simon also sought him, and since we answered him nothing, I do not know what came over him: he declared himself to be Faustus but was not believed, and, weeping and beating himself, he threatened to kill himself and rushed off as though toward the sea.”

source_issues.issue: The nine printed dots mark unavailable wording after “Peter” and before the surviving fragment διώτατα, apparently the end of an incomplete word or expression. The exact gap is retained and the fragment is transliterated; its interpretation remains provisional, and no restoration has been supplied.

The ten printed dots mark unavailable wording after Annoubion and before the surviving fragment όγον, apparently the end of an incomplete word. The exact gap is retained and the fragment is transliterated; its interpretation remains provisional, and no completion has been supplied.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὁ θεὸς τὰ πράγματα ἡμῶν οἰκονομεῖ
lexical_decisions.chosen: God orders our affairs
lexical_decisions.rationale: οἰκονομεῖ denotes managing or arranging affairs; “orders” preserves that sense without adding an explanation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: will thereafter discuss nativity
lexical_decisions.rationale: In the context of Annoubion and astrological discussion, γένεσις concerns birth or nativity, while τοῦ λοιποῦ means thereafter or henceforth.

lexical_decisions.chosen: more sincerely, as a friend
lexical_decisions.rationale: γνησιώτερον can mean more genuinely, sincerely, or candidly; the comparison concerns the openness expected from a friend.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐπανῆλθον εἰς τὴν Λαοδίκειαν τὸν Σίμωνα προπέμψαντες Ἀππίων καὶ Ἀθηνόδωρος ἐπιζητοῦντες τὸν πατέρα
lexical_decisions.chosen: Appion and Athenodorus returned to Laodicea, having sent Simon ahead, seeking the father
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle ἐπιζητοῦντες presents their seeking in connection with their return; the rendering does not add a separate onset or subsequent beginning of the search.

lexical_decisions.chosen: what came over him
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally “what seemed good to him,” the phrase idiomatically refers to what entered his mind or prompted his conduct.

lexical_decisions.chosen: weeping and beating himself
lexical_decisions.rationale: κόπτομαι can depict striking oneself as an expression of grief; the bodily image is retained.

lexical_decisions.chosen: rushed off as though toward the sea
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὡς qualifies the reported direction and does not state that he reached or entered the sea.

passages.text: On hearing this, Appion and those with him wailed and beat themselves, saying, “Why did you not receive him?” And just as Athenodorus was about to say to me, “It was Faustus, your father,” Appion forestalled him and said, “We learned from someone that Simon, after finding him, sent him away ............................... the truth, Faustus himself having begged him, because he did not wish to see that his own sons had become Jews. When we heard this, we came for this reason, seeking him. But since he is not here, the person who told us appears to have spoken truthfully. As, therefore, we heard it from him, so we have told you.” But I, Clement, understood Peter’s purpose: he wanted to plant in them the suspicion that he was going to look for the old man among them, so that they would become afraid and flee. I therefore joined in his plan and said to Appion, “Listen, my dearest Appion. We were eager to give him, as our father, the things we regarded as good. But if he himself did not wish to receive them and, on the contrary, was disgusted with us and fled—I will say something rather harsh—we do not care about him either.” When I said this, they left, taking offense as though at cruelty, and (as we learned the next day) of us ......., they set out in Simon’s tracks for Judea.

source_issues.issue: The thirty-one printed dots mark unavailable wording connecting ἐξώρμησε with τὰ ἀληθῆ. The exact gap is retained, and no missing action, negation, or speech has been restored.

The seven printed dots mark unavailable wording that governed or completed the genitive ἡμῶν. The resulting fragment is preserved in its source order without conjecturally supplying its syntactic relation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: wailed and beat themselves
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verbs portray loud lamentation and bodily striking in grief, so both actions are retained.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Simon, after finding him, sent him away
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐξορμάω may be intransitive, “set out,” or causative, “send out.” Taking αὐτόν as also supplying the object of ἐξώρμησε supports the causative rendering, though the following lacuna prevents certainty and the intransitive alternative remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to plant in them the suspicion
lexical_decisions.rationale: The image of sowing or planting suspicion is preserved.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς τὸν γέροντα ζητεῖν μέλλων παρ’ αὐτοῖς
lexical_decisions.chosen: that he was going to look for the old man among them
lexical_decisions.rationale: παρ’ αὐτοῖς has the dative and directly allows a locative or associative sense: “among them,” “at their place,” or “in their keeping.” Context could construe looking for someone in their keeping as demanding him from them, but the main rendering preserves the more source-transparent locative construction.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I therefore joined in his plan
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression literally describes running together with his purpose and contextually means cooperating with or furthering the plan.

lexical_decisions.chosen: was disgusted with us and fled
lexical_decisions.rationale: βδελύσσομαι expresses abhorrence or revulsion, stronger than simple dislike.

lexical_decisions.chosen: taking offense as though at cruelty
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὡς presents cruelty as their construal of Clement’s words rather than an unqualified judgment by the narrator.

passages.text: Nevertheless, after ten days had passed, ......... from Antioch, from the father, reporting to us how the father, dēmo........., by denouncing his appearance and speaking well of Peter, had moved the entire city of the Antiochenes into longing. He also reported that, as a result, everyone desired to see him, but that some, angry with him as though he were Simon because of their surpassing affection for Peter, even wanted to lay hands on Faustus as though he were Simon; and that therefore Faustus, fearing that he might be killed, had sent to ask Peter to come immediately, so that Peter might reach him while he was still alive and make a timely appearance before the city while its longing for him was at its height. When Peter heard this, he gathered a great many people for assembly, appointed one of his followers as bishop, baptized and healed, and, after remaining three days in Laodicea, hastened to set out for nearby Antioch.

source_issues.source_quote: ἡμερῶν δέκα διελθουσῶν ......... ἐκ τῆς Ἀντιοχείας παρὰ τοῦ πατρὸς ἀγγελῶν ἡμῖν
source_issues.issue: The nine printed dots mark unavailable wording after the genitive absolute and before the phrase beginning ἐκ τῆς Ἀντιοχείας. The missing wording apparently included main-clause material, potentially a subject and finite verb, with ἀγγελῶν describing the reporting mission. The exact gap is retained without inventing a messenger or finite verb.

The nine printed dots follow the surviving fragment δημο and mark unavailable continuation of the word or phrase. The fragment is transliterated and the exact gap retained; its interpretation remains provisional, and no adverb such as “publicly” has been restored.

lexical_decisions.chosen: denouncing his appearance
lexical_decisions.rationale: αὐτοῦ may refer to the father’s present appearance, Simon’s appearance, or the person represented by it. The non-reflexive “his” preserves that referential ambiguity.

lexical_decisions.chosen: speaking well of Peter
lexical_decisions.rationale: In this public-speech context εὐλογέω can mean praising or speaking favorably of someone rather than pronouncing a blessing.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν πᾶσαν Ἀντιοχέων πόλιν εἰς πόθον μετέθηκεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: had moved the entire city of the Antiochenes into longing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves the source image of transferring or moving the city into a state of longing.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐνίους δὲ καὶ χαλεπαίνοντας αὐτῷ ὡς Σίμωνι διὰ τὴν πρὸς Πέτρον ὑπερβάλλουσαν στοργὴν
lexical_decisions.chosen: some, angry with him as though he were Simon because of their surpassing affection for Peter
lexical_decisions.rationale: The Greek expresses “the surpassing affection for Peter” without an explicit possessor. “Their” takes the affection as belonging to the townspeople and as motivating their anger against the man they took for Simon, which best fits the report that the city longed for Peter. Alternatively, the phrase could refer to the supposed Simon’s conspicuous affection for Peter.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐξαυτῆς ἐλθεῖν πέμψαντα ἀξιοῦν· τὸν Πέτρον
lexical_decisions.chosen: had sent to ask Peter to come immediately
lexical_decisions.rationale: τὸν Πέτρον is taken as the delayed object of ἀξιοῦν. Alternatively, it may be read as an anticipatory accusative identifying Peter as the implicit subject of the following purpose clause. The printed punctuation makes the attachment conspicuous, so the main construction remains provisional, though both readings identify Peter as the one asked to come.

lexical_decisions.chosen: so that Peter might reach him while he was still alive
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπικαταλαμβάνω here means to catch up with or reach someone; ζῶντα describes the endangered Faustus.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῇ πόλει ἀκμαζούσῃ πόθῳ τῷ πρὸς αὐτὸν
lexical_decisions.chosen: before the city while its longing for him was at its height
lexical_decisions.rationale: The city is portrayed as being at its peak or flourishing in its longing; the pronoun most naturally refers to Peter but remains formally pronominal.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he gathered a great many people for assembly
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐκκλησιάζειν can denote convening or addressing an assembly and need not imply a later formalized church service.

lexical_decisions.chosen: appointed one of his followers as bishop
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπίσκοπος denotes the appointed overseer; “bishop” preserves the narrative’s office term.
